Contents of the texts

The table of contents of each of the 56 books and articles this site is built from, with an overview of every chapter (608 overviews). Open a book for a short overview of the whole work, a note on how far East and Southeast Asia and their participation in exhibitions are discussed in it, and its contents; open a chapter to read its overview. Chapter overviews were written by machine from a full reading of each chapter; the book overviews and Asia notes were written from those chapter overviews and from the passages of each text that name the region. None of it has been checked by a person.

Allwood, John, Ted Allan and Patrick Reid. The Great Exhibitions: 150 Years. London: Exhibition Consultants, 2001.Asia: substantial18 chapter overviews

Overview

Allwood, Allan and Reid trace the international exhibition from medieval fairs and national shows to the world expositions of 1851 to 2000, asking why nations keep staging them despite frequent losses. Their argument is that the medium was driven first by trade and then by national prestige, and moved from subject-based halls and national showcases towards thematic display and civic legacy. The book runs chronologically from London in 1851 to Hanover in 2000, through chapters built around a few named fairs such as Chicago 1893, St Louis 1904 and Expo 67. Appendices list the events and the BIE documentation. The final chapter argues that the recognised-event system has allowed more fairs than the medium can sustain, and sets out steps for future hosts.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia gets substantial attention, mostly concerning Japan. Japanese material appears from the early fairs: at London in 1862 and Dublin in 1853 (chapter 3), and through the Japanese delegation to Vienna in 1873 (chapter 4). Chapter 14, 'The Eastern Hemisphere', is mainly about Japan's state-led expositions from Okinawa 1975 to Osaka 1990, with the Aichi 2005 bid, and also covers Korea's Taejon 1993 and China's Kunming 1999. Osaka 1970 is treated as a Japanese event in chapter 12, while Chinese pavilions at Knoxville 1982 and New Orleans 1984 appear in chapter 13. Asian states are shown as exhibitors and hosts, and Asian visitors mostly as Japanese crowds at home.

Southeast Asia is slight, appearing mainly as displayed peoples and colonial architecture. The Philippines is shown through Igorrots on the Pike at St Louis 1904 (chapter 8), an ASEAN plaza at Vancouver 1986 (chapter 13), and the Manila 1992 bid, which was dropped (chapter 14). Angkor Wat reproductions appear at Paris 1889 and 1931 (chapters 6 and 9), and Thai temples at St Louis, Seville 1992 and Hanover 2000 (chapters 8 and 15). The Tonkin colonial exhibition of 1902-03 in French Indo-China (chapter 7) showed Japanese, Chinese and Siamese exhibits, and Javanese villages formed part of the Chicago Midway (chapter 6). Singapore appears only as one of the Straits Settlements in a list of colonies (chapter 5), and Malaya and Borneo not at all.

Preface

The preface has two parts. Allwood's first-edition note admits that a complete history of international exhibitions from 1851 is an ambitious undertaking, given the volume of documentation and its discrepancies, and hopes to revive interest in events that historians have neglected. The second-edition note by Allan and Reid explains the new material covering the thirty years since, the use of 'World's Fair', 'Exhibition' and 'Exposition' as interchangeable, and a dedication to expo veterans such as Marcel Galopin.

Introduction

Allwood, Allan and Reid ask why nations have kept staging international exhibitions for 150 years despite frequent losses. They trace the exhibition back to medieval fairs and industrial displays, and argue that its driving motive has always been showing off, first for trade and later for national prestige. The introduction moves from London in 1851 to Paris in 1867, where the first thematic display appeared, and ends with the threats now facing expositions, from lack of finance to instant communications.

London 1851Paris 1867
1The Beginnings

Allwood, Allan and Reid trace the origins of the exhibition in English and French fairs, prize shows and national displays before 1851. The chapter starts with the Royal Society of Arts' first industrial exhibition of 1761 and its permanent hall, then turns to France, where the Marquis d'Aveze's unsold royal manufactures led to a series of National Exhibitions from 1798 to 1849. English attempts fared worse: the National Repository of 1828 was dubbed the 'toy-shop' by critics, and Birmingham's 1849 hall, visited by Prince Albert, was the nearest British equivalent to the French shows. The authors conclude that British indifference to French-style shows left Britain to hold the first International Exhibition.

2‘This Cristial Exhibition’

Allwood, Allan and Reid explain how the Great Exhibition of 1851 was planned, from the Society of Arts' prize shows and Henry Cole's talks with Prince Albert to the Royal Commission and the choice of Hyde Park. Most of the chapter concerns the building: Joseph Paxton's glass and iron design was accepted at a tender of £79,800, and the building was handed over in seventeen weeks despite protests over the site and the elm trees. The authors then describe the classification, the foreign sections and the crowds, including the excursions run by Thomas Cook. The chapter ends with the profit of £186,437, which bought the South Kensington site of museums and colleges, and with the Crystal Palace's move to Sydenham, where it stood until its fire in 1936.

London 1851
3The Copyists, the First Paris ‘Exposition Universelle’ and London Againp. 19

The chapter follows the copies of the 1851 exhibition staged in other cities, and asks why most of them failed. Allwood, Allan and Reid cover the Dublin Exhibition of 1853, financed largely by William Dargan, whose southern hall roof was destroyed by a storm and whose five-shilling entry charge kept most people away. New York's Crystal Palace of 1853 ran up debts despite a large site, lost the backing of P T Barnum and burned down a few years later. The Paris Exposition Universelle of 1855 had a government-financed palace with poor ventilation, made a loss of over eight million francs, and included the Exposition Economique, an early thematic display. The final section covers London's 1862 International Exhibition, condemned as an ugly shed and rescued from a loss by Sir John Kelk. The authors conclude that repetition without royal patronage or a central site could not ensure success.

Dublin 1853New York 1853Paris 1855London 1862
4The Big Step Forward and the American Centennial Expositionp. 31

Allwood, Allan and Reid trace the shift from the London exhibitions to the wider fairs of the 1860s and 1870s. The main case is Paris in 1867, which introduced national pavilions, Frédéric Le Play's concentric galleries including the History of Work, and a building by Gustave Eiffel, and which was overshadowed by the Tsar's near-assassination and news of Maximilian's execution. The London International Exhibitions of 1871 to 1874 failed as a thematic series, while the Vienna exhibition of 1873 was undone by a stock-market collapse and high hotel prices, its income reaching only a sixth of its cost. Philadelphia's Centennial Exhibition of 1876, whose grounds were planned by Herman Schwarzmann, is presented as the first properly landscaped international exposition, with the Corliss engine and Bell's telephone among its displays. The chapter ends with the Centennial's funding from public money and concessions, and with the later demolition of its main buildings.

Paris 1867Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876
5Paris, Australia and all the Worldp. 46

Allwood follows the exhibition circuit from Paris to the Antipodes in the 1870s and 1880s. The chapter opens with Paris 1878, set against the aftermath of the Franco-Prussian war and the Commune, and describes the Krantz building, the Rue des Nations, the ventilation system devised by the architect Hardy, and landmarks such as Doré's vase. Sala's complaints about exhaustion, dear restaurants and the dominance of large firms serve as evidence that exhibitions were turning from individual craftsmanship towards commerce. Most of the chapter then covers the Sydney exhibition of 1879 and the Melbourne exhibition of 1880, using visitor numbers, the Garden Palace and art sales to show their effects. The central figure is Jules Joubert, whose shows in Adelaide, Perth, Christchurch, Calcutta and Tasmania are traced in detail. The chapter ends with London's Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886, which led to the founding of the Imperial Institute.

Paris 1878Sydney 1879Melbourne 1880
6Eiffel’s Tower and Chicago’s White Cityp. 56

Allwood treats international exhibitions as public relations exercises in which each event had to outdo the last. The chapter sets two cases side by side. Paris 1889, held to mark the centenary of the Revolution, is discussed through the Eiffel Tower, which artists and writers opposed before it became a profitable structure for Eiffel, and through Dutert's Galerie des Machines, with its hinged steel roof. Electricity, Edison's phonograph and the colonial villages are described as the main attractions. Chicago 1893 is presented as a failure of nerve: its lakeside site laid out by Olmsted, its uniform Neo-classical Florentine architecture, and the criticism of Louis Sullivan and the Belgian engineer Vierendeel are set against the Midway, the Ferris Wheel and the Cairo street. The chapter argues that Chicago's classicism shaped American public and business architecture for decades. It closes with the San Francisco Midwinter Exposition of 1894, which carried Chicago's exhibits and style westwards.

Paris 1889Chicago 1893
7An Architectural Fantasiap. 69

Allwood treats Paris 1900 as the high point of Art Nouveau in exhibitions, and as the point where spectacle began to outrun financial sense. The Grand Palais, the Porte Monumentale, the Rue des Nations and the Palace of Electricity are described, along with the architects behind them and the contrasting Finnish, Swedish and British pavilions. The chapter then turns to new forms of display: Grimoin-Sanson's Cinéorama, the Trottoir Roulant moving walkway and the Olympic Games. It argues that the exhibition lost money because high concession rents were passed on to visitors. Buffalo 1901 is treated through its Electric Tower, its Midway and the assassination of President McKinley. Glasgow 1901 and Turin 1902 are briefly compared for their architecture and their Art Nouveau displays, and the chapter ends with the Tonkin colonial exhibition of 1902-03.

Paris 1900Buffalo 1901
8The Louisiana Purchase Exposition and Two Great Firesp. 83

Allwood sets two American fairs against the difficulties of organizing them. The St Louis Louisiana Purchase Exposition of 1904 is described as bigger than any previous exhibition, spread over 1,272 acres with a walk of thirty-five miles around it. Its white Ivory City, the Festival Hall and the Pike amusement area are compared with Chicago, and the automobile, wireless and aeronautics displays are used to argue that St Louis excelled Chicago in showing science in motion. The living ethnological displays and the Olympic Games are also covered. The second half concerns the Panama-Pacific International Exposition of 1915 in San Francisco, which the author presents as a success against earthquake, fire, war and depression. Its colour scheme by Jules Guerin, the Tower of Jewels, Bernard Maybeck's Palace of Fine Arts and the Stella attraction are described. The chapter closes with San Diego's exhibition and the Rio centenary of 1922-23, and points forward to London's Empire exhibition.

St Louis 1904San Francisco 1915
9Between the Warsp. 96

Allwood surveys the exhibitions of the 1920s and 1930s. It begins with the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley in 1924-25, where the stadium, the Neverstop Railway and the amusement park are described, and where advertising designers, more than architects, gave the event its character. The chapter moves to Paris 1925, whose Art Deco name it traces, and to Le Corbusier's Pavillon de l'Esprit Nouveau, which was fenced off and nearly denied its prize. Barcelona 1929 and Mies van der Rohe's German pavilion, with its Barcelona chair, follow, along with the 1928 convention that tried to limit how often exhibitions were held. The argument is that these events were increasingly designed for commerce and display rather than education, and that their losses mounted. Chicago's Century of Progress of 1933-34, with its science pavilions and the Sky Ride, is treated at length. The chapter ends with Paris 1937, where the German and Soviet pavilions faced one another across the Champ de Mars, and where the approach of war ended the exhibition's run.

Wembley 1924Paris 1925Barcelona 1929Chicago 1933Paris 1937
10World’s Fair Competitionp. 116

Allwood compares the New York World's Fair of 1939-40 with the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island in San Francisco, which opened in the same year. The New York fair, with its theme of 'The World of Tomorrow', the Trylon and Perisphere, its planned sectors and the reclaimed Corona Dumps site, is described first, along with the Aquacade, Railroads on Parade and the Swedish and Finnish pavilions. The chapter argues that the ambition for planned sectors and a unified architectural style was undone by exhibitors who ignored the plan, by loud flags and murals, and by an organizing body with little authority. The San Francisco fair is then set against it: an island built for the Bay Bridge and an airport, a site walled against the wind, a colour scheme that combined Guerin's 1915 palette with Urban's 1933 colours, and the Tower of the Sun. The chapter ends as war closes the fair and Treasure Island becomes a naval station.

New York 1939San Francisco 1939
11The Resumption of a Great Traditionp. 128

Allwood's final chapter covers the post-war revival of international exhibitions, starting with the Festival of Britain of 1951. Its South Bank site, the narrative display theme compiled by Ian Cox, the Dome of Discovery and the routing of crowds that gave rise to 'Townscape' are described. The chapter then turns to Brussels 1958, the first international exhibition after the war, centred on the Atomium and the Water Ladder, with the Philips pavilion by Le Corbusier and the American and Soviet pavilions. Italia 61 in Turin is discussed as an attempt to organize exhibitions around the theme of 'Man at Work', which the author judges a failure, though Nervi's Palazzo del Lavoro is valued. The Seattle Century 21 fair of 1962, with its Space Needle, Monorail and United States Science Pavilion, is the last case, and the chapter concludes that it left the city a ready civic centre and a profit. The argument is that exhibitions moved from subject-based halls towards thematic display and from national showcases towards science and civic legacy.

London 1951Brussels 1958Turin 1961Seattle 1962
12Madison Avenue, the Computer and the Rising Sunp. 132

Allwood traces how exhibitions of the late 1960s and early 1970s moved from national statement towards commercial showmanship. The main case is New York 1964-65, where Robert Moses's fair, without major foreign exhibitors, filled its grounds with company pavilions, among them IBM's building by Eero Saarinen, Ford's Disney-designed display and the Johnson Wax film To Be Alive, and was hit by protests, poor site planning and a financial loss. Montreal's Expo 67 is presented as a high point, with Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67, Buckminster Fuller's geodesic American pavilion and the Labyrinth film. Osaka 1970 is treated as a Japanese event of record attendance, organised around Kenzo Tange's Festival Plaza and the Tower of the Sun, and remembered for the rush to see the American pavilion's moon rock. The chapter ends with a run of picture captions on later fairs and legacies, including Expo 98, Hanover 2000 and the London Dome, which carry its argument forward without comment.

New York 1964-65Montreal 1967Osaka 1970
13The North American Experiencep. 147

Allwood's chapter examines the American and Canadian exhibitions of 1974 to 1986 and argues that the United States' refusal to take responsibility for international fairs, combined with exhibitions used to fund urban renewal, weakened the medium. It moves through Spokane 1974, the first fair devoted to the environment, which drew only nine foreign participants; Knoxville 1982, whose energy theme gave way to commercial display and whose host pavilion was sold to the city for one dollar; and New Orleans 1984, where bankruptcy followed a site that housed its international exhibitors in a long, nondescript building. Its main case is Vancouver's Expo 86, which the chapter treats as a rare successful specialised exposition. The federal government left the financing to British Columbia, and a transport and communications theme was pursued through specialised periods, symposia and street theatre, while the Canada and British Columbia pavilions drew the largest crowds. The chapter closes by setting this success against the management style of the Expo 86 Corporation, and concludes that a successful exposition needs considerable financial and creative investment from its host.

Spokane 1974Knoxville 1982New Orleans 1984Vancouver 1986
14The Eastern Hemispherep. 161

Allwood's chapter covers the exhibitions held in Japan, Australia and Korea between 1975 and 1999, and argues that Japan turned the medium into a state-led tool of regional and economic development, which its neighbours then copied. It opens with Okinawa 1975, where an ocean theme and the Aquapolis floating platform were set on a former battlefield, and moves through Tsukuba 1985, which used computers, robots and audio-visual display to promote a science city. Its main case is Osaka 1990, a garden exposition that the organisers turned into a hybrid expo within the BIE's rules, with 82 nations and a record attendance. The chapter then surveys Brisbane 1988, whose shaded riverside site and state pavilions are described, Taejon 1993, where Korean corporate pavilions overshadowed the international exhibitors, and the Kunming 1999 garden expo. It ends with the Philippines' withdrawal from a recognised exposition for Manila in 1992, and concludes that developing nations were still denied a realistic route to hosting.

Okinawa 1975Tsukuba 1985Osaka 1990Brisbane 1988Taejon 1993
15The European Scenep. 72

Allwood argues that European exhibitions between 1984 and 2000 were marked by cancelled projects, and that the few that went ahead were judged on finance, management and their ability to hold visitors. The chapter explains why Paris 1989 and the Vienna and Budapest proposals fell through, and why the Milan Triennale lost its standing, and traces the Liverpool Garden Festival of 1984 as an attempt to copy Japan's use of expositions for urban regeneration. Its main case is Seville 1992, where a state corporation, the restored Carthusian monastery and the Lago de Espana were built on a barren island, while visitor queues, the cost per visit of the Canadian and British pavilions and the reduced US pavilion were set against its budget. Genoa's Colombo 92 and Lisbon 1998 are shown as smaller events tied to their waterfronts, and Hanover 2000 and the London Dome as millennial exhibitions with low attendance and heavy criticism. The chapter ends with an irate reader's letter comparing the Dome to a tower left unfinished, and uses it to close its account of European decline.

Seville 1992Genoa 1992Lisbon 1998Hanover 2000London 2000Liverpool 1984
16What of the Future?p. 193

Allwood's concluding chapter argues that the world exposition has lost its role as a forum for international exchange, and that the Bureau International des Expositions has failed to control the medium. It starts from Hanover 2000, whose low attendance, overrun budget and absent US pavilion are set against the nineteenth- and twentieth-century fairs whose inventions and national displays drew mass audiences. The chapter then traces how television, corporate retreat and the 1988 Protocol's five-year registration cycle changed the medium, and contrasts universal with specialised events, citing Vancouver 1986 and Genoa 1992 as models. It argues that the recognised category has allowed more events than the medium can sustain, that attendance figures are inflated, and that host governments should bear the responsibility set out in the 1928 Convention. The chapter ends with seven steps for future hosts and a call for an international conference, perhaps under the United Nations, to decide the medium's future.

The Publisher
Badger, Reid. The Great American Fair: The World’s Columbian Exposition and American Culture. Chicago: Nelson-Hall, 1979.Asia: slight21 chapter overviews

Overview

Badger uses the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 as a test case for what the great world's fairs say about the societies that made them. He argues that the fairs expressed a Victorian faith in progress, order and culture, and that the White City's unity answered the fears of an unsettled age rather than describing American society. The book opens with a background of the London, Paris, Vienna and Philadelphia fairs and the American role in them. It then treats the Chicago fair in detail: its origins, organisation, site and design, finance and promotion, congresses, exhibits and Midway, and its legacy. Four parts and an epilogue carry the story to the fire and violence of 1894.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are slight in this book, and most of the material is in lists and quotations. Japan appears as an exhibitor and as a government. Chapter 3 (America and the Great World's Fairs) notes that Japanese displays at Philadelphia in 1876 showed how far America still had to go in the decorative arts. Chapter 9 (Finance and Promotion) says that of the fewer than twenty governments that had accepted by June 1891, only Germany, Turkey and Japan seemed enthusiastic. Chapter 14 (The Midway) lists Persian, Japanese and Indian bazaars, a Chinese village and a Dutch settlement with what the text calls South Sea island villages, without naming the islands. Chapter 13 (The Exhibits) discusses the ethnic displays on the Midway, where Indians, Eskimos, Egyptians and Africans are named, and quotes an Indian visitor. Chapter 12 (The World's Congress) quotes Barrows wanting Christianity to advance in China, and Chapter 15 (Achievement and Influence) quotes an 1890s passage that names the 'innocent Siamese' among peoples threatened by armaments. East Asian and Southeast Asian peoples are never treated as observers, as people on display in Asia, or as the subject of an exhibition held in Asia.

Contents

Prefacep. ix

Badger explains why he chose the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 as a test case for cultural history. He wants to know how far the great world's fairs represented the age that produced them, and what a single fair can reveal about American society in the 1890s. The preface then acknowledges the colleagues, students, archives and institutions that supported the work.

Chicago 1893
Prologue: Opening Dayp. xi

The prologue reconstructs the opening day of the Columbian Exposition on 1 May 1893, when President Cleveland set the fair in motion from Chicago. Badger draws on newspaper reports to describe the parade, the crowd in the Court of Honor, the speeches and the crush before the platform. He closes by noting that the celebration of American progress took place during a deep depression, and that the Pullman strike and the Spanish-American War lay only a few years ahead.

Chicago 1893
Introduction: The Great World’s Fair and Victorian Culturep. xv

Badger argues that the great world's fairs expressed the Victorian faith in progress, a belief that industrialism, nationalism, urbanisation and science would bring steady improvement without disorder. The fairs grew into a self-conscious attempt to display culture in all its dimensions, and their symbolic meaning came to outweigh their practical purpose. The introduction closes by holding that this balance could not last, and that the fairs lost their original significance once it cracked.

Part OnePart One: The Backgroundp. 1
1The Crystal Palace and the Origins of the Institutionp. 3

Badger treats the London exhibition of 1851 as the first world's fair in the modern sense, a deliberate attempt to show the forces of change in industry, science and culture in one popular display. Prince Albert, the Royal Society of Arts and Joseph Paxton's glass and iron building stand at the centre of the account. Badger shows how the scheme was attacked in advance as a threat to public order, morality and the economy, and how it was judged a triumph once it opened and drew six million visitors. He then assesses its effects: British trade seemed to grow, the monarchy's popular standing rose, and the fair gave a national confidence that could also be turned to competitive nationalism. The chapter ends by weighing the fair's legacy of national self-confidence against the fact that few contemporaries foresaw the Crimean War that followed close upon it.

London 1851
2The Growth and Character of the Institutionp. 7

Badger examines the world's fair as an institution, which between 1851 and 1925 became a standard part of Western culture. Each fair claimed to display the latest stage of progress, from British machinery and Bessemer steel in London to German motors at Paris in 1867 and the telephone and typewriter at Philadelphia in 1876. Architecture and the arts had to show refinement, which gave them a largely functional role, and the congresses held alongside the fairs seldom did more than reflect current thought. National purposes shaped many fairs, from Austria's recovery in Vienna in 1873 to Napoleon III's rivalry with London in 1855 and 1867. Badger then turns to finance, showing that governments subsidised fairs and that few made a profit, and to the city, which he treats as the greatest exhibit of any fair. The chapter closes by arguing that the claimed economic gains to host cities, hard to measure, were used to win public money from city governments.

London 1851Paris 1855Paris 1867Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876
3America and the Great World’s Fairsp. 13

Badger follows American participation in world's fairs from London in 1851 to the Philadelphia centennial of 1876. He argues that the United States was hesitant and privately organised, so that its first display in London, rescued by a private banker's money, was mocked by Punch and only later won respect for its machinery and agriculture. Later fairs at Paris and Vienna brought more official backing but also mismanagement, while American design and the fine arts still looked weak to European critics. The New York World's Fair of 1853, a failed Crystal Palace imitation, leads into a discussion of features peculiar to American fairs: little government control, rivalry between cities and a strong appetite for popular entertainment, illustrated by Philadelphia's Shantyville. The centennial, the chapter's main case, looked back to the American past, and the chapter closes with the late 1880s plans for a Columbian fair that would have to outdo Paris.

London 1851New York 1853Philadelphia 1876Paris 1889
Part TwoPart Two: The Settingp. 23
4Energy and Uncertaintyp. 25

Badger uses the Philadelphia centennial of 1876 to examine how Americans understood the industrial changes of the post-Civil War decades. The opening ceremonies looked back to the nation's past: the committee chose Whittier to write a hymn while Whitman was ignored, and the Corliss engine drew admiration for its power rather than for the functional design that might have pointed to a new artistic tradition. Badger argues that businessmen, lacking models for enterprises of national scale, sought security and reassurance, and turned to statistics and social science to discover the laws of industry. He then describes the depressions, labour conflicts and rapid urban growth of the period, when urban real estate had come to be worth twice the value of farms by 1890. The chapter ends by setting the industrial city, with its chaotic growth, against the older rural community, and by pointing towards Chicago as the place where these contrasts were most visible.

Philadelphia 1876
5The Representative Cityp. 31

Badger explores Chicago's rise from frontier town to national metropolis, arguing that its growth and conflicts made it a representative American city. He divides the story at the Great Fire of 1871, which destroyed four square miles and left about a hundred thousand people homeless, but which gave the city a new identity built on regeneration. Rebuilding brought skyscrapers and the Chicago School of architecture, while immigrants from many countries formed dense ethnic districts and the wealthy moved south along Michigan Avenue. Badger describes slum conditions, sweatshop labour, city bossism and the strikes of 1877 and 1886, the latter ending in the Haymarket bombing and the trial of anarchists whom the author treats as a convenient scapegoat. The chapter argues that Chicago's civic pride was a response to this insecurity, and it closes by describing the city as the place where the nation's major forces were most visible, which sets up the fair that follows.

Part ThreePart Three: The Great Fairp. 41
6Genesis and Growth of the Ideap. 43

Badger traces how the idea of a Columbian world's fair in 1892 developed in the decade after the centennial, from scattered proposals in Baltimore, Mexico City and Washington to a contest between Chicago and New York. Chicago's clubs, newspapers and businessmen built a campaign that stressed the city's centrality and its claim to speak for the West, while New York papers portrayed it as a raw outpost boasting of its grain, lumber and meat. The chapter follows the lobbying in Congress, the House vote of February 1890 that gave the fair to Chicago, and the ten million dollar guarantee that the city's committee pledged without consulting its citizens. Paris in 1889 overshadows the story, because American visitors measured their plans against it and judged the national display there a discredit. The chapter ends by noting that Chicago now had to make good its claim, and that the dual structure of the local company and the national commission would complicate the work.

Paris 1889Chicago 1893
7Organizationp. 59

Badger describes how the World's Columbian Exposition was organised once Chicago had won the fair, and why its structure was awkward. The local Chicago Company, responsible for raising money and building, and the National Commission, appointed under the act, disputed authority, each accusing the other of extravagance or usurpation. Badger traces the choice of site, from the lakefront, which the Illinois Central and the War Department contested, to Jackson Park, a swamp that Frederick Law Olmsted proposed to turn into lagoons and a wooded island. He then shows how Congress's refusal to fund the commission's expenses forced it into an advisory and judicial role, and how George Davis was made director-general and a Board of Reference and Control was set up to settle disputes. The chapter ends with the creation of a third organisation to run fifteen departments under that joint board.

Chicago 1893
8The Site, the Plan, and the Designp. 63

Badger traces how the Chicago Company and the National Commission chose the site for the World's Columbian Exposition and how its plan and buildings were designed and built. The lake front proved unworkable, so the planners turned to Jackson Park, and Daniel Burnham, appointed chief of construction in late 1890, took control of the work while Root, Olmsted and Codman supplied the main elements of the plan. Badger shows how the grand court, the basin and the wooded island drew on the French exposition of 1889, how the architects were chosen and the classical style agreed, and how Burnham imposed an all-white color scheme without consulting the color director. The chapter then follows the construction, with its swamp drainage, staff-covered steel frames and some seven thousand workers, and closes with the sculpture and decoration commissions. Badger's emphasis is on the unity of the design, which came from one controlling chief working through strained cooperation among artists, engineers and committees.

Chicago 1893Paris 1889
9Finance and Promotionp. 73

Badger examines the money, publicity and special programs that accompanied the Chicago fair. The first budgets proved wrong because contracts were let before the money arrived and because the classification of exhibits kept growing during construction, so the Chicago Company sought a federal appropriation. Congress cut the request to $2.5 million in souvenir coins and required Sunday closing, and the company made up the shortfall by selling the coins for a dollar each. The central case is Moses P. Handy's Department of Publicity and Promotion, which mailed a weekly newsletter to over fifty thousand domestic addresses, printed it in fourteen languages and shaped press coverage at home and abroad. Badger then turns to the women's role that led to a Board of Lady Managers and Sophia Hayden's Women's Building, and to the Midway, where Paris 1889 provided the model for concessions and Thomas Palmer's plan for a dignified ethnological display gave way to Sol Bloom's amusements. The chapter credits the Promotion Department with fixing the fair's pre-opening image as a symbol of American culture, and ends with the Midway's commercial turn under Bloom.

Chicago 1893Paris 1889Philadelphia 1876
10Dedication Dayp. 83

Badger describes the dedication of the buildings on October 20 and 21, 1892, moved from October 12 after New York claimed that date. A parade of nearly one hundred thousand people and the speeches in the Manufactures Building are set out. Most of the crowd could not hear the speakers, yet they stayed on. The chapter ends with the feeling that the fair marked the end of an old America as much as the start of a new one.

Chicago 1893
11Final Preparationsp. 87

Badger covers the last months before the opening, when a harsh winter, a partial collapse of the Manufactures Building roof and a wet April left the grounds unfinished on May 1, 1893, and the Chicago Company was short of cash after Congress withheld money for judges and awards. The chapter then shifts to Chicago itself, where Carter Harrison's return to the mayoralty and the city's wide-open reputation are set beside a civic pride that Badger ties to the new University of Chicago. Much of the chapter is practical, covering the seven routes to Jackson Park, the electric railway and lagoon craft, the water and sewage systems, and the Westinghouse lighting that made the White City shine at night. The most detailed case is the music program, where Theodore Thomas's concerts were undone by the dispute over Paderewski's Steinway and Thomas resigned in August. The chapter ends with the courts' conflicting orders on Sunday opening.

Chicago 1893
12The World’s Congressp. 95

Badger examines the World's Congress Auxiliary, the program of congresses that ran alongside the fair, and the religious and social pressures that shaped it. The campaign for Sunday closing and Reverend John Barrows's call to use the fair to reaffirm Christian values show how many religious people hoped the exhibition would stand for tradition, and the Parliament of Religions in September 1893 is treated as the most ambitious of the congresses. Badger then surveys the education, authors', architects' and labor congresses. Woodrow Wilson argued for liberal education, Hamlin Garland clashed with Mrs. Catherwood over local color, and Louis Sullivan's paper on polychrome challenged classical imitation. The Labor Congress rally on the lake front, which followed a clash with police, is given particular weight, and the chapter also covers the Congress of Representative Women, chaired by May Wright Sewell. Badger's argument is that the congresses forbade open controversy, so conflict was contained under the ideal of peace and harmony. The chapter ends with a French commissioner's verdict that the women's activities, the Parliament of Religions and the congresses were outstanding efforts in the realm of ideals.

Chicago 1893
13The Exhibitsp. 103

Badger looks at the individual exhibits that most visitors passed by, from agricultural and manufacturing displays to the Fine Arts Palace and the state and federal buildings. Pratt's rejection of the offer to run the Indian exhibit and the exclusion of black Americans from the fair's management are the sharpest cases. The chapter argues that the sheer number of displays overwhelmed visitors, and asks whether the ethnic exhibits encouraged viewers to see nonwhite peoples as primitive.

Chicago 1893
14The Midwayp. 107

Badger follows the Midway from its delayed construction to its popularity, by which time the management had given up the dignified ethnological display that Putnam was to direct. The chapter describes the concessions in detail, among them the Streets of Cairo, the Algerian and Tunisian villages with their dancers, an African village, Irish and German displays and a captive balloon ride, and it gives most attention to George Ferris's wheel, the most popular attraction of the entire fair. Using attendance figures, Badger shows how the Midway's amusements, newspaper coverage and better weather drove a rise from a disappointing May to 6,818,864 visitors in October. The chapter suggests that the Midway gave many Americans a release from the fair's idealism, and it closes with the Chicago Company's final payment of its debts, which Badger calls a genuine triumph for the city.

Chicago 1893
Part FourPart Four: The Culturep. 111
15Achievement and Influencep. 113

Badger assesses what the fair achieved and argues that its effects have been overstated. The chapter credits the exposition with reinforcing American admiration for technology and electricity, with opening wider export trade for firms and for farm products such as Oregon fruit, and with feeding a nationalism that Badger traces to Columbus Day and the Pledge of Allegiance. For Chicago, the fair's role in art clubs, the American Academy in Rome, the Field Museum and the City Beautiful movement is set against the claim that Burnham sold out to eastern academics, a claim Badger finds unsupported. The longest case is Louis Sullivan, whose Transportation Building and golden doorway Badger reads against his later account of the fair as a betrayal of American democracy. The chapter concludes that the fair reflected the cultural conflicts of the period more than it shaped them.

Chicago 1893
16A Confusion of Symbolsp. 119

Badger argues that the fair presented a culture full of contradictions, and that foreign and American observers read it differently. The chapter draws on James Muirhead's view of America as a land of stark contrasts and on Henry Adams's later verdict that the Exposition denied philosophy, then sets the Court of Honor against the Midway and the Ferris wheel against Richard Morris Hunt's planned golden dome. The main case is the representation of women, where the Board of Lady Managers, the Women's Building and the women's congresses offered competing images, and where Susan B. Anthony, Jane Addams and Bertha Palmer stand for three different models of the American woman. Frederick Jackson Turner's frontier thesis supplies a second theme, the worry about cultural continuity once the frontier closed. The chapter concludes that the Victorian faith in control and order was the fair's chief reassurance, so that foreign visitors saw a confusion of symbols where Americans saw a convergence.

Chicago 1893
17The Vision of Unityp. 125

Badger argues that the White City's unity answered the fears of an unsettled age, so it was a vision Americans wanted rather than a picture of their society. The congresses, the Parliament of Religions and the Court of Honor's illumination are read as efforts to impose harmony. Howells's Altrurian utopia and Schuyler's view of the White City as holiday architecture close the case, and the chapter ends by naming Chicago itself, not the architects, as the fair's hero.

Chicago 1893
Epiloguep. 129

Badger's epilogue traces the fair's end, from Carter Harrison's assassination on the fair's next-to-last day to the winter unemployment of 1893 and 1894 and the burning of the buildings during the 1894 railway strike. It then follows the later careers of Burnham, Gage, Bloom and Monroe, and the afterlife of the Art Palace, the Midway and the site. The chapter ends with the fair's dream of order ending in violence and flame.

Chicago 1893
Appendicesp. 131

Bell, Leonard. Colonial Constructs: European Images of Maori, 1840–1914. Auckland: Auckland University Press, 1992.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

Bell studies European paintings, watercolours, drawings and prints of Maori made for, exhibited in or published in Australasia and Britain, from the first organised settlement in New Zealand to the emergence of an independent nation. Its argument is that every image is a construction shaped by European conventions, patrons, racial theory and audiences, so it is better read as ideology than as a neutral record. The chapters follow artists and periods in turn: Angas and others in the 1840s and early 1850s, Gilfillan and Strutt, the artists active in New Zealand in the 1860s, the historical paintings of the 1890s and 1900s, Lindauer's pictures of customs and legend, and Dittmer's Te Tohunga of 1907. The conclusion considers later uses of these images, including their reuse by contemporary Maori artists and the 1987 Te Maori exhibition.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are slight in this book, which is about European images of Maori and the colonial settings in which they were made. No Asian display, participant or visitor is mentioned in any of the exhibitions discussed. Asia appears only as subject matter, in passing and mostly as a comparison for European painting: the Siamese twins among the Egyptian Hall's entertainments in London in the 1840s (chapter 1); the Orient of illustrated travel books (chapter 1); belles from Tahiti, the Philippines, India and China in Chevalier's 1872 London exhibition (chapter 3); Chinese heads among Hutchinson's sculptures shown at the A.S.A. in 1901 (chapter 5); and the European romanticisation of Africa, Asia and Oceania, to which Bell relates Dittmer's rhetoric (chapter 6). The Orientalism Bell discusses refers mainly to North Africa and the Middle East. South Asia enters only through the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London, where New Zealand exhibits were shown.

Contents

List of Illustrationsp. vi
Acknowledgementsp. XV
Abbreviationsp. xvi
Introductionp. 1

Bell's introduction defines the scope of a study of European visual representations of Maori from the first organised European settlement in New Zealand to the emergence of an independent nation. It sets aside a general survey, and a history of Maori or of colonisation, to concentrate on a small group of oil paintings, watercolours, drawings and prints made for, exhibited in, or published in Australasia and Britain. Drawing on Kristeva, Said, Goodman and Barthes, Bell argues that every representation is a construction shaped by European conventions, patrons, racial theory and audiences, so these images are better read as ideological constructs than as neutral records. The introduction then sketches the colonial context: the conversion of most Maori to Christianity by the early 1850s, the wars of the 1860s, land confiscations and a falling Maori population. This background frames the image types the following chapters examine, including the supposedly vanishing Maori of ethnographic record and the romantic or picturesque figure. It closes by acknowledging that the author's own text is situated and leaves gaps.

1The 1840s and Early 1850s: G. F. Angas, S. C. Brees, R. A. Oliver, J. J. Merrett, C. Clarke, W. Beetham, and J. W. Carmichaelp. 9

Bell examines how a group of artists, most of them linked to Governor Grey or to colonial settlement, represented Maori in the 1840s and early 1850s. Angas comes first: his watercolours, shown at London's Egyptian Hall in 1846 and reissued as lithographs in The New Zealanders Illustrated (1847), served as ethnography and popular entertainment at once. Its plates turn Maori women and children into keepsake types and present men as passive, Christianised and reconciled to settlement. Brees's panorama and book, Oliver's lithographs and Merrett's sketches draw on the same picturesque and keepsake conventions. Clarke's expedition drawings for Grey are set against his imaginative scenes for John Logan Campbell's memoir. The chapter ends with the portraits of Te Puni and Tamihana, which show Maori absorbed into colonial order, and with Carmichael's painting of the Erebus and Terror, a studio fiction built from marine conventions rather than a record of Ross's 1841 visit.

London 1846London 1849
2Gilfillan and Struttp. 53

Bell examines John Gilfillan and William Strutt, the first two professional artists to exhibit oil paintings featuring Maori in the 1850s. Both had substantial careers in Britain before going to New Zealand, and both later worked in Australia rather than as artists in the colony. Their New Zealand drawings are read as genre studies drawn from Scottish peasant imagery and as colonial landscapes in which Maori stand for unimproved wilderness beside European farms and towns. The main cases are Gilfillan's lithograph Interior of a Native Village, displayed at the Great Exhibition among New Zealand products, and his Melbourne oil Korero, shown in 1853 as a decorative fine art spectacle. Strutt's Hare Pomare and Family, shown to Queen Victoria, is analysed as a Holy Family analogy that makes a Maori group acceptable to Victorian viewers. Bell argues that idealisation and ideology worked together: peaceable Maori served colonial needs, while hostile Maori were cast as savages. The chapter ends by concluding that these were parts of one colonial outlook, not contradictory impulses.

London 1851Melbourne 1853
3Representations of Maori by Artists Active in New Zealand in the 1860sp. 94

Bell surveys the European artists active in New Zealand in the 1860s, when few professionals worked there and few paintings with Maori were exhibited. Albin Martin, J. C. Symons and William Ewart are treated briefly, and Ewart's portrait of John Hobbs is read as an ideal friendly Maori for a governor. The main cases are Horatio Robley and Gustavus von Tempsky. Robley's watercolours and sketches, made in the Bay of Plenty in 1864-66, are read as reportage, with unidealised faces and carefully recorded moko, though the Illustrated London News engravings after them turned his scenes towards conflict or conciliation. Von Tempsky's 1867 exhibitions in Auckland and Wellington were fictions that romanticised Maori in banditti and picturesque settings, and cast them as savages when they resisted. The chapter ends with Nicholas Chevalier and Domett's Ranolf and Amohia, whose Maori could be exotic figures of nostalgia or inferiors to be controlled, depending on the function of the image.

Auckland 1867Wellington 1867London 1879
4Late Nineteenth-/Early Twentieth-Century Historical Paintingsp. 147

Bell argues that the Maori historical paintings European artists produced in New Zealand in the 1890s and 1900s were part of a settler effort to acquire a past. Auckland's art society, public gallery and patrons prized such pictures, and reviewers treated them as the most important works in national exhibitions. The main cases are Steele and Watkins's The Explosion of the Boyd, Wright's The Burning of the Boyd, Steele and Goldie's The Arrival of the Maoris and Watkins's The Phantom Canoe, about the 1886 Tarawera eruption. Bell sets each against its European models, from Gericault's Raft of the Medusa to Gilsemans's engraving, and against the ethnological texts its painters used. He shows how the works mixed ethnographic detail with melodrama, violence and eroticism, and how Maori figures are often dark, dead or decorative. The chapter concludes that these paintings cast Maori history as a dualism of savagery and romance, and that this construction helped naturalise European possession of New Zealand.

Auckland 1908
5Lindauer's Paintings of Maori Customs and Legendp. 195

Bell turns to Gottfried Lindauer's large oil paintings of traditional Maori activities and legend, the series commissioned by the Auckland collector Henry Partridge and shown in his Lindauer Gallery from 1901. He argues that the pictures, among them Tohunga under Tapu, Digging with the Ko and Happy Days, were composites built from staged photographs by museum men such as Hamilton, earlier engravings and Puvis-style compositional devices, and that Partridge and James Cowan shaped how viewers read them as records of a vanishing culture. The chapter then takes Hinemoa and The Laughing Girl as cases, setting them against European nude and Ariadne traditions and against photographs of Polynesian women. Its last section contrasts these works with The Time of Kai, the only Lindauer of contemporary Maori life, which breaks the idealised order of the others. Bell concludes that Lindauer's 'old-time' Maori were a European construct that gave settler culture an antiquity and cast present-day Maori as decadent.

London 1886
6Wilhelm Dittmerp. 222

Bell examines Wilhelm Dittmer, a German-born painter and illustrator who lived in New Zealand from 1898 to 1905 and later published Te Tohunga (1907), a lavishly illustrated book of Maori legend. The chapter argues that his Maori images, from the oil portrait Mana of the chief Te Heu Heu Tukino to the paintings of elderly figures and young women, conform to colonial stereotypes of a dying and passive people, even where they borrow forms from Maori art. Bell compares Dittmer with Goldie and Lindauer, showing how Mana turns a powerful political figure into a mask, while Dittmer's mature women, unlike Goldie's, look out with strength. The bulk of the chapter traces the European sources of the Te Tohunga drawings in Symbolism, Art Nouveau and Jugendstil, and shows how the text reshapes Maori legends such as Hinemoa and Mahuika to suit European tastes. Bell concludes that the book, underwritten by Prime Minister Joseph Ward, helped to fashion a second, indigenous culture for the settler nation.

Conclusionp. 256

Bell's conclusion argues that colonial representations of Maori have no single fixed meaning. Dittmer's illustrations have inspired some contemporary Maori artists, and Lindauer's portraits were shown at the 1987 Te Maori exhibition as testimony to survival and continuity rather than to a dying race. Against these uses, the chapter sets the fact that most of these images were made for European audiences and buyers, objectified Maori as cultural and commercial commodities, and now sell as investments. Bell also shows that portraits could carry meanings outside European contexts, for instance at tangi, where they embodied the presence of ancestors and became taonga. Such images remain central to contested questions of ownership, control and the authority to narrate the past. The book offers interpretive possibilities rather than a single authentic picture, and it hopes to open a field for further study of cross-cultural representation in New Zealand.

Notesp. 260

Benedict, Burton. The Anthropology of World’s Fairs: San Francisco’s Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915. London and Berkeley: Scolar Press, 1983.Asia: occasional7 chapter overviews

Overview

The volume studies the Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915 in San Francisco and, in its lead essay, world's fairs in general. It grew from a Lowie Museum exhibition built from the fair's Japanese mannequins, Swedish dolls and Chinese temple model. Burton Benedict's main chapter treats fairs as modern rituals of competition in which nations, companies and cities compete through displays, and traces classification schemes and the display of colonised peoples from London 1851 to New York 1939, which Benedict sees as the point where fairs became trade shows. Four chapters then examine the 1915 fair: Marjorie Dobkin on its politics and site selection, Gray Brechin on its architecture, Elizabeth Armstrong on its public sculpture and gender, and George Starr on its allegory and how visitors read it.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia appear occasionally, as examples within a wider argument about display. The preface begins with the Japanese mannequins, Swedish dolls and Chinese temple model from the 1915 San Francisco fair. Most references sit in chapter 3, 'The Anthropology of World's Fairs': Japan's pearl models of Mount Vernon and the Liberty Bell at Chicago in 1933 and New York in 1939, and Japan's gardens at St. Louis in 1904. Southeast Asia appears mainly in colonial and ethnic displays: the Philippine exhibit at St. Louis in 1904 with six villages of imported inhabitants, Indochinese people at Paris in 1889, and Java and Cambodia in village and panorama displays at Chicago in 1893 and Paris in 1900.

Dobkin (chapter 4, 'A Twenty-Five-Million-Dollar Mirage') gives the region a political role: the Japanese and Chinese governments exhibited at the 1915 fair although they opposed California's 1913 anti-alien land act, and the fair's directors argued that its prize was trade with the Orient. Benedict's chapter 3 also records the Chinese Republic's objection to the 'Underground Chinatown' concession, which showed Chinese in an opium den. Brechin (chapter 5) and Starr (chapter 7) use 'Oriental' and 'Chinese' mainly for architectural and figurative imagery, and Armstrong (chapter 6) quotes the 'mystic East' in a mural description. Korea, Taiwan and Mongolia are not named in the matched passages, and Asian visitors and observers are not discussed.

Contents

PrefaceBurton Benedictp. vii

Benedict describes how the book began: the Lowie Museum at Berkeley held Japanese mannequins, Swedish dolls and a model of a Chinese temple from the Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915, and he was invited to curate a show from them. He recounts his own childhood visits to fairs and how he and his colleagues gathered images, postcards, a tower of glass jewels and souvenirs from the 1915 exhibition. He ends by noting that oral histories and a boy's diaries gave the research a perspective that documents could not.

San Francisco 1915
Acknowledgmentsp. xi

Benedict thanks the staff of the Lowie Museum and the two museum scientists who researched, collected specimens and wrote essays for the exhibition. He names advisers, the libraries and collections that lent material, including the Bancroft Library and the San Francisco History Room, and the designers and proofreader of the book. He closes with thanks for a National Endowment for the Humanities grant. The page ends with his initials.

List of Illustrationsp. xiii
The Anthropology of World's FairsBurton Benedictp. 1

Benedict argues that world's fairs are modern rituals of competition, comparable to the potlatch, in which nations, companies and cities compete through ever larger displays of goods, towers and allegorical symbols. He shows how classification schemes from the 1851 Great Exhibition onward ordered the world, and how the display of colonised and Native peoples ranged from trophies and curiosities to evolutionary villages at St. Louis in 1904. He treats the amusement zone as a parody of the main fair. His examples come chiefly from London 1851, Paris 1889, Chicago 1893, St. Louis 1904, San Francisco 1915 and New York 1939, and he takes the Panama Pacific exposition as a case study. He concludes that the New York fair of 1939 marked a watershed after which world's fairs became trade shows, and that the 1915 San Francisco exposition was the last collective outburst of nineteenth-century optimism.

London 1851Paris 1889Chicago 1893St. Louis 1904San Francisco 1915New York 1939
A Twenty-Five-Million-Dollar MirageMarjorie M. Dobkinp. 66

Dobkin argues that the Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915 was an attempt to restore confidence in San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake, fire and graft trials, and that its promised permanent improvements were dropped as business and political interests pulled apart. She traces the fair from Reuben Hale's 1904 proposal and the failed Burnham plan, through the split between reform leaders such as James Phelan and the business elite who formed the Board of Directors, which excluded the prosecutors. The main case study is site selection: Golden Gate Park, Lincoln Park and a composite plan were each argued for until Charles Moore's support secured Harbor View. Dobkin also covers the rivalry with New Orleans and San Diego for federal recognition, the Board's opposition to Governor Johnson's anti-alien land acts, the labour truce with unions, and a publicity campaign built on projected investment. Her conclusion is that the economic claims were inflated, that the fair cost about half of what had been predicted, and that the First World War, not the exposition, delivered the prosperity its sponsors wanted.

San Francisco 1915
Sailing to Byzantium: The Architecture of the FairGray Brechinp. 94

Brechin argues that the Panama Pacific International Exposition was an architectural fantasy of a walled Byzantine city, sustained for nine months, that stood in deliberate contrast to the disordered San Francisco it rose from after 1906. He reviews the abandoned citywide plans for permanent improvements and then the fair as built: Ernest Coxhead's compact court layout, in which eight palaces formed an inner core, the night lighting supervised by William D'Arcy Ryan, the Tower of Jewels with its Novagems, and Jules Guerin's colour scheme. A large part of the chapter is on the artificial travertine that gave the buildings an illusion of age, and on the Oriental and Mediterranean imagery visitors read into the fair. Brechin then follows the fair's influence on the later work of Kelham, Mullgardt and above all Maybeck, and its revival at the 1939 Treasure Island fair, which he presents as a stripped Moderne copy and a nostalgic nod to the past. He concludes that the fair was a brief realisation of a Byzantine myth of perfection, and that the city's future lay in urban redevelopment rather than in arcaded dream cities.

San Francisco 1915San Francisco 1939
Hercules and the Muses: Public Art and the FairElizabeth N. Armstrongp. 114

Armstrong argues that the public art of the 1915 fair, sculpture and murals alike, celebrated male strength, mastery over nature and Social Darwinian progress, while women were cast as ethereal, subdued or passive. Her starting point is Perham Nahl's Thirteenth Labor of Hercules poster, chosen over designs with ethereal female figures, and the commissioned works that followed its spirit: Arthur Mathews's mural The Victory of Culture over Force, A. Stirling Calder's Fountain of Energy, his Nations of the West with its pioneer imagery, Hermon MacNeil's Adventurous Bowman and the Burden-Bearers beneath it, and William de Leftwich Dodge's Atlantic and Pacific. She sets these against the Darwinian sculpture of Mullgardt's Court of the Ages, the Native American figures of Fraser and Borglum, and the female allegories of Weinman's Descending Night and the weeping women on Maybeck's Palace of Fine Arts. The chapter ends by noting that the fair's explicit bravado was dismantled while the brooding Muses of the Palace of Fine Arts outlasted it.

San Francisco 1915
Truth Unveiled: The Fair and Its InterpretersGeorge Starrp. 134

Starr argues that the 1915 fair was saturated with allegory, and that its visitors, guidebook writers and critics treated it as a text to be decoded, which made much of the art stilted and turned the exposition's uplift into an obligation. He opens with Tocqueville and Santayana to frame American attitudes to symbolism, then works through the guidebooks of John D. Barry, Rose Berry, Stella Perry and Sheldon Cheney. His cases include the wings attached to supposedly weight-bearing figures, Charles Harley's Triumph of the Fields, Ulric Ellerhausen's weeping women on the Palace of Fine Arts, and Aitken's Fountain of Earth in the Court of the Ages. The most effective parts, he suggests, were those visitors could enjoy directly: the Court of the Ages by night, the lighting and steam around the Tower of Jewels, and Guerin's colour scheme. He concludes that Maybeck's Palace of Fine Arts, by accepting its own transience, reached visitors in a way the didactic allegories did not.

San Francisco 1915
Bennett, Tony. Pasts Beyond Memory: Evolution, Museums, Colonialism. London: Routledge, 2004.Asia: slight10 chapter overviews

Overview

Bennett's book asks how nineteenth-century natural history, ethnological, geological and archaeological museums made the deep, pre-documentary past visible and used it to govern visitors and citizens. Its argument is that evolutionary displays organised time and space together, so that museums became instruments of liberal government working on the layered, archaeological structure of the person. Britain is the primary case, with Australia and the United States as contrasting contexts, and the colonial dimension is central: colonised peoples were denied historical depth and managed as if already museum specimens. The chapters run from the historical sciences and typological display to habit and cultivation, Osborn's racial museum, colonial Australia and labelled displays, ending with a postscript on slow modernity.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present in this book, and the coverage is slight. Across the whole text the regions are named only in a handful of passages, none of them in a chapter on either region, and none concerning an exhibition, a national pavilion, an Asian commissioner or merchant, or an Asian visitor. The museums studied are overwhelmingly British, Australian and American. The only Japanese reference in the front matter is an acknowledgement of Masaaki Morishita's work on Japanese art museums.

The body of the book mentions the region only in passing. In Chapter 1 Bennett lists museums opening in Bangkok (1874), Japan (1871), China (1905) and Korea (1908) as part of the spread of the museum form beyond Europe and America. In Chapter 2 Huxley's racial sequence runs through Asia and includes the Chinese, the 'Xanthrocoi', one of the 'two great stocks' that originated civilisation. In Chapter 4 a Balzac museum tour passes the dawn of Chinese civilisation. In Chapter 5 Osborn's 'homo sapiens asiaticus or Mongolian' is one of three primary human stocks, treated as quasi-zoological. The idea of 'Asian despotism' in the Introduction and Chapter 4 (Mill, Bagehot) concerns India, which is South Asia. Southeast Asia is not mentioned in any matching passage.

Contents

List of figuresp. ix
Acknowledgementsp. xi

Bennett's acknowledgements say the book took ten years to write and was supported by the Australian Research Council, which funded Robin Trotter's research assistance. Thanks go to the staff of museums and libraries from the Pitt Rivers Museum to the Queensland Museum, and to colleagues and students whose discussion shaped it, among them Ivan Karp, Corinne Kratz, Anne Coombes and Donna McAlear. The book is dedicated to the memory of the author's mother, who died before it was completed.

Introductionp. 1

Bennett takes the title Pasts Beyond Memory from Conrad's Heart of Darkness and uses it for the deep, pre-documentary pasts that geology, palaeontology, archaeology and anthropology made visible in the later nineteenth century. The argument is that evolutionary museums of natural history, ethnology and geology made these pasts public and, in doing so, became instruments of liberal government, working on the layered, archaeological structure of the person. Britain is the primary case, with Australia and the United States as contrasting contexts in which the same sciences were used differently. In colonial settings, the book argues, indigenous populations were denied historical depth and were managed as if they were museum specimens, so the museum's role there has to be sought in colonial administration. The theoretical frame is Foucault's governmentality, set against accounts of museums as ideology, and the chapters move from the historical sciences to typological display, the American Museum of Natural History, Australian museums, and the politics of vision in evolutionary arrangements.

1Dead circuses: expertise, exhibition, governmentp. 12

Bennett asks how late-nineteenth-century natural history and ethnological museums governed their visitors, and argues that they defined themselves against the living spectacle of circuses, fairground shows and the midway zones of world's fairs. In this model the expert stood as a showman behind glazed cases, and the public could look at and learn from the displays but had no access to the work behind them. The evidence comes from Huxley's proposals for museum cases, from Melbourne's National Museum under McCoy and Baldwin Spencer, and from the contrast between Macleay's circular Quinary system in Sydney and Huxley's linear display of fossil horses. The chapter then argues that evolutionary displays organised time and space together, drawing on Latour's centres of calculation and Foucault's account of governmentality, and it ties this to the new liberalism, the new education movement and adult education. It concludes that museums sought to instil a temporal conscience in their visitors, and it criticises McClintock for treating time as mainly ideology.

2The archaeological gaze of the historical sciencesp. 36

The chapter argues that geology, natural history, archaeology and anthropology became historical sciences in the nineteenth century, reading objects and fossils as traces of pasts beyond memory that were arranged into a single developmental time. Bennett takes Whewell's palaeontological sciences, Huxley's piece of chalk and Geikie's The Story of a Boulder as examples of how the present came to be read as a stack of sedimented pasts. Cuvier's catastrophism and Werner's stratigraphy are set against Lyell and Darwin, whose account of the imperfect geological record shows the difficulty of filling in time. The argument then turns to the disputes between Owen and Huxley over dinosaurs and the place of man among the apes, illustrated by paired skull and skeleton figures, and to Thomsen's three-age system, Pitt Rivers's excavations and Lubbock's account of civilisation. The chapter ends with colonial Australia, where this archaeological gaze made Aboriginal people primitive but not ancient, and with Tylor's stratified model of human institutions, which prepares the discussion of museums that follows.

3Reassembling the museump. 64

Bennett argues that the typological method developed by Pitt Rivers, and taken up by evolutionary curators, reorganised museum collections so that objects became substitutable parts of universal developmental series. He traces how the method was adopted in British museums such as Liverpool under Forbes, the Horniman and the British Museum (Natural History), and how it spread to the Smithsonian, the American Museum of Natural History and the Field Columbian Museum in Chicago, which drew on materials from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The chapter shows how this grammar let collections circulate between institutions and fill gaps in sequences, and it presents the method as a black box for evolutionary thought. Colonial cases follow, including the Indian ethnographic survey and Australian administration, where colonised peoples were treated as if already in a museum. German anthropological museums, by contrast, rejected labels and evolutionary arrangements, a difference Bennett uses to show how anthropology related to Bildung. The chapter ends by describing the museum as an evolutionary accumulator, and it sets up the discussion of mnemotechnics in the next chapter.

4The connective tissue of civilisationp. 85

Bennett argues that the nineteenth-century museum was a device for governing the self through the historical past. The chapter starts from Maleuvre's reading of the art museum as a technology of memory and from Balzac's curiosity-shop episode, then moves to evolutionary thought, which pictured the person as a layered store of inherited habits. Most of the argument reads Walter Bagehot's Physics and Politics, where habit is both the engine of social progress and a danger that can freeze a society, and Pitt Rivers's account of inherited intellectual and automaton minds. Huxley's Evolution and Ethics, with its colonial garden analogy, is presented as the decisive break that moved accumulation out of the body and into culture, giving the state a role in cultivating character. Bennett also shows how this model excluded women, the working classes and colonised peoples from the developmental self. The chapter concludes that the evolutionary museum was an accumulator of the past meant to shape citizens, and that its address was uneven across class, gender and race.

5Selective memory: racial recall and civic renewal at the American Museum of Natural Historyp. 114

Bennett examines the American Museum of Natural History under Henry Fairfield Osborn, whose presidency treated the past as a selective store for renewing white Americans of northern European descent. Osborn drew on Huxley and on Weismann's theory of heredity to argue that the race plasm could be revived by contact with primal scenes of the struggle for existence, and the chapter reads the museum's displays, including the African Hall dioramas and the life groups, as devices for stripping away civilisation to reach that inherited core. Bennett then turns to the museum's educational work, which made it a distribution network reaching the children of immigrants in New York schools, with nature study offered as a moral antidote to tenement life. Against Haraway's reading of the museum as a rich men's peephole, Bennett argues that its hybrid public and private status shaped a governmental programme that other museums copied. The chapter concludes that the museum addressed adults of northern European stock through a restorative memory, while the migrant child was to be integrated through a shared language of nature.

6Evolutionary ground zero: colonialism and the fold of memoryp. 136

Bennett argues that Australia functioned in evolutionary thought as an "evolutionary ground zero" placed outside developmental time, so that Aboriginal culture was read as static and its material culture was displayed as an unchanging record. The chapter traces how Australian archaeology avoided stratigraphic digging, in line with Pitt Rivers's prediction that colonial archaeology would stay on the surface, and how anti-evolutionary curators such as McCoy and the Macleays shaped the Australian Museum and the National Museum of Victoria. Baldwin Spencer, trained at the Pitt Rivers Museum, reorganised the Victorian collections along evolutionary lines, and his assimilation policy for people of mixed descent is examined through the photographs and reports of his Northern Territory work. Drawing on Foucault's biopolitics and on Patrick Wolfe, Bennett shows how colonial time was separated from settler time. The chapter concludes that the colonised were denied the layered self that the museum and the state were meant to cultivate, and that assimilation tried to supply that depth through degrees of whiteness.

7Words, things and vision: evolution ‘at a glance’p. 160

Bennett examines how British and Australian evolutionary museums of the late nineteenth century tried to make evolution visible, and why they needed words to do it. Evolution works through imperceptible changes and gaps in the fossil record, so curators could not simply show it; they had to fill the spaces between objects with arrangement and text. The chapter draws on Pitt Rivers's typological displays, Baldwin Spencer's boomerang series in Melbourne, the Horniman Museum's labelling programme and a Dublin label on Paludina snails. It sets these against the Renaissance cabinet of curiosities and the Enlightenment museum, where meaning lay in conversation or classification, and links the anxiety about gaps in evolutionary sequences to fears of political and social mutation, including working-class politics, feminism and Stoker's Dracula. It closes by arguing that the evolutionary museum's authority rested on expert mediation that presented itself as the lesson of things, and that its speed of time set it apart from other technologies of modernity.

Postscript: slow modernityp. 187

A short postscript, 'Slow modernity', answers readings that set art museums in modern time against archaic natural history and ethnographic museums. Bennett argues that these museums belonged to modernity and helped shape its relation between past and present, organising progress through long continuities rather than sharp breaks. Drawing on Ray, Bourdieu and Latour, it treats 'pasts beyond memory' as objects produced by the historical sciences and mobilised for social and colonial ends. The museums are therefore institutions of slow modernity.
