Boone, M. Elizabeth. “The Spanish Element in Our Nationality”: Spain and America at the World’s Fairs and Centennial Celebrations, 1876–1915. University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2019.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Boone follows Spain's presence at a sequence of international expositions and national centenaries between 1876 and 1915: Philadelphia 1876, Barcelona and Paris in 1888 and 1889, Chicago 1893, the 1910 centenaries in Buenos Aires, Santiago de Chile and Mexico City, and the San Francisco and San Diego fairs of 1915. Its argument is that these displays helped define national identities in the United States and Latin America, and that Spain was repeatedly refused, misread or pushed into the past, so that its modern role and its links to the Americas were forgotten. Using paintings, ephemeral architecture, posters, postcards and press responses, the chapters proceed chronologically, each a case study of one fair or pair of fairs. The introduction ends by considering present-day consequences, including the Spanish-speaking population of the United States.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are slight in this book, which is about Spain, the United States and Latin America. The Philippines are the main Southeast Asian presence, and only as a Spanish colony: hemp from the islands was shown at Philadelphia in 1876 (chapter 1), and abacá fibre from the Philippines sat in the Spanish agricultural gallery at Chicago in 1893 (chapter 3). Japan is the most concrete case. Pellicer, reviewing the Barcelona fine arts display in 1888, asked whether the Japanese had stopped being artists since becoming industrious (chapter 2). In 1910 the Oriental Steamship Company of Japan organised a Japanese decorative arts exhibition in Mexico City alongside the Spanish show, and its sales were far stronger than the Spanish display's (chapter 4). China appears only as one of the national vendors in a satirical image of the Centennial restaurants (chapter 1).

None of the other regions on the list (Korea, Siam, Indonesia, Indochina) appears. Asia enters only as a category: Asian identity is named among the challenges to the Protestant national image in the Chicago chapter (chapter 3), and Asia is listed as a trading region the Panama Canal would link in the chapter on 1915 (chapter 5). The Orientalism discussed concerns North Africa and the Middle East, not East Asia.

Contents

List of Illustrationsp. ix
Acknowledgmentsp. xiii

Boone's acknowledgments thank colleagues and archivists in Spain, Chile, Argentina, Mexico and the United States, along with students, friends and funders. The book was finished in 2018 while the author was a visiting research professor at the Universidad de Alcalá de Henares, and all translations are the author's own.

Introductionp. 1

Boone opens with Walt Whitman's 1883 insistence that Spanish character must be recognised in American identity, and argues that an English-only national story has erased Spain from United States history. The book examines Spain's presence at five celebrations: Philadelphia 1876, Chicago 1893, San Francisco and San Diego in 1915, the Barcelona and Paris fairs of 1888 and 1889, and the 1910 centenaries in Buenos Aires, Mexico City and Santiago. Using paintings, ephemeral architecture, posters and press responses, it asks why Spain was displayed, refused or misread at each event, and how these displays helped shape national identities across the Americas. Boone draws on theories of exhibition, memory and transnational study, treating fairs as exercises in using the past to imagine a national future. The introduction ends by considering present-day consequences, including the contested reputations of Junípero Serra and Bernardo de Gálvez and the large Spanish-speaking population of the United States.

Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893San Francisco 1915San Diego 1915Barcelona 1888Paris 1889Buenos Aires 1910Mexico City 1910Santiago de Chile 1910
1Inventing America at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennialp. 15

Boone argues that the Philadelphia Centennial of 1876 invented a singular US national identity by excluding Spain's point of view. The chapter's main case is Spain's display: Antonio Gisbert's history painting Disembarkation of the Puritans in America, which the critic Earl Shinn thought a Spanish painter had no business making, and a set of mostly unremarkable paintings and products sent under a budget cut by the restored monarchy. Spain's commissioners built a triumphal arch with medallions of Ponce de León and De Soto, a neo-Gothic agricultural arch, and an Islamic-inspired soldiers' quarters, but American critics read the displays as museum clutter and Catholic excess. Boone sets this against the Colonial Revival, the Anglo-Protestant myth of origin and the Black Legend. The chapter concludes that the centennial allowed some European nations to speak while asking others, Spain among them, to stay silent.

Philadelphia 1876
2Defining (and Defending) Spain in Barcelona and Paris, 1888 and 1889p. 49

Boone asks how Spain was defined at two fairs held a year apart, the Exposició Universal in Barcelona in 1888 and the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1889. Spain's Restoration monarchy was divided between Liberals and Conservatives, and Catalan nationalists opposed any collaboration with Madrid, so each fair offered a different Spain. Barcelona is the main case: the chapter follows the fair's organisation, its site in the Parc de la Ciutadella, and the inauguration attended by the queen regent and the young Alfonso XIII. It then examines the fine-arts display, arranged by province and reviewed by Pellicer and Yxart. In Paris the official presence was a food pavilion by Arturo Mélida, built in neo-Mudéjar style, and a painting gallery where the jury gave its top prize to Luis Jiménez Aranda's hospital scene rather than to the government's history canvases by Gisbert and Casado. French critics dismissed those canvases as gruesome and theatrical, while Pardo Bazán defended them. The chapter concludes that the fairs turned a contested nation into a simpler story, one that was most persuasive outside Spain.

Barcelona 1888Paris 1889
3Marginalizing Spain (and Embracing Cuba) at the 1893 Columbian Expositionp. 87

Boone examines Spain's presence at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, which marked four centuries since Columbus's voyage. The Spanish built replicas of Valencia's silk exchange, a Toledo cloister and a Valladolid cloister, presenting 1492 and the Catholic Monarchs as the origin of the nation. The chapter's strongest material concerns Cuba, where the agricultural display promoted sugar and tobacco and Cuban visitors read it as evidence of a nation rather than a colony; a painting of Columbus in chains was altered before it could be hung. U.S. visitors instead consumed Spain as fantasy, through a replica of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, a Moorish Palace on the Midway and the Monastery of La Rábida. Princess Eulalia's exhausting visit, shaped by tensions over Cuba, shows the gap between royal expectations and American tastes. Boone concludes that Spain was pushed into the past, so that its links to the United States were forgotten.

Chicago 1893
4Reasserting Spain in America at the 1910 Centennial Exhibitionsp. 121

Boone examines the Spanish art and industry displays mounted for the 1910 independence centenaries in Buenos Aires, Santiago de Chile and Mexico City. Spain used these events to reassert its presence in America, and the republics used them to define their own national identities. In Buenos Aires the Spanish colonia financed the Pabellones de España, and José Artal's fine-arts exhibition, whose works were for sale, drew Zuloaga's Return from the Harvest into an Argentine collection. In Santiago a Spanish-funded statue of Alonso de Ercilla sat beside a satirical cartoon about the O'Higgins monument, which exposed the class and anti-Spanish tensions beneath the celebrations. In Mexico City a Spanish exhibition of about 250 works sold poorly, while a Mexican counter-exhibition of mostly Indigenous subjects showed that Spanishness there was complicated by large Indigenous and mestizo populations. The chapter concludes that Spanish art gave these republics a strategy for making a modern national art of their own.

Buenos Aires 1910Santiago de Chile 1910Mexico City 1910
5Using Spain to Ignore Mexicans at the 1915 California Fairsp. 155

Boone opens with a 1915 photograph of four Mexican gardeners posed in suits before a painted backdrop reading 'Meet Me in San Diego', and uses it to ask how Spanishness in the United States spoke to Mexican migrants. The chapter compares the two California fairs of 1915. In San Francisco, the Panama-Pacific International Exposition went ahead without a Spanish government pavilion, despite years of lobbying by local boosters; Spain's presence was reduced to past conquistadors in sculpture and a generalized Mediterranean style. In San Diego, the Panama-California Exposition built a Spanish colonial city, drawing on the Portola Festivals, the novel Ramona, the restored Estudillo House and mission bells. Boone reads postcards, photographs and newspapers closely, showing how visitors were pictured inside the architecture and how the Mexican workers who built the park remain nearly invisible. The chapter concludes that erasing Spain's modern role left the United States unable to embrace its Spanish-speaking population, and it argues for recognising Spanishness in all its complexity.

Brown, Kendall H. “Fair Japan: Japanese Gardens at American World’s Fairs, 1876–1940.” Journal article.Asia: central5 chapter overviews

Overview

Brown's article examines the Japanese gardens built at American world's fairs from Philadelphia in 1876 to the New York and San Francisco fairs of 1939–40, and the commercial gardens set up outside the gates. Brown argues that these gardens were official images of a timeless, pre-modern Japan that served an imperial government's political aims. It moves from staged performances to the commercial 'Fair Japan' enclaves and their postwar afterlife, and asks whether the propaganda delayed American responses to Japan.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the whole subject of this article: Japan alone, with its gardens, pavilions and wartime context, is discussed in every chapter. The attention is central, concentrated in 'Performing on the World Stage' and 'Fair Japan', with 'In The Wake of Exposition Gardens' on the later relations with the United States. Japan appears as an exhibitor in two forms: the official gardens and national pavilion, built by workers from Japan under government sponsorship from Philadelphia in 1876 onward, and commercial 'Fair Japan' enclaves set up outside the gates by entrepreneurs such as Yumindo Kushibiki. Japan was also the largest or second-largest renter of space in the industry halls at major American fairs.

China figures only as the setting of Japan's wars: the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 and the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05, the invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and coastal China in 1932, and the 'Sacred War' in China during the 1939–40 fairs. The Pacific coast fairs of 1907–1915 are set against anti-Japanese immigration. Southeast Asia is marginal: one passage, on the French colonial displays at the 1900 Paris Exposition, notes a Siamese pavilion and Angkor Wat among colonial holdings, and colonised Asia generally appears as territory displayed by its conquerors as trophies. Korea does not appear in the text as read. Japanese women in kimonos and geisha figures are the performers in the gardens, not visitors or observers.

Contents

[no heading printed: opening section, pp. 13-14]p. 13

Brown opens with a moss garden in New York State, tended by a gardener named Morrell who treats the work as meditation, and introduces the aesthetics of wabi-sabi. The section then turns to the Japanese gardens built at American world's fairs from 1876 onward. They were official images of a timeless Japan, and many survived as parks and private gardens. Brown frames them as political tools that presented a pre-modern nation while Japan was industrialising and expanding.

Philadelphia 1876San Francisco 1894New York 1939
Performing on the World Stagep. 14

Brown argues that Japanese gardens at world's fairs were staged performances, not neutral displays of beauty. Japan's official image split into a modern, industrial pavilion and a timeless, feminine garden. Brown ties this to fairs timed around Japan's wars, from Chicago in 1893 to San Francisco and New York in 1939 and 1940. The gardens, he concludes, naturalized a politically charged message, presenting Japan's imperial present as the natural expression of an unchanging culture.

Chicago 1893St. Louis 1904San Francisco 1939New York 1939
Fair Japanp. 15

Brown turns to the Japanese gardens built by commercial entrepreneurs outside the fair gates. Run by businessmen such as Yumindo Kushibiki, these small gardens competed with attractions like the Bavarian Beer Garden, and others stood in Atlantic City and on a New York rooftop. Brown argues they served Japan's interests more effectively than the official pavilion, since they were not tied to the government. The name 'Fair Japan' puns on 'fair' to suggest beauty and virtue at once.

In The Wake of Exposition Gardensp. 16

Brown considers the gardens' legacy as relations between Japan and the United States soured from about 1913. American fascination with Japanese culture was separated from views of Japan as a political power, and the feminine, pastoral image became easy to dismiss once Japan was a threat. He asks whether the propaganda delayed American responses to Japanese expansion, citing the St. Louis displays of 1904 and the New York and San Francisco fairs of 1939 and 1940.

St. Louis 1904New York 1939San Francisco 1939
Gardens as Performance Artp. 16

Brown argues that fair gardens were performance art, meant to entertain and persuade a public, with spectacles such as dance and fashion shows. They aimed to fix an unchanging image of modern Japan, and the main garden worked as a transitional space that prepared visitors for the national pavilion. Brown traces their afterlife in postwar American homes, sister-city displays and theme parks. He concludes that their deepest legacy was to make Asian culture part of American public space.

Burris, John P. Exhibiting Religion: Colonialism and Spectacle at International Expositions, 1851–1893. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 2001.Asia: substantial8 chapter overviews

Overview

Burris's book is a cultural history of how the international exposition tradition helped create the academic field of religion. Its cases are the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London, the Paris expositions of 1867 and 1889, the New York Crystal Palace of 1853, the Philadelphia Centennial of 1876 and the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition of 1893, whose World's Parliament of Religions is the central event. Burris argues that fair displays of peoples as primitive or civilised carried social evolutionism into comparative religion, and that the Parliament's exclusions of Native Americans and African Americans followed the fair's cultural hierarchy. The work is limited to Britain and the United States. It has an introduction, five chapters, a conclusion on the 1993 centenary meeting, and notes, bibliography and index.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a substantial strand, concentrated in chapter 4, 'Exhibitionism, American Style', and chapter 5, 'Exhibiting Religion at Chicago's Columbian Exposition'. In chapter 4 Japan and India appear as participants at Chicago: Japan's Ho-o-den Palace in White City, a Japanese bazaar and teahouse on the midway, and an Indian pavilion whose attendants spoke with British accents. China appears on the midway as a display arranged by others, a 'Joss House' museum, since the Chinese government boycotted the fair. Javanese and Samoans in the midway's Dutch Settlement are among the village peoples shown as primitive. Chapter 5 treats Asians as speakers at the World's Parliament of Religions, where about half a dozen Asian delegates spoke in English and the Chinese papers were read through translators. Chapter 2 notes that China and Japan sent no exhibits to the Great Exhibition.

Southeast Asia receives much less attention. Indochina appears only through Cochin-Chinese families in the colonial section of the Paris exposition of 1889, and Java through the Javanese at that fair and on the Chicago midway. Siam appears only as religious objects from the Siamese government in the Chicago Anthropology Building. Burma, Malaya and Borneo are not discussed in the passages examined.

Contents

List of Illustrations
Acknowledgments

Burris thanks the people who shaped the book, beginning with Charles H. Long, whose seminar and unpublished paper 'Fair: No Fair' helped set its blueprint. He names his dissertation committee, the editors and copyeditor at the University Press of Virginia, and the libraries consulted in London and Chicago. He acknowledges funding and teaching at Syracuse University, and closes by thanking his parents and his wife, Kathy, who is a librarian.

Introduction

Burris opens with the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 in Chicago, arguing that the international exposition tradition helped form a field of religion. The introduction names four elements that made that field possible: its comparative basis in colonial encounters, its appeal to popular culture, the spread of social evolutionism through displays of peoples as savage or primitive, and a division that placed the least industrial peoples under anthropology while civilisations were classed by religion. Its key case is the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions, which excluded peoples defined culturally rather than religiously. Burris describes the book as a cultural history limited to Britain and the United States, rather than a single-thesis study, and previews a final chapter on the Parliament's centenary.

London 1851Chicago 1893
1International Expositions in Historical Contextp. 1

Burris places the nineteenth-century international expositions in four historical contexts: commerce, spectacle, interculturalism and cross-cultural discourse. The chapter traces the ancestry of the exposition in medieval and early modern trade fairs, especially the Champagne and Piacenza fairs, which Burris reads as places where value was set across unfamiliar borders by hosts with political power. It then turns to national industrial exhibitions in France and Britain and to the carnivalesque midway, where colonised peoples were shown beside industrial displays. Burris links this to medieval relic display, eighteenth-century curiosity collections and the British Museum, and argues that Christian ways of naming foreign peoples shaped how they were exhibited. The chapter ends by asking whether religion can unite peoples across cultures or is the most guarded of cultural possessions.

London 1851Chicago 1893
2Britain’s Great Exhibition: Ideology Materializedp. 23

Burris reads the Great Exhibition of 1851 as a source for the emergence of a field of religion, arguing that its displays and awards produced a global hierarchy of cultures and religions based on industrial capacity. The chapter follows the planning: Prince Albert's decision that the exhibition should be international, the choice of Hyde Park, Paxton's glass building nicknamed the Crystal Palace, the arrangement of displays by country and the awards juries. It then shows how the press ranked nations, with Britain first, France as the only serious rival, and the United States, whose thin display was mocked, placed between civilised and savage. Colonised and primitive peoples appear mainly through British collections, such as the Indian Court and Queen Pomare's Tahitian mats, shown as objects of trade. Burris shows that religious commentators, including the Archbishop of Canterbury and Edward Higginson, linked industrial success with divine favour. The chapter ends with the jury disputes, and argues that religion had been absorbed into judgments of industrial prowess.

London 1851
3Social Evolutionism and International Expositions: A Cultural Historyp. 63

Burris argues that social evolutionism, the idea that human societies form a single hierarchy of progress comparable to a chain of being in nature, was popularised and given authority by the international exposition tradition, and that this in turn helped create a field of religion. The chapter traces the doctrine back to the decades before the Great Exhibition of 1851, when geology, the higher criticism and new ethnology began to loosen biblical accounts of human origins, and then follows its fate through Darwin and Spencer to a neo-Lamarckian version that proved more popular in Britain. Its evidence is the display of peoples at exhibitions: the ethnographic arrangement of the Great Exhibition, the Paris expositions of 1867 and 1889 with their photographs and mock native villages, and the Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London in 1886. The chapter concludes that displaying non-Western peoples as curiosities made their religions appear too obscure to count as religion, so that Western comparative religion rested on evolutionary categories.

London 1851Paris 1867Paris 1889London 1886
4Exhibitionism, American Stylep. 86

Burris asks why religion became a theme at the Chicago fair of 1893, and answers by tracing the three nineteenth-century American international expositions that came before it. American fairs differed from European ones because the United States had no colonies to display, so the peoples classed as primitive lived inside the country, and the hierarchies shown at the fairs carried direct political meaning for American social order even though they were staged as carnival entertainment. The chapter works through the New York Crystal Palace of 1853, with its commercial shanties and collapse, the Philadelphia Centennial of 1876, with its racially divided displays and Native American sections, and Chicago's White City, Midway Plaisance and anthropological Department M. Its evidence includes the Kwakiutl performances, the Dahomean village, the exclusion of African Americans, and the protests of Frederick Douglass and Ida B. Wells. The chapter concludes that the midway placed peoples deemed primitive in a carnival setting that implied their religion was not serious, which shaped who could speak at the World's Parliament of Religions.

New York 1853Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893
5Exhibiting Religion at Chicago’s Columbian Expositionp. 123

Burris examines how religion was displayed and debated at the 1893 Columbian Exposition in Chicago, with the World's Parliament of Religions as its central event. He argues that the exposition tradition had turned religion into a separable category that could be exhibited and compared, and that the Parliament reproduced the same hierarchy of civilised and primitive peoples as the fair around it. The evidence includes religion-based displays in the Smithsonian and Anthropology Building, midway shows that cast Dahomeans and Native Americans as fetishists, and the congresses on evolution, anthropology and Africa. Burris is most concerned with absence. Native Americans were not invited to speak, while African Americans were admitted through Bishop Benjamin Arnett and Fannie Barrier Williams as Christians rather than as a culture. Asian speakers, Catholics and Jews gained visibility, although the Asian delegates were invited partly to ease Catholic-Protestant tensions. The chapter concludes that the Parliament's exclusions followed the cultural hierarchy of the fair rather than religious judgment.

Chicago 1893
Conclusion: A Parliament for the World’s Religions?p. 167

Burris's conclusion follows what happened after the 1893 Parliament, from the Christian and academic commentary that interpreted it to the Atlanta exposition of 1895, which gave African Americans a separate building but segregated audiences. It then turns to the 1993 centenary meeting in Chicago, retitled 'A Parliament for the World's Religions', which drew neo-pagans and Native American groups but few mainline Protestants, Catholics or Jews. Burris describes the scientist Gerald Barney's appeal to religious leaders on population and food, an Orthodox metropolitan's rejection of the idea that religion could reshape a scientific and economic order, and the failure of Hans Küng's 'Global Ethic' statement to win the assembly's endorsement. Burris argues that the 1893 exclusions rested on a hierarchy of primitive and civilised peoples inherited from the exposition tradition, and that the field of religion has not fully broken from it. The chapter ends by urging the discipline to keep its categories from absorbing the political climate in which they were formed.

Chicago 1893Atlanta 1895

Cotter, Bill, and Bill Young. The 1964–1965 New York World’s Fair: Creation and Legacy. Charleston, SC: Arcadia, 2008.Asia: slight10 chapter overviews

Overview

Cotter and Young, The 1964-1965 New York World's Fair, is a picture book of photographs, concept art, models and captions that follows the fair from its creation to its afterlife. Its main argument, made most directly in the closing chapter, is that Robert Moses used the fair chiefly to finish the Flushing Meadows park he had planned for the 1939-1940 site, spending leftover money on grounds rather than repaying creditors. The scope is one fair in one city: the 1959 proposal and planning, construction, the 'phantom fair' of cancelled and altered pavilions, the two seasons, the sale and demolition of the buildings, and the restored park. The introduction is followed by nine chapters that run roughly in chronological order, with captions doing much of the narrative work.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia barely figure in this book. Three passing mentions are all the text contains, and none is developed. Japan is named once, in chapter 4, The Phantom Fair, as one of the exhibitors whose names filled the site map by the autumn of 1962, a list the chapter then qualifies by describing how many announced exhibits never got built or were cut back. Chapter 6, The Changing Fair, records the early closure of the Indonesia Pavilion, one of the most beautiful international pavilions, after political and financial trouble left unpaid rent; for the rest of the fair the building stood empty behind barricades. Chapter 8, The End of the Fair, shows a sign left in place to mark the site of the Korea Pavilion, which still advertised gift shop bargains after demolition. In each case the country appears as an exhibitor or a site, not as a subject of display, and no Asian people, colonial display, Asian visitors or Asian-held exhibitions are discussed. Japan and Korea get no further description, and the book makes no comparison with Asia.

Contents

Acknowledgmentsp. 6
Introductionp. 7

Cotter and Young introduce a sequel to their earlier book on the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair, covering how the fair was created, built and left as a legacy. Cotter explains that many pavilion-building organisations have gone and corporate records were lost, so the book relies on photographs and personal collections. Young sets out its scope, from five years of design and construction to two years of park restoration.

New York 1964
1Why a Fair?p. 9

Cotter and Young trace the fair to a 1959 proposal by New York businessmen led by Thomas J. Deegan to mark the city's 300th anniversary. They argue that New York won federal backing over Seattle, Los Angeles, Chicago and Washington largely through politics, and reproduce a 1959 New York Times report. The chapter ends with Robert Moses being chosen to head the corporation, which the authors present as his chance to finish the park left unfinished after the 1939-1940 fair.

New York 1964
2Designing the Fairp. 13

Cotter and Young explain that the fair reused the roads and utilities of the 1939 fair site at Flushing Meadows, and that its pavilions used space-frame structures, fiberglass and a relaxed building code to keep costs down. Most of the rest is photographs and captions showing concept art, scale models, and rejected or altered designs for pavilions such as Kodak, DuPont, Wisconsin and Africa, along with changes to the Unisphere logo and a 1964 site plan of the fairgrounds.

New York 1964
3Building the Fairp. 29

Cotter and Young open with the scale of construction, listing miles of water mains and high-voltage cable, about 250,000 tons of steel, $550 million in exhibit and construction spending and some 12.9 million man-hours by Labor Day 1963. The rest is captions following the building of the Unisphere, the Tent of Tomorrow roof at the New York State Pavilion, the 1963 dedication ceremonies and late work on the Belgian Village and Hall of Science, and the chapter ends with the rainy opening day and protests over racial injustice.

New York 1964
4The Phantom Fairp. 51

Cotter and Young examine exhibits that were announced for the fair but never built, or were abandoned during construction, which they call the phantom fair. The chapter argues that exhibiting was too expensive for most sponsors, so many dropped out or cut back, and it illustrates unbuilt or altered designs such as Rheingold's Little Old New York, the Swiss Sky Ride, the Texas-NASA pavilion and the Rocky Mountain and Southwestern States pavilion. The World of Food Pavilion is the main case, since construction began before fair officials ordered it demolished and court battles followed. The authors also cover the difficulty of attracting foreign governments, which were reluctant because of a dispute with the Bureau of International Expositions, and they end with Georgia's planned plot near the Unisphere, another project that stalled for lack of funds.

New York 1964
5Promises of the Fairp. 61

Cotter and Young test the fair's predictions about the future, drawing on pavilions that promised space travel, computers, satellite communication and new consumer goods. They credit the fair with anticipating the moon landing, the home computer and optical character recognition, and show Telstar and the Green Bank radio telescope as examples of genuine advances, but they list predictions that failed, including Picturephone, Norge's disposable Dishmaker, a four-hour workday, Corfam and fluid-logic computers. The chapter gives most space to General Motors' Futurama ride, which made the most predictions and got the most wrong, and ends by asking whether its climate forecasts anticipated global warming.

New York 1964
6The Changing Fairp. 71

Cotter and Young describe how pavilions and shows were altered between the two seasons, either because they failed or because crowds and new products demanded change. Failures included the Texas Pavilions' To Broadway, With Love, which closed after 97 performances, and Leon Leonidoff's Wonder World in the Amphitheater, which lasted less than three months before the Florida Water Ski Show replaced it. The chapter also covers the Hall of Education and its Demonstration Center successor, the Greek Pavilion's remodelled windows, the renamed Bourbon Street, and the closures of the Indonesia Pavilion and the Sierra Leone Pavilion, which became the United Nations Pavilion in 1965. It ends with James Bond's Aston Martin DB5 added to the AMF exhibit for 1965.

New York 1964
7The Fair on Salep. 83

Cotter and Young describe the sale of the fair's contents on the morning after it closed, when exhibitors sold furnishings, steel and whole pavilions to any buyer with cash. The AMF monorail went for 20 cents on the dollar, Greyhound sold its Glide-a-Ride trains to 29 buyers, and the Wisconsin Pavilion was taken out on a flatbed truck before union demolition crews noticed. The chapter then traces where pieces went, including the Austrian Pavilion, which became a ski lodge near Jamestown, New York, the Christian Science Pavilion, which became a church in Poway, California, before its demolition in 2006, and the Disney shows that moved to Disneyland. Its last examples are the Parker Pen Pavilion, reused as a lodge shelter, and the Hall of Free Enterprise plaques, which went to the Amway headquarters in Michigan.

New York 1964
8The End of the Fairp. 99

Cotter and Young describe the demolition after the fair closed, which exhibitors were required to finish within 90 days under the lease for Flushing Meadows Park. Many exhibitors defaulted, so the corporation spent over half a million dollars removing about 35 abandoned pavilions before the park was handed to the city in June 1967. The chapter then covers the final days, when visitors took plants and fittings, and photographs of demolition at the Kodak, General Motors, Ford and Bell System pavilions and the United States Pavilion, whose piles were later reused for the Arthur Ashe stadium. It closes with the restored park, which the authors say the fair improved through new roads, sports fields and the permanent Hall of Science, though not on the scale Moses had planned.

New York 1964
9The Fair's Great Legacyp. 117

Cotter and Young trace what remained of the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair in Flushing Meadows-Corona Park. Their central claim is that Robert Moses used the fair chiefly to finish the park he had planned for the earlier 1939-1940 site, spending the leftover cash on the grounds rather than repaying creditors. Most pavilions were demolished within months, and only a few survived, including the administration and press buildings, the Singer Bowl, the Space Park, the New York State Pavilion and the Hall of Science. Each caption pairs a photograph of a place, such as the entrance canopy, Gotham Plaza, the Unisphere, the New York City Building panorama or the monorail station, with its present state, showing what has gone, what survives and what has decayed. Later pages cover the time capsules, the statues and the Queens Zoo, and the chapter concludes that the pavilions are gone but the fair survives in memory.

New York 1964-1965
Cotter, Bill. The 1939–1940 New York World’s Fair. Charleston, SC: Arcadia, 2009.Asia: occasional11 chapter overviews

Overview

Cotter, The 1939-1940 New York World's Fair, is a picture book that argues the fair is remembered for its optimism about the future rather than for any single exhibit. It relies on candid photographs of visitors among gardens and sculptures, with only about a dozen publicity or aerial images among more than 200, and Cotter concedes that no single book can capture the fair's hundreds of buildings. The scope is the 1939 season and the 1940 season that followed under new management, covering the fair's planning, its Theme Center, and each of its zones: transportation, communication, food, government, community interests, production and distribution, and amusement. The book is organised as an introduction, ten chapters built around zones and topics, and captions that carry most of the descriptive detail.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia appear only in passing, in a book about the fair's Western and American exhibits. The densest material is in chapter 6, The Government Zone. Japan is mentioned three times there: its government pavilion, modelled on an ancient Shinto shrine, included a Formosa Tea Garden, where the caption notes that Taiwan was then under Japanese rule; a stone lantern in the Japanese garden, inscribed as a token of American-Japanese friendship, is linked to the Pearl Harbor attack; and a Japanese business display in the Hall of Nations is set apart from the government pavilion. The Netherlands pavilion is said to present the Dutch East Indies as one of three parts of the empire. Chapter 9, The Amusement Area, describes Frank Buck's Jungleland, where guests could see Malayan workers from his expeditions in a re-created native village, a display of people organised by someone else, and the Chinese Lama Temple, a replica of the Potala of Jehol with a Tibetan design. In chapter 10, The 1940 Season, the American Bureau for Medical Aid to China occupies the former Siam pavilion and works for a China at war. Asian visitors and exhibitions held in Asia are not discussed, and beyond these passages the region is not mentioned.

Contents

Title Page
Copyright Page
Acknowledgments
Introduction

Cotter, who first saw a world's fair in 1964 and later collected 1939 material, argues that the 1939 fair is remembered for its optimism about the future rather than for any single exhibit. Publicity photographs of empty pavilions miss the crowds, so the book relies on candid shots of guests strolling past gardens and sculptures, with only about twelve publicity or aerial images among more than 200. Cotter concedes that no single book can capture the fair's hundreds of buildings.

New York 1939
1Creating the World of Tomorrow

Cotter describes how the 1939-40 fair began in 1935 as a plan by New York business and political leaders to profit from a Queens landfill. The chapter covers the financing, the design committee that approved every pavilion, and the engineering needed to make the site ready, from a diverted river to 10,000 trees. Captions show the design process, from concept paintings and models to blueprints for the Perisphere, and the murals and reliefs. It ends with the Administration Building.

New York 1939
2The Theme Center

The chapter explains the Theme Center, the Trylon and Perisphere, which tied the fair's themed zones into one design and helped visitors find their way. It covers the Perisphere's gypsum surface, the Democracity model seen from the Magic Carpet balconies, and the Helicline ramp, along with the sculptures that lined the approaches. Cotter's captions add dimensions, admission prices and anecdotes. The chapter ends with the Perisphere lit as a jack-o'-lantern on Halloween, when the 1939 season closed.

New York 1939
3The Transportation Zone

The chapter covers the Transportation Zone, one of the fair's most popular areas, where railways, automakers and airlines competed for visitors. It describes the Railroads pavilion with its model layout and streamlined locomotives, and the General Motors Futurama, which predicted automated highways and planned cities for 1960. Ford's Road of Tomorrow and the tyre exhibits at Goodrich and Firestone are briefly described. It notes that cars overtook trains, one prediction that came true, and ends with the Aviation Building.

New York 1939
4The Communication and Business Systems Zone

The chapter describes the Communication and Business Systems Zone, the smallest at the fair, whose exhibits Cotter calls pedestrian. Its main draws were the RCA and AT&T pavilions, where visitors saw a working television set, a tape recorder and a long-distance call. It also covers the Communications Building's murals, the statues Speed and Builders of Tomorrow, and the Star Pylon that guided crowds to the railway station. Hollywood, Cotter notes, was absent.

New York 1939
5The Food Zone

The chapter describes the Food Zone, where food and drink companies used the fair to promote convenience foods, frozen products and bottled drinks. It covers the Swift, Coca-Cola, Continental Baking, Heinz, Beech-Nut and Sealtest pavilions, along with Borden's Rotolactor and the Turkish and Swedish pavilions, both of which sat in this zone. Cotter notes tobacco and alcohol sponsors and the draw of free samples. It closes by contrasting the fair's fine restaurant meals with its many snack bars.

New York 1939
6The Government Zone

The chapter covers the Government Zone, the fair's largest collection of foreign pavilions, arranged around the Lagoon of Nations and Court of Peace. It explains how Grover Whalen secured about 60 nations by skirting the BIE rule, and why Germany had no pavilion. Cotter describes national pavilions for Japan, Italy, Poland, Czechoslovakia and France, several making political statements about the war, and the state pavilions. It ends with the nightly fountains and fireworks.

New York 1939
7The Community Interests Zone

The chapter covers the Community Interests Zone, which had two railway stations and subway access, yet which most visitors walked through. Cotter describes its uninspiring pavilions, including radiators, vacuum cleaners and a Fuller Brush display, and the more successful Gardens on Parade and Coty Charm Center. It ends with the Temple of Religion and the Hall of Special Events, which was mostly used for evening dancing.

New York 1939
8The Production and Distribution Zone

The chapter covers the Production and Distribution Zone, which Cotter says redeemed the fair's weaker zones. Its large corporate pavilions tried to link industrial products to consumers, and the chapter describes Westinghouse and its robot Elektro, the Petroleum and Electric Utilities buildings, Kodak's photo garden, U.S. Steel's dome and the Glass Center. It ends with the Carrier pavilion, where air-conditioning drew visitors on hot days.

New York 1939
9The Amusement Area

The chapter covers the Amusement Area, which is generally regarded as the fair's least successful zone, built on the softest ground beside a lake made by diverting the river. It describes Billy Rose's Aquacade, the most successful attraction, along with Frank Buck's Jungleland, the Parachute Jump, the Loop midway and Sun Valley. Many exhibits failed, and some left no record. It ends with the Water Bugs ride and the world's largest cash register.

New York 1939
10The 1940 Season

The chapter covers the 1940 season, when Harvey Dow Gibson took over from Grover Whalen, dropped the zones and leased pavilions to any paying exhibitor. Cotter describes the American Jubilee show, the Great White Way that replaced the Amusement Area, and the For Peace and Freedom theme as war spread in Europe. It notes flags at half-mast, the July 4 bombing that killed two officers, and the bankruptcy. It ends by asking whether the fair was a success.

New York 1939New York 1940
Coté, Joost. “Staging Modernity: The Semarang International Colonial Exhibition, 1914.” Journal article.Asia: central8 chapter overviews

Overview

Coté's article examines the International Colonial Exhibition held in Semarang, Dutch East Indies, in 1914. It was organised by the city's chamber of commerce rather than the colonial government, and it opened as war broke out in Europe. Coté argues that colonial exhibitions shared the didactic aims of European world's fairs but faced a particular problem: the colonised visitor was both audience and exhibit, so the pedagogy of progress could not be fixed in meaning. He reads the plan, architecture, native section, thematic layout, women's pavilion and poor attendance as expressions of a settler vision of colonial modernity. The article moves from an opening survey through chapters on the exhibition's visible and invisible meanings, its design, its ordering of visitors, the spectator, the women's pavilion and outcomes, to a conclusion.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

Southeast Asia is the whole subject: the exhibition was held in Semarang, Java, and the article concerns the Dutch East Indies throughout. Its Javanese and colonial materials are read closely in chapter 1 (visible and invisible meanings), chapter 3 (Defining a colonial utopia, on the native section, the regional houses and the temple), chapter 4 (Establishing proper order, on the native agriculture and housing displays) and chapter 7 (Outcomes, which analyses attendance of 306,795 Javanese against 370,472 Europeans). The Javanese spectator and the nationalist reading of 'tradition' are the subject of chapter 5 and the conclusion, which mentions Minangkabau architecture. No other Southeast Asian territory is discussed. The comparison with British India and Australia marks South Asia as a contrast only.

East Asia enters as foreign participation and as a political reference point. The opening section names the official Japanese and Chinese displays and reads them against the European war and suspected Japanese ambitions in the region, describing the Japanese buildings as impressive. Chapter 4 treats the Chinese pavilion, financed by Oei Tiong Ham, as the one community that escaped European control, and the women's pavilion in chapter 6 includes a Chinese girls' school. The conclusion calls the Japanese and Chinese displays 'provocative models for an autonomous Asian future'. These passages are brief and comparative: neither country is examined as an exhibitor in its own right, and no exhibition held in East Asia is discussed.

Contents

Untitled opening section (no heading in text)p. 1

Coté opens by placing the Semarang International Colonial Exhibition of 1914 within the history of world's fairs, which he presents as stages for a discourse of progress and a pedagogy of mass education. Colonial exhibitions, he argues, carried the same didactic aims as European ones but faced a particular problem: could native audiences read them correctly? Drawing on Prakash's account of British India and on Dutch participation in world exhibitions from London in 1851 to Paris in 1931, he shows how the Netherlands used such displays to present itself abroad. The Semarang exhibition, planned in 1912, postponed from 1913 and staged by the city's chamber of commerce rather than the colonial government, is described through its scale, its architecture, its electric lighting and the foreign pavilions of Japan, China and two Australian states. Coté concludes that the exhibition, opening as war began in Europe, was a settler-led showcase whose meanings could not be fixed, and that it marked the beginning of the end of the imperial future it celebrated.

Semarang 1914
The colonial exhibition of Semarang: visible and invisible meaningsp. 5

Coté argues that the Semarang exhibition, though framed as a display of colonial achievement, was also meant to model a harmonious future society that would win over both the settler community and the Javanese urban population. He frames this through the idea of colonial modernity, which combined a reformist faith in progress with tighter surveillance of racial boundaries. Drawing on Stoler and Mrazek, he shows how the discourse of urban reform gave colonial officials a neutral-seeming, scientific language for regulating native life in towns. He then sets the exhibition within the politics of 1914, when the Aceh war had only just ended, the colonial bureaucracy was still being built and nationalist demands were beginning to appear. Coté concludes that the organisers saw the exhibition as a new colonial beginning and a blueprint for a future Indies society, but that it was also, unknown to them, the start of the end of the future it celebrated, and that gaps between plan, layout and visitors already revealed disagreement.

Semarang 1914
Educating the spectatorp. 11
Defining a colonial utopiap. 11

Coté turns to the architecture and layout of the Semarang exhibition, using the 1920 account of its designer, Henry Maclaine Pont, as his main evidence. The entrance arch, the electric lighting and the tram and road links announced a colonial modernity, while reconstructed regional houses set beside them gave European-ness its contrast. Coté places these native displays within a long European habit of exhibiting villages and live craftsmen, but argues that in a colony the native was also meant to be a member of the audience. Maclaine Pont's plan, with Western buildings in plain view, eastern forms hidden along a winding path and a temple overlooking all, was a utopian vision of separate but connected communities. The plan was never fully carried out, for financial reasons, which left the native section to read as orientalist nostalgia. He concludes that a utopia laid out in a tropical landscape could not be felt through its buildings alone, however carefully reconstructed.

Semarang 1914
Establishing proper orderp. 17

Coté examines how the Semarang exhibition was ordered to educate visitors, though official accounts never named pedagogy. Organised by theme and labelled throughout, its layout worked like a school textbook. The strongest displays were government departments and European agriculture, including a pair of sugar factory models, one from the 1840s and one modern. In the native section, a journalist's guide read regional buildings and crafts as an evolutionary sequence, while native agriculture and model housing drew on the health reformer Tillema's warnings about disease. The live kampung tukang is read as an economic display, and the Chinese pavilion, financed by Oei Tiong Ham, as the one community that escaped European control. Coté concludes that the exhibition's order expressed a settler vision of progress in which each community had a designated place.

Semarang 1914
The spectatorp. 26

Coté asks whether the native spectator would have recognised the invitation to take part in colonial modernity, and argues that the exhibition's evolutionary message was hard to read against. He shows that the exhibition was a private Semarang initiative without government backing, and that its European audience, especially the Eurasian working class, was divided by economic and political grievances. The chapter concludes that settler progressives on municipal councils could make the exhibition stand for settler nationalism as readily as for colonial success.

Semarang 1914
Women and the Semarang International Colonial Exhibitionp. 28

Coté treats the women's pavilion as the one place where colonial and indigenous interests seemed to meet. The European section reused exhibits from the Amsterdam exhibition De Vrouw 1813-1913, and the pavilion also honoured Kartini and the teacher Dewi Sartika and included a Chinese girls' school. Coté shows, however, that the souvenir commentary by Maria Kooy-van Zeggelen treated indigenous women as needing awakening by Western ideas, so that progressivism shaped even this display.

Semarang 1914
Outcomesp. 30

Coté weighs why the Semarang exhibition failed: 306,795 Javanese visitors against 370,472 Europeans, and a financial loss. He sets out four explanations: that it was too modern, that rumours of danger scared people away, that the native was too thrifty after official warnings, and, most likely, that growing anti-colonial opposition kept the masses out. He concludes that visitors were mainly the better off and educated, the group the object lesson was meant for.

Semarang 1914
Conclusionp. 34

Coté concludes that the colonial exhibition, meant to reinforce colonial order, introduced ambiguities unlike those of European exhibitions, because the native was a participant as well as an object. He identifies two ways it could feed nationalism: by showing the extent and diversity of the colonised population, and by defining native tradition in ways that anti-colonial movements could use. He argues that the pedagogic project depended on the viewer's involvement, so the educated Javanese visitor could consume the knowledge without accepting the colonial vision.

Semarang 1914

Della Coletta, Cristina. World’s Fairs Italian-Style: The Great Expositions in Turin and Their Narratives, 1860–1915. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2006.Asia: substantial7 chapter overviews

Overview

This book argues that Italy's exhibitions between 1860 and 1915 were tools of nation building rather than imitations of French and British fairs. Della Coletta reads the fairs as consensus-making machines that repeated ideas about national identity, imperial competition and progress, while their counter-narratives survived as silences and contradictions. Turin, which sponsored more national and international fairs than any other Italian city, is the main case: chapters cover the Turin fairs from 1850 to 1911, including 1911, which marked fifty years of unity. Two chapters then read texts that carry exposition habits into literature, Emilio Salgari's adventure novels and Guido Gozzano's writing on India and the 1911 fair. An introduction and a conclusion frame the argument.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are present but not central. Their fullest treatment is chapter 3, Emilio Salgari: Writing Exposition Style, where the Malay archipelago, Borneo and Siam supply the settings and ethnic inventories of the jungle novels, and Sandokan's Borneo kingdom, destroyed by British and Dutch allies of the sultan, is read against Garibaldi's campaigns. Here the concern is fiction and the European ranking of peoples, not exhibitions. Chapter 1 mentions a Chinese-pagoda kiosk at the 1884 Turin fair. Chapter 2, Turin 1911, has the most exhibition material: Pourtauborde's Oriental fairground, which evoked China, Siam, Japan and Indochina as 'Oriental peoples'; the Filipino villages at the 1904 Saint Louis fair, cited as a model for 'native' displays; and Barzini's Beijing-to-Paris race reports, read as a fair-like image of a motionless East. Chapter 4 touches Japan only through war photographs in illustrated magazines.

Asia appears as a theatre of display and fiction, never as exhibitor: no Asian state, commissioner or merchant is discussed, no fair held in Asia is considered, and Asian observers barely appear. South Asia gets much more space, through Gozzano's India letters in chapter 4, which lie outside this question. The colonial sections of Turin 1911 concentrate on Eritrea and Somalia, so Southeast Asia is reduced to a list.

Contents

Acknowledgmentsp. ix

Della Coletta thanks the colleagues and readers who commented on the manuscript, the archives in Rome and Turin that supplied materials on Italian fairs, and the University of Virginia for fellowships and image-reproduction funds. The author credits the University of Toronto Press editors, notes that two sections of chapter 4 first appeared in earlier journal and volume versions, and thanks family members for their support.

Introduction: The Spectacle of Inventing a Nation: World’s Fairs and Their Narratives in Italy, 1860–1915p. 3

Della Coletta argues that Italy's exhibitions between 1860 and 1915 were active tools of nation building rather than imitations of French and British fairs, and that they carried their own contradictions. The introduction reads expositions as a 'signifying practice' combining realist and spectacular codes, drawing on Said's account of culture and on critiques of binary imperial thinking. Its main case is Turin, the city that sponsored more national and international fairs than any other in Italy. Turin 1911 tried to give the Turin baroque a national meaning and to present Italy's colonial achievements, but the revival stayed regional and the colonial displays revealed dependence on France and Britain. The introduction then previews the later chapters: Emilio Salgari's jungle novels, read against Dumas's memoirs of Garibaldi, and Guido Gozzano's letters from India and exposition pieces. Della Coletta concludes that these hybrid narratives undercut the fairs' binary logic, and that Gozzano's writing reflects a shift toward unstable forms of knowledge.

Turin 1911
1Prologues to World’s Fairs: National Expositions and Nation Building in Turinp. 15

Della Coletta argues that Turin's decline after 1864, when it lost the capital to Florence and then Rome, has been overstated. The city kept presenting itself as the moral and industrial core of Italy, and it used national expositions to do so. The chapter traces this through the Turin fairs of 1850, 1858 and especially 1884, held in the Valentino park, whose pleasure gardens, exotic kiosks, toboggans and electric illumination are read as tools for turning industrial display into popular amusement. Strikes and revolts at the Palermo, Milan and Turin fairs of 1891 to 1898 show the limits of that consensus. The chapter also reads De Amicis's guide Torino 1880 and Manzotti's ballet Excelsior as versions of the same message. The argument is that fairs fused nationalism, bourgeois consensus and a Western story of progress. The chapter ends by setting Turin's rivalry with Rome against the wider nation-building programme of the expositions.

Turin 1884Turin 1898Milan 1881
2Turin 1911: The ‘Fabulous Exposition’p. 79

Della Coletta argues that the 1911 Turin exposition, staged to mark fifty years of Italian unity, combined industrial display with propaganda for the nation, a national architectural style and colonial expansion. The chapter starts with the architecture, where the organizers adopted the Turin baroque of Juvarra as the fair's overall style and the Rome exhibition of the same year used a classical revival instead. It then turns to the colonial displays for Eritrea and Somalia, the Somali village, and the 'Oriental' fairground that the Frenchman Pourtauborde laid out across the Po. Official magazines, Touring Club guides, press coverage of Scipione Borghese's Peking-to-Paris motor race and of Luigi Amedeo's polar expedition supply further evidence. The argument is that the fair prepared public consent for the war on Turkey, declared on 30 September 1911 while it was open, and that the Turin baroque never became a shared national symbol. The chapter ends by calling Turin 1911 the last act of the fairs' drama of progress.

Turin 1911
3Emilio Salgari: Writing Exposition Stylep. 123

Della Coletta reads Emilio Salgari's popular adventure novels as 'exposition narratives', texts that carry the encyclopedic and classifying habits of the world's fairs into fiction. The chapter opens with the 1883 publicity stunt that launched Sandokan, the Malayan Tiger, and shows how Salgari assembled his jungle cycle from borrowed travel and scientific passages taken from periodicals and illustrated volumes. It then examines the ethnic inventories in I pirati della Malesia and Le pantere di Algeri, which rank peoples against a white European baseline. Sandokan's exoticism, the chapter argues, is only skin-deep: he is a Risorgimento hero modelled on Garibaldi as Dumas presented him in the Memoirs of Garibaldi, and the novels' anti-British plots leave their colonial stance unresolved. The final section turns to Le meraviglie del Duemila, a 1907 novel set in a technocratic New York of 2003, where Della Coletta pits the natural sublime against the technological sublime and reads the protagonists' madness and the fall of the utopia as a victory for entropy. The chapter concludes that Salgari's faith in science heralds no rebirth.

4Guido Gozzano’s Imperial Ambiguitiesp. 176

Della Coletta reads Guido Gozzano's Indian letters against the single volume that Borgese assembled from them as Verso la cuna del mondo (1917), and against the newspapers and magazines where they first appeared. She argues that Gozzano's travel writing borrows its method from the World's Fair displays and illustrated periodicals of the time: it piles up catalogues of visual contrasts and leaves Western assumptions intact. The evidence is close reading of particular sketches: the harbour of Bombay as a 'compendium of the world', the temples of Elephanta and Madura, a Devadasi's dance, the Parsee Towers of Silence, the 1857 Cawnpore massacre, and Goa, where parody of Camoens and a borrowed Heredia sonnet turn the epic into elegy. Gozzano's essays on the 1911 Turin exposition, including his two readings of Dürer's Melancholia, show the same ambivalence towards spectacle. The chapter ends with Agra and Hyderabad, where Gozzano's ideal of an art cut off from profit turns out to depend on British grain shipments, so that aesthetics and the market cannot be kept apart.

Turin 1911
Conclusionp. 269

Della Coletta closes the book by arguing that World's Fairs were consensus-making machines that repeated a few ideas about national identity, imperial competition and progress, while their counter-narratives survived as disruptive silences and contradictions. Drawing on Said, she claims the book shows these rival narratives were part of the imperial story itself rather than outside it. The Italian case, with its belated and hybrid nation-making, is presented as especially revealing of this tension.

Notesp. 273

Indexp. 339
Denton, Kirk A. Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2014.Asia: central14 chapter overviews

Overview

Denton's Exhibiting the Past surveys how museums and memorial sites in the People's Republic of China represent the national past, from dynastic times onward. The introduction sets out a narratological method that reads exhibits as visual stories and compares Chinese museums with memory museums elsewhere. The thirteen chapters are organised by museum type rather than by theme: premodern history, the Museum of the Chinese Revolution, revolutionary history under the market, martyrs' memorials, military museums, sites of Japanese atrocity, memorial halls for model heroes and leaders, ethnographic museums and theme parks, red tourism, and municipal urban planning halls. Denton argues that state museums remain politically directed while adapting to market reform, nationalism and the decline of socialism. The conclusion ties these displays to neoliberal narratives of past, present and future.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the book's whole subject, because every chapter treats museums and memorial sites in the PRC, so its coverage is central. The concern is how China displays its own past, not how Asian states or peoples take part in international exhibitions. Chapter 6 (Heroic Resistance and Victims of Atrocity) is the most concentrated treatment of another East Asian country: Japan is the aggressor in the War of Resistance Memorial Hall at Wanping, the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall and the Unit 731 Museum in Harbin. Chapter 1 (National Origins and Local Identity) treats Korea through the contested kingdom of Koguryo/Gaojuli. Taiwan and Hong Kong recur in chapters 1, 3, 5 and 6, as partners in a shared memory of resistance or as commercial context.

Exhibitions in Asia and Asian visitors appear mainly in chapter 2, on the 1929 West Lake Exposition in Hangzhou, which the book says drew some one thousand foreign visitors, among them from Japan, Korea and Indonesia. Southeast Asia is slight. Vietnam appears as a comparison in chapter 2, through Hanoi's revolution museum, and in chapter 9, through its ethnic museum, while Indonesia, Thailand and Burma are cited only in a note to chapter 5 on military museums. No Southeast Asian pavilions, displays or peoples on show are discussed.

Contents

Preface and Acknowledgmentsp. vii

Denton's preface explains how a 1999 conference paper on revolutionary history paintings in the Museum of the Chinese Revolution in Beijing led the author from Republican-era literary studies into museum studies. It thanks the funders and institutions that supported research trips to China, Taiwan and Hong Kong, along with the Chinese museums and scholars who met the author, and the press editor and reviewers. It also lists where earlier articles were reprinted, and closes with a dedication to family.

Introductionp. 1

Denton opens with the Road to Revival exhibition, which reopened the National Museum of China in 2011 and presents modern Chinese history as a party-led story of national humiliation and revival. Alongside it, an Enlightenment art show and luxury-brand displays for Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari illustrate the several faces of postsocialist China. Denton argues that state museums and memorial sites remain politically directed, yet that official memory has adapted to market reform, nationalism and the decline of socialism. Comparing China with memory museums in South Africa, Latin America, Korea, Taiwan and post-Soviet Europe, the introduction sets out a narratological method that reads exhibits as visual stories. It closes with a history of Chinese museums, from imperial collections and the Nantong Museum through the Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution and the post-1989 boom, and explains why the chapters are organized by museum type rather than by theme.

Beijing 2011
1National Origins and Local Identity: Museums of Premodern Historyp. 27

Denton argues that museums of premodern history, which display China's prehistoric and dynastic past, help invent a national origin for the modern state. Drawing on Hobsbawm's idea of the invention of tradition, the chapter shows how archaeology supplies these museums with artifacts and how contested claims to ancient sites, such as Koguryo/Gaojuli, bind a nation to its territory. It then traces how the Marxist sequence of primitive, slave and feudal society shaped the Museum of Chinese History, from its 1961 building on Tiananmen Square through the Cultural Revolution to the dynastic exhibit of the late 1990s and the 2011 Ancient China hall, which stresses cultural continuity and imperial glory. The second half turns to local culture museums, including those for Liangzhu, Sanxingdui, the Zhejiang Provincial Museum and the Western Han King of Nanyue in Guangzhou, which present regional origins that fit a plural, multiethnic nation. Denton concludes that these museums respond to nationalism and globalization, offering a nostalgia for a local identity that seems untouched by the state.

Beijing 1961Beijing 2011
2Exhibiting the Revolution: The Museum of the Chinese Revolutionp. 45

Denton traces how the Museum of the Chinese Revolution in Beijing, the state's most official exhibition of party history, has represented the revolution since the 1920s. The chapter starts with the Nationalist Revolutionary Memorial Hall at the 1929 West Lake Exposition in Hangzhou, and argues that its party-led narrative of progress, its martyrs and its father figure of the revolution reappear in the Communist museum. It then follows the exhibits from the 1961 History of the Chinese Revolution, shaped by factional fights over Mao's place, through the Cultural Revolution merger and the post-Mao revisions of 1979 and 1990, to the Modern China hall of 1996 and Road to Revival in 2011. Denton shows how each version cut text, added art and dioramas, and retreated from Mao while keeping the telos of the party's victory. The chapter closes by arguing that the final exhibit elides the famine, the Cultural Revolution and Tiananmen, and presents modernization as the end point of revolutionary history.

Hangzhou 1929Beijing 1961Beijing 1990Beijing 1996Beijing 2011
3Commodification and Nostalgia: Revolutionary History in the Era of the Market Economyp. 75

Denton examines how revolutionary history museums in China have adapted to the market economy since the 1990s, when officials and scholars judged them to be in crisis and the revolution had come to seem a fading tradition. The chapter works through three responses. At the Red Crag Revolutionary Memorial Hall in Chongqing, a popular, diorama-rich exhibit sits beside a conventional one on the CCP Southern Bureau, and Denton argues that the popular display turns revolutionary history into a commodity for red tourism. The Nanjing Presidential Palace museum presents Republican-era capitalism and the Nanjing decade positively, and drops class from its narrative. The Shanghai Municipal History Museum, moved to Pudong, offers a nostalgic, model-based image of the commercial old city that sets the revolution aside altogether. Denton concludes that these museums are changing in content and form, but that their nostalgia and their downplaying of class tie them to the neoliberal ideology of the present.

4Martyrdom and Memory: Monuments, Memorials, and Museums for Dead Heroesp. 95

Denton examines the state's use of martyrs in museums and memorial parks, and argues that the post-Mao party has kept the cult of revolutionary martyrdom alive even as the market economy has made martyrs seem remote. The chapter first traces a longer history, from the loyal martyrs of imperial China and the Yue Fei shrine in Hangzhou to the commemoration of anti-Manchu and Republican dead, to show that the modern cult has older roots. It then turns to the Mao-era cult, with its Martyrs Memorial Festival and iconic women such as Zhao Yiman, and to two post-1989 sites. The Longhua Martyrs Memorial Park in Shanghai has a glass pyramid, execution-ground ruins and online flower-giving. The Yuhuatai Martyrs Park in Nanjing is framed by a call to pursue modernization. Denton concludes that market ideology increasingly absorbs martyrs into a generalized spirit of sacrifice for development, yet these sites keep alive a leftist memory that the nostalgic Shanghai museum has erased.

5Martial Glory and the Power of the State: Military Museumsp. 116

Denton examines the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution in Beijing, the most official of China's state military museums, and argues that it ties the present authoritarian state to a long martial tradition. The chapter first sketches a Chinese culture of war, from Qing displays of victories to Liang Qichao's call for martial spirit and Mao-era militarization. It then traces the museum's history from its founding as one of the Ten Great Structures to its post-Mao revisions, which added imperial military exhibits in 1988 and dropped much of the Maoist class-struggle emphasis. Denton focuses on the entrance hall with its statue of Mao, the Ancient Warfare exhibit that links Sunzi and imperial unification to revolutionary legitimacy, and the contemporary PLA hall, which avoids the army's role in 1989. The museum presents glory and heroic sacrifice, with little attention to the suffering of soldiers. Denton concludes that it presents strong state power as the norm in Chinese history, which justifies the CCP's authoritarian rule.

6Heroic Resistance and Victims of Atrocity: Negotiating the Memory of Japanese Imperialismp. 133

Denton examines how museums of the Japanese occupation in the PRC have moved from a heroic story of resistance toward one of victimization, and argues that this shift serves nationalist and economic aims. The chapter analyses three post-Mao sites. The Memorial Hall of the War of Resistance in Wanping moves between a chronological overview, dioramas of atrocity and a martyrs hall, and its 2005 revision stresses national confidence. The Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall, designed by Qi Kang, uses a bleak cinderblock aesthetic, mother-and-child sculptures and the figure of 300,000 dead. The Unit 731 Museum in Harbin relies on authentic ruins and artifacts rather than spectacle. Denton links these shifts to the decline of class-struggle narratives, to popular culture and to Holocaust memorial precedents. The chapter concludes that the museums use shared suffering to channel resentment toward Japan, though the victim narrative sits uneasily with the CCP's heroic resistance narrative.

7Heroic Models and Exemplary Leaders: Memorial Hallsp. 153

Denton examines post-Mao memorial halls devoted to heroic models and exemplary leaders, arguing that they carry a strong Confucian moralism centred on the individual's duty to the nation rather than on the family-state relationship. The chapter opens with Ha Jin's poem about a dead soldier who still venerates Mao, and uses it to frame the move from Maoist political sacrifice to a market-era ethic of moderation and loyalty. Its main case is the Lei Feng Memorial Hall in Fushun, where Denton shows how exhibits recast the soldier as a model of study and thrift, and how revisionist books and blogs on his staged photographs and diary push against that image. The chapter then turns to the Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping halls in Huai'an and Guang'an, which present the leaders as humane, approachable and morally upright. It concludes that these sites offer the party a benign face, and wonders whether citizens, now online and aware of corruption, still accept that mythology.

Fushun 1965Huai'an 1992Guang'an 2004
8Literary Politics and Cultural Heritage: Modern Literature Museumsp. 177

Denton examines literary museums in the PRC, arguing that they use writers to build a canon of modern Chinese literature and a sense of national identity. The chapter opens with a scene from the 1964 film Stage Sisters, in which a woodblock print of a Lu Xun character raises a woman's political consciousness, and then turns to Lu Xun, the most heavily commemorated writer. Denton compares the Lu Xun memorial halls in Shanghai, Beijing and Shaoxing, showing how each stresses a different phase of his life, and then focuses on Shaoxing, where a redeveloped Lu Xun Old Home District and the Lu Village theme park recast him as a native son and tourist attraction, with nostalgia replacing his iconoclasm. The second half analyses the Modern Literature Museum in Beijing, opened in 2001, which privileges May Fourth realists and leftist writers, leaves the Cultural Revolution unrepresented, and was founded to restore the memory of Republican-era writers. The chapter concludes that the museums keep a socially critical May Fourth tradition on display, but that nostalgia and the rhetoric of personal growth in the market era blunt its edge.

Shaoxing 2003Beijing 2001
9Ethnic Minorities and the Construction of National Identity: Ethnographic Museumsp. 199

Denton examines how museums and theme parks in the PRC display China's ethnic minorities, arguing that the displays build a unified nation in which difference is shown but subordinated to a shared political ideology. The chapter begins with the critique of Western ethnographic museums and the Soviet model that China borrowed, then traces the Chinese tradition of classifying non-Han peoples back to the Qing. It describes the Nationalities Culture Palace in Beijing, now partly given over to commerce, and the Yunnan Museum of Nationalities, where political discourse frames the exhibits. Its central case is the Chinese Nationalities Museum and Ethnic Culture Park in Beijing, a for-profit re-creation of minority villages that reads as a miniature nation, and the chapter ends with the Suojia Miao ecomuseum in Guizhou, whose staged performances show how living heritage becomes a tourist display. Denton concludes that ecomuseums are no more authentic than the state's versions, since living traditions cannot be protected from modernization.

Beijing 1994Kunming 1995
10Revolutionary Memory and National Landscape: Red Tourismp. 214

Denton asks why the PRC state has promoted revolutionary tourism since 2004 and how far visitors accept its aims. The chapter argues that red tourism is a collective, ritualised and commodified form of pilgrimage that ties a revolutionary narrative to particular landscapes, with the state using it for patriotic education, rural development and urban branding. Denton first sketches a history of revolutionary and premodern tourism, then examines three sites: Jinggangshan, where Mao's poems and popular songs filter the experience; the Hunan 'golden triangle' of Shaoshan, Huaminglou and Peng Dehuai's memorial, where Liu Shaoqi is recast in Confucian terms; and Xibaipo, where Hu Jintao's appropriation of Mao's 'two duties' is traced. Its evidence includes tour-group practices, wreath-laying, costumed photographs and the documentary New Socialist Climax. The conclusion is that red tourism keeps the revolution safely in a commodified past, where it cannot be turned against the present.

Shaoshan 1964Xibaipo 1978Huaminglou 1988
11Museums of the Future: Municipal Urban Planning Exhibition Hallsp. 243

Denton asks how the urban planning exhibition halls that have spread through Chinese cities since the late 1990s present the future. The argument is that their utopian images of modern cities serve the market-reform programme of the Chinese Communist Party, replacing the Maoist promise of socialist happiness with a neoliberal one. The evidence is three halls. Shanghai's has a large city model, a golden-future sculpture and a nostalgic 1930s street. Suzhou's stresses literati heritage and the city's bid for World Heritage status. Chongqing's, under Chaotianmen Plaza, shows skyscrapers and empty streets. Beijing, Nantong and the Dalian museum linked to Bo Xilai are cited for comparison. Throughout, models, lighting and video invite visitors to identify with urban growth, while displays omit displaced residents, migrant workers and factories. Denton concludes that the halls project a collective fantasy of development that links to individual dreams of success.

Conclusionp. 265

Denton's conclusion begins with Xi Jinping's 2012 'China Dream' speech, urging looking back, examining the present and gazing forward. Denton argues that the book's museums and its urban planning halls share one logic: past, present and future are intertwined and filtered through present-day neoliberal agendas. It lists the narratives now on offer, from nostalgic modernization to red tourism. It closes by noting that most visitors accept prevailing narratives because their own dreams are bound up with them.
