Filipová, Marta, ed. Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840–1940: Great Exhibitions in the Margins. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015.Asia: substantial16 chapter overviews

Overview

The volume, edited by Marta Filipová, gathers fifteen chapters on international exhibitions held in the regional and provincial margins of Europe, the Americas, Asia and Australia between 1840 and 1940. Its argument is that these smaller events were not copies of London or Paris but adapted the medium to local agendas such as regional identity, municipal promotion, colonial and national self-presentation, linking local modernities to a global one. The case studies range from Budapest, Barcelona, Berlin and Bohemia to Wolverhampton, Rio de Janeiro, Ghent, London and Edinburgh, Dunedin, Launceston, Nancy, Helsinki, Naples and Osaka. The chapters are grouped in five parts: exhibition as a concept, constructing identities, historicity and modernity, art and design exhibited, and international ambitions.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia receive substantial attention, but it is concentrated in one chapter. Chapter 15, by Jeffer Daykin, on the 1903 Osaka Exposition, is the only study of an Asian host, and treats Japan as host, exhibitor and colonial power. Its Formosan section presented Taiwan as a foil that made Japan the civilised spectator, while the Jinrui Kan concession outside the grounds displayed live Chinese, Korean and Okinawan people, alongside Malayan and Javanese people among others. Chinese and Korean protests, backed by official pressure, led to the removal of the Chinese and Korean exhibits. Daykin also notes the Netherlands-India section's bilingual catalogue.

Elsewhere the coverage is occasional. Muñoz Torreblanca (chapter 2, Barcelona 1888) notes a Tagalog cigarette-making group in a tobacco company pavilion and a thin Spanish colonial display that lacked the Philippine material shown at Madrid in 1887; the Chinese, Japanese and Turkish presence there was token. Depelchin (chapter 8, Ghent 1913) places a Philippine village on the edge of 'Old Flanders' and Japan among the international hall's participants. Rezende (chapter 7, Rio 1922) lists Japan among thirteen nations with pavilions and a Japan Day, alongside Japanese immigrants in Brazil. Filipová (chapter 6, Wolverhampton) notes Japanese arts and crafts in 1902, and Japanese enamels and Chinese weapons in the 1884 display. Albert (chapter 5, Bucharest 1906) mentions only a reproduction of Port Arthur. Siam, Indochina, Burma and Borneo do not appear in the passages.

Introduction: The Margins of Exhibitions and Exhibitions StudiesMarta Filipováp. 1

Filipová argues that exhibitions held in the regional and provincial margins of Europe, the Americas, Asia and Australia were not simply copies of London or Paris, but adapted the medium to local agendas such as regional identity, municipal promotion and nation-building. The introduction opens with George Wallis's report on the New York Exhibition of 1853, which compares American and European manufactures, to show how early the exhibition became a vehicle for national comparison. It then maps the volume's sections, on exhibition as a concept, constructing identities, historicity and modernity, art and design, and international ambitions, and their case studies, from Budapest and Barcelona to Wolverhampton, Dunedin, Osaka and Rio de Janeiro. It extends the period beyond the conventional 1851 to 1939 frame, and concludes that marginal exhibitions show how universal values were combined with regional and national agendas, linking local modernities to a global one.

Rio de Janeiro 1922Ghent 1913Wolverhampton 1869Wolverhampton 1902Dunedin 1865Dunedin 1889Launceston 1891Nancy 1909Helsinki 1876Naples 1938Osaka 1903Barcelona 1888Berlin 1844Budapest 1896
Exhibition as a Conceptp. 21
1A Capital in the Margins: Concepts for a Budapest Universal Exhibition between 1867 and 1917Miklós Székelyp. 23

Székely argues that the proposals for a universal exhibition in Budapest between 1867 and 1917 show how a semi-sovereign state presented itself at home and abroad. Within the Dual Monarchy Hungary had its own government but no independent foreign or military policy, so its exhibitions asserted a 'sovereign' and 'Hungarian' identity through pavilion architecture, the revival of historic styles and vernacular art, and commemoration. The chapter follows three planning efforts: Szilárd Blána's utopian permanent exhibition of 1874, Count Jenő Zichy's proposal to mark the 1896 Millennium with a universal exhibition, and Leo Lánczy's 1911 scheme for 1917, the fiftieth anniversary of Franz Joseph's coronation. Its evidence comes from Hungarian displays at Paris in 1867 and 1900, the forestry pavilion and ethnographic village at Vienna in 1873, and the Turin pavilion of 1911. Székely concludes that none of the Budapest universal exhibitions was realised, and that the plans show a modernising nation looking to its glorious past while displaying its present achievements abroad.

Budapest 1896Budapest 1917Vienna 1873Paris 1867Paris 1900Turin 1911
2Barcelona’s Universal Exhibition of 1888: An Atypical Case of a Great ExhibitionMarina Muñoz Torreblancap. 45

Muñoz Torreblanca asks whether the Barcelona Universal Exhibition of 1888 belongs with the great exhibitions of Paris and London, or was a set of good intentions of little lasting significance. Muñoz Torreblanca first sets out the institutional background, noting that exhibitions before the 1928 Paris convention had no shared regulatory framework and that terms such as 'universal' and 'international' were often used as synonyms. The planning story runs from Spain's unrealised national exhibition projects to Eugenio Serrano de Casanova's private proposal, which the city council took over, and the evidence includes the Ciutadella site, the Palace of Industry, the magic fountain and captive balloon, the rejected tower projects, and a thin colonial display that the chapter ascribes to Spain's weakening colonial position. It also compares numbers, with about 12,000 exhibitors and just over two million visitors set against London in 1851 and Paris in 1867. The chapter concludes that the exhibition was more a regional event promoting Catalonia than a universal one, though its most lasting effect was the transformation of Barcelona itself.

Barcelona 1888
3A Marginal Exhibition? The All-German Exhibition in Berlin, 1844John R. Davisp. 69

Davis argues that the All-German Exhibition held in Berlin in 1844, which falls outside the standard canon that begins with the Great Exhibition of 1851, deserves study in its own right. The chapter sets out the German background of 39 sovereign states after 1815 and the Zollverein customs union of 1834, which shaped the exhibition's aims of technical education and market integration. It then traces how Bavarian proposals and the Mainz exhibition of 1842 pushed Prussia to host the event, the first to apply to all German states and the source of procedures for later Customs Union exhibitions. Its evidence comes from archives in Berlin and Munich, the official report, and the display in the Zeughaus, whose militaristic setting, late arrivals and aesthetic arrangement drew criticism at home. Davis concludes that the exhibition was a step between local and international forms, that it influenced the 1851 London exhibition and fostered later national-liberal networks, and that it has received too little historical attention.

Berlin 1844Mainz 1842
Constructing Identitiesp. 89
4‘Witness to the Momentous Significance of German Labour in Bohemia’: Exhibitions in the German-Speaking Regions of Bohemia before the First World WarTomáš Okurkap. 91

Okurka asks how German-speaking regions of Bohemia used regional exhibitions between the 1890s and the First World War to make political claims. Early exhibitions in the 1870s and 1880s were neutral trade and agricultural shows, but the Czech Jubilee Provincial Exhibition in Prague in 1891, which most German producers boycotted, prompted German organizers to stress German identity in their titles, as at Most in 1898. The core case is the German-Bohemian Exhibition in Liberec in 1906, which Okurka reconstructs from its invitations, its enormous grounds, its architecture and the exclusion of Czech exhibitors. He shows how the town's leaders used it to present Bohemian Germans as a unified economic force and to argue for a separate German territory, while the Czech and German press read it in sharply opposed ways. Attendance of about 1.27 million was a record for German exhibitions in Bohemia, but it fell short of the organizers' hopes and left a deficit of roughly half a million crowns. The conclusion argues that these exhibitions were not mirrors of the Czech-German conflict but active participants in it.

Prague 1891Most 1898Liberec 1906
5The Nation for Itself: The 1896 Hungarian Millennium and the 1906 Romanian National General ExhibitionSamuel D. Albertp. 113

Albert compares two smaller national exhibitions that sit at the margins of the great world's fairs: the Hungarian Millennium Exhibition in Budapest in 1896 and the Romanian National General Exhibition in Bucharest in 1906. He argues that these events were aimed deliberately at national or regional audiences, and that this self-limitation, together with a historiography built on the large fairs, has kept them marginal. In Budapest the Historical Exhibition presented a thousand years of Magyar history in reconstructed period buildings, and the Ethnographic Village included houses of non-Magyar groups under Hungarian rule, subsumed into a Hungarian state identity. The Ős-Budavára amusement area turned three centuries of Ottoman and Habsburg rule into entertainment. Bucharest was built on virgin ground, centred on King Carol I and his link to Trajan, and its pavilions and medals claimed populations outside the kingdom. Albert concludes that the Hungarian exhibition looked inward and the Romanian outward, but that in both cases the nation was the chief beneficiary.

Budapest 1896Bucharest 1906
6The Forefront of English Commercial Centres: Wolverhampton’s Exhibitions of 1869 and 1902Marta Filipováp. 137

Filipová asks what two exhibitions held in Wolverhampton, a town in the Black Country with a poor reputation, were meant to achieve. The South Staffordshire Exhibition of 1869 at Molineux House drew about 220,000 visitors and displayed local goods such as locks, iron, engines and coal, with an art section that mixed fine art and industrial objects. The Wolverhampton Arts and Industrial Exhibition of 1902, inspired by Glasgow's exhibition of 1901, had purpose-built halls, a Canadian pavilion and a separate fine art section in the new Art Gallery, but it lost about 30,000 pounds and drew few visitors from outside the region. Filipová reads both against the region's industrial identity, its rivalry with Birmingham and the decline of local industry by 1902. A smaller show in 1884 is discussed as the event that gave the Art Gallery its collection. She concludes that the events aimed at local education and civic pride, and that their limited reach reflected economic change and the exhibition fatigue of the period.

Wolverhampton 1869Wolverhampton 1884Wolverhampton 1902
Historicity and Modernityp. 161
7Nature and the Brazilian State at the Independence Centennial International Exhibition in Rio de Janeiro, 1922Livia Rezendep. 163

Rezende examines the Independence Centennial International Exhibition held in Rio de Janeiro in 1922, the first international exhibition on Brazilian soil. She places it within a republican government's need for foreign investment and public consent after the First World War, and within the urban reforms that Mayor Carlos Sampaio carried out in the name of sanitation. The central case is the razing of the Morro do Castelo, whose earth was used to fill the bay for the exhibition site, a process illustrated magazines presented as progress. Rezende then turns to the national section, especially the Pavilion of Statistics and the Festivities Palace, which were designed to teach a largely illiterate public how Brazil had advanced under the republic, and whose pantheon of heroes passed over the monarchy. A further section sets the amusements against the foreign warships in Guanabara Bay, using a journalist's remark about two exhibitions, to show the contradictions of modernity. The conclusion argues that the exhibition made the nation itself an object for public appreciation.

Rio de Janeiro 1922
8The Ghent Universal and International Exhibition of 1913: Reconciling Historicism, Modernity and ExoticismDavy Depelchinp. 183

Depelchin asks why the Ghent exhibition of 1913, which was formally universal and international, gave so little prominence to the exotic, which usually featured so strongly in universal exhibitions. He places Ghent within Belgium's run of international exhibitions from Antwerp in 1885 to Ghent itself, and within the city's need to define itself through local history. The chapter then describes the fairground: the white Beaux-Arts Court of Honour, the 'Old Flanders' and 'Modern Village' sections that promoted architectural regionalism, and the Belgian city pavilions in historical styles. Its central case is the colonial and non-Western pavilions. Persia had the only prominent orientalist building on the Avenue of Nations, the Congo pavilion took a hybrid style, and the Moroccan, Tunisian and Algerian pavilions were pushed into a wooded area and presented as trading showcases. The French colonial displays were more commercial than picturesque. Depelchin concludes that the organizers' emphasis on local history suppressed exoticism, and that Ghent reshaped the universal exhibition to fit local ambitions.

Ghent 1913
9Old London, Old Edinburgh: Constructing Historic CitiesWilson Smithp. 203

Smith examines the 'historic city', a reconstruction of a host city's old streets built inside a modern exhibition. He takes two examples: Old London, shown at South Kensington from 1884 to 1886, and Old Edinburgh, at the Edinburgh International Exhibition of 1886. Old London, designed by the antiquarian architect George Birch, reproduced about 25 demolished buildings, aged with distressed finishes, and was funded by the City of London Corporation and the Livery Companies. Smith argues it defended the Livery Companies at a time when their wealth was under attack, and that visitors were asked to suspend disbelief. Old Edinburgh, by Sydney Mitchell, was a self-funding venture: its facades hid rented shops staffed by costumed saleswomen, and its handbook told Scottish history from a Liberal and Presbyterian viewpoint. Smith ends with three paradoxes: the backward-looking attraction inside an exhibition of progress, a site-specific type that nonetheless spread between fairs, and the tension between scholarly authenticity and commerce. The chapter concludes that each exhibit told its host city's own story, and that consuming the past came to mean consumption in the present.

London 1884Edinburgh 1886
Art and Design Exhibitedp. 229
10A Red-Letter Day: Evaluating Progress in New Zealand’s Art at Dunedin’s International Exhibitions, 1865 and 1889Rebecca Ricep. 231

Rice compares the fine art sections of the two international exhibitions held in Dunedin, the New Zealand Exhibition of 1865 and the New Zealand and South Seas Exhibition of 1889-90, to ask what they show about progress in New Zealand art. Her evidence is mainly the critical reception. In 1865 reviewers, chiefly 'Rambler' (identified as William Fox), praised colonial watercolours as equal to the best work at home, and read the display as proof of colonial taste. By 1889 the verdicts were sharper: reviewers faulted New Zealand painters for relying on landscape and for having little genre or history painting. Rice explains the change through James Belich's idea of recolonization and through the new historical consciousness of 1889, shown in the Early History, Maori and South Seas Court and in a group of John Gully's works. She concludes that the 1865 exhibition helped build an art infrastructure, but that by 1889 the colonial moment was seen as past, which brought anxiety rather than triumph.

Dunedin 1865Dunedin 1889
11International Exhibitions and Urban Aspirations: Launceston, Tasmania, in the Nineteenth CenturyAnne Nealep. 251

Neale asks how Launceston, a small northern Tasmanian city, came to host an international exhibition in 1891-92, and argues that civic pride and a wish to be seen as up to date drove the event. Launceston's leaders had long been ahead in water supply and parks, and the idea, first raised in 1883, was held back by a lack of Tasmanian government money. The fair drew about a quarter of a million visitors and made a profit. Neale argues that the Albert Hall, a rare surviving permanent building, owes as much to Gordon McKinnon, a New South Wales architect, as to the council's approved architect. Two fountains form the chapter's other focus, a cast-iron French design first shown in Paris in 1855 and a terracotta copy of a Dublin fountain of 1853. Neale traces both through catalogues, council minutes and surviving examples, arguing that each is among the oldest public fountains in Australia. The conclusion reads the movement as a commercial network, with Launceston's survivors proving it was as strong at the margins as at the centre.

Launceston 1891Paris 1855Dublin 1853
12‘Urbi et Orbi’: Decentralization and Design in Nancy’s International Exposition of Eastern France, 1909Claire O’Mahonyp. 273

O'Mahony examines the International Exposition of Eastern France, held at Nancy in 1909, as an attempt to present a border city that had stayed French after the 1871 annexation of Alsace-Lorraine as a centre of regional and international exchange. She begins with Claudin's official poster, whose Lorraine girl releasing pigeons and rococo and medieval landmarks set out the balance between loyalty to France and regional pride. She then shows how the Chamber of Commerce, the mayor and local entrepreneurs organised the fair and gave the pavilion commissions to Lorraine architects. Her evidence is the site itself, including the Ecole de Nancy pavilion, the Palace of Mines and Metallurgy, a transplanted Alsatian farmhouse and the Palais des Fêtes, together with the official report and press coverage. O'Mahony argues that the exposition joined art, craft and industry into a regional vision that anticipated the regional economic model of the 1920s. She concludes that Nancy's fair was a model of decentralisation, and that Etienne Clémentel chose the city as the template for the regional economic alliances set up in 1919.

Nancy 1909
International Ambitionsp. 293
13Merging Peripheries and Centres: The Transnational Interconnectedness of the Helsinki National Exhibition of 1876Taina Syrjämaap. 295

Syrjämaa uses the first Finnish national industrial and art exhibition, held in Kaivopuisto Park in Helsinki in 1876, to test whether exhibitions formed a chain led by the great fairs. She argues that the Swedish-speaking businessmen, engineers and architects who organised it drew on many models, above all the Stockholm Nordic exhibition of 1866, whose wooden pavilion, central rotunda, fountain and porcelain display the Helsinki event closely resembles. The rotunda also recalls Vienna, but the Stockholm parallels are stronger. Her second case is the ethnographic section, a set of cottage interiors built by student unions after Artur Hazelius's collection in Stockholm, which later went to the Paris exhibition of 1878 and gained a prize. The sources are the official catalogue, Finnish newspapers and the business archives of Forssa Ab. The chapter concludes that the Helsinki exhibition was a hybrid appropriation of earlier models, and that small and permanent displays could feed back into the great fairs, so that the medium formed a bundle of threads rather than a single line.

Helsinki 1876Stockholm 1866Paris 1878
14The Last Exhibition of the Italian Colonial Empire: Naples 1938–40Giovanni Arenap. 313

Arena examines the Mostra Triennale delle Terre Italiane d'Oltremare, a colonial exhibition planned for Naples that opened on 9 May 1940, less than a month before Italy entered the Second World War and the show closed. He places it in a sequence of Italian colonial shows that begins with Tripoli's trade fair of 1927 and the Turin colonial exhibition of 1928, and continues with the Antwerp colonial exposition of 1930, where the regime stressed imperial Rome and modernised colonial economies. The Naples site in the Fuorigrotta district combined pavilions, gardens planted with colonial species and a plan meant to renew the city, while its historical, geographical and manufacturing sections used photomontages, ethnographic recreations and a 46-metre Fascist Party tower. Arena draws on the bylaws, the artists involved, especially Melkiorre Melis and his Libya pavilion café, and archival drawings. He concludes that the propaganda depended on the close integration of architecture and art, and that much of that decoration was destroyed in the bombing of the war.

Naples 1940Tripoli 1927Turin 1928Antwerp 1930
15International Ambitions of an Exhibition at the Margin: Japan’s 1903 Osaka ExpositionJeffer Daykinp. 333

Daykin asks what it meant for Japan to host an international exposition in 1903, using Osaka's Fifth National Industrial Exhibition in Tennoji Park as the case. The event was planned as a domestic show and became international only when foreign applications far exceeded the space reserved for them, so a Foreign Samples Building and separate national pavilions had to be provided. Daykin uses the Japan Weekly Chronicle, foreign-language guides and the commissioners' introductions to show how the awards policy and language arrangements lagged behind the event. His central example is the Jinrui Kan, a live 'native peoples' concession outside the grounds, which was altered after protests from Chinese and Korean students and officials and from the Okinawan press. The Formosan section, by contrast, presented Taiwan as a colonial foil that made Japan the civilised spectator. Daykin concludes that Osaka was a marginal international exposition, one that asserted Japan's equality with the West just two years before the Russo-Japanese War.

Osaka 1903
Indexp. 351
Findling, John E., and Kimberly D. Pelle, eds. Encyclopedia of World’s Fairs and Expositions. Jefferson, NC: McFarland, 2008.Asia: substantial8 chapter overviews

Overview

The Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions, edited by Findling and Pelle, is a reference work of about a hundred entries, each on one fair, arranged in date order from London in 1851 to Shanghai in 2010. Each entry is signed by a contributor and closes with its own bibliography. The foreword by Vicente Gonzalez Loscertales of the Bureau of International Expositions argues that expos remain valuable and sets out criteria for a theme. The preface, by the editors, traces fairs from medieval trade fairs through the Crystal Palace and argues that American fairs grew out of European experience, with more weight on civic pride and entertainment. Appendixes cover the BIE, fair statistics, officials, excluded fairs and planned fairs that were never held. The back matter holds a general bibliography, internet resources, contributor notes and an index.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a real but secondary strand. Full entries on fairs in the region, all within the Entries chapter, are Hanoi 1902-1903 (Rydell: French Indochina, with exhibits from the Philippines, Malaya, Siam, Japan, China, Formosa and Korea), Nanking 1910 (Pelle: China's first world's fair, with fourteen foreign nations and fifteen provinces), Osaka 1970 (Anderson: the first expo held in Asia, with Hong Kong among its participants), Okinawa 1975-1976 (Manning: Japan's ocean expo on the Ryukyu island), Tsukuba 1985 (Narita: a Japanese science fair with 47 countries), Taejon 1993 (McGregor: Korea's first fair, with 108 international participants), Aichi 2005 (Heller: Japan, with a seventeen-country Asia Common) and Shanghai 2010 (Fernsebner: China's urban-themed fair). Tokyo 1996 and Manila 2002, both planned and never held, have entries in Appendix E.

Asian participation is more often treated within entries on other fairs. St. Louis 1904 (Boger) built a Philippine Reservation of over a thousand Filipinos, including Igorots and Filipino scouts, presented as part of American imperial rule. Seattle 1909 had Japanese naval officers, a Japanese Day and an Igorot village on the midway. Okinawa 1975 lists pavilions for Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and the Republic of Korea. Apart from Hanoi, fairs planned or held in Southeast Asia are few: Manila 2002 would have been the first sanctioned fair hosted by a developing country, but the Manila effort collapsed in 1999.

Contents

ForewordVicente Gonzalez Loscertalesp. 1

Gonzalez Loscertales, Secretary General of the Bureau of International Expositions, argues that expos remain valuable in the twenty-first century because they draw large crowds, transform host cities and give governments, companies and civil society a platform. He sets out criteria for a theme, which should be of global interest, future-oriented and a priority for governments, and says expos now serve sustainable development and public education. He ends by thanking the editors and contributors.

Prefacep. 3

The editors trace world's fairs from medieval trade fairs and English prize shows through the French national exhibitions and mechanics institute displays to the Crystal Palace of 1851. They argue that American fairs grew out of European experience and gave more weight to civic pride and entertainment. They explain that fair, exhibition and expo are used interchangeably, though the terms differ. The volume offers essays on more than ninety-five fairs from 1851 to 2005, plus appendixes and bibliographies.

London 1851
106Entries: London 1851 to Shanghai 2010p. 9

The body of the encyclopedia: entries on individual fairs in chronological order, from London 1851 to Shanghai 2010, each by a named contributor and each ending with a bibliographical note. The entries were not summarised one by one. The list below gives the entry headings that could be picked out of the text by script (it may miss a few or include a stray heading); headings in colour link to this site's study page for that fair.

AAppendix A: The Bureau of International ExpositionsVicente Gonzalez Loscertalesp. 411

Gonzalez Loscertales traces international exhibitions from medieval trade fairs to London in 1851 and then explains how the diplomatic conferences of 1912 and 1920 led to the 1928 convention and the creation of the Bureau of International Expositions. He summarises the protocols of 1948, 1966 and 1972, and the BIE's current role in distinguishing registered expos from smaller recognised specialised exhibitions. The text is a short institutional history that sets out the BIE's rules on frequency and participation.

BAppendix B: Fair Statisticsp. 413

Appendix B is a table of fair statistics: opening and closing dates, site size, paid and total attendance, and profit or loss for the fairs in the volume. The introduction warns that these figures are inconsistent across sources and should be used with caution. In this extraction the rows are rotated and scrambled, so only occasional dates, city names and numbers can be read.

CAppendix C: Fair Officialsp. 418

Appendix C is a list of the principal officials of each fair in the volume, from London in 1851 to Shanghai in 2010, giving commissioners, presidents, general managers and chief architects where known. The entries are dense and sometimes incomplete, because the editors note that reliable information was not always available. It shows which individuals ran the fairs, though it makes no argument.

DAppendix D: Fairs Not Includedp. 422

Appendix D is a chronological list, by year and city, of exhibitions held after 1851 that were excluded from the main body, mostly regional, specialised or short-lived events such as the Cork Irish Industrial Exhibition of 1852 and the Glasgow Garden Festival of 1988. The introduction explains that the list shows how widespread fairs were, especially in the nineteenth century. Names are given in the host country's language unless it is not a common Western tongue.

EAppendix E: Fairs That Never Werep. 428

This appendix to the Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions lists expositions that were planned but never held, from New York 1913 and Baltimore 1914 to Calgary 2005, each as a short history. It does not argue a thesis; it records how each proposal was made, which sites and themes were chosen, and where it stopped. The causes recur: world wars and the Great Depression, economic slumps, doubts that a city could afford the cost, governments and mayors withdrawing support, and rival bids that won the BIE vote. Several entries are detailed, notably Philadelphia 1976, Los Angeles 1981, Paris 1989, Chicago 1992, Tokyo 1996 and Manila 2002, which trace the bidding, financing and political fights. Some entries show a fair's afterlife, such as Tokyo 1940 tickets honored at Osaka 1970. The appendix ends with Calgary's defeat by Aichi for 2005.

Findling, John E., and Kimberly D. Pelle, eds. Historical Dictionary of World’s Fairs and Expositions, 1851–1988. New York: Greenwood Press, 1990.Asia: substantial8 chapter overviews

Overview

Findling and Pelle's Historical Dictionary of World's Fairs and Expositions (1990) is a reference work. Its core is about ninety-five short entries, arranged chronologically, on international fairs from London in 1851 to Glasgow in 1988, with bibliographies for each. The introduction traces the fairs from medieval trade fairs and early national exhibitions to the Crystal Palace of 1851, and argues that they moved from single halls to national pavilions with fine arts and amusements, serving national prestige and, in the American case, civic rivalry. Appendixes cover the Bureau of International Expositions (John M. MacKenzie), fair statistics (Ted Allan), fair officials, fairs not included, fairs that never were, and fairs yet to come, followed by a general bibliography and index.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a secondary but steady presence. Five entries concern fairs held in the region: Hanoi 1902-1903, a French colonial exposition in Tonkin with pavilions for the Philippines, Malaya, Siam, Japan, China, Formosa and Korea; Nanking 1910, China's first world's fair; Osaka 1970, described as the first world exposition in Asia; Okinawa 1975-1976, a Japanese ocean exposition; and Tsukuba 1985, a Japanese government fair on technology and the environment. The Osaka entry is the fullest: 2.7 percent of its 64 million visitors were foreign, Asian nations shared an International Place pavilion, and China and North Vietnam were not invited. Japan's planned fairs of 1912, 1917 and 1940 appear in the chapter on fairs that never were.

Asian participation in other fairs is handled as national display. Japan and China are the most frequent, at Vienna 1873, Amsterdam 1883, New Orleans 1884-1885, Barcelona 1888, Liege 1905, Portland 1905, Chicago 1933-1934 and New Orleans 1984. Southeast Asian people appear mainly as displayed people: native villages from Dutch colonies at Amsterdam 1883, the Philippine reservation at St. Louis 1904, an Igorot village at Seattle 1909, and the 55 Filipinos at Ghent 1913, who went unpaid after their agency went bankrupt and nine of whom died of exposure. Indochina appears as colonial display at Paris 1931, with an Angkor Wat replica. South Asia (Calcutta 1883-1884, Ceylon at Wembley) is treated alongside, as contrast.

Contents

Copyright Acknowledgment

Findling and Pelle open with a copyright acknowledgment thanking World's Fair quarterly for permission to publish Arthur Chandler's chapters on the Paris expositions of 1867, 1878 and 1937. A dedication follows, and most of the unit is a contents list running from London in 1851 to Glasgow in 1988, then the appendixes. It gives students a quick map of the book's arrangement.

Prefacep. xi

Findling and Pelle's preface explains that the book grew out of a 1982 seminar on world's fairs at Indiana University Southeast. It sets two aims: basic information on more than ninety fairs in over twenty countries from 1851 to 1988, with annotated bibliographies, and a guide for researchers who want to go further. It thanks the librarians, collectors and staff who helped, and closes with a dedication to the editors' children.

Introductionp. XV

Findling and Pelle trace the roots of world's fairs to medieval trade fairs, the Royal Society of Arts exhibition of 1761, French national exhibitions up to 1849, English mechanics institute shows, and the first public art exhibition in London in 1760. They argue that these strands came together in the Crystal Palace exhibition of 1851, which set the pattern of industrial display with an international component. The introduction then shows how fairs moved from one large hall toward thematic and national pavilions, and added fine arts and amusements, so that they came to display national lifestyles as well as industrial progress. Nationalism runs through the account, since fair managers, often with government support, sought to make their host country look better than its rivals. The authors contrast the American case, where fairs were privately managed, tied closely to civic pride and city rivalry, and gave more weight to entertainment, and they close by defining fair, exhibition and exposition, which the book uses interchangeably.

London 1851
95Entries: London 1851 to Glasgow 1988p. 3

The body of the dictionary: entries on individual fairs in chronological order, from London 1851 to Glasgow 1988, each by a named contributor and each ending with a bibliographical note. The entries were not summarised one by one. The list below gives the entry headings that could be picked out of the text by script (it may miss a few or include a stray heading); headings in colour link to this site's study page for that fair.

Appendixesp. 371
ABureau of International Expositionsp. 372

This appendix explains the Bureau of International Expositions, the Paris body set up under the 1928 convention to regulate international fairs and revised by protocols in 1948, 1966 and 1972. It argues that the bureau was founded to restrict expositions rather than promote them, and that its controls have worked best on large universal fairs. It ends with a proposed 1989 protocol that would allow one registered event of six months every five years.

BFair Statisticsp. 315

This appendix is a table of statistics for the fairs in the book, giving opening and closing dates, site size, paid and total attendance, and profit or loss. Its introduction warns that attendance and financial figures vary widely between sources and depend on how each fair kept its accounts. The table itself is badly garbled in the scan, so individual figures are not reproduced here.

CFair Officialsp. 382

This appendix lists the principal officials of each fair from London in 1851 to Glasgow in 1988, giving names with titles such as president, commissioner general, general manager or chief architect. The same figures recur from fair to fair, for example Henry Anthony Hedley, Jules Joubert and Petr Spurney, and royalty and heads of government appear as patrons or chairmen. Entries are brief and uneven, since the appendix admits that reliable information was missing for some fairs.

DFairs Not Includedp. 395
EFairs That Never Werep. 403

Findling and Pelle close the dictionary with a list of world's fairs that were planned but never held, arranged by year and city from New York 1913 to Chicago 1992. Each short entry gives the reason a project collapsed, such as a world war, the Great Depression, rival cities, or the financial demands on the host, and notes any surviving legacy, such as Rome's partly built E42 site or Portland's commemorative medal. Taken together the entries show how often plans were overtaken by war, economic crisis or shifting politics, and how the Chicago 1992 scheme fell apart under public scrutiny of its finances and property deals.

Finnegan, Diarmid A., and Jonathan Jeffrey Wright, eds. Spaces of Global Knowledge: Exhibition, Encounter and Exchange in an Age of Empire. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015.Asia: substantial13 chapter overviews

Overview

The volume brings together eleven case studies, grouped as encounters and identity, collection and display, and circulation and translation, on how knowledge was made and moved across empires in the long nineteenth century. Its introduction questions what 'global knowledge' meant and warns against easy claims of globality, while the afterword by Withers proposes connections, institutions and languages as ways of testing those claims. The sites are varied: fur-trade posts in Rupert's Land, ships at sea, a Cyprus excavation, a Belfast museum, Kew's Museum of Economic Botany, Malthus's Essay on Population, a Haitian imperial court, a Bihar mission and Livingstone's French and German editions. Exhibitions recur in only a few chapters, mainly the Kew and Haitian ones.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a substantial but concentrated presence, carried by two chapters. Chapter 1, by Johnson, on Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe, is set wholly in Burma: the expedition to Yado over the Karen hills, the panoramic survey at Thandaung, Italian priests at Leiktho and a local account of the Sittang's changed course. Burmese labour, guides and knowledge are shown as indispensable to her botanical painting and mapping, while her descriptions of Shan, Karen and Padong peoples keep the colonial hierarchy in view. Chapter 3, by Finnegan, on Thomas Workman, covers Southeast Asia through his trips of 1883 to 1892: Singapore, Malayan spiders, Javan specimens, and a 1889 Singapore lecture with views of Chinese graveyards. In both chapters Asia is a field for British observers, and Asian people appear as guides and informants rather than as exhibitors or visitors.

Elsewhere the coverage is slight. Chapter 7, by Wright, on the Belfast museum, records a Burmese idol and a Burmese god among donations of 1831 to 1832; Thomson's travels reached China and Japan. In chapter 6, Cornish quotes a visitor who remembered the figures in the Kew indigo model as Chinese, though the model is an Indian object. Workman's 1887 lecture on China and Manila appears only in a footnote. No chapter discusses East or Southeast Asian exhibitions, state pavilions, commissioners or displays of Asian people; Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines and Indochina do not appear.

Contents

List of Figures and Tablesp. vii
List of Contributorsp. ix
Acknowledgementsp. xi
Introduction: Placing Global Knowledge in the Nineteenth CenturyDiarmid A. Finnegan and Jonathan Jeffrey Wrightp. 1

Finnegan and Wright introduce Spaces of Global Knowledge by asking what 'global knowledge' meant in the long nineteenth century, from the late eighteenth century to the early twentieth. They open with Cook's first Pacific voyage and Banks's collecting to show how exploration, empire and science were bound together. Reviewing recent work on global history and the global history of science, they weigh its promise against the risk of flattening local difference and of returning to a universal history. Their working definitions treat global knowledge both as knowledge that moved across many territories and as an aspiration held by historical actors. The volume's case studies, grounded in archival work and a 'bottom up' method, show knowledge economies that were uneven and shaped by imperial power. The introduction then outlines three sections, on encounters and identity, collection and display, and circulation and translation, and summarises most chapters, from Johnson's Burmese botany to Henderson's study of Livingstone's translations. It ends by urging scepticism toward easy claims of globality. Exhibitions appear only in passing, such as the Haitian emperor's use of a world-fair display language.

Part 1Encounters and Identityp. 17
1Global Knowledge in a Local World: Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe’s Encounters with Burma 1901–1902Nuala C. Johnsonp. 19

Johnson reconstructs one year, 1901 to 1902, in the life of Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe, a civil engineer's wife who painted Burmese orchids and plants and sent seeds and paintings to Glasnevin. The argument is that her knowledge of Burma was shaped by colonial assumptions about class, gender and race, yet depended on Burmese labour, guides and local expertise. The main evidence is her letters to her mother, held in the National Botanic Gardens archive, with surviving paintings and a map. Johnson follows the couple's expedition to Yado over the Karen hills, with two elephants and about 600 pounds of equipment, and a survey trip to Thandaung, where Wheeler Cuffe sketched a panorama to scale. The chapter also looks at Italian priests at Leiktho, a local account of the Sittang's changed course, and the wine and shoes carried back on the voyage home. It concludes that her knowledge was a collaborative exercise carried out in the contact zone between European and Burmese people.

2Archaeology, Empire and the Field: Exploring the Ancient Sites of Cyprus, 1865–1876Polina Nikolaoup. 39

Nikolaou examines how the British consul Robert Hamilton Lang and the American consul Luigi Palma di Cesnola excavated and exported antiquities from Ottoman Cyprus in the 1860s and 1870s. The chapter argues that Cypriot archaeology was built through networks that joined imperial diplomacy, local knowledge and metropolitan scholarship. It works through four themes drawn from the consuls' letters: their motives, which were financial as well as antiquarian; their dealings with Ottoman authorities, who issued firmans and an Antiquities Law that was weakly enforced; their reliance on local labourers and intermediaries, as at Athienou; and the recording of finds. Cesnola's disputed provenance, discussed in the Feuardent lawsuit and Stillman's report, contrasts with Lang's correspondence with Charles Newton at the British Museum, which made his finds credible. Nikolaou concludes that the place of discovery, and the methods used to record it, decided whether collecting counted as science, and that archaeology in Cyprus was a collective, networked and contested enterprise.

3Webs of Science, Webs of Commerce: The Life-Worlds of a Merchant NaturalistDiarmid A. Finneganp. 57

Finnegan follows Thomas Workman, a Belfast linen merchant and amateur naturalist (1843-1900), through his travels to North America, Brazil and South East Asia and through the spaces in which he turned them into knowledge. The chapter argues that Workman's global vision was held together by commerce and science at once: his trips were sales journeys for linen and muslin, and his collections of tropical spiders were scientific capital. Its method is to pause at a series of places: his father's Bedford Street warehouse, which hosted the British Association's soiree in 1852; Camp Supply in Indian Territory, where his letter-book descriptions of the Kiowa and Cheyenne reveal a detached, romanticising observer; the coasts of Brazil, where ship and shore mediated his sense of tropical difference; and the Belfast Museum and Craigdarragh House, his home on Belfast Lough. Finnegan uses Workman's journals, letters and lectures, and the Society's records, to show how shifting priorities made his foreign donations and lectures less valued locally. The chapter concludes that Workman's global knowledge was fragile and patchy, and that his death in 1900 marks the decline of the amateur merchant-naturalist.

4Scientific Practice and the Scientific Self in Rupert’s Land, c.1770–1830: Fur Trade Networks of Knowledge ExchangeAngela Byrnep. 79

Byrne examines how fur traders at posts in Rupert's Land, c.1770-1830, built scientific identities for themselves. The chapter argues that their practice operated on two planes at once: observations were shaped by local conditions and by Hudson's Bay Company expectations, yet they circulated across a borderless republic of letters. Its evidence comes from fur trade correspondence, journals and reports, especially those of Peter Fidler, Andrew Graham and James Hargrave. Byrne traces two practices. The first is the exchange of books, magazines and news, which kept traders connected to British scholarship. The second is kitchen gardening at trading posts, where traders recorded crop success and failure in ways that documented climate and natural history, while showing reluctance to adopt the native crops and methods that First Nations offered. Byrne concludes that these networks were fragile, but that traders' observations, often unacknowledged, were absorbed into major British natural histories and expeditions, so that local and global knowledge were assembled together.

Part 2Collection and Displayp. 97
5Sampling the South Seas: Collecting and Interrogating Scientific Specimens on Mid-Nineteenth-Century Voyages of Pacific ExplorationSarah Louise Millarp. 99

Millar examines the collecting of specimens on three voyages of the 1830s and 1840s: the French corvettes Astrolabe and Zelee under Dumont d'Urville, the United States Exploring Expedition under Charles Wilkes, and James Clark Ross's British Antarctic expedition in Erebus and Terror. The chapter argues that the ship was a scientific space in its own right: its layout, its limited room for dissection and drawing, and the authority of its captain shaped what could be collected and studied at sea. Millar compares the three voyages through their sailing instructions, which gave commerce a prominent place for the French and Americans but a narrower, magnetic focus for the British. Evidence comes from the letters and published narratives of crew and naturalists, including Midshipman William Reynolds's letters from the Vincennes and Ross's narrative. Shooting birds, dredging the seabed and catching penguins are shown to be both science and pastime, and conflicts over space, time and personal collections divided the 'Scientifics' from officers and crew. Millar concludes that the knowledge gathered at sea was made by men at sea as much as by men of science, and that the line between them was blurred.

6Curating Global Knowledge: The Museum of Economic Botany at Kew GardensCaroline Cornishp. 119

Cornish uses the biography of one object, a clay model of an Indian indigo factory, to trace how the Museum of Economic Botany at Kew Gardens produced global scientific knowledge. The model was made in Krishnanagar, commissioned by T.N. Mukharji of the Indian Department of Agriculture, and shown at the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London before Kew acquired it. Cornish follows its path through Kew's display practices, its circulation in guidebooks, the Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information and a novel, and its reception by visitors, who responded to it in terms of both wonder and resonance. Her main claim is that the knowledge produced at Kew was global in its acquisition networks, in its circulation and in its impacts. She ends by conceding the limits of that knowledge: the indigo work neither improved conditions for Indian labourers nor reversed the decline of natural indigo before synthetic dyes.

London 1886
7‘A Depot for the Productions of the Four Quarters of the Globe’: Empire, Collecting and the Belfast MuseumJonathan Jeffrey Wrightp. 143

Wright asks how the Belfast Natural History Society, which opened its museum in 1831, came to hold a collection of objects from across the world, and what knowledge its displays produced. He argues that the museum was a global space made possible by empire, although its holdings also came from North America and from merchants and seamen outside imperial channels. Drawing on the society's donation and letter books, he shows a deliberate policy of 'global' collecting from the 1820s, pursued through naval contacts and returning travellers such as Gordon Augustus Thomson and James Emerson Tennent. Wright looks closely at a New Zealand mokomokai, or tattooed head, and treats its acquisition as an exercise of imperial power. He then traces how after 1868 the society turned towards local collections, and how the displays of the 1880s and 1890s set the foreign apart as 'savage'. The chapter concludes that the museum conveyed a message about British global reach to its middle-class members and to the working-class visitors admitted on Easter Mondays.

8Malthus’s Globalisms: Enlightenment Geographical Imaginaries in the Essay on the Principle of PopulationRobert J. Mayhewp. 167

Mayhew asks how Thomas Robert Malthus engaged with the global world of his day, using the first and second editions of the Essay on the Principle of Population (1798 and 1803). He argues that Malthus's global imaginary was Enlightenment in character, not attentive to geographical difference: he sorted the world into stages of hunters, shepherds and settled commercial societies, following the Scottish stadial theory of Hume, Robertson and Smith. In 1798 Malthus claimed to rely on observation but cited almost no travel accounts, whereas in 1803 he added a vast body of evidence, drawn from voyages by Cook and Vancouver, Asiatic Researches, Gibbon and census returns. The 1803 Essay, Mayhew shows, divided the world more starkly into positively and preventively checked societies, while colonies, the 'forced' populations of China and India, and the ambiguous edges of Europe complicated it. Mayhew concludes that Malthus's work was Eurocentric and confirmatory rather than testing, and that it belongs to an Enlightenment worldview before the Victorian shift towards comparative anthropology.

Part 3Circulation and Translationp. 185
9Brokering Knowledge in an Age of Mis-Recognition and Ignorance; or Displaying Haiti to the MassesKaren N. Saltp. 187

Salt examines how Faustin I, the last emperor of Haiti, used objects and images in the 1850s to counter pejorative views of Haiti in the Atlantic world. She argues that Faustin I deliberately circulated knowledge about Haiti, through Haiti's presence at the 1853 Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations in New York, through pamphlets by his commercial agent B.C. Clark, and through an album of daguerreotypes and lithographs of the imperial court. The chapter works through Clark's two 1853 pamphlets, which pressed for Haiti's recognition, and through an 1856 Illustrated London News article whose text mocked the emperor while its engravings copied the album's portraits of him and Empress Adelina. Salt set these items against the caricatures of Daumier and Cham and against the racialised American debates over recognition. She concludes that the material traces are fragmentary and that the reach and purpose of the album remain open questions, though a positive 1852 Gleason's article suggests that other objects circulated too.

New York 1853
10‘Throughout Bihar and Beyond’: Dublin University Mission and the Structuring of a ‘Global’ Medical PracticeSarah Hunterp. 209

Hunter studies the medical work of the Dublin University Mission, which reached Hazaribagh in the Chota Nagpur region of Bengal in January 1892. She argues that medicine gave the missionaries access to villages and to the secluded quarters of women, but that their practice was reshaped by local customs and Indian practitioners, producing a hybrid medicine rather than western knowledge diffused unchanged. Her evidence comes from the Mission's annual reports and magazine: Irish nurses visiting zenanas, upper-caste women in purdah attending from 1896, Digby Fund scholarships that trained Indian men such as Masih Charan Pankaj, and the female side of the work, from the first female doctor, Eva Jellett, in 1905 to the nurses' school at St Columba's Hospital, opened in 1912. The chapter concludes that the Mission's survival depended on Indian staff who knew the language and geography of the district, and that the medicine it practised was altered by contact with the place.

11Historical Geographies of Textual Circulation: David Livingstone’s Missionary Travels in France and GermanyLouise C. Hendersonp. 227

Henderson follows David Livingstone's Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa (1857), a best-selling travel narrative, into its French and German editions. Her argument is that a book's meaning changes as it travels: translators, publishers and reviewers reworked the text, its prefaces and its illustrations, so that Livingstone lost authority over his account. She draws on copyright law of the period, including the 1838 act and the later Anglo-French and Anglo-Prussian agreements, and on the John Murray archive. Her main cases are Lotze's authorised German translation for the publisher Costenoble, Otto Spamer's shorter, illustrated rival, which Costenoble attacked as plagiarism, and Hachette's French edition alongside Paumier's cheaper summary. Henderson concludes that unauthorised editions reached readers who could not afford the originals, and that a 'global Livingstone' is a worthwhile question, though one that could underplay the nuances of local reception. The chapter ends by calling for a geography of the book that links production, circulation and reception.

Afterword: Connections, Institutions, LanguagesCharles W.J. Withersp. 245

Withers, in an afterword, reflects on what the volume's chapters show about 'global knowledge' in the nineteenth century. He opens with Harriet Martineau's 1858 remark on the shrinking globe, then argues that a claim to global knowledge needs more than connections between distant places; it must show how each shaped the other. His main concern is the category itself. Terms such as 'global', 'transnational' and 'international' are slippery, and broad studies tend to become thematic networks, while fine-grained work risks assuming the connection rather than explaining it. He proposes three lines of enquiry: connections, through letters, print, steam shipping and the telegraph; institutions, such as museums and libraries, whose administrators brokered between imperial knowledge and its publics; and languages, since translation changes meaning. He ends by noting, with Rupke, that the categories are 'assignments', and by reminding readers that most contemporaries, unlike Martineau, had little access to the world they read about and saw displayed.

Bibliographyp. 257
Indexp. 281
Ganz, Cheryl R. The 1933 Chicago World’s Fair: A Century of Progress. Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 2008.Asia: slight11 chapter overviews

Overview

Ganz's book is a history of A Century of Progress, the 1933-34 Chicago fair, which was privately financed during the Depression to revive the city's economy and reputation. Its argument is that the organisers used cooperative science exhibits and the idea of progress to generate optimism, presenting technology rather than people as the driver of progress, while Midway entertainment, women, African Americans, ethnic communities and aviation pressed their own meanings on the fair. Chapters move from the Sally Rand shows and the Chicago boosters who financed the fair to its architecture and corporate exhibits, then to women's spaces, the Du Sable cabin, ethnic pavilions and the Graf Zeppelin and stratosphere balloon, and end with an epilogue on the fair's objects and afterlife.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia have a slight place in this book, which is concerned with Chicago, its Midway and its organisers rather than with foreign participation. The only Asian national presence named is a Japanese Pavilion, mentioned in the epilogue as the source of items bid for in the fair's sale of surplus (a phonograph, a rug and lights). Tokyo enters the introduction only as one of the cities that surpassed Chicago in size. Chapter 7, Ethnic Identity and Nationalistic Representations of Progress, concerns European immigrant communities, Mexico and Italy, and has no Asian national section.

Chapter 1, Sally Rand and the Midway, holds nearly all the remaining material, and there the Asian reference is mostly a concession name. The Oriental Village was one of the Midway's attractions, where Little Egypt recreated her Streets of Cairo show, where Rand moved her production in 1934, and where the mayor judged Hot Cha San's dance acceptable in 1933. The book does not say that these performances were Asian in origin. The 'Siamese' twins listed among the Living Wonders freak show are named as one of the displayed bodies, with no discussion of where they came from. Southeast Asia is otherwise absent, and the book does not discuss Asian visitors or exhibitions held in Asia.

Contents

Acknowledgments

Ganz thanks the scholars, archivists and institutions that made the book possible. The section describes research in Chicago archives and collections, including the University of Illinois at Chicago and the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, and names the funders who supported travel and fellowships. It acknowledges earlier writing on international expositions and ends with thanks to the publisher, editors and family. It makes no argument about the fair itself.

Introduction

Ganz introduces A Century of Progress, the 1933–34 Chicago fair financed privately during the Depression to revive the city's economy and reputation. The chapter argues that organizers, unlike the competitive exhibitors of 1893, used cooperative science exhibits and the idea of progress to generate optimism, presenting technology rather than people as progress's driver. It notes that women, African Americans and fan dancers pressed their own meanings of progress on the fair, and it left a lasting mark on Chicago.

Chicago 1933Chicago 1893
1Sally Rand and the Midway

Ganz examines Sally Rand's fan and bubble dances and the Midway shows around them at the 1933 Chicago fair, arguing that the fair's need for crowds and revenue, combined with lax policing, turned popular entertainment into sexual spectacle. Rand's Lady Godiva ride through the Streets of Paris in May 1933 led to a paid engagement and record box-office receipts. Evidence comes from court cases in which judges declined to close the shows, from the shifting nudity rules, and from peep shows such as Visions of Art and the Olympia show. The chapter also traces the repeal of Prohibition, which let concessions sell liquor, and the Hollywood codes that followed. Ganz concludes that Rand, more than the Sky Ride, became the fair's enduring icon of optimism.

Chicago 1933Chicago 1893
2Chicago Boosters Set the Stage

Ganz traces how Chicago's business and civic leaders, led by the Dawes brothers and Lenox Lohr, moved from the idea of a centennial celebration in 1926 to a financed world's fair in 1933. The chapter argues that the fair's management reflected the business, military and engineering model of its leaders, and that earlier failures, including the Hurley plan, the 1927 cancellation and the 1929 federal resolution, shaped what came next. It draws on committee records, the Chicago press, the Dawes brothers' letters and the organization charts Lohr adapted from earlier expositions. Ganz concludes that the Dawes brothers and Lohr, through bond sales, cash-basis building and a strictly hierarchical structure, turned an uncertain civic idea into a fair ready to reshape Chicago's lakefront and reputation.

Chicago 1933Chicago 1893Philadelphia 1926
3A New Vision for a World’s Fair

Ganz examines how the fair's organizers turned the idea of progress into an architectural and exhibition program. The chapter argues that they rejected competitive state and national pavilions in favour of cooperative industrial exhibits, and that architecture, colour, lighting and science displays were chosen to show science as the engine of progress. Its cases are the Administration Building, which tested new wallboard, and Paul Cret's Hall of Science, with Joseph Urban's colour scheme and neon lighting. It also discusses Louise Woodruff's Fountain of Science with its robot figure, the National Research Council's advisory role, and the corporate pavilions of Sears, General Electric, IBM and Ford. It concludes that the fair's architecture and exhibits gave Depression-era visitors a magical escape grounded in modern technology.

Chicago 1933Chicago 1893
4The Vision on Display

Ganz examines how the organizers of A Century of Progress, Chicago's 1933 fair, tried to make exhibits that taught visitors about science and industry during the Depression. The chapter argues that fair leaders wanted cooperative, industry-wide exhibits rather than competitive displays, and that this effort mostly failed: only a few industries, such as dairy, staged joint displays, while corporations such as General Motors and Ford built their own pavilions. Ganz works through the dioramas made by Edward Ashenden's workshop, the Sky Ride, the AT&T telephone exhibits, and the GM and Ford pavilions, including GM's assembly-line display. The chapter also shows how business leaders used the fair to promote their image and confidence in recovery, culminating in Alfred Sloan's 1934 GM conference, which opposed New Deal regulation. It concludes that the fair set a model of corporate showmanship and a pioneering idea of progress that shaped later fairs.

Chicago 1933
5Women’s Spaces at the Fair

Ganz asks what space women were given at A Century of Progress and argues that male organizers, working with society women, denied them a distinct women's building. The chapter first sets the 1933 fair against earlier American fairs: the 1893 Woman's Building in Chicago, where the Board of Lady Managers beat the suffragist Queen Isabella Association, and the narrower roles women were given at Buffalo, St. Louis and Philadelphia. Its main case is the Temple of Womanhood, a concession proposed by Dorthea Goodrich in 1932 and cancelled after clubwomen and Martha McGrew learned of her past under another name. Ganz follows the rivalry between Helen Dawes and McGrew, the role of Helen Bennett, and the National Council of Women's exhibit in the Social Science Hall, then closes with the Chicago Woman's Club headquarters just outside the main gate. The chapter concludes that privileged women protected their own status while professional women accepted the fair's male-led progress, so that no collective women's space emerged inside the grounds.

Chicago 1893Chicago 1933
6African Americans and the Du Sable Legacy

Ganz describes how African Americans were treated at A Century of Progress and how the clubwomen of the National De Saible Memorial Society won a place at the fair with a replica of Jean Baptiste Point Du Sable's cabin. The chapter argues that fair organizers gave black Chicagoans few jobs and let concessionaires stage stereotyped 'Negro' attractions, so that the progress theme largely excluded the city's African American community. It works through Negro Day at Soldier Field, which drew only about four thousand paying visitors, and through the NAACP's lawsuits over denied restaurant service. The core case is the Du Sable cabin, which Annie Oliver's society campaigned to build from 1928, overcoming fair officials' refusals with letters and a city appropriation. Ganz shows how the cabin, its booklet and the clubwomen's hosting made the women an exhibit in their own right. The chapter ends with the clubwomen's 1936 campaign to rename a Chicago high school after Du Sable.

Chicago 1933
7Ethnic Identity and Nationalistic Representations of Progress

Ganz examines how Chicago's ethnic communities were recruited to A Century of Progress and how the fair presented their homelands. The chapter argues that Major Felix Streyckmans's Committee on Coordination of Nationalities used a melting-pot ideal and competing ethnic committees to win European immigrants' support, while African Americans and Mexicans in the city were largely left out. It works through the Old European Village scheme, which failed, and through the Mexican and Italian presences. The Mexican case covers the replica Mayan temple, the presidential train, and the Old Mexico concessions, whose floor shows featured Euro-American dancers in costume. The Italian case centers on Italo Balbo's flight to Chicago, the 450-exhibit Italian Pavilion, and the Columbus statue. Ganz argues that most ethnic groups embraced American capitalism and rejected revolution, and the chapter ends by contrasting the rail of Mexico's train with the aviation that the fair used to display progress.

Chicago 1933
8Aviation, Nationalism, and Progress

Ganz examines how aviation carried political meaning at the 1933 Chicago fair. The chapter centres on the visit of the German airship Graf Zeppelin, whose tail fins bore the swastika, a flag Eckener preferred to keep out of view. Ganz follows the disputes it provoked among German American groups, Jewish organisations and the German consulate, and the politically charged receptions held for Eckener and Ambassador Luther. It then turns to A Century of Progress, a stratosphere balloon built by a joint venture of Dow, Goodyear and Union Carbide, whose failed and successful flights were presented as American achievements although Auguste Piccard designed the gondola. Ganz argues that the fair made aviation a test of national prestige, and that the swastika episode forced German Americans to choose between their ethnic loyalty and their American identity.

Chicago 1933
Epilogue

Ganz's epilogue follows the 1933 fair from its last day, 31 October 1934, into its afterlife. It describes the closing ceremony, the midnight fireworks and the vandalism that followed, then traces what became of the fair's objects and buildings: the Piccards' gondola and the Pioneer Zephyr went to the Museum of Science and Industry, the House of Tomorrow was moved to Indiana, and only a Roman column remains on the lakefront. Ganz looks at the people who ran the fair, including Rufus Dawes, Lenox Lohr and the women whose careers grew from it. The chapter argues that the fair left lasting civic and ethnic effects, from the fourth star added to Chicago's flag to immigrant families' pursuit of home ownership and upward mobility. It ends with Sally Rand, whose bubble dance became the fair's icon.

Chicago 1933
