Gelernter, David. 1939: The Lost World of the Fair. New York: Free Press, 1995.Asia: slight29 chapter overviews

Overview

Gelernter asks what the optimism of the 1939 New York World's Fair meant and why it has since vanished. He argues that the fair rested on a civic faith in America and a utopian future, that many of its promises came true in suburbs and highways, and that the faith itself has died. The book is built around the diary of Hortense Glassman, who walked the grounds with the engineer Mark Handler in 1939, and around later interviews with Mrs. Levine, who was Glassman. Early chapters follow the couple through a single day and set the pavilions beside essays on politics, technology, architecture and social rules. Later chapters follow Handler and Levine to his death in 1943, and the epilogue turns to the fair's history and to religion.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive slight attention. Japan is the only regional power that recurs, and nearly always as a backdrop to war. The Prologue notes anti-Japanese aggression signs in Chinatown and Japan as a source of paper flowers. Chapter 3 (Color Coded) mentions Japan's threat in Asia alongside Roosevelt's response to fascism. Chapter 15 (Technology: Frightening) cites the Japanese bombing of Shanghai, and Chapter 16 (When Life Turns Out to Be a Sand Castle) ends with Pearl Harbor, in a passage quoting Mrs. Levine. The fair itself is touched in two places. Chapter 22 (Obsession) notes that China and Germany were the only large countries not represented, and that China was then under Japanese invasion. The epilogue repeats that China did not sign up and places a Japanese pavilion on the grounds at closing. The notes add a few Japanese restaurants in Manhattan and observe that the fair's 90 percent representation claim would have ceded Chinese Manchuria to Japan. No East or Southeast Asian exhibit, commissioner or visitor is described, and Southeast Asia appears only through a passing mention of Sumatran rubber in the Prologue.

Contents

Author's Notep. vi
Prefacep. xi

Gelernter's preface sets out sources and aims. Most of the material comes from the fair's own period, in newspapers, guidebooks, picture books and magazines. Among modern studies it recommends Harrison's essay collection and Rydell's World of Fairs, which it finds tendentious but instructive. The stated goal is to convey what the fair was like, and the preface admits that much has been left out. It ends by thanking the people who shared memories and helped with research and editing.

1Prologue: The Center of Timep. 1

The Prologue sets New York in 1939 against the present, a city of new bridges, skyscrapers and La Guardia's reform government. Long conversations with Hattie Levine, a fairgoer who recalls the Futurama and the Trylon and Perisphere, give the fair its texture. Gelernter argues that its optimism rested on a civic religion in which the American creed and a utopian future were believed, and that the fair's promises were largely fulfilled, notably in suburbs and highways. Evidence includes the exhibits, a 1940 Roper poll in which a plurality stayed optimistic after France fell, and the Polish and Palestine pavilions, which were shadowed by war. The chapter concludes that the faith has since died, and ends by inviting readers on a tour of the fair.

New York 1939
2Into the Fairp. 56

Gelernter reconstructs a single day, Thursday 18 May 1939, from the diary of Hortense Glassman, who walked the grounds with the engineer Mark Handler. Their visit to Democracity inside the Perisphere leads to a discussion of the model city, which the chapter reads as a forecast of postwar suburbia, and to comparison with the film The City and with Levittown. Between diary passages, the chapter sketches the high thirties through the New Deal, the CIO, Turing and von Neumann, the Spanish Civil War and the big bands. It ends on the Helicline, where Handler and Glassman quarrel over whether the United States can win a war against Hitler and whether they should have children, a dispute the diary records with some tension.

New York 1939
3Color Codedp. 73

Gelernter introduces La Guardia, Robert Moses and Franklin Roosevelt as the three figures who shaped New York and the fair, drawing on Caro's biography of Moses and on the Flushing Meadow site that Moses had cleared beside the Grand Central Parkway. The argument is that all three had ferocious will, and that Moses's public works made the era's faith in government tangible. The chapter then surveys 1939 at home and abroad, from the waning New Deal and the Court fight to the Spanish Civil War and Roosevelt's response to Hitler. It turns to the fair's layout under the Board of Design, with its radiating avenues and the Lagoon of Nations, and to its color code of theme colors, which Gardner Harding and Talbot Hamlin judged in different ways. The chapter ends by walking the grounds past the Parachute Jump toward the Transportation Zone.

New York 1939
4The Necktiep. 89

Gelernter opens with the yearbook label that called Hortense Glassman a 'famous cold beauty', then follows her and Mark Handler past the guide chairs and onto the Helicline. The chapter's main argument is that in 1939 America was a community of faith held together by countless distinctions, among them adults and children, clothes for home and for the fair, and men's and women's roles. Its evidence for the later loss of these distinctions is a set of modern news items, including a Half Moon Bay proposal to ban homework and a Westchester parent who fears giving a curfew, along with Fitzgerald's The Last Tycoon, in which the hero takes off his tie at 3 A.M. The chapter ends with the Theme Center's commission to Wallace Harrison and Andre Fouilhoux, the gypsum-board surface over the steel frame, and the note that four thousand tons of steel went into the structure.

New York 1939
5The Monkey Goddessp. 99

Gelernter follows Hortense Glassman and Mark Handler through the Heinz pavilion, with its Goddess of Perfection fountain and free food, and then into the Borden building, where cows are milked on a turntable. Handler argues that the fair's exhibits make a case for rational hope rather than simply asserting that the future is bright, and the chapter reads the commercial pavilions as arguments of that kind. The most tense passage comes when a man in the crowd shouts 'Munchen!' and 'Greater Germany!' at the couple, and another onlooker makes an antisemitic remark, which sends Glassman back to a memory of a Russian man whose family had been killed in a pogrom. The chapter ends with Handler's plan for a Perisphere wrapped in steel lattice and lit from behind, and his suggestion that they stop at the Consumers building next.

New York 1939
6Doughnutsp. 112

Gelernter uses the Consumers building to examine what the fair said about income and the economy. Egmond Arens's focal exhibit set four official income levels, from subsistence to luxury, and proposed that abundance could be distributed to 'Three-Thirds of a Nation.' Gelernter sets these figures against 1935 household data and modern incomes, and concludes that the country is far richer than in 1939. Other exhibits, including Gilbert Rhode's show on interdependence and Russel Wright's Food Zone with its sixty-foot egg, are read as expressions of the fair's faith in planning and wonder. The chapter then moves to a doughnut shop, where Handler predicts Hitler's next moves through Austria, Munich and Czechoslovakia while Glassman's diary records their talk about war and having children, before the two set off towards the Transportation Zone.

New York 1939
7Haven't We Met Somewhere Before?p. 124

Gelernter examines the Amusement Area, where the Crystal Lassies show and Salvador Dali's Dream of Venus pavilion offered girlie shows, and argues that the performers and spectators of 1939 were individuals who knew what they were doing. The chapter sets out parallels with the present, including divided opinion on pornography, the place of women in work and marriage, and the meaning of 'liberal' in a period when La Guardia, sitting as a magistrate, fined the managers of a 'Miss Nude of 1939' show. Other evidence includes the use of 'clients' for welfare recipients, the 1930s idea that social causes explain crime, and a Times supplement's forecast of federal health insurance. It ends by observing that the society differs from 1930s America, though not necessarily in the ways we suppose.

New York 1939
8Partyp. 134

"Party" introduces Mark Handler, a young architect, through interviews with Mrs. Levine, who was Miss Glassman in 1939 and now looks back on that year. Gelernter begins with her memory of a late-1937 party in Brooklyn Heights, where Handler held court among admirers while Sarah Abbot, a wealthy non-Jewish woman, watched him closely. The narrative moves through Tuesday-night arguments at a Manhattan delicatessen over Handler's designs for worker housing, his affair with a separated woman, and the courtship that followed. Diary entries give the chapter its texture, along with a vivid picture of a sobbing woman that Mrs. Levine admits she may have imagined. Her reflections on the optimism and political anxiety of the period frame the personal story. The chapter ends with her refusal to explain Handler fully, leaving the reader to puzzle him out.

9Choosing Fordp. 147

"Choosing Ford" follows a diary kept by Miss Glassman during a day at the 1939 New York World's Fair with Mark Handler, an outing that turns into a half-serious marriage proposal. Gelernter alternates her diary entries with notes on the exhibits they pass. Handler suggests they marry and put off the question of children, and after a playful exchange she insists she has not agreed. Their walk takes them into the Transportation Zone past the General Motors, Goodrich, Railroads and Chrysler pavilions, and into the Ford building, where the Ford Cycle of Production turntable, the Mercury sculpture and the Road of Tomorrow are described. Gelernter's notes add the Crosley car, the Masterpieces of Art loan show, Chrysler's rocket display and the Ford courtyard's Novachord, showing how the fair mixed commerce, art and education. The chapter ends in the courtyard, where the couple rest in the sun, listening to the cars and fountains, with the question still unsettled.

New York 1939
10Technology: Gorgeousp. 162

"Technology: Gorgeous" argues that the 1939 fair treated machines as objects of beauty and almost spiritual feeling, and that art and engineering were so closely joined that visitors saw no conflict between them. Miss Glassman's diary places the couple in the Ford courtyard, where a Novachord concert was advertised, and Gelernter uses that ensemble, led by Ferde Grofe, to introduce Gershwin as the decade's representative composer. The main evidence is the fair's murals, about half of which had technological themes, and the work of Stuart Davis, Leger and de Kooning. A quoted diary of a WPA muralist shows the Federal Art Project's commitment. Industrial designers such as Loewy and Dreyfuss, who redesigned refrigerators and telephones, show how the fair's machines were made presentable, while bridges, skyscrapers and streamlined trains show the thirties faith in progress. Gelernter compares the calm 1939 reaction to television with present-day alarm and concludes that the split between art and technology has alienated us from the future. The chapter ends with the Futurama's Polyrhetor, a twenty-ton sound system that the New York Times called the outstanding technological contribution of the fair.

New York 1939
11Flight in Spacep. 177

"Flight in Space" uses the fair's Transportation Zone to show how 1939 imagined the airplane. Miss Glassman and Mark Handler walk past the Aviation, Marine Transportation and Firestone buildings, and Gelernter sets their diary against a wider account of thirties aviation, in which planes were pictured as cars, ships or luxury liners. The chapter cites Norman Bel Geddes's Airliner Number 4, a nine-deck design with a gymnasium, the Hindenburg disaster of 1937, and the interiors Bel Geddes produced for Pan American. It contrasts the comfort of the Pullman train with present-day air travel, which Gelernter argues is faster but far less pleasant than 1939 expected. The Firestone Factory of Tomorrow and its tire-making process are treated as a case of technology that was homely and laborious rather than remote. The chapter ends with Miss Glassman's wry remark that her prospects are improving, as the couple cross the bridge back toward the main grounds.

New York 1939
12Playgroundsp. 187

"Playgrounds" reconstructs the autumn of 1939, when Mark Handler, working for Robert Moses's Parks Department, designed inexpensive visionary playgrounds for an exhibit at the Brooklyn Museum that December. Gelernter draws on a second interview and Mrs. Levine's diary to show how the show was entangled with Moses's high-handedness, the withdrawal of the collaborator Norman Ryerson, and Ryerson's violent car crash three days before the opening. The chapter also sketches the couple's daily life: Mrs. Levine's cataloguing job at the New York Public Library, Handler's economical lunches at the Automat, and an uneasy visit to his parents, whose Zionism and insistence on a professional career she resented. The opening and Handler's speech are reported, and Moses's dismissal of Handler the next day is set against Handler's belief that the crash, not the exhibit, was the cause. The chapter ends with Mrs. Levine bringing out the typed pages of his opening remarks.

13His Own Wordsp. 202

"His Own Words" gives the text of Mark Handler's notes for the playground exhibit, which Mrs. Levine reads from typed pages. Four designs are described in detail: a set of swings inside a concrete half-cylinder, a twenty-foot chain-link cube maze with ivy and extra exits, a long inclined platform with ten slides of varying length, and a wading pool with fountains and blue-glass grottoes. Between readings, Mrs. Levine speaks about the economic reality of 1939, when a working woman might have only a few dollars a week after rent, and traces Handler's stubbornness to his father's wartime wound and his family's journey to New York. Gelernter uses these passages to argue that hunger and money shaped everyday life far more than they do now. The chapter closes with Mrs. Levine's reflections on women's choices and feminism, and her view that the past should not be lived in. She then sends Gelernter home with the three typed pages and a portrait.

14Dynamite, Manhattan, 1939p. 209

"Dynamite, Manhattan, 1939" opens with Life's 1939 portrait of America and a photograph of an unguarded dynamite store on a New York construction site, and asks why people then could be trusted with such risks. Gelernter's answer is that 1939 lived in an ought culture, in which daily conduct followed rules that people kept because they were expected to. The chapter catalogues these rules: how to greet a stranger, when to remove a hat, who stands for whom, which clothes suit which occasions, and how porters, filling-station attendants and housecall doctors served the public. Emily Post's 1937 etiquette book, film scenes and a La Guardia anecdote show that such rules were enforced and not merely decorative. Gelernter then turns to the larger oughts governing sex, divorce and contraception, and argues that good conduct is built by practice, as Theodore Roosevelt and traditional Judaism both suggest. The chapter closes by setting these habits against present-day ones, arguing that the loss of small oughts helps explain why the dynamite could no longer be left unguarded.

15Technology: Frighteningp. 222

"Technology: Frightening" sets the fair's optimism against the fear of war and crime that Mark Handler voiced to Miss Glassman as they walked the Court of Power, the Plaza of Light and the Pharmacy and Metals buildings. Her diary describes the tulip beds, the Helicline and a lunch at the Brass Rail, while Handler's worry that bombs would one day fall on children in neighboring houses is met with her reassurance that every life carries risks. Gelernter then shifts to the 1930s: the Lindbergh kidnapping, the FBI's pursuit of Dillinger, the rapid execution of Hauptmann, and La Guardia's crime-fighting displays at the New York Building. The chapter's central case is Picasso's Guernica, the 1937 painting of an air raid that was shown in New York in 1939 and captured public fear of bombing from the sky. The closing argument is that airplanes overhead at the fair looked, to visitors, like bombers that could kill them.

New York 1939
16When Life Turns Out to Be a Sand Castlep. 232

"When Life Turns Out to Be a Sand Castle" follows Mark Handler and Mrs. Levine from 1940 to the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Gelernter presents the chapter through a third interview and extracts from Mrs. Levine's diary. Handler's choice of engineering at Yale over architecture, a path his parents had urged and for which a letter from Robert Moses helped secure admission, postponed their marriage and set him on a demanding course. The couple's life is described as serene and dutiful, with Friday-night meals and disputes over Jewish observance, before the wealthy Tierney commissions Handler to design a progressive school whose amphitheater-like building is described in detail. Gelernter then recounts Handler's question at a New School lecture on the Moscow trials, the couple's 1941 walk on the Brooklyn Promenade, and their evenings at Roseland and Luna Park. The chapter ends with Pearl Harbor, Handler's enlistment and the collapse of the school project, and the dimout as an image of a life that was built on sand.

17Technology: Goodp. 254

"Technology: Good" argues that the technological changes of the 1930s, such as electrification, the automobile and the household appliance, altered daily life far more than the computer has altered ours. Miss Glassman's diary takes the couple across the Plaza of Light, past the Con Edison and Electric Utilities buildings, through the Street of Yesterday with its gaslights, and out along the Avenue of Tomorrow past a forty-foot waterfall. Her memories of the old street lead Gelernter to the household revolution of the era, with the rise of vacuum cleaners, washing machines and refrigerators between 1923 and 1939. The chapter then turns to the present, comparing the computer's effect on text, architecture and games with earlier changes, and it reproduces a late-thirties list of forty-five years of discoveries. Its last image is La Guardia's rusty spade at the groundbreaking, which Gelernter uses to show how thoroughly 1939 had improved ordinary life.

New York 1939
18The Art of the Microcosmp. 264

"The Art of the Microcosm" describes the Con Edison City of Light diorama, which Miss Glassman's diary calls the most dramatic show at the fair, with a model of Manhattan, a thunderstorm and nightfall. Gelernter argues that the fair's enthusiasm for dioramas expressed a thirties wish to hold the city whole from an overview. The chapter ends by noting that the buildings were designed by Harrison and Fouilhoux and that their fountains were choreographed by Calder.

New York 1939
19Robot!p. 267

"Robot!" follows Miss Glassman and Mark Handler through the Westinghouse building, where the time capsule sealed in 1938 for opening in 6939 is described along with its contents and the Book of Record sent to libraries. The diary then turns to Elektro, a seven-foot robot and its dog Sparko, which Miss Glassman finds clunky and unimpressive, and Gelernter uses it to show the fair's faith in automation. At General Electric the couple watch an artificial lightning demonstration, staged to test field equipment, which overwhelms the audience. Gelernter presents the show as an example of the fair's taste for spectacle and danger. The chapter ends with Handler silent and half-smiling after the show as the couple head for the International Zone.

New York 1939
20The Landscape and Its Sanctityp. 273

Gelernter argues that Americans in the 1930s believed they could control both the landscape and the future, and that this confidence has since drained away. The evidence is the decade's building programme: New York's parkways, bridges and tunnels, Boulder Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, the planned town of Radburn and Margaret Bourke-White's photograph of Fort Peck Dam under construction. Architects' drawings, Lewis Hine's photograph of an engineer on a skyscraper and the fair's slogan 'Building the World of Tomorrow' show an almost spiritual faith in building. Set against this is a present-day view of nature that leaves people passive, illustrated by the decades that passed before the West Side highway, which collapsed in 1974, was replaced and by the stalled debate over public toilets in New York. The result is a busy society that goes nowhere, a 'postutopian' condition in which activity adds up to nothing. The chapter closes by doubting that a nation which has given up its claims on space can keep its claims on time.

New York 1939
21Sudden Darkp. 282

This chapter is built almost entirely from extracts of the diary kept by Hattie Glassman, who records the months before her fiancé Mark Handler, an architect, was called up for military service. Gelernter lets the diary carry the story, so the reader hears Handler's dry self-doubt ('I am terrified') alongside Glassman's strained and sometimes painful intimacy with him in a borrowed, unheated house near New Haven. Small domestic details, such as learning to light a fire from library books, the Gershwin records and the Beethoven quartets, and Handler's design for an improbable house of pitched-roof boxes, show the couple trying to hold on to a future that the war was taking away. The chapter ends with the induction notice, the farewell at Penn Station with Handler's parents and the narrator's last words, a Greek prayer, Kyrie eleison. The fair appears only in memory, and the chapter's weight comes from what the reader already knows about the war that follows.

22Obsessionp. 291

Gelernter argues that the 1930s combined vicious anti-Semitism with extraordinary Jewish prominence, and that the historical record has told only one side. The chapter opens with the fair's Freedom Pavilion, planned to show work by Germans exiled by the Nazis, which collapsed after Grover Whalen withdrew support. At a meeting organised by Herbert Bayard Swope, Monsignor Lavelle warned against provoking trouble, and the effort fell apart. Gelernter sets this failure against the Czechoslovak pavilion, which the fair completed in defiance of the Nazi government in Prague. The chapter then catalogues Jewish figures in the fair's planning, design and music, and in Hollywood, New Deal politics, the press, the arts and sport. Its final claim is that American tolerance allowed this achievement, and that the present decline of American Jewry makes remembering it urgent. The argument moves from the fair to the country at large, and much of its evidence is a long list of names.

New York 1939
23At Lastp. 299

Gelernter follows a single day at the 1939 fair through the diary of Hattie Glassman, who visited it with Mark Handler in the months before they married. The day moves from the Government Zone to the French pavilion, where the diary notes the souvenirs, model rooms and travel films, and on to the Soviet building, with its Stalin and Lenin facade, a trompe l'oeil staircase and a life-size Moscow subway station. Glassman then records about half an hour of near-silence beside the Lagoon of Nations, where Handler proposes. Parenthetical notes by Gelernter supply context, including the unfinished Palestine pavilion and Robert Kohn's remark that the fair's buildings would be thrown away within a couple of years. The chapter ends with the couple's talk of having children as an act of courage in an extraordinary time, and with a little girl who brings news of another engagement. It shows the fair as a place where private hopes were tested against public optimism.

New York 1939
24Parachute Jumpp. 306

Gelernter continues Hattie Glassman's diary through an evening in the Amusement Area. Visits to Billy Rose's Aquacade, the Music Hall, a dinner at Caruso's and the Sun Valley ice rink come before the couple ride the Parachute Jump, where Glassman's nerves supply the humour and Handler's teasing the tension. Parenthetical notes give the Aquacade's stars and takings, the ride's origin as a training device for aviators, its popularity with more than half a million visitors in 1939, and its move within the area in 1940 before its later transfer to Coney Island. The chapter is less an argument than a close description of how the fair entertained people. Its evidence beyond the diary is press reviews, guidebook quotations and the fair's own promotional copy. It ends with the couple walking back to the main grounds for the lights and fireworks.

New York 1939
25Late Afternoonp. 314

Late Afternoon is the first chapter in which Gelernter, as interviewer, records Hattie Levine's account of what happened to Mark Handler after the fair. It covers his training as an engineer and officer in upstate New York and Maryland, the lists of instructions he left for Levine, and the 1943 Sicily campaign in which he was shot in the stomach. Levine describes travelling to Tunisia on a plan made possible by her father's connections, and nursing Handler, who by then was too weak to sit up and still drawing. Gelernter reproduces her memory of his last designs: a parliament building for a Jewish Palestine, shaped as a seven-branched menorah, and a folly for an oval pool. Handler died on 19 September 1943 and was buried with Levine's essay 'On the Transcendent Beauty of Building'. The chapter's emotional centre is her uneasy recognition that the family connections she resented were what got her to Tunisia.

26Unfinished Businessp. 323

Unfinished Business continues the Levine narrative with her 1946 meeting with Sarah Abbot, the wealthy patron whose family had helped stage Handler's architectural exhibition and whom Levine suspects of having been his lover. The confrontation turns on whether Abbot had seen Handler before he left, why his Jewish father opposed a marriage to a non-Jew, and a Hebrew Bible Handler carried, which Levine has never opened, convinced that three strands of Abbot's hair lie marked inside. Later quarrels over a memorial playground and Levine's regrets about her own pride follow. Gelernter then describes Levine's death at the end of September, the letter from Frances Lasker enclosing the diaries, and a white button with blue lettering, which ends the chapter with the line 'I have seen the future'. Levine's earlier view, that time need not move forward and that imagination can make it run another way, frames the chapter's sense of a future that has since disappeared.

27The Voice of the Perispherep. 332

This chapter gives a night at the 1939 fair from Hattie Glassman's diary, written after the proposal. It follows the couple along the illuminated mall past the Trylon and Perisphere, past the Petroleum building, to the Lagoon of Nations, where a water, gas and fireworks show plays to music. Gelernter's parenthetical notes explain that the Voice of the Perisphere was a piano wire amplified in a box beneath the sphere, and that the Lagoon show ran on a thousand water nozzles, 400 gas jets and noiseless fireworks devised by John Craig, operated from a console inside the United States building. Contemporary critics, quoted by Gelernter, praise the fountain displays as a new art. The chapter ends at the Rainbow Grill, where the couple finish a bottle of champagne above the city, and with a dawn reflection on perfect happiness. It is the book's most lyrical account of the fair, and it presents the fair's optimism as an experience rather than an argument.

New York 1939
28Epilogue: Herein Utopiap. 339

The epilogue has three parts. The first traces the New York fair's history from the 1934 businessmen's meetings and the rival origin stories of Grover Whalen and Joseph Shadgen, through its financing, its deal with Robert Moses to turn the Flushing Meadow ash dump into a park, and the attendance and debts of the 1939 and 1940 seasons. Gelernter then weighs the charges of commercialism, bigotry and racism, arguing that the fair mirrored an America that was both brave and biased, and that its corporate exhibits were not a plot to sell highways. The second part, on religion, argues that the 1939 faith in the future has disappeared because America has achieved a comfortable utopia, so that people can no longer see the future at all. The coda returns to an evening in May 1939 and shows Mark Handler and Hattie Glassman dancing at the Rainbow Grill, the book's last image.

New York 1939

Geppert, Alexander C. T. Fleeting Cities: Imperial Expositions in Fin-de-Siècle Europe. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010.Asia: occasional9 chapter overviews

Overview

Geppert studies five imperial expositions in Berlin, Paris and London between 1896 and 1931 (Berlin 1896, Paris 1900, London 1908, Wembley 1924, Vincennes 1931), arguing that they formed overlapping transnational networks in which organisers borrowed pavilions, colonial villages and old-town sections from one another. Against the 'identity' reading of national display, he proposes a method of space, time and personae and treats each exposition as a medium. Chapters 2 to 6 are chronological case studies, each built around one fair, its site and its impresario or planners. Chapter 7 traces 'exhibition fatigue' from German debates to the 1928 convention that created the Bureau International des Expositions, and proposes a theory of exposition practice; a short coda considers the photographs, postcards, posters and films that fixed the fairs.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are a minor, scattered thread in this book rather than a theme. Japan and China appear among the foreign colonial displays at the Trocadéro in chapter 3, Paris 1900: The Exposition Universelle as a Century's Protean Synthesis, and China is one of the countries 'visited' by the Tour du Monde panorama. Chapter 4, London 1908: Imre Kiralfy and the Franco-British Exhibition, mentions the Japan-British Exhibition of 1910 within the bi-national pattern, and describes Burmese artisans and a Buddhist priest among the performers Kiralfy recruited for his 1896 India and Ceylon Exhibition, with the terms of their contract. Chapter 5, Wembley 1924: The British Empire Exhibition as a Suburban Metropolis, has a Burma Pavilion and a Burmese Pagoda, lists Malaya and Hong Kong among the colonies, and quotes observers on the 'atmosphere of Orientalism'.

The fullest Southeast Asian material is in chapter 6, Vincennes 1931: The Exposition Coloniale as the Apotheosis of Imperial Modernity. Indochina is the centrepiece of its colonial section, where a reconstruction of Angkor Wat on the Avenue des Colonies is described as Indochina's contribution and one of two chefs-d'oeuvre. A Times correspondent notes Annamites and Cambodians going about their business among visitors, and the chapter reports the burning of the Dutch pavilion, which the Surrealists read as contempt for the peoples whose objects it held. Geppert does not discuss exhibitions held in Asia, Asian commissioners or merchants, or Asian visitors, and Japan's Expo '70 at Osaka appears only in the introduction. Ceylon and India receive far more attention than the Southeast Asian territories.

Contents

Figures and Platesp. ix
Acknowledgmentsp. xiii

Geppert thanks the advisers, colleagues and archives behind a book based on his PhD thesis, 'London vs. Paris: Imperial Exhibitions, Transitory Spaces, and Metropolitan Networks, 1880-1930'. He names his supervisors John Brewer, Luisa Passerini and Bernd Weisbrod, the European University Institute in Florence, and the Donald G. Larson Collection at Fresno. He also thanks funders, translators, editors at Palgrave, and his parents, to whom the book is dedicated.

Abbreviationsp. xvi
1Introduction: How to Read an Expositionp. 1

Geppert opens with a 1896 review by Georg Simmel of the Berliner Gewerbeausstellung, which he uses as a model for reading an exposition as a medium rather than a mirror of national identity. The book studies five imperial expositions in Berlin, Paris and London between 1896 and 1931, among them the Exposition Universelle of 1900, the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908 and the British Empire Exhibition of 1924-25. Geppert argues that these events formed overlapping transnational networks, since organizers borrowed pavilions, colonial villages and 'old town' sections from one another, and that the 'identity' framework of earlier work is too simple. He sets out a method of space, time and personae, drawing on Lefebvre and Chartier, and surveys the rise of exposition studies since the 1980s. The introduction admits that its choice of cases is partial, and it closes by promising five virtual visits that compare London, Paris and the would-be world city of Berlin.

London 1851Paris 1900Berlin 1896London 1908London 1924Paris 1931
2Berlin 1896: Wilhelm II, Georg Simmel and the Berliner Gewerbeausstellungp. 16

Geppert asks why Germany never hosted an international exposition like those in London, Paris or Vienna, and what the Berliner Gewerbeausstellung of 1896 was in their place. He traces three failed phases of the 'exhibition question' (1878-82, 1891-92, 1907-10), in which businessmen's associations and government debated and dropped plans, and attributes the final failure largely to Wilhelm II's personal opposition, with cost and site problems behind it. The chapter then turns to the privately financed fair: its layout, the colonial section with its 'native villages', the Egyptian quarter Kairo and Alt-Berlin. Reading Georg Simmel's 1896 review beside the Kaiser's letters and the press, Geppert argues that the fair tested Berlin's claim to be a world city and found it wanting next to Paris. It concludes that the fair left few urban traces but was publicised as a rehearsal for a later world exhibition.

Berlin 1896Paris 1900Chicago 1893Vienna 1873
3Paris 1900: The Exposition Universelle as a Century’s Protean Synthesisp. 62

Geppert places the 1900 Exposition Universelle within Paris's long history as the leading exhibition city, and argues that the claim of a decisive break in 1900, after which the medium became commercialised and lost its seriousness, needs closer examination. He traces the choice of the Champ de Mars, a site weighed down with revolutionary associations, and the 1895-96 press debate in which Barres, Mirbeau and others attacked the principle of further expositions. The chapter then works through the fair's paradoxes: its spill beyond the city limits, the moving sidewalk, the stereoscopic souvenir map, the national and colonial sections at the Trocadero, the Rue des Nations, the retrospective Vieux Paris and the Palais d'Electricite. It ends with the dispute over the fair's central attraction, or clou, and the Eiffel Tower's uncertain status. The chapter concludes that the medium's apparent decline reflected a shift in its function rather than a simple rupture, and that the 1911 and 1920 proposals for another Paris fair came to nothing.

Paris 1900Paris 1889
4London 1908: Imre Kiralfy and the Franco-British Exhibitionp. 101

Geppert uses the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908 at London's White City to examine Imre Kiralfy, the Budapest-born impresario who turned international exhibitions into a private commercial business. The chapter traces his earlier London ventures at Olympia and Earl's Court, and the transnational networks, from Barnum to Coubertin, through which he borrowed ideas, above all from Chicago 1893. It then analyses the 1908 fair's bi-national design, its Court of Honour, its white architecture and the commercial purpose behind the Entente cordiale rhetoric. The key evidence comprises the Flip-Flap, the Ceylon, Senegalese and Irish 'villages', Old London, the Paris pavilion, press reviews and visitors' postcards. The chapter concludes that the fair's imperial spectacle was bound up with its dual nature, that its claims to diplomatic rapprochement rested more on faith in the medium than on evidence, and that the White City's fame proved short-lived.

London 1908
5Wembley 1924: The British Empire Exhibition as a Suburban Metropolisp. 134

Geppert examines the British Empire Exhibition of 1924 and 1925 at Wembley, and the stadium built for it, treating the site as a suburban metropolis rather than a simple national display. The chapter opens with the 1990s plan to demolish the stadium, then recovers a forgotten layer of the ground: Watkin's Folly, an unfinished imitation of the Eiffel Tower abandoned in 1895, which ties Wembley to the London–Paris rivalry. The exhibition, revived in 1920 to answer London's lack of a monumental image as an imperial capital, is shown to order the Empire spatially through its symmetrical layout, Kipling's street names, reinforced-concrete pavilions and the Wembley lion emblem. The main cases are the Government Pavilion with its illuminated world map, the Indian pavilion, the West African 'Walled City' and a 1924 student protest over a newspaper article about it. Visitor accounts, from schoolchildren to a young Somali and German official reports, show how readily the imaginary world tour was accepted. The chapter concludes that Wembley was a self-referential celebration of Empire that also marked the beginning of its end.

Wembley 1924
6Vincennes 1931: The Exposition Coloniale as the Apotheosis of Imperial Modernityp. 179

Geppert examines the Exposition Coloniale Internationale held in the Bois de Vincennes in Paris from May to November 1931, presenting it as the apogee of French imperial display and the penultimate great French exposition of the century. The chapter first traces its prehistory: a rivalry between Paris and Marseilles over a colonial fair, repeated postponements that delayed it by eleven years, and the appointment of Lyautey as commissioner general in 1927. It then walks through the site, from the Porte d'Honneur and the Musée Permanent des Colonies to a reconstruction of Angkor Wat and the Avenue des Colonies, where a pavilion for each colony stood along one axis beside more than 3000 people displayed as ethnographic exhibits. The later sections turn to protest: the Communist press, the Surrealist manifesto 'Ne visitez pas l'Exposition coloniale', the fire that destroyed the Dutch pavilion, and the counter-exhibition 'La Vérité sur les colonies'. Geppert concludes that the fair aimed to create a colonial consciousness among French visitors, yet it exposed cracks in its own representational system, which survive in the one building still standing, now a museum of immigration.

Paris 1931
7Conclusion: Exhibition Fatigue, or the Rise and Fall of a Mass Mediump. 201

Geppert's concluding chapter asks why world and imperial exhibitions, at their height around 1900, also drew sustained criticism. It traces the German term Ausstellungsmüdigkeit ('exhibition fatigue') from the diaries of the engineer Max Eyth, who worked at fairs in London, Vienna and Paris, through German debates from the 1880s to similar complaints in France and Britain. It then follows the institutional response: a German permanent exhibition commission, a British Board of Trade branch, and the 1928 convention that created the Bureau International des Expositions. A proposed Anglo-German exhibition at the White City, which German officials blocked, shows how these fears worked in practice. The second half turns to sites. Geppert compares the Eiffel Tower, the Ferris wheels at Earl's Court and Paris, and the Berlin Funkturm, and treats the grounds in London, Paris and Berlin as 'cities within the city' that were absorbed into urban life in different ways. The chapter closes by proposing three elements of a theory of exposition practice: transience, the movement from space to place, and the chronotope of time and space.

London 1851Vienna 1873Paris 1878Berlin 1896London 1908Paris 1889Paris 1900Paris 1931
Coda: Pictures at an Exhibitionp. 248

The coda considers the pictures that fixed exhibitions: sketches, engravings, photographs, postcards, posters, maps and, from 1900, films. Geppert notes that the official report of the 1851 Great Exhibition already contained more than 150 early photographs. The coda argues that visuality was central to the medium, since expositions overwhelmed visitors and resisted full representation. It explains how the illustrations were chosen, to argue as well as illustrate, and ends by calling expositions a meta-medium of the fin-de-siècle metropolis.

London 1851Paris 1900

Giberti, Bruno. Designing the Centennial: A History of the 1876 International Exhibition in Philadelphia. Lexington: University Press of Kentucky, 2002.Asia: occasional7 chapter overviews

Overview

Giberti's book is a study of the 1876 Centennial exhibition in Philadelphia, read through the problem of order. Its argument is that early world's fairs displayed goods through a dual system of classification by country and by type, and that the Centennial tried to impose this system on its real space but never fully ordered it. Chapters follow the classification, the architecture (including the 1873 building competition and the engineers who shaped the buildings), the installation in the Main Building, visitors' ways of seeing, the American System of Awards that replaced medals and juries, and the permanent institutions that grew out of the fair in Philadelphia. Precedents from London 1851, Paris 1855 and 1867, and Vienna 1873 frame the argument.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East Asia is discussed occasionally in this book, and Southeast Asia barely at all. China and Japan appear as places in plans and as national sections. The densest passages are in chapter 3, The Installation in the Main Building. The proposed installation by nations put China and Japan at the far end of an American-centred world map, and the realised plan placed them in the west wing, behind Germany and Austria-Hungary, since 'no specific provision had been made for the Asian countries'. Chapter 2, The Architecture of the Exhibition, makes a related point about Vienna in 1873, where China and Japan sat at the eastern transepts.

Chapter 4, Ways of Seeing the Exhibition, lists China and Japan among the enclosed sections of smaller or less developed countries, while noting that they were the exceptions in mounting displays of metal and ceramic wares. Chapter 6, The Exhibitionary Complex in Philadelphia, has the most material: Japanese and Turkish bazaars as freestanding pavilions, American purchases of Chinese and Japanese enamels and porcelain, a Chinese costume procession in the 1880 programme of the permanent exhibition, and an Asia gallery in Kimball's Main Street arrangement at the Pennsylvania Museum. Southeast Asia appears only through Siam, named once among the Asian and African powers placed at the far end of the 1876 proposed map. The book does not treat Asian visitors or exhibitions held in Asia.

Contents

Preface

Giberti explains that the book began as a study of British design reform after the 1851 Great Exhibition but turned to the 1876 Centennial in Philadelphia and its organisers' obsession with order. The argument is that early world's fairs displayed goods through a dual system of classification by country and by type, which the Centennial tried to impose on its real space. Foucault, Martin Jay and Jonathan Crary are named as influences.

Philadelphia 1876
1The Order of the Exhibition

Giberti argues that the organisers of the 1876 Centennial were preoccupied with classification, and that this preoccupation shaped the whole exhibition. The chapter traces the classificatory logic from the French national expositions of 1798-1849, through London in 1851, where Playfair's thirty classes gave way to a geographic installation, to Paris in 1855 and 1867, where Napoleon's dual system of country and type produced a wheel-like plan. Vienna in 1873 is the counter-case, a developmental order realised as national courts along one nave. The Philadelphia scheme, drafted by a committee that included William Blake, combined these models in ten departments and a decimal notation modelled on Philadelphia's street numbers. The classification was then cut to seven departments to fit the buildings, and the official catalogue was late and disordered, which Giberti presents as evidence that the exhibition was never fully ordered. The chapter ends by arguing that the organisers had to keep revising their project in the face of conditions they could not foresee.

London 1851Paris 1855Paris 1867Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876
2The Architecture of the Exhibition

Giberti argues that the architecture of the Centennial was shaped by the split between architecture and engineering, and that engineers had more influence on the fair than architects did. The chapter takes three precedents, the Crystal Palace of 1851, the elliptical hall of Paris in 1867 and Vienna's industrial palace of 1873, and reads each for its vista, its plan and its flaws. The central case is the 1873 competition, which drew forty-three entries and whose four prizes all went to Philadelphia firms, though the committee then declined to endorse any winner. Giberti follows the unpremiated Pavilion Plan of Vaux and Radford, a timber-and-iron hall of uniform bays that the chapter treats as the most modern scheme entered, and then the process by which Pettit and Wilson, both engineers, produced a rectangular iron-and-brick building with shedlike wings. The chapter concludes that the Centennial was an engineer's landscape, whose utilitarian buildings anticipated twentieth-century modernism while architecture was still weak as a profession.

London 1851Paris 1867Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876
3The Installation in the Main Building

Giberti examines how the Centennial's Main Building was planned, built and filled with exhibits. The chapter starts with the 1873 site plan and the formal axial layout of the grounds, which drew on the Vienna and Paris fairs and set buildings across the fairground in the new pavilion pattern. It then turns to the Main Building itself, a prefabricated iron-and-wood shed that Giberti reads as a rationalised industrial loft, and to the two schemes for installing displays inside it. The first, a dual grid of nations and departments taken from Paris, was abandoned; the second, an installation by races centred on the four industrial powers, was only partly realised. Giberti argues that the organisers wanted the arrangement to make the classification visible, yet the last-minute scramble for space and the demand for striking displays along the avenues undid that transparency. The chapter closes by suggesting that the exhibition's ideal of legibility gave way to the glance of a mobile crowd.

Philadelphia 1876Paris 1867
4Ways of Seeing the Exhibition

Giberti turns from the planning of the Centennial to the visitor's experience of it, asking how the exhibition looked and felt from inside. Walking the nave, visitors faced a street of national sections that contemporaries compared to a shopping arcade, and most reported bewilderment rather than clear understanding. The chapter then examines particular national courts, including Sweden, France and Frank Furness's Brazilian court, and the ways exhibitors built their displays, from goods piled on the floor to vitrines, compound showcases and walk-in structures such as the Doulton temple. It works through the technique of more and the model room, and argues that mannequins, wax figures and even the living body blurred the line between goods and people. Views from the towers and the balloon overview let visitors see the whole, but the chapter concludes that the exhibition encouraged a distracted, mobile glance and turned objects into commodities loosened from their origins.

Philadelphia 1876
5The American System of Awards

Giberti explains how the Centennial replaced the medal-and-jury system of earlier fairs with an American System of Awards based on signed judges' reports. The chapter begins with Judges' Hall and with the defects of juries that critics such as Beckwith and Francis Walker had identified, then sets out the new system's articles, its bronze medal and the Grouping for the Judges' Work that replaced the original classification. Its central case is the revolt of the Group 27 judges on the Fine Arts, who could not rank paintings as they ranked sewing machines, and the Committee on Appeals, which added 628 further citations. Giberti shows how the mass of undifferentiated reports levelled goods, and reads the art judges' protest as an attempt to protect the aura of the artwork from the market. The chapter follows the system to Chicago in 1893 and 1933 and concludes that the new art institutions of the period express anxiety about the value of things.

Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893Chicago 1933
6The Exhibitionary Complex in Philadelphia

Giberti examines the institutions that grew out of the Centennial in Philadelphia: the Permanent International Exhibition of 1877 to 1881 in the Main Building, the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Art in Memorial Hall, and John Wanamaker's Grand Depot department store. Giberti argues that the exhibition was an ambiguous institution, neither quite museum nor quite market, and that its problems of order, architecture, installation, display and evaluation reappeared in each successor in a different form. The evidence is mainly documentary: the International Exhibition Company's bulletins and finances, the museum's acquisitions and trustees' reports, Wanamaker's own statements, and photographs of Memorial Hall and the Chestnut Street store. Giberti sets the museum's vitrines and Moore Memorial Room against the circular counters of the Grand Depot, and reads the store's plan as an echo of the dual classification at the 1867 Paris exposition. The conclusion is that the department store came closest to the exhibition's ideal of a unitary panorama of goods, while the museum drifted toward representational architecture and art-historical display, so that the Centennial's design problems were carried into the permanent institutions of the modern city.

Philadelphia 1876Philadelphia 1877Paris 1867

Gilbert, James. Perfect Cities: Chicago’s Utopias of 1893. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991.Asia: occasional8 chapter overviews

Overview

Gilbert uses the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 to ask how urban middle-class audiences made sense of a Chicago full of immigrants, cultural diversity and disorder. The fair is read as a model of the city, divided between the neoclassical White City of Burnham and Olmsted and the commercial Midway Plaisance organised by Sol Bloom. Four urban environments are examined: the city imagined in guidebooks, the fair, George Pullman's company town and Dwight Moody's evangelical city. Gilbert argues that the contest between commercial popular culture and a culture of history and morality was never resolved. The seven chapters move from the guidebooks and the fair to Pullman, Moody and the 'gray city' that replaced the White City after the fire of 1894.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia appear occasionally, almost all in Chapter 4, 'First City: Form and Fantasy', which treats the Midway of the 1893 fair. The Japanese pavilion is discussed as Japan's own participation, with a range of consumer products that 'obviously contradicted racial stereotypes about Asians' staged in the anthropological exhibits. Japan also appears in the Japanese Bazaar on the Midway and in the Japanese garden and temple on Wooded Island, which Olmsted accepted only as a compromise. Displays organised by others include the Chinese Village and the Javanese Village, which a guidebook invokes in its account of the Dahomey Village as showing 'striking degrees of barbarism'.

Elsewhere the region is barely present. A Chinese theatre is one item in a list of attractions at the White City Amusement Park of 1905 in Chapter 7, and the Preface and Chapters 1 to 3 do not name either region. The Midway's 'Oriental' centre, with its belly dancing, is Middle Eastern in the book's own description, so the word is not evidence of East Asian coverage. Asian visitors and observers are not discussed, and Southeast Asia is confined to the Javanese Village.

Contents

Illustrationsp. vii
Prefacep. ix

Gilbert opens with childhood train trips into Chicago from a suburb on the city's southeast edge, and with the 1948 Railroad Fair at Burnham Park. These memories lead to a reflection on the gap between the child's Chicago and the grander city of the 1890s that the book reconstructs. The preface also raises unanswered questions about Gilbert's own family and recalls a neighbour campaigning to save Louis Sullivan's buildings. It ends with thanks to archives and colleagues.

Chicago 1948
1Itinerariesp. 1

Gilbert uses the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 in Chicago to ask how urban middle-class audiences tried to make sense of a city full of cultural diversity. Four total urban environments are examined: the city imagined in guidebooks, the fair itself, the Pullman company town and the evangelical city founded by Dwight Moody and Turlington Harvey. Gilbert defines the middle class, the elite, commercial culture and popular culture, supported by census tables on occupational growth and city populations, and draws on Robert Wiebe's account of the new professions. The fair is presented as an uneasy compromise between the controlled White City and the commercial Midway, and the audience itself had to reconcile the two. The chapter ends with tourism, which gave visitors a familiar setting in a strange place, and with the fair's classicism, which looked to the past to reassure visitors about the future.

Chicago 1893
2Chicago: Two Profilesp. 23

Gilbert opens with Chicago around 1893 as a flat, grid-planned city of immigrants, factories, slums and new skyscrapers, which its middle class experienced as disorder and strangeness. He traces how rapid growth, suburbanization and a largely foreign-born population unsettled residents, and how elites and the new middle class answered with cultural institutions and a moral order. His main evidence is biographical. The principal figures behind the World's Columbian Exposition, among them Dwight Moody, Turlington Harvey, George Pullman, Marshall Field and Harlow Higinbotham, nearly all came from the evangelical burned-over district of western New York, and Gilbert argues that this upbringing led them to see commerce and culture as sanctified by religion. He sets them against Sol Bloom, a Chicago entrepreneur of popular street culture for whom success and popularity replaced moral judgement. The chapter ends by framing the book's story as a contest between these two outlooks.

Chicago 1893
3Approaches: Discovery from a Distancep. 45

Gilbert examines how Chicago's guidebooks and urban journalism shaped visitors' expectations before the 1893 fair. Writers such as George Ade, Finley Peter Dunne and Henry Fuller, and guidebook authors such as Rand McNally, Harold Vynne and Louis Schick, presented a city of bewildering diversity but kept it at arm's length through itineraries, hotel lists and reassuring tones. Gilbert works through close readings of these texts, including Ade's detached sketches, Stine's inventories of institutions and the guides' brief treatment of the Haymarket affair and the Great Fire. He argues that the guidebooks presented Chicago as a city of the future, its past dissolved in the fire's rebuilding, and that separating cultural diversity from moral intensity made the city safe for middle-class consumers. The chapter concludes that the genre let the middle class find its place in an unfamiliar urban world by masking the city's real conditions.

Chicago 1893
4First City: Form and Fantasyp. 75

Gilbert reads the 1893 Columbian Exposition as a model of Chicago itself, set out as two opposed cultures: the White City of neoclassical staff buildings, planned by Daniel Burnham and Frederick Law Olmsted, and the commercial Midway Plaisance, organized by Sol Bloom. Drawing on visitor diaries, official minutes, concession agreements and guidebooks, he shows how the fair administration tried to police the Midway, rejecting African American and union applications and closing indecent dances. Key cases include the German and Irish villages, the Dahomey Village, the Ferris Wheel, the Woman's Building and Hovenden's painting Breaking Home Ties, which Gilbert reads as a sentimental image of the prodigal son. Failures such as the Sunday-closing dispute and Theodore Thomas's empty concerts show commerce gaining ground. The chapter concludes that the fair anticipated a reproducible modern mass culture, and that the contest between commercial culture and a culture of history and morality remained unresolved.

Chicago 1893
5Second City: Our Townp. 131

Gilbert opens with the special train that carried Chicago's elite to the company town of Pullman in January 1883, and uses that evening to treat the town as a staged environment. The chapter argues that George Pullman planned his houses, arcade, church and clock tower, along with his sleeping cars and his wife Hattie's social life, as one project to shape the behaviour of workers, customers and visitors. It works through the town's amenities and their controls: the Arcade library and theatre, the ban on saloons, and pressure on rents and votes, along with the promotional literature prepared for the 1893 World's Fair, when thousands of visitors came to see the town. Gilbert sets this paternalism against the Fair's balance of White City and Midway, and draws on the Pullmans' letters and diaries for the family's social life. The chapter concludes that the 1894 strike exposed the gap between the town's appearance and its residents' lives, and that Roseland's saloons and cheap amusements eventually washed back over the model community.

Chicago 1893
6Third City: The Evangelical Metropolisp. 169

Gilbert opens with Dwight Moody preaching the parable of the Prodigal Son in Chicago's Haymarket Theatre during the 1893 World's Fair. The chapter argues that Moody, unlike George Pullman, did not try to banish popular culture from his city but tried to master it, adopting theatres, circus tents, newspaper advertising and mass-produced tickets for evangelism. It traces Moody's career from shoe salesman and YMCA worker to evangelist, and places him in the lineage of Charles Finney. The main evidence is the 1893 campaign, with its 220 staff, Sunday services in theatres and at Forepaugh's Circus, and the 'Gospel Wagons', together with the temperance town of Harvey, Illinois, which Turlington Harvey marketed to Fair visitors. Gilbert concludes that the campaign reached mostly Protestants, and that its fusion of revivalism and mass media anticipated Fundamentalism, even as Moody grew more pessimistic about the city after 1893.

Chicago 1893
7Exit: The Gray Cityp. 209

Gilbert's closing chapter follows Chicago from the burning of the White City in 1894 to the realist and sociological image of a 'gray city' that replaced it. It argues that the fires, the Pullman strike and the depression swept away the fiction of a unified, elite-led city, and that later schemes, from Burnham's 1909 plan to the White City Amusement Park of 1905, either ignored or commercialised the popular culture the Fair had pushed onto the Midway. The evidence includes the fates of Pullman and Moody, Stead's If Christ Came to Chicago, the Hull-House maps and labor museum, the new Field Museum and Museum of Science and Industry, and the novels of Herrick, Dreiser, Sinclair and London, and the University of Chicago sociologists. Gilbert concludes that the city came to be seen as diverse, private and disorganised rather than as a pageant under command, and that the cultural problems posed in 1893 kept returning through twentieth-century American life.

Chicago 1893

Gosden, Chris, and Chantal Knowles. Collecting Colonialism: Material Culture and Colonial Change. Oxford: Berg, 2001.Asia: occasional12 chapter overviews

Overview

Gosden and Knowles's Collecting Colonialism (2001) studies four collections from western New Britain, made between 1910 and 1937 by Albert Buell Lewis, Felix Speiser, John Alexander Todd and Beatrice Blackwood. Its argument is that colonial relations, not vanishing cultures, shaped what the collections contain: objects are processes whose meanings changed between village and museum, and contact produced new forms of difference rather than acculturation. After an introduction and a history of the district under German and Australian rule, the book gives one chapter to each collector, then compares the four collections, examines the varieties of colonialism and ends with its morality. The scope is one region and one kind of collecting, museum collecting in the field, with the Chicago museum's origins in the 1893 Columbian Exposition touched on.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia appear occasionally, and never as places of exhibition. The main Asian presence is the colonial population of Chinese and Japanese traders, shopkeepers and labourers. Chapter I notes that patrol officers in Rabaul were sent to a Chinese tailor, and that a cargo-cult leader prophesied that all the Chinese would leave New Guinea. Chapter II records labour for Europeans or Chinese on the plantations and a Chinese dwelling at Arawe Plantation, and chapter VII a Chinese storekeeper killed in the Upper Watut. Chapter IV, on Albert Buell Lewis, gives the fullest account, of the Japanese merchant Isokichi Komine, whose collection of over 3,000 objects Lewis bought in 1911 for Chicago; its material came from the Admiralties and New Ireland, not Asia. The same chapter reports that the Kilenge said most of their masks were destroyed by the Japanese in the Second World War.

Southeast Asia enters mainly as culture-historical comparison. Blackwood's blowpipes in chapter I are compared with Borneo. Speiser, in chapter V, links Arawe ceremony and tooth-blackening with Nias, west of Sumatra, and with Indonesia, a theme of his 1938 Copenhagen paper; his 1946 survey counts one style as imported from 'Indonesia and mainland Asia'. Chapter IX suggests that recent exchange may link New Guinea with southeast Asia. Dorsey's Field Museum expeditions, in chapter IV, were 'mainly focused on East Asia and Melanesia', but the book does not follow that programme.

Contents

List of Figures
List of Maps
List of Tables
Acknowledgements

Gosden and Knowles thank the Leverhulme Trust and the British Academy for funding the multi-sited study, which took them to four museums and several archives. They acknowledge the New Britain scholars whose work shaped the project and the staff of the four museums, and they name readers who commented on drafts, especially Jim Specht. They also say that a second volume on German museum collections from the region is in preparation.

Preface

Gosden and Knowles argue that colonial New Guinea was one field of mutual influence, not two societies in collision, so museum collections record outcomes of colonial exchange. They study four collections from New Britain made between 1910 and 1937 by Lewis, Blackwood, Speiser and Todd, setting each collector's background beside patrol reports and mission archives. The preface also asks how objects made human relations real for colonial people and claims that museum collections hold research potential for colonial history.

1People, Objects and Colonial Relations

Gosden and Knowles open with a strip of barkcloth that Beatrice Blackwood collected in 1937 from Möwehafen in New Britain, cut from a man's belt and used to bind an infant's head. From this one object they trace successive lives: its use as male dress, its recycling, its purchase and documentation, and its present place in the Pitt Rivers Museum. The chapter then sets out their model of colonial New Guinea, in which Melanesians, Europeans and Asians were bound together through exchange, yet white writers stressed their separateness and never acknowledged their dependence on local people. Cargo cults, the staged dress and flag ceremonies of patrol officers, and planters' and anthropologists' accounts serve as evidence. Through the production and exchange of trochus-shell armbands, the authors argue that objects are processes whose meanings change between village and museum. The chapter ends by stressing the experimental, unstable character of colonial relations, which produced new forms of difference rather than acculturation.

2Colonial Culture and History in West New Britain

Chapter Two bridges the general argument and the detailed fieldwork by giving a history of western New Britain. It describes pre-colonial societies organised in small cognatic hamlets, linked by Siassi trade, languages and ceremonies, and shows how colonial rule reshaped them. The core is a division into two periods: German rule from 1884 to 1914, when a recruiting and trading economy gave way to plantations, head taxes, luluai and tultul offices and large coastal villages; and Australian administration from 1914 to 1942, under military rule and then the mandate, with foot patrols, the Expropriation Board and competing Anglican and Catholic missions on the south coast. The authors draw on patrol reports, letters and plantation records, using the 1888 Ritter collapse, the epidemics of the 1890s, the recruiting ban and Arawe Plantation as cases. They close by noting that the collectors worked as temporary members of this colonial society, and turn to the collections.

3The Collectors and their Collections

This chapter introduces the four museum collections of Lewis, Speiser, Todd and Blackwood and the method used to analyse them. Gosden and Knowles place their project alongside work on collecting in Africa and Papua New Guinea, and set out each collector's dates, institution and share of the objects. They argue that collections are direct records of the colonial relations that produced them, not distorted proxies for vanishing cultures. The main evidence is Blackwood's diaries and notebooks, which record purchases of 275 items from some twenty-four named people using trade goods, money, tobacco and knives. Human skulls were sold for 10s each, generally by men, and a field assistant, Magnin, sold socially marked items. Speiser and Blackwood could still buy mokmok and singa stones in the 1930s, which the authors read as a temporary devaluation after the missions arrived, while gold-lip shells and large pig's-tusk ornaments stayed expensive. The chapter then compares the collectors' priorities, summarises an alphabetical list of Arawe material culture, and explains how 901 objects were recorded by category, gender and provenance. It closes with the fieldwork and archive research carried out for the book.

4Albert Buell Lewis

Chapter Four turns to Albert Buell Lewis, who collected on the south coast of New Britain for eight weeks in 1909-10 during a wider Melanesian survey for the Field Museum, Chicago. It first traces the museum's history, from its founding on the Columbian Exposition of 1893 to George Dorsey's policy of expedition collecting aimed at salvaging traditional objects before they vanished. Lewis's position in German New Guinea, among plantation managers, Governor Hahl and rival collectors such as Schoede, shaped what he could buy. A diary entry and a notebook account of the same inland visit show a big man removing objects from sight, which the authors read as local control over the collection. The 330 New Britain objects are then examined by category, from shields, blowpipes and masks to valuables, and the authors note that gold-lip shells are absent except where Lewis bought the Komine collection. They argue that these gaps reflect the limits of purchase rather than a lack of collecting interest. The chapter ends with the long delay before the collection was catalogued and displayed, Lewis's modest publication record, and later research on exchange networks.

Chicago 1893
5Felix Speiser

Gosden and Knowles reconstruct the collection that Felix Speiser made on the south coast of New Britain in 1929 and 1930, and the relations that shaped it. Speiser worked from Gasmata, Kandrian and the Arawe Islands, and the chapter shows how his collecting depended on the district officer Calcutt, the planter Harry Bond and, above all, the big man and luluai Aliwa, whose knowledge of the past became Speiser's main source. Speiser's interest in culture history and ceremony led him to acquire blowpipes, pig's-tusk ornaments, head-binding items and Kuiunke masks, which no other collector obtained. The authors also show that Speiser collected for exchange as well as for study: duplicates were set aside for sale, and the central collection went to the Basel museum for 25,000 Swiss francs. They conclude that Speiser's collection, the smallest of the four, carries the most anthropological detail, and that its ceremonial objects record a shift from male-only rituals to rites involving the whole community.

6John Alexander Todd

Gosden and Knowles examine John Alexander Todd, a Sydney University student who made a collection on the south coast of New Britain in 1933-4 and returned there in 1935-6. The chapter argues that Todd's collection was a minor part of his fieldwork, and that his notes and diaries are lost, so the objects must be read alongside his published articles and a catalogue he compiled. The authors place Todd within the Sydney anthropology department, where Radcliffe-Brown and Rockefeller funding shaped what students could do, and they read his article on native offences and European law as evidence of his interest in colonial rule. The collection is analysed for its women's material, including skirts and looped vine bags, its valuables such as dogs'-teeth ornaments and cassowary-quill belts, and what its absences reveal, notably the scarcity of stone tools. The chapter ends with Todd's move into law in 1937 and the partial loss of the 245 objects he left at Sydney, of which 186 survive.

7Beatrice Blackwood

Gosden and Knowles examine the collection that Beatrice Blackwood made in the Arawe region of New Britain in 1937, during a four-month stay centred on Kandrian and Gasmata. The chapter stresses her interest in process: she gathered raw materials, tools and partly made objects, especially for barkcloth, blowpipes and head deformation, and copied canoe-paddle designs into a sketchbook. Her relations with the local men Magnin and Alip and with Owas are reconstructed from her diaries, which show how knives, tobacco and shillings were negotiated, and how Magnin sold her a pig's-tusk ornament with his father's teeth attached. The authors also place her within colonial society, noting that she lodged in a government house and found white visitors and rival missions disrupting her work. The chapter ends with the fate of the collection at the Pitt Rivers Museum, where most of it went into storage and her unpublished manuscript on Arawe material culture was never produced.

8Comparing the Collections: Experiment, Social Relations and Agency

Gosden and Knowles compare the four collections made in western New Britain between 1910 and 1937 to argue that colonial rule changed the community, its exchange relations and its objects in distinct ways. They treat objects as processes of production, exchange and use, following stone axes, obsidian, shell skills and barkcloth to show how the shift from stone to steel altered garden work, social differentiation and relations with Europeans. Tables of 809 classified items and of artefact-type percentages show that warfare, stone tool, container and music objects declined while valuables increased, and the authors find that the formal qualities of pig's-tusk ornaments, shields and barkcloth changed little, although shield backs stopped being painted. Their central claim is that exchange networks widened, with the Siassi trade and the plantations drawing in more people, and that European goods were exchanged but never became socially marked. The chapter concludes that community was remade around large villages and wider exchange, and that objects bound to names and identities carried continuity through these changes.

9Varieties of Colonialism

Gosden and Knowles argue that colonial culture in New Guinea was varied, and that the variety has two sources: the chance of personalities and events, and the long regional histories that shaped how each area dealt with Europeans. They sketch a spectrum of exchange with whites, from refusing to trade, through trading existing objects, to making goods for sale, and illustrate it with Manus obsidian daggers and spears made for European collectors, Trobriand carvings promoted by a trader's wife, and Tanga's split between kastam and bisnis. Beneath the variety lies a common pattern: New Guineans treated whites as ancestral figures, traded with them, and often built cargo cults, which the authors read as attempts to reach the sources of white power rather than as resistance. The second half turns to prehistory, using Lapita pottery and the Siassi exchange system in western New Britain and the sweet potato and pig herds of the Highlands. The chapter concludes that colonial relations were experiments, and that Arawe's stable objects took on new meanings, a point that leads on to the morality of colonialism.

10The Morality of Colonialism

Gosden and Knowles argue that colonialism reordered the moral world of New Guineans, who had to decide which relationships were proper and how to reach white wealth. Objects had no fixed value in this experimental arena. In western New Britain, population decline, labour migration and changed ritual did not produce the collapse the salvage paradigm predicted; people drew on local kinship and ceremony instead. In Arawe, the authors conclude, objects kept their forms while their meanings shifted.
