Greenhalgh, Paul. Ephemeral Vistas: The Expositions Universelles, Great Exhibitions and World’s Fairs, 1851–1939. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1988.Asia: substantial11 chapter overviews

Overview

Greenhalgh's book is a study of how international exhibitions from 1851 to 1940 gained legitimacy as a medium of national expression and kept it through a traumatic period. It concentrates on Britain, France and the United States, treating about thirty major events in detail, and argues that the exhibitions were saturated with liberal ideology and imperial display. After an introduction and a chapter on origins, chapters on funding, imperial display, human showcases (peoples exhibited in native villages), national profiles, design and architecture, women's exhibiting, and the fine arts are organised by theme. A short postscript on the surviving Crystal Palace at Sydenham closes the argument.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia receive substantial attention, concentrated in chapters 3 and 4, and mostly as objects of imperial display rather than as exhibitors. Chapter 3, Imperial display, centres on the Japan-British Exhibition of 1910, where Japan's Colonial Palace showed Formosa, Korea and Manchuria and the Japanese army was shown, and on the Indochinese section at Paris 1889, the Dutch Indies at Paris 1900 and the Philippine displays at Buffalo 1901 and St Louis 1904. Chapter 4, Human showcases, covers the Tonkinese village and Cambodian elephant at the Paris expositions, the Kampong-Javanese village, a private undertaking subtitled 'Life in the Dutch Indies', the Chinese and Japanese teahouses and Javanese villagers at Chicago, and the St Louis Philippine villages, arranged by stage of civilisation from Negritos to Moros. Chapter 11, The prefabricated and the mass-produced, treats Japanese art as a source of Western design reform, shown from London 1862 onwards.

Asia is a comparison within a wider empire story. India and Ceylon, outside this question, get far more space in the imperial and village chapters. Korea and Manchuria appear only in one quoted 1910 guide passage, and the Chinese figure mostly as crowds, villagers and tea-house staff. Burma, Malaya, Hong Kong and Sarawak appear mainly in lists of colonies at Wembley in 1924 and Glasgow in 1938.

Contents

List of illustrationsp. vi
General editor's forewordp. ix

MacKenzie, the general editor of the series, presents Greenhalgh's book as a study of imperialism as a habit of mind and of the exhibitions as one of its cultural products. He argues that the fairs displayed imperial economics and racial hierarchy through spectacle, yet also allowed Asian music and African art to influence European composers and painters. The foreword concludes that exhibitions bound the world into patterns of dependence while permitting unexpected and mutual contacts.

Acknowledgementsp. xi
Dedication
Introductionp. 1

Greenhalgh opens with a Geddes quotation and a picture of exhibitions as temporary cities that drew millions between 1851 and 1939. The book concentrates on Britain, France and the United States, treating about thirty major events in detail. It asks how exhibitions gained legitimacy as a medium of national expression and kept it through a traumatic period. The text is then arranged by theme after two introductory chapters, to highlight correlations and divergences in exhibiting policy.

1Origins and conceptual developmentp. 3

Greenhalgh traces how international exhibitions grew out of earlier national and local shows before the first international event, London's Great Exhibition of 1851. The chapter begins with the French national exhibitions from 1797, which the state used to revive trade after the Revolution, and follows their growing scale to 1849, alongside the English Society of Arts displays and the Mechanics Institutes shows of the 1830s. Its argument is that the idea of an international exhibition developed slowly: Boucher de Perthes's call for foreign exhibitors in 1834 and the failed French attempt of 1849 prepared the ground for Henry Cole and Prince Albert. The second half surveys the mature tradition, including the Paris show of 1855 as a reply to London, the Convention of 1928, and the four rationales used to justify the events: peace, education, trade and progress. It ends by noting that the chapter has only described the bare bones of these events, which later chapters will flesh out.

Paris 1797Paris 1798London 1851Paris 1855Paris 1867Paris 1889
2Funding, politics and societyp. 27

Greenhalgh examines who paid for exhibitions and who controlled them, arguing that the events were saturated with liberal ideology and that backers wanted to maximise attendance, publicise a political position and make a profit. The Great Exhibition of 1851 is the model case: a Royal Commission, thousands of small sponsors and over four hundred local committees raised the money, and the event is read as a counter-revolutionary display staged after 1848. The chapter then compares French state funding for the Expositions Universelles with the company-run American fairs, from Philadelphia in 1876 to New York in 1939, and with Imre Kiralfy's commercial White City shows in London. It shows how attendance came to depend on popular entertainment, from the amusement areas of Paris in 1867 to the Chicago Midway in 1893, and it weighs apparent losses against the permanent buildings the fairs left behind. The chapter concludes that empire was the theme most likely to sustain audiences, which the next chapter takes up.

London 1851Paris 1867Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893London 1908New York 1939
3Imperial displayp. 52

Greenhalgh argues that empire was the theme most fully displayed at international exhibitions, and that its presentation changed between 1851 and 1940 while its presence never slackened. The chapter opens with India, the most carefully staged possession from the Great Exhibition onward, and traces how Indian courts grew from 30,000 square feet in 1851 to the Wembley palace of 1924, which cost £180,000 for the Indian site. It then turns to the handling of the white dominions and smaller colonies, to French displays of Algeria and Tunisia from 1839 through the Paris Exposition of 1889 to the colonial exhibition at Vincennes in 1931, and to the Portuguese, Dutch and Belgian sections, especially the Antwerp exposition of 1930. Buffalo in 1901, St Louis in 1904 and the Japan-British Exhibition of 1910 close the survey, with the American and Japanese displays of empire. The chapter concludes that exhibitions joined a rhetoric of progress to organised exploitation, and so embodied neither good nor evil in any simple sense.

London 1851Paris 1889Paris 1900London 1908London 1924Paris 1931Antwerp 1930St Louis 1904
Figuresp. 82
4Human showcasesp. 82

Greenhalgh examines the practice of displaying people at international exhibitions between 1889 and 1914, when colonised and other non-Western peoples were housed in reconstructed villages and watched by paying crowds. He sorts the displays into four types (imperial, educational, commercial and ambassadorial) but argues that they overlapped, and that the imperial type was the most numerous and lavish. The chapter works through the Paris 1889 and 1900 native villages, the Jardin d'Acclimatation's peopled exhibits that preceded them, Imre Kiralfy's London spectacles, and the Chicago, Buffalo and St Louis fairs, where Native American, Filipino and Dahomeyan residents were placed within a supposed evolutionary hierarchy. Commercial examples include the Cairo Street and the Indian tea-houses, and the Senegalese and Dahomeyan troupes, who toured under private entrepreneurs, receive detailed attention. Greenhalgh concludes that the displays did lasting damage by teaching mass audiences that non-European peoples were inferior, and that this harm was never repaired.

Paris 1889Paris 1900London 1908London 1909London 1911Chicago 1893Buffalo 1901St Louis 1904
5The national profilep. 112

Greenhalgh argues that international exhibitions were a main vehicle for presenting national character, and that each country built its profile from different materials. France relied on the fine arts, which it claimed as proof of its role as civiliser, and the chapter follows this from the Trocadéro of 1878 to the Paris Exposition of 1937. Britain, as its industrial lead faded at the end of the century, invented an 'Olde Englande' of Tudor villages, Shakespeare and royalty, which the Royal Pavilion of 1900 and the New York fair of 1939 both used. America's profile rested on pioneer, republican and progress themes, shown in classicism until the 1930s and then in modernist forms such as the Perisphere at New York in 1939. The main cases are the national pavilions at Paris 1900 and 1937, where the German, Soviet, Italian, Spanish and British sections are compared, and the Irish and Scottish villages, which Greenhalgh reads as a periphery to the English core. The chapter concludes that the 1937 fair, with Guernica in the Spanish pavilion, was the climax of nationalist rivalry, after which exhibitions became more muted and neutral.

Paris 1867Paris 1889Paris 1900Philadelphia 1876Paris 1937New York 1939
6The prefabricated and the mass-producedp. 142

Greenhalgh traces how the international exhibitions shaped design and architecture from 1851 to 1939, and argues that the historicist-to-modernist shift was neither linear nor complete. The Great Exhibition revealed the tension between machine production and ornament, and critics often blamed industrial methods for what was really a question of symbolic taste. The chapter then follows the buildings: Paxton's prefabricated Crystal Palace, the Model House for the Working Classes, the housing section at Paris in 1867, and the engineering halls of Paris in 1889, set against the stone-clad Grand Palais of 1900. It shows art nouveau at Paris in 1900, Turin in 1902 and London in 1908, and the arrival of full modernism at Paris in 1925, Paris in 1937 and New York in 1939. Its conclusion is that international modernism failed through its methods, losing sight of ordinary urban life, and that the earlier exhibitions had more to teach than the later ones.

London 1851Paris 1867London 1862Paris 1889Paris 1900Chicago 1893London 1908Paris 1925Paris 1937New York 1939
7Women: exhibiting and exhibitedp. 174

Greenhalgh examines what women did at exhibitions and how they were presented there, arguing that the women's buildings were both a platform and a constraint. The chapter follows the Woman's Building at Philadelphia in 1876, paid for by a women's committee after the Centennial Board withdrew its promise of space, and the Columbian of 1893, where a more radical Board of Lady Managers filled its building with international work, a mural by Mary Cassatt and a dress-reform conference. Later women's sections, at Atlanta, Buffalo, St Louis and San Francisco, were rapidly taken over by anti-suffrage forces and church-linked groups. The Palace of Women's Work at the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908 presented women as domesticated and voteless, while women working on the same site did twelve-hour shifts with only one rest room. The chapter's statistics show women making up about 3.5 per cent of the work in the Paris fine arts palaces from 1855 to 1900. Greenhalgh concludes that visibility was the one real gain the exhibitions gave women, and that women artists were little better represented in the twentieth century than in the nineteenth.

Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893London 1908Paris 1900London 1924
8The fine artsp. 198

Greenhalgh argues that fine art at exhibitions conferred status rather than attracting visitors, and that the Paris Expositions Universelles set the standard for it. The chapter follows how juries chose work: in 1878 the Beaux-Arts establishment excluded Millet and the impressionists and allowed Courbet a single canvas, while in 1900 the heaviest showing of impressionism came through Roger Marx's Centennale. Courbet's private pavilion of 1855 shows how the avant-garde protested from outside official control. Britain's sections at South Kensington and the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908 are set against the French model, with the Spielmann brothers promoting the Pre-Raphaelites. The most lasting influence, Greenhalgh suggests, came from the imperial and ethnographic displays, which shaped Gauguin, Picasso and Matisse through their contact with Oceanic, African and North African art. The chapter concludes that the fine art palaces were overrated as a source of artistic change, yet an exhibition without them would have been unsatisfactory.

Paris 1855Paris 1878Paris 1889Paris 1900London 1862London 1908
Postscriptp. 225

The Postscript visits the surviving fragments of the Crystal Palace at Sydenham and uses them to sum up the exhibitions. Greenhalgh grants that they were among the few nineteenth-century creations aimed at the masses with something other than work in mind. Yet they spread irrational pride, racial and class division and an obsession with power, and Greenhalgh concludes that their ideology still shapes the banal urban environment.

Hale, Dana S. Races on Display: French Representations of Colonized Peoples, 1886–1940. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 2008.Asia: central11 chapter overviews

Overview

Hale asks how the Third Republic represented its colonial subjects and, through them, its own identity. Using trademark labels registered in Paris and Marseilles from 1886 to 1940 and the colonial sections of the fairs in those cities, the book compares sub-Saharan Africans, North Africans and Indochinese. Part I (1886–1913) covers the empire, racial theory and the Paris fairs of 1889 and 1900; Part II (1914–1940) covers the Marseilles and Paris expositions of 1922, 1931 and 1937. A final chapter treats France's self-image as parent and brother to its colonial children. Hale argues that the images stressed human difference and French superiority, and that this framework still shapes France's ties with its former colonies.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East and Southeast Asia are central to the book, but almost entirely through Indochina, one of the three colonial groups the study is built around. Chapters 4 ('Indochinese: Gentle Subjects') and 7 ('Indochinese: Fils Doué') are devoted to it, covering trademarks and the 1900, 1922, 1931 and 1937 fairs. Chapter 1 covers Indochina's conquest and its pavilions at the 1889 Paris fair, and chapter 8 treats the Indochinese as part of France's self-presentation. Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos appear as conquered territories and as exhibits: the Angkor Wat reconstructions of 1922 and 1931, the Cambodian royal ballet, the Théâtre Annamite, the dragon procession and the Rue Annamite, with artisans, soldiers and performers housed on the fairgrounds. Asian visitors include the prince of Annam in 1889.

East Asia gets only passing attention. Chinese appear as neighbours seen as troublesome in the Tonkin affair that opens chapter 4, and as workers in pay and hours disputes (chapter 4), and as rickshaw pullers whose planned employment in Paris in 1931 was dropped after the Chinese consul protested (chapter 7). Japan and Korea get no discussion, though kimono-clad women recur on trademarks. In Southeast Asia, Thailand appears only as a threat to Cambodia, and the Javanese dancers of 1889 and the Malays of the 1931 ethnographic directives are passing mentions; the Philippines, the Dutch East Indies and Burma are absent.

Contents

Acknowledgmentsp. ix

Hale thanks the people and institutions behind the book, which began as a doctoral thesis at Brandeis University under Paul Jankowski. They name a year of research in France supported by a Ford Foundation fellowship and an exchange with the Ecole Normale Supérieure, Howard University grants and an American Historical Association award that extended the study to 1940, and the archivists in Paris, Provence and Washington who guided the research. Hale also thanks family, friends and the editors at Indiana University Press.

Introductionp. 1

Hale asks how a state defines its own identity and that of peoples it treats as outsiders, and argues that the Third Republic built a national self-image of France as an imperial power after its defeat in 1870. The book draws on comparative studies of world's fairs, cultural anthropology and French colonial history. Its evidence comes from colonial expositions in Paris and Marseilles and from trademark images registered in those cities between 1886 and 1940, with the 1900 Exposition universelle as a leading case of how Africans, North Africans and Indochinese were staged. The introduction outlines the book's two halves, covering the years 1886 to 1913 and the period from World War I to 1940, and summarises the chapters on each group. It concludes that French images of race stressed cultural supremacy and a civilising mission, and that the same framework still shapes France's ties with its former colonies.

Paris 1900
Part IPART I. ON THE PATH TO CIVILIZATION, 1886–1913p. 7
1Overseas Empire and Race during the Third Republicp. 9

Hale's first chapter explains how the Third Republic acquired its empire and how officials and businessmen used racial ideas to justify it. It surveys the conquests of Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco, West Africa, Madagascar and Indochina, and argues that French notions of race were unstable and hierarchical, placing Europeans at the top, Asians and Arabs below, and sub-Saharan Africans at the bottom. Its main evidence is the colonial sections of the Paris expositions, above all those of 1878 and 1889, where separate pavilions, concessions, indigenous villages and African troops first appeared. The chapter then introduces the trademark survey, which shows how commercial images of colonial peoples reinforced official displays. It ends by concluding that race-based trademarks and colonial exhibitions together stressed human difference and French superiority, a theme the later chapters test.

Paris 1878Paris 1889
2Sub-Saharan Africans: “Uncivilized Types”p. 23

Hale traces how French images of sub-Saharan Africans as uncivilized types took shape between the 1880s and the First World War, testing them against commercial trademarks and the colonial sections of the 1900 Exposition universelle in Paris. The chapter starts with the scientific and popular background, including anthropologists' racial rankings and the display of Africans at the Jardin d'acclimatation. It then surveys 316 French trademark labels from 1886 to 1913, focusing on the recurring black head, cleaning products that wash blackness away, and coffee and chocolate labels that cast black men as servants or plantation workers. At the fair, Hale compares the Malagasy, Dahomean and Senegalese displays, the language classes held for them, and the official ethnographic notices that ranked peoples by labour value and moral character. The chapter concludes that both sources present Africans as exotic and subordinate, capable of progress only through French tutelage, and that the notices condemned African vices that French society shared without ever making the comparison.

Paris 1900
3North Africans: Mysterious Peoplesp. 46

Hale examines how French trademarks and the 1900 Paris exposition presented North Africans as mysterious Muslims, while also promoting Algeria and Tunisia as economically integrated parts of France. The chapter begins with racial theories that placed Arabs and Berbers as a lesser white group, which made the Maghreb easier to accept as part of the nation. It then sorts trademark labels for soap, coffee, dates, flour and wine, showing North Africans as farmers, merchants, warriors and devout Muslims, often on products with no link to the region. The core case is the official Algerian and Tunisian sections, including the Tunisian souk and the privately run Algerian Attractions, where a diorama company exhibited a woman in Moorish dress, her head and wrists locked in a stock, as an 'Arab custom', while the commissioner's office struggled to enforce rules requiring crafts to be made on site. Hale concludes that the fair offered two images, a modernising economic colony and a mysterious Oriental culture, and that the contradiction served the same propaganda purpose of encouraging trade and investment.

Paris 1900
4Indochinese: Gentle Subjectsp. 67

Hale argues that French officials and trademark designers presented the peoples of Indochina as diligent, gentle and skilled subjects, a portrayal that suited the political and economic aims of Governor General Paul Doumer. The chapter opens with the Tonkin affair and French views of the Chinese as troublesome, then analyses trademarks for tea, cloth, tobacco and lacquer, which show Asians in tranquil domestic scenes or at manual work, rarely under European supervision. At the 1900 Paris exposition, the Indochinese section copied Vietnamese and Cambodian buildings, and its artisans, militiamen and theatre company were presented as docile. Hale gives particular attention to the labour disputes among the Chinese workers over pay and hours, which officials described as laziness and placidity. The official notices divided the population into robust groups and indolent ones, and presented the majority Annamites as the model submissive worker. The chapter concludes that the image of the gentle Asian subject supported deeper French control and the commercial development of the region.

Paris 1900
Part IIPART II. CHILDREN OF FRANCE, 1914–1940p. 85
Introduction to Part 2p. 85

Hale introduces Part II by noting that the First World War changed French views of the empire, since African, Malagasy and Indochinese labourers and soldiers kept French industry running and the army supplied. The text sketches the planning of colonial fairs, from the 1906 Marseilles exposition through the 1922 Marseilles event to the Paris exposition of 1931. It ends by previewing the trademark and exhibition chapters on 1914 to 1940.

Marseilles 1906Marseilles 1922Paris 1931
5Sub-Saharan Africans: La Force Noirep. 91

Hale asks how French images of black Africans changed after the First World War, when the tirailleurs sénégalais were praised as defenders of France and the empire was described as a family. The chapter reads trademarks registered in 1914 to 1940, which show black soldiers as friendly, childlike figures, alongside comic children, banana caricatures and entertainers. It then turns to the colonial expositions at Marseilles in 1922 and Paris in 1931, where African troops, dancers and village artisans were displayed, and where Franco-African brotherhood was preached alongside images of primitive strength. Hale describes the parades, festivals and Paris performances built around African soldiers, and the ethnographic notices that graded groups by labour value. The last case is the 1937 Paris fair on the Ile des Cygnes, where craftsmen were housed on site and two Cameroonian artisans were overcome by carbon monoxide from an illegal stove. Hale concludes that the force noire image endured, and that the language of fraternity changed the rhetoric of colonial power without changing the status of Africans.

Marseilles 1922Paris 1931Paris 1937
6North Africans: Fils Aînép. 118

Hale argues that French images of North Africa between the wars cast Algeria, Tunisia and Morocco as the firstborn son of the colonial family while keeping their Arab and Berber inhabitants inside Orientalist stereotypes. The first evidence is commercial trademarks registered in Paris and Marseilles from 1914 to 1940, which used veiled women, warriors, camels, Turkish pipes and Islamic motifs to sell products from coffee and tobacco to grain, wine and insecticide. The chapter then turns to the 1922 exposition in Marseilles, the 1931 exposition in Paris and the 1937 world's fair, examining Moorish palaces, reconstructed souks and cafés, staged performances such as the Fantasia and the Rifle Dance, and the rival claims of officials such as Lyautey and Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire. Arab and Berber candidates were absent from the 1937 Meilleur Mariage Colonial contest, which Hale reads as a limit to the eugenic argument for colonial marriage. The chapter concludes that officials presented North Africans both as exotic entertainers and as children needing French training, a blindness that it ties to the bloody struggle for independence that followed.

Marseilles 1922Paris 1931Paris 1937
7Indochinese: Fils Douép. 141

Hale argues that French officials and entrepreneurs praised Indochinese as the most gifted of the colonial children, the fils doué, while treating them as subordinates who needed French guidance. Trademarks registered in Paris and Marseilles show the same pattern: tea, cloth, soap and paint labels used straw-hatted workers, servants and exotic women, and registrations barely rose after 1914. The chapter then follows the official display at the 1922 exposition in Marseilles, where a full-scale Angkor Wat, Cambodian royal dancers, a Rue Annamite and a dragon procession carried the message, and at the 1931 exposition in Paris, where ethnographic directives sorted peoples into barbarian and advanced groups and a plan to use Chinese rickshaw pullers was dropped after a protest by the Chinese consul. The 1937 Khmer-style pavilion and artisan workshops on the Ile des Cygnes are read as a claim to protect a declining civilisation. The chapter concludes that this gentle and talented image masked Vietnamese opposition to French rule, which the French public discovered only abruptly a decade after the 1937 fair.

Marseilles 1922Paris 1931Paris 1937
8La Mère-Patrie and Her Colonial Children: France on Displayp. 161

Hale examines how the colonial expositions and trademarks of the Third Republic presented France to its own public, portraying sub-Saharan Africans, North Africans and Indochinese as children of a parental mère-patrie. Trademark counts from Paris and Marseilles (656 for sub-Saharan Africa, 628 for North Africa and 259 for Indochina) open the argument, followed by a survey of the Paris exposition of 1900, the Marseilles exhibitions of 1906 and 1922, the Paris exposition of 1931 and the 1937 world's fair, showing how organisers such as Charles-Roux and Lyautey used colonial troops, living displays and performances. Hale distinguishes a parental, hierarchical France from a fraternal image of brothers that appeared after the war, and reads the second as a response to colonial military service and to anti-imperialist protest, including a surrealist tract against the 1931 exposition. The chapter concludes that colonial peoples were displayed as objects of protection and entertainment, and that the soldiers of the empire, ironically, were the ones who defended France in its hour of need.

About the Authorp. 217
Harvey, Penelope. Hybrids of Modernity: Anthropology, the Nation State and the Universal Exhibition. London: Routledge, 1996.Asia: occasional7 chapter overviews

Overview

Harvey's Hybrids of Modernity is a reflexive study of Expo'92, the Seville universal exhibition, written by an anthropologist whose access to the fair was as a journalist with press credentials. Its main argument is that the nation state, the universal exhibition and social anthropology are linked modernist institutions, and that the hybrid forms of late twentieth-century culture do not dissolve them but carry effects their founders did not expect. The scope is one fair in one year, with comparison to earlier exhibitions such as London in 1851 and Osaka in 1970. The chapters take up anthropology's handling of culture and context, the nation state in the national pavilions, technology among multinational exhibitors, and visitors as citizens and consumers, and a conclusion sets representational knowledge against embodied practice.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia receive occasional attention, and nearly all of it concerns one case: Japan's pavilion at Expo'92. Chapter 2 (Anthropology) describes the Japanese pavilion, a wooden building by Tadao Ando sited opposite Fujitsu's spherical cinema, and says Japan concentrated on tradition rather than technology. Chapter 3 (The nation state) quotes the official guide on Japan's emergence as a technological power at Osaka in 1970, and Chapter 4 (The universal exhibition) notes that Fujitsu's staff denied any special link between Japan and the company. Chapter 5 (Hybrid subjects) reports visitors' disappointment that Japan showed tradition instead of the latest technology. Southeast Asia appears once, in Chapter 2, where an Indonesian procession passes through the site and the author, as a tourist, cannot interpret it. Chapter 3 cites the Expo press dossier's eighteen Asian participating countries, and the conclusion quotes a Swatch executive on Asian production. The book does not discuss Chinese or Korean pavilions, colonial display of Asian peoples, or Asian visitors.

Contents

List of figuresp. vii
Acknowledgementsp. viii

Harvey thanks colleagues in the Department of Social Anthropology at the University of Manchester and the many audiences who commented on early versions of the work in Britain, the United States and Latin America. The project began as a joint study of Expo'92 in Seville with Laura Rival, funded by the British Academy, but changed shape during fieldwork. Harvey also names friends and colleagues whose conversations shaped the book, and family and a partner who gave space to write.

1Introductionp. 1

Harvey opens by turning Timothy Mitchell's idea of the world as exhibition into a question about late twentieth-century culture, using Expo'92, the Seville universal exhibition, as the case. The Expo, with its bridges, reclaimed island and national pavilions, is presented as a place where representation and reality blur, and Harvey's position as a journalist with press access becomes the problem for an anthropologist. The chapter argues that hybrid forms now seem to dissolve old dualities of nature and culture, and that the nation state, the universal exhibition and social anthropology are linked modernist institutions built on the relation between the universal and the particular. It then defends a reflexive auto-anthropology against a divide between anthropology and cultural studies. The chapter ends by previewing the rest of the book, which takes up culture and context, the nation state, technology and consumers at the Expo, and concludes that the hybrid institutions of modernity carry effects their founders did not expect.

Seville 1992
2Anthropology: can we do anthropology when culture and context become self-evident?p. 29

Harvey asks what anthropology can still say about culture and context once both have become visible as constructs, using Expo'92 as the test case. The chapter traces how the notion of culture as construct led anthropologists to see ethnographic monographs as partial and power-laden, and it sets Strathern's Melanesian contrast between fragmentation and Western accumulation against the cultural constructionism on show at the fair. Its evidence comes from pavilions that played with their own artifice: Switzerland's exhibit declaring that Switzerland does not exist, the Czechoslovak glass sculpture, the Irish display built around the fictional scientist Deselby, and the Siemens auditorium that circled its own displays. Harvey's brief, journalistic fieldwork also shows how participant observation at a fleeting event produced distance rather than understanding. The chapter concludes that the cultural construct now reproduces itself endlessly, and asks whether anthropologists should stop interpreting or simply add more perspectives.

Seville 1992
3The nation statep. 50

Harvey examines how nation states were presented at Expo'92 and argues that the model of the nation as an egalitarian community of equal, bounded units persists even when it is questioned. The chapter opens with Spain's bid, which rested on 1492 as a national origin and on supranational corporate sponsors, and then turns to the standard devices of nationhood such as flags, anthems, capital cities, National Days and canonical objects that made pavilions equivalent. Harvey compares the European Community pavilion, which presented a multicultural nation writ large, with Spain's own display of its autonomous communities, the British pavilion whose shop failed, and the Hungarian and Czechoslovak pavilions, which had to reconcile socialist pasts with new national claims. The Swiss pavilion, which deconstructed national culture through irony, is treated as the limit case. The chapter concludes that the contemporary nation state no longer needs cultural homogeneity or territorial integrity, and that the individualist model absorbs such critiques rather than being undone by them.

Seville 1992
4The universal exhibition: changing relationships between technology and culturep. 99

Harvey uses the Expo'92 in Seville to ask how the universal exhibition now links technology to national culture. Nations and multinationals depend on each other there: Siemens, Fujitsu and Rank Xerox mounted their own pavilions beside the national ones, Coca-Cola sponsored national pavilions, and the nations themselves were presented as brands. The chapter then sorts the exhibits into three relationships between technology and culture: technology as an invisible aid to displaying high culture (the Pavilion of Art and Culture around 1492), technology as the improvement of a way of life (the Italian exhibit on perspective and the Siemens and Rank Xerox histories of communication), and technology as cultural artefact in its own right (Fujitsu's Echoes of the Sun and the Spanish Moviemax). Drawing on Haraway's informatics of domination, Harvey argues that such simulation technologies erase the social conditions of their production. She concludes that the fair now displays commodified culture and simulated experience, though its older narratives of national progress persist alongside the new ones.

Seville 1992
5Hybrid subjects: citizens as consumersp. 131

Harvey turns from the exhibitors to the visitors of Expo'92, based on interviews and observation on site. She argues that visitors were addressed as both citizens and consumers: realist displays invited them to identify with nations, while the choices offered and the play with reflexivity invited them to consume. Harvey sets Baudrillard's account of consumption as frustrated desire against de Certeau's consumers, who turn exhibits to their own uses. Her cases include the American Spirit Home, which Spanish visitors read as American condescension; visitors wading into the ornamental pools; the joke about missing 3-D glasses at the Venezuelan pavilion; Expo passports whose stamps could pass between people; and bookmarks taken from a shop at the Israeli pavilion. She concludes that people are not simply consumers: visitors enjoyed simulated sensation yet still attended to political realities, so the experience was at once embodied and commodified.

Seville 1992
6Conclusionp. 170

Harvey brings the argument together by setting two approaches to culture against each other. Representational knowledge treats context as foundational, while knowledge as embodied practice treats context as emergent, and Harvey holds that the two cannot simply be added together. The Expo, the nation state and anthropology are all presented as hybrid institutions that objectify cultural forms while deconstructing them; the Swiss and Czech pavilions show the nation as an imagined form, read through Lyotard's distinction between modern and postmodern presentation. Harvey draws on Baudrillard, Jameson and Mitchell, and the monastery of Santa Maria de las Cuevas serves as an example of layered origins. She concludes that critical anthropology should attend to its own representational practice and to the effects of cultural self-awareness, and that anthropology and cultural studies could work together. The chapter ends by asking how Expo'92 could be less good than Disney yet better than the Welsh Garden Festival.

Seville 1992

Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014.Asia: central9 chapter overviews

Overview

Assimilating Seoul by Henry studies how the Japanese colonial government in Keijo, the capital of colonial Korea, used public spaces between 1910 and 1945 to draw Koreans into imperial rule. Henry's argument is that colonial governance reached the main arteries and monuments of the city but faltered in everyday life, and that settlers, Korean elites and poor residents each shaped those spaces to their own ends. The book has an introduction, five chapters and an epilogue, each concerned with one domain of public life: urban planning, Shintō shrines and festivals on Namsan, the expositions held on the Kyŏngbok Palace grounds, sanitation and hygiene, and wartime imperial subjectification. The argument rests on colonial and Korean newspapers, official plans, police records and visitor accounts, and the epilogue follows the postcolonial remaking of the same sites.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the whole subject: the book studies one city in colonial Korea, so attention to the region is continuous and central. Japan is present throughout as metropole and colonizer, through the Government-General, the settler community and imperial shrine cults. Chapters 2 and 5 treat Japanese religious and state displays in Seoul, including the 1940 Great Keijo Exposition. Exhibitions with East Asian participation are concentrated in chapter 3, Material Assimilation: Colonial Expositions on the Kyŏngbok Palace Grounds, where a Korean journalist's critique of the 1929 Korea Exposition notes Taiwanese bananas, Mongolian sheep and Manchurian soybean products in its halls. Chapter 4, Civic Assimilation: Sanitary Life in Neighborhood Keijo, covers the 1933 Disease Prevention Exhibition.

Taiwan, Manchuria and Mongolia appear mainly as sources of goods or as comparisons: a Taiwanese amulet registration rate is cited in chapter 5, and a planner's trip to Manchuria appears in chapter 1. Chinese people are not studied as visitors, exhibitors or residents, and Chinese cities figure only through comparison, such as the Tianjin treaty port in chapter 4. Southeast Asia is absent: none of its countries, colonies or peoples is discussed, and the only related item is a Philippines title in the bibliography.

Contents

List of Illustrationsp. vii
Note on Place Namesp. ix

Henry explains the place-name conventions used in the book. The city of the title has carried several names under different regimes, from Namgyŏng and Hanyang to Hwangsŏng, Keijo and Seoul. Henry uses precolonial Korean names for places that predate colonial rule and Japanese terms for places the colonial authorities later controlled, with exceptions where Koreans dominated. Most of the unit is a chart of key sites, giving Korean, Japanese, Chinese and English names for palaces, streets, shrines and districts.

Preface and Acknowledgmentsp. xiii

Henry describes how the book began, with exchange years in Argentina, Milwaukee and Osaka that led to graduate work and a specialty in colonial Korea. The preface reflects on the author's own position as a scholar and then thanks teachers, mentors, colleagues and archivists in Japan, Korea and the United States who supported the research. It names the institutions that funded the dissertation and later revisions, and ends by dedicating the book to family.

Introduction. Assimilation and Space: Toward an Ethnography of Japanese Rulep. 1

Henry opens in 1925 with the Korea Shrine on Namsan, built by the colonial government in Keijo, and with an official's report of Koreans who looked around but did not worship there. This failure of assimilation frames the book, which treats the city's public spaces as a crucible for Japanese rule. Henry reads assimilation as a set of contested projects in spiritual, material and civic life, and argues against top-down accounts by looking at how shrines, expositions and neighborhoods were used by settlers, Korean elites and poor residents. The introduction sets out three periods, 1910–25, 1925–37 and 1937–45, and the five chapters that follow. It draws on Mary Louise Pratt's idea of contact zones and explains that the sources are limited by the colonial archive, so the book reads Japanese-language newspapers and Korean papers against the grain.

Keijo 1915Keijo 1929
1Constructing Keijō: The Uneven Spaces of a Colonial Capitalp. 22

Henry traces how the Government-General remade Hanyang, the royal capital of the Chosŏn dynasty, into the colonial capital Keijō between 1910 and 1936. Colonial planning reshaped the city's arteries and monuments far more than its everyday neighbourhoods: palaces became parks, museums and offices, and roads such as Taihei Boulevard were widened to display Japanese modernity, while the Korean-populated northern village kept much of its precolonial street pattern and district names. Henry follows this unevenness through urban reforms (1910–25), city planning as cultural rule (1925–34) and the years after the Town Planning Act of 1934, each of which met resistance from Korean residents and from Japanese settlers guarding their own interests. The evidence comes from official plans and maps, the Keijō nippō and Maeil sinbo newspapers, and planning journals. The chapter concludes that colonial governance reached the main arteries but faltered at the capillaries of everyday life, and it leads on to the public spaces of the city's microsites that the following chapters examine.

2Spiritual Assimilation: Namsan’s Shintō Shrines and Their Festival Celebrationsp. 62

Henry examines how the Government-General tried to draw Keijō's colonized population into emperor worship through Namsan's Shintō complex, the settler-run Seoul Shrine and the state-built Korea Shrine of 1925. The chapter argues that this spiritual assimilation was makeshift. Seoul Shrine's settler leaders admitted few Koreans, and their grand festival became a procession of play, with geisha, kisaeng and boisterous crowds, rather than solemn prayer. Henry draws on Keijō nippō and Maeil sinbo reports and festival photographs, and tracks the procession route, which entered Chongno after 1919 and Korean neighbourhoods after 1926, along with the inclusion of kisaeng, a royal musical troupe and native deities such as Tan'gun. Koreans, the chapter shows, mostly watched rather than worshipped, and they gave few donations. The chapter closes on pickpocketing during the festivals of the early 1930s, which Henry reads as the limit of spiritual assimilation before 1937.

3Material Assimilation: Colonial Expositions on the Kyŏngbok Palace Groundsp. 92

Henry argues that the expositions staged on the grounds of Kyŏngbok Palace were a central means of 'material assimilation', by which the colonial government sought to make Koreans identify with Japanese rule as a route to progress. The chapter follows three events. The small 1907 Keijo exhibition, dominated by Japanese merchants and overshadowed by the protectorate's forced treaty, was mostly a market and a festival. The 1915 Industrial Exhibition cleared many palace buildings and used Western-style halls, museum-style classification and a contrast between a backward Korean past and a modern Japanese present to teach visitors to see development. The 1929 Korea Exposition, financed by coerced donations and rural tour groups, drew nationalist critics who condemned its 'pure Korean style' halls. Drawing on newspapers, police records and visitor accounts, Henry shows that crowds came mainly for amusements and giveaways, that tour guides struggled to make the displays meaningful, and that some visitors turned the event to their own ends. The chapter concludes that the expositions exposed the unevenly shared rewards of colonial modernity.

Seoul 1907Seoul 1915Seoul 1929
4Civic Assimilation: Sanitary Life in Neighborhood Keijōp. 130

Henry examines how the Government-General and Korean elites used public hygiene in the Korean neighbourhoods of Keijo to build what the author calls 'civic assimilation', a habit of self-regulation that would bind residents to colonial norms of cleanliness. The chapter traces the dual surveillance of sanitation cooperatives and police from the protectorate years through the 1910s, when semiannual cleanups were enforced through fines, home inspections and roadside lectures, and shows how residents evaded these measures or tidied up only before inspectors came. Henry argues that the system failed poorer Koreans, who could not pay fees, relied on well water and lacked toilets, so that colonial and nationalist critics alike used disease statistics to make claims about the city. The chapter also follows Korean cooperative leaders, medical students and the 1933 Disease Prevention Exhibition, which drew nearly eighty thousand visitors and seems to have drawn wary residents into sanitary rule. It concludes that after 1935 the colonial state turned to harsher, centralised measures, narrowing the room for Korean elites to reshape assimilation.

Seoul 1933
5Imperial Subjectification: The Collapsing Spaces of a Wartime Cityp. 168

Henry examines how the late colonial state, after war with China began in 1937, tried to make Koreans in Keijo (Seoul) loyal subjects of the emperor, a process the chapter calls imperial subjectification. Its evidence comes from the Keijo nippo's coverage of the 1940 Great Keijo Exposition, the torch relay from Ise to Korea Shrine and a school tour of Japan's sacred sites, and from the Namsan shrines, the militarised autumn festival, Seoul Nation-Protecting Shrine and the campaign to install Ise amulets and miniature shrines in homes. Henry sets the official claim that rising shrine visits proved growing reverence against the complaints of Shinto priests about coercion and formality, and against photographs that show Koreans bowing in a Confucian manner or keeping their hats on. The chapter argues that loyalty was performed under observation and that the state could measure it only by counting. It ends by showing how the cult fell short in the home, where amulets were discarded and shrines misused, and by noting a Christian seminary professor who visited Namsan while keeping his own faith.

Keijo 1940
Epilogue. After Empire’s Demise: The Postcolonial Remaking of Seoul’s Public Spacesp. 204

Henry follows the sites of colonial Keijo after 1945, when the Namsan shrines were demolished under pressure from Koreans and with the agreement of the US Army. The ground was then given over to Christian Easter services, a memorial to the patriot An Chung-gŭn and a statue of Syngman Rhee. The chapter then traces Kyŏngbok Palace, where the former Government-General building served as Capitol Hall and then the National Museum before its demolition in 1995, and where restorations since 1996 have produced a 'Chosŏn renaissance' of uncertain authenticity. Evidence comes from the press, official statements, the monuments and museums themselves, and disputes such as the 1958 Yatsugi visit and the 1982 textbook controversy. Henry argues that these monuments silence the colonial past they replace, and that recreated palaces and a turn to tourism leave Seoul's history of imperial subjectification unexamined. The closing pages turn to Seoul Station and the old city hall, kept as cultural spaces, and to the new city hall, which more than three-quarters of Koreans think clashes with its surroundings, as signs of a fragile move towards engaging that history.

Hoffenberg, Peter H. An Empire on Display: English, Indian, and Australian Exhibitions from the Crystal Palace to the Great War. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001.Asia: slight11 chapter overviews

Overview

Hoffenberg's book examines popular exhibitions in England, Australia and India from the Great Exhibition of 1851 to the Festival of Empire in 1911. Its main argument is that exhibitions were social texts, written by commissioners and read in varied ways by visitors, and that they helped imagine a tripartite empire of England, India and settler Australia while masking inequalities of class, race and labour. The scope covers London, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide and Calcutta shows, along with the afterlife of their collections. The book is organised in eight chapters on commissioners, state power, commerce, the Australian and Indian courts, machinery, visitors and ceremonies, followed by a short epilogue, three appendices, notes and a bibliography.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia figure only slightly, and in passing, in a book centred on India, Australia and England. The preface describes a Chinese village with tea houses at the 1884 International Health Exhibition. Japanese visitors to London in 1862 are noted for their curiosity (chapter 7). At Adelaide in 1887 Japanese earthenware sold among 'Eastern goods', and the manager of the Japanese Village paid the commission a share of receipts (chapter 3). Chinese teas are the rivals that Indian tea merchants sought to displace in Australia (chapter 4), and Chinese commissioners in national costume lead the Adelaide opening procession (chapter 8). Malays and the inhabitants of Perak appear once, in a list of peoples at London in 1862 (chapter 6).

East and Southeast Asian people appear as visitors, sellers or passing comparisons rather than as commissioners of their own courts, and the book does not discuss their participation. Chapter 5 says the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition represented Australia and India in a self-contained imperial world without non-British societies, including China and the Ottoman Empire. Otherwise the regional material concerns India and Australia, with South Asia the main colonial case throughout.

Contents

List of Illustrationsp. xi
Prefacep. xiii

Hoffenberg's preface sets out the aim: to examine popular exhibitions in England, Australia and India from the Great Exhibition of 1851 to the Festival of Empire in 1911. It argues that exhibitions were social texts, written by commissioners and read in varied ways by visitors, and that they helped imagine a tripartite empire of England, India and settler Australia. It also engages Said, Cohn and MacKenzie, and debates over the state's cultural role.

London 1851London 1862
Acknowledgmentsp. xxv

Hoffenberg's acknowledgments trace the book to a family trip to England and Scotland and to a postcard from Thomas Metcalf showing a Sydney exhibition medal. They thank archives and libraries in Britain, Australia and North America, and the funders, including Fulbright-Hays and the University of California, Berkeley. They also name colleagues and advisers, and dedicate the book to family.

1Exhibitions and the New Imperialismp. 1

Hoffenberg argues that the popular exhibitions held in London and in colonial cities such as Sydney, Melbourne and Calcutta between 1851 and 1914 deserve as much study as the Great Exhibition that overshadows them. The chapter shows how colonial commissioners used these shows to present Australia as a progressive settler society and India as a restored tradition. Its evidence includes the Doulton 'Impasto' panels at the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition, the Zenana Days in Calcutta, and Aboriginal Australians displayed at Sydney and Adelaide, cases in which visitors and exhibits sometimes returned the colonial gaze. The chapter also traces the afterlife of the shows in museum collections, catalogues and the classifications used to organise them. It argues that the exhibitions promoted an imperial market and a federated commonwealth, while masking inequalities of class, race and labour. It closes by claiming that exhibitions shaped social order through participation rather than coercion, and that their ideas about imperial federation carried into the Commonwealth.

London 1851London 1862London 1886Sydney 1879Calcutta 1883Melbourne 1888
2The Exhibition Wallahs: Commissioners and the Production of Imperial Knowledgep. 31

Hoffenberg's chapter examines the commissioners who organized Britain's and its colonies' exhibitions in the Victorian and Edwardian eras, and how their work turned exhibitions into networks of imperial and colonial knowledge. The argument is that these cultural bureaucrats, who were often scientists, art experts, botanists and museum officials, created and circulated the categories by which the empire and its colonies were known, and that their exchanges of objects and information strengthened ties between metropole and periphery. Hoffenberg works through South Kensington first: Henry Cole, Cunliffe-Owen and Purdon Clarke, whose handbooks, purchases and loans linked London to Australian and Indian museums. The bulk of the chapter then compares Australian commissioners such as Redmond Barry, William Macarthur, Edward Combes and Ferdinand von Mueller with Anglo-Indian and South Asian ones, above all Buck, Watt, Lockwood Kipling and Trilokya Nath Mukharji, whose catalogues and overseas travels form the chapter's fullest case study. The conclusion argues that this participation was not simply hegemonic: colonial experts became nationalist intellectuals, so that imperial knowledge could also undermine imperial rule.

London 1851London 1862Calcutta 1883London 1886Melbourne 1880
3Commissioners and the State: Power and Controversy at the Exhibitionsp. 63

This chapter asks how exhibition commissioners justified their authority as a new cultural elite, and why that authority drew criticism. Hoffenberg argues that commissioners presented themselves as disinterested experts serving the state, yet their work of selecting, pricing and displaying objects exposed them to charges of self-interest and commerce. The main evidence is the Crystal Palace of 1851, where the executive commissioners forbade price tags, and the London International of 1862, which radical papers denounced as a jobbery run by a 'Science and Art clique'. Colonial cases, including the Melbourne Centennial Exhibition, the Adelaide Jubilee show of 1887 and the sales rules at Calcutta in 1883-84, show how on-site selling set commissioners against local merchants. Hoffenberg then compares state funding in Australia and India, which was direct and generous, with England's ad hoc royal commissions, and traces critics from Babbage to the radical press who attacked the commissioners from opposite sides. The chapter ends by treating exhibitions as contests for public opinion, in which the shows revealed the tensions they were meant to conceal.

London 1851London 1862Calcutta 1883London 1886Adelaide 1887
4Consumers, Producers, and Markets: The Political Economy of Imperial Federationp. 99

Hoffenberg examines how Australian and Indian commissioners, merchants and critics used international exhibitions to argue about the economics of empire. The displays of wool, coal, wine, cotton, silk and tea are read as political economies in their own right rather than neutral reflections of trade. Hoffenberg follows the Australian and Indian commodity courts from the Great Exhibition of 1851 through the London International Exhibition of 1862 and the Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886, with further material from Sydney in 1879 and Calcutta in 1883. Tea provides the chapter's clearest case: the Indian Tea Districts Association sold samples in London and then in Australia and North America, and the chapter traces how James Inglis and Jules Joubert encouraged direct trade between Australia and India without English middlemen. The argument is that colonial producers pursued independent commerce within an imperial framework, and that critics such as Carlyle and the radical press rejected the market ideals the shows celebrated. The chapter ends by noting that the displays both reinforced imperial economic unity and exposed its strains, which opens onto the question of colonial trade policy.

London 1851London 1862London 1884London 1886Calcutta 1883Sydney 1879Chicago 1893
5Terrae Nullius?: Australia and India at Overseas Exhibitionsp. 129

Hoffenberg asks how Australian and Indian commissioners represented their colonies at overseas exhibitions, from the Paris Universal Exposition of 1855 to the London shows of 1862 and 1886. The chapter argues that the displays drew on a contrast between settler Australia, shown through mining machinery, wool, photographs, maps and emigrant literature, and an Oriental India, shown through artware, village bazaars, ethnographic models and casts of ancient monuments. Its evidence comes mainly from commissioners' letters, official catalogues and guidebooks, and from objects such as the working quartz-crushing battery of the Queensland court at South Kensington in 1886. Hoffenberg shows how Australian commissioners tried to correct an image of frontier violence and rough labour by exhibiting paintings, books and pictures of towns, and how both colonies courted emigrants, with Canada as the main rival. In India, commissioners built a traditionalist past through casts of the Sanchi Tope, the Gwalior Gateway and reconstructed bazaars where artisans worked and sold goods to visitors. The chapter concludes that these exhibits reinforced imperial authority over the past, yet also supplied colonial nationalists with the materials they later used to challenge it.

London 1851London 1862Paris 1855Paris 1867Philadelphia 1876London 1886Calcutta 1883
6Machines-in-Motion: Technology, Labor, and the Ironies of Industrialismp. 166

Hoffenberg examines the working machines that drew crowds at English, Australian and Indian exhibitions from 1851 onwards. Machinery courts, reapers and steam-powered demonstrations presented industrialism as something visitors could watch and test, but the chapter argues that the same displays hid the labour that built and ran them. Machinery halls were framed as idealised factories, and visible hand workers, such as Indian artisans and women in the craft courts, were placed beside self-acting machines to suggest a harmonious industrial order. Hoffenberg shows this with Doulton panels at the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition, and with the building sites of London in 1862 and Sydney in 1879, where accidents and strikes were left out of official albums. Exhibitions did help diffuse new technology across England and the colonies, and machines kept on in museums and technical schools extended that reach. The chapter ends with the armaments displays, where guns and warships were admired as beautiful objects, so that the peaceful pledge of 1851 was undercut by war.

London 1851London 1862London 1886Sydney 1879Melbourne 1888Nagpore 1865
7Imperial and National Taxonomies: Entertaining and Policing Exhibition Visitorsp. 203

Hoffenberg turns from exhibits to the people who visited exhibitions and to the ways commissioners classified, entertained and policed them. Visitors to the Great Exhibition of 1851, the London International of 1862 and the Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886 are treated as a visible social mass that organisers sorted by nation, race, class and gender. The evidence includes reduced fares for London workers, the appeal to guilds from neighbouring colonies for the Melbourne Intercolonial of 1866 to 1867, and the controversial zenana day at the Calcutta International of 1883 to 1884, when women in purdah were admitted to the grounds. Maori and Fijian performers at Sydney in 1879, and Aboriginal visitors from mission stations at Adelaide in 1887, are set against the static ethnographic models shown elsewhere, and the separate entrances at Nagpore in 1865 show how race and rank were policed at the door. Hoffenberg argues that exhibitions offered social integration and imperial federation in economic and cultural terms, a citizenship that was real but not political. The chapter closes by linking these practices of ordering visitors to later management of migration in the twentieth century.

London 1851London 1862London 1886Sydney 1879Adelaide 1887Calcutta 1883Nagpore 1865
8The Imperial Pilgrims' Progress: Ceremonies, Tourism, and Epic Theater at the Exhibitionsp. 242

Hoffenberg argues that visitors to the British and colonial exhibitions were active participants rather than passive spectators, and that their ceremonies, tourism and pageants helped create the Victorian public and an imperial civil society. The chapter begins with Lord Curzon's 1903 Delhi Durbar Art Exhibition and draws on Crystal Palace ceremonies, Australian and Indian shows, and the memoirs of colonial visitors such as Alexander Dobbie and Edward Ogilvie, for whom exhibitions were stops on an imperial pilgrimage. Opening ceremonies in London, Dublin, Calcutta, Sydney and Melbourne placed the Crown, viceroys, Indian princes and trade unionists in a visible hierarchy, though Anglo-Indian boycotts in Calcutta during the Ilbert Bill dispute exposed its limits. Pageants, above all the 1911 Festival of Empire at Sydenham, and closing ceremonies and souvenirs then fixed the shows in public memory. The exhibitions, Hoffenberg concludes, were a contested process that constituted the public rather than merely reflecting it, and their rituals drew colonial subjects into an imperial order that also nurtured colonial nationalism.

Delhi 1903London 1851London 1886London 1911Dublin 1853Melbourne 1880Melbourne 1888Adelaide 1887Philadelphia 1876
Epilogue: Recessional: Imperial Culture and Colonial Nationalismp. 273

The epilogue argues that exhibitions from 1851 to 1914 presented a traditionalist vision of empire, built on relics, royal ceremony and the preservation of supposedly disappearing cultures, and that this vision later served colonial nationalism as well. Hoffenberg cites the Sanchi Tope cast shown in London in 1871, the Gwalior Gateway at South Kensington in 1886, and Irish antiquities shown at Dublin in 1853 as examples of preservation that gave commissioners authority and their sponsoring states legitimacy. Antiquarian protection laws in England and the colonies supplied the legal frame. Displays of Indian art and labour were later claimed by the Indian National Congress for its swadeshi movement, while the Melbourne Trades Hall Council used the exhibition form to promote Australian goods and labour. The contrast between the neoclassical Australian pavilion and the durbar-style Indian pavilion at Wembley in 1924-25 shows how architecture still encoded hierarchy. The conclusion is that a neoimperial network of Commonwealth exhibitions continues to shape identities into the postcolonial era.
