Hollengreen, Laura, Celia Pearce, Rebecca Rouse and Bobby Schweizer, eds. Meet Me at the Fair: A World’s Fair Reader. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2014.Asia: occasional46 chapter overviews

Overview

Meet Me at the Fair, edited by Laura H. Hollengreen and Rebecca Rouse, is a 2014 volume of new essays on world's fairs. The introduction sets the fair against the early modern curiosity cabinet and against scholarship that reads fairs as displays of imperial and racial power, and argues that the fair is polyvalent: a shrine to science, a marketplace and a site of nation-building. The essays range from London's Crystal Palace in 1851 to Shanghai in 2010, with most attention to Chicago in 1893 and 1933 and to New York in 1939 and 1964-65. They are grouped under eight 'pavilions': anthropology and ethnology, American identity, science and industry, design and architecture, operations and urban planning, arts and media, amusements and recreation, and the future.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia receive occasional attention, in about twenty chapters, almost always briefly. The one sustained treatment is chapter 8.2 (the Japan Pavilion), where Walters reads Japan's display as an industrial challenge to American manufacturers rather than a cultural exchange: national industrial rankings, the Shinkansen, Seiko's Tik-Tok, Sony's Videocorder, Matsushita and Hitachi advertising, and Toray's kimonos of synthetic fibre. The Shanghai Expo of 2010 recurs. Aelbrecht (8.4) calls Shanghai the closest follower of Lisbon's Expo '98 model, Caramellino (5.4) reads it as city regeneration, and Schrenk (3.3), Tran (7.4) and Hellier-Tinoco (1.6) mention its GM pavilion, its food rules and a Mexican mask in its gallery. Chinese exhibitors and visitors are rarely discussed in their own right.

Older fairs show the region mainly as displayed peoples and places. Santesso (1.3) sees the unfinished Chinese exhibit at Philadelphia in 1876, with working carpenters, as living authenticity, and places Chicago's Javanese (1893) and Chinese (1933) villages in the zoo tradition. Robles (1.4) notes Tonkinese villagers at Paris in 1889, Crompton (2.3) lists Siam and Chinese markets on the Midway, Lukas (7.1) a Chinese theatre and an Igorot village, and Kamerbeek (6.5) the Filipino Village at Buffalo in 1901. Jacobson (6.2) discusses the Japanese Village in Edison's Buffalo films. Japan appears as a source of prints (Whitfield, 2.1) and of Osaka's Expo 70 (Pearce, 3.5), while Telotte (7.2) and Warren (7.5) mention Disney's Tokyo park and Epcot's Japan pagoda.

Contents

Table of Contents: Tours
PrefaceRobert W. Rydellp. i

Rydell's preface opens with Charlotte Brontë's 1851 response to the Crystal Palace and argues that fairs work by 'make-believe', persuading others to occupy a reality. It traces the fair movement from the Great Exhibition, set against the revolutions of 1848, to the Cold War and the Shanghai Expo. Exhibitions, Rydell argues, served elite authority, and women, minorities and workers contested them. The preface ends by introducing the volume's themed 'pavilions' of essays on picnics, architecture, theme parks and souvenirs.

London 1851New York 1964
IntroductionLaura H. Hollengreen and Rebecca Rousep. 1

Hollengreen and Rouse introduce Meet Me at the Fair, a collection of new short essays on world's fairs by scholars from several countries and disciplines. They open by comparing the fair with the early modern curiosity cabinet, since both mixed wonder, art and science. They then trace the scholarship since the 1980s, which reads fairs as displays of imperial and racial power, and set against it the techno-optimism of fairs from London's Crystal Palace in 1851 to Chicago in 1933 and New York in 1964-65, where corporate sponsorship came to dominate. The fair, they argue, is polyvalent, a shrine to science, a marketplace and a site of nation-building, and the volume's pavilions mirror that. They also describe seven alternative tours through the chapters. The introduction ends by asking whether the fair has a future at all, since travel, television, the internet and theme parks now do what fairs once did.

London 1851Chicago 1933New York 1964-65
1Anthropology & Ethnology Pavilionp. 15
1.1When “The Present European Family” Contemplates “The Phases of Human Existence”: The Court of Natural History at the Crystal Palace, Sydenham, 1854-1866Fanny Roblesp. 17

Robles examines the Court of Natural History at the Crystal Palace in Sydenham, which opened in 1854 after the building was moved from Hyde Park. There, life-size plaster figures of 'natives' from five continents stood in painted habitats among plants and stuffed animals. It reconstructs the aims of the curator Robert Gordon Latham and the Ethnological Society, who presented the Court as an educational guide to human difference. Robles then sets these aims against the responses of visitors and critics. Harriet Martineau noticed that the largest crowds gathered in the Natural History department, Elizabeth Eastlake condemned the figures as a kind of moral cannibalism, and Punch mocked the display. Drawing on cartoons, a music-hall monologue and the Palace's own guides, Robles argues that the Court's ethnology was bound up with comparisons between 'savages' abroad and the urban poor at home. The chapter concludes that popular entertainment undermined the Court's educational claims, but that its tableaux had a long afterlife, continued in the Field Museum's 1933 'Races of Mankind' exhibition.

London 1851Sydenham 1854
1.2Displaying Cultural History: The Smithsonian Institution and the World’s FairsKathleen Curranp. 31

Curran examines the Smithsonian Institution's part in American fairs, centring on George Brown Goode, who rose through the United States National Museum to become assistant secretary of the Smithsonian. The chapter argues that the museum's displays drew on Gustav Klemm's idea of 'cultural history', which arranged objects by stages of development rather than by place of origin, and that Goode and Otis Mason adapted this into a 'synoptic' method of exhibition. The method's first large showing came at the Cincinnati exhibition of 1888, where transport was presented as a sequence from canoes to locomotives. Curran then turns to Mason's life groups of North American peoples, prepared for Chicago in 1893, and to Franz Boas's criticism of the typological arrangement of Eskimo artefacts, which pushed the museum towards habitat displays. The chapter ends with Goode's draft classification for the Chicago fair, which aimed to make the exposition 'an illustrated encyclopedia of civilization'. Cultural history, adopted piecemeal at earlier fairs, thus became the framework for the whole Columbian Exposition.

Chicago 1893Cincinnati 1888
1.3Living Authenticity: The World’s Fair and the ZooAaron Santessop. 41

Santesso argues that the world's fair and the zoo grew out of the same desire for authenticity, and that the zoo's 'African village' is the lasting successor to the exotic villages of the fairs. The chapter begins with the close ties between the two institutions, from the Philadelphia Zoo and the Centennial Exhibition of 1876 to the origins of the St Louis Zoo in the 1904 fair. It then reconsiders the Dahomey Village at Chicago in 1893 and the case of Ota Benga, which are usually read only as expressions of power and racism. Santesso adds that fair visitors were preoccupied with the artificial, as at the Corliss steam engine and the unfinished Chinese exhibit in Philadelphia, where living workmen supplied a sense of authenticity. The chapter traces this through the German zoo directors Bodinus and Hagenbeck, whose animals in exotic replicas and living panoramas were copied at colonial fairs in Paris and at Chicago in 1933. It ends with today's zoo 'African villages', where visitors take the place of the people once displayed and so find themselves inside the living panorama.

Chicago 1893Philadelphia 1876St Louis 1904Chicago 1933
1.4Blanche et Noir, by Louise Faure-Favier: When France Falls in Love with Senegal at the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1900Fanny Roblesp. 53

Robles reads the Senegalese village at the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1889 alongside Louise Faure-Favier's novel Blanche et Noir (1928), which begins with the fair. The chapter traces how native villages developed from the displays at the Jardin d'Acclimatation, where Nubians, Ceylonese and others had been shown since the 1870s. In 1889 the Senegalese, brought to Paris by a colonial officer, were praised by a journalist for their industry and beauty, while other visitors called them apes. Robles then turns to the novel, in which a widowed Frenchwoman falls for a Senegalese jeweller at the fair and elopes with the jeweller to Senegal. Robles argues that its sympathy is limited, since it relies on women leading a civilising mission. Set against this is the real jeweller's complaint that the huts did not represent Senegal. The chapter also considers interwar negrophilia and the protests of 2011 at the Jardin, and it ends by noting the Quai Branly exhibition 'The Invention of the Savage' as a belated reckoning with this history.

Paris 1889
1.5Debating the African VillageDeborah L. Hughesp. 61

Hughes examines the protests of 1929 against the 'African Village' at the North East Coast Exhibition in Newcastle, where West African performers from a touring troupe were shown in a commercial entertainment pavilion. The chapter follows the letters from the West African Students' Union, the Anti-Slavery and Aborigines Protection Society and the League Against Imperialism, which asked the Home and Colonial Offices to halt the display on grounds of exploitation and racial prejudice. The government's response turned on whether the performers were British subjects, and the Home Office, which had licensed the show, found no grounds for objection. Hughes argues that by the 1920s academic anthropologists had distanced themselves from popular ethnological display, leaving such shows to showmen, and that once their scientific justification had gone they became open to anti-colonial criticism. The 1924 Wembley exhibition set the precedent for these complaints. The chapter concludes that the controversy made Newcastle another site where the rights of colonial subjects were contested, even though the show went ahead.

Newcastle 1929Wembley 1924
1.6Embodying Touristic Mexico: Virtual and Erased Indigenous BodiesRuth Hellier-Tinocop. 71

Hellier-Tinoco examines two Mexican exhibits from twenty-first century world's fairs: a 3D film of the Night of the Dead ritual on Janitzio island, shown at Hannover in 2000, and a suspended mask of the Dance of the Old Men from Jarácuaro, displayed at Shanghai in 2010. The chapter argues that both present indigenous P'urhépecha people as authentic, timeless and pre-industrial, when both were reshaped from the 1920s into national icons and tourist attractions. It traces how the Janitzio ritual and the dance were staged in Mexico City theatres, photographed, filmed and sold in guidebooks and postcards, and how the mask later appeared in the Mexican Tourist Board's European campaign of 2006. The chapter calls this process 'performism' and places it within the long history of indigenous bodies at fairs, which serve as the 'final authenticator'. The Hannover pavilion replaced the absent villagers with the bodies of visitors, and the Shanghai gallery kept the mask after the body had been erased, so the fairs turned indigenous display into economic exchange value.

Hannover 2000Shanghai 2010
2American Identity Pavilionp. 81
2.1Frontiers of the World’s Columbian ExpositionStephen J. Whitfieldp. 83

Whitfield argues that the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 can be understood through six kinds of frontier, each a dividing line that can also be crossed. The fair took place in Chicago, a city that had grown from a trading post into an industrial metropolis, and it marked the boundary between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as America became an imperial power. It also exposed the gap between rich and poor, and gave rise to the mass popular culture of the Midway Plaisance, with its Ferris wheel and ragtime. The chapter describes Olmsted's drained lakeside site and the White City, but dwells on the fair's racial exclusions, including Frederick Douglass's objection to the Dahomean village and the near absence of black Americans from its tributes. It then turns to labour unrest outside the grounds, the depression of 1893 and the rise of mail-order consumerism, before ending with Frederick Jackson Turner's frontier thesis, first given at a meeting of historians in Chicago. The fair, the chapter concludes, stood between the desperation of the city's poor and a vision of communal harmony.

Chicago 1893
2.2Fixing Race: Visual Representation of African Americans at the World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893Bridget R. Cooksp. 97

Cooks examines Peter Newell's fifteen-part Johnson Family cartoon series, published in Harper's Weekly from July to November 1893 while the World's Columbian Exposition was open in Chicago. The series is anomalous in a magazine that rarely printed racist images of African Americans, and Cooks argues that it did three things. It helped fix racial categories as segregation was being formalised, it offered a black family as a comic counterpart to the all-American family readers could identify with, and it reassured white readers that African Americans were kept out of the fair's celebration of the nation. The reading draws on minstrelsy, coon songs and the uncle, mammy and pickaninny types. The cases are the cartoons themselves: the family on the Midway's Cairo Street, a reunion with a former master at the Kentucky State Building, and the caption about a spotted mule at the White City. These are set against a construction photograph by C. D. Arnold that shows a black worker, and against Ida B. Wells's preface to The Reason Why. The chapter concludes that the cartoons reinforced black inferiority and anticipated the colour line.

Chicago 1893
2.3Staging Gentility at the Columbian Exposition: White Masculinity on and off the MidwayConstance Cromptonp. 113

Crompton uses the rival performances of the strongman Eugen Sandow and the boxer James J. Corbett on the Midway of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition to ask what white middle-class muscles meant once Frederick Jackson Turner had declared the frontier closed. The chapter first sets out the fair's divisions of space and race, including the Woman's Building, a single Colored Peoples Day and the Midway's ethnic villages, where bodies were displayed alongside goods. It then follows Corbett, whose 'scientific' boxing and vaudeville act at the Natatorium were ended by the fair's directors, a decision Crompton reads as proof that boxers could not be recast as genteel. Sandow turned his muscles into a spectacle, posing and lifting rather than fighting, and was promoted through backstage visits and newspaper accounts that were both scientific and sexualised. Crompton draws on Edison's kinetoscope and Buffalo Bill's Rough Riders to show how the Midway framed these bodies. It concludes that Sandow's posed, scientific physique became the model of middle-class manhood while Corbett faded, and that the fair's visual technologies helped bring that shift about.

Chicago 1893
2.4Picturing Female Patriotism in Three Dimensions: High Street at the 1926 SesquicentennialLydia Mattice Brandtp. 127

Brandt examines High Street, the reconstructed colonial street of replica houses that the Women's Committee built in the south-west quadrant of the 1926 Sesquicentennial International Exposition in Philadelphia, where it became the fair's most popular destination. The argument is that the women's organisations used the replicas to present the home as the moral foundation of citizenship, at a moment when the male organisers were embroiled in scandal. The committee's conservative view of women's civic role drew on earlier female-led preservation and municipal housekeeping movements. The chapter then turns to the individual buildings: the Washington House, furnished from an inventory of the president's possessions; the Jefferson boarding house, fitted with reproductions based on Monticello; and the Shippen House, finished by Good Housekeeping as a modern home behind a colonial facade. Brandt shows that these interiors promoted Colonial Revival goods available for purchase, so that a woman's consumption became part of her civic duty. The chapter concludes that the committee made the colonial past stylish and attainable, and presented its own members as proof that the founders' values survived in modern homes.

Philadelphia 1926
2.5Ethnic Pride on Display at the 1933 Chicago World’s FairCheryl R. Ganzp. 143

Ganz examines the souvenirs that ethnic groups produced and sold at A Century of Progress, the Chicago fair of 1933 and 1934 held in the depths of the Depression. Chicago's immigrant communities, who made up about two-thirds of the city's population, were given their own events and sales, and Ganz argues that their souvenirs expressed both ethnic pride and a stake in the city's progress. Three souvenirs are examined. The first is a porcelain plate honouring Mayor Anton J. Cermak, a Bohemian-born politician shot in Miami in 1933 and mourned across ethnic lines. The second is the German-American Group's campaign to bring the Graf Zeppelin to Chicago, which produced a 50-cent airmail stamp and cacheted envelopes that pointedly omitted the swastika flag. The third, and longest, is the African American clubwomen's replica of Jean Baptiste Point Du Sable's cabin and the postcards they sold in 1933 and 1934 claiming that Du Sable was Chicago's first settler. The chapter concludes that the African American postcards carried the most contested message at the fair, and that surviving souvenirs now offer a window into the fair's optimism and its challenges.

Chicago 1933
2.6Plump, Moist, and a Bit of a Chump: Elmer and the Average American and the 1939 World’s FairKatie Uvap. 149

Uva examines the 1939 New York World's Fair, which promised a streamlined, peaceful future but drew disappointing crowds, and Elmer, the folksy mascot introduced for the 1940 season to revive it. Elmer, Uva argues, was an ambiguous figure: praised as an amiable, all-American man of simple values, but also derided as a rube. The chapter sets out the fair's problems, which were admissions of 26 million against a projected 45 to 60 million, high prices and a public uneasy about automation when one in six Americans was unemployed. It then traces the replacement of the promoter Grover Whalen by Harvey Dow Gibson, the cut in admission price, the shift of theme from 'The World of Tomorrow' to 'For Peace and Freedom' as war spread across Europe, and the Westinghouse Middletons as a more modern model of family life. Attendance and press reactions show the campaign had mixed results. The chapter concludes that Elmer's reception reflected the fair's central conflict: it tried to sell a radically different future while retreating into a nostalgic American past.

New York 1939
2.7Deconstructing the Unisphere: Hip-Hop on a Shrinking Globe in an Expanding UniverseNettrice R. Gaskinsp. 155

Gaskins examines the Unisphere, the twelve-storey steel globe that was the symbol of the 1964-65 New York World's Fair, and the hip-hop and urban artists who later used it as a backdrop. The fair's promise of progress and 'Peace Through Understanding' sat uneasily with the civil rights struggle, and its lack of African American presence, together with Robert Moses's road and bridge building, shaped how the site was experienced. Gaskins reads the Unisphere through Langdon Winner's idea of artifacts as political and Deleuze's notion of a plane of immanence, and links it to Afrofuturism, tracing a line from Sun Ra and P-Funk to Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock'. The main cases are two music videos: Craig Mack's 'Flava in Ya Ear' (1994), which uses the site as a bling-era prop, and Talib Kweli's 'In this World' (2010), which orbits the rings around the rapper. The conclusion is that the Unisphere now stands for urban life and global culture rather than the fair's vision of progress, and that artists have made its remains a stage of their own.

New York 1964
3Science & Industry Pavilionp. 167
3.1The Price of Things: Art, Industry and Commodity Culture at the Exposition Universelle of 1855 in ParisKatie Hornsteinp. 169

Hornstein examines the Exposition Universelle of 1855 in Paris, the first European world's fair to combine industrial products and fine art. The French government intended the pairing to show that industry and the arts were allied, but Hornstein argues that it produced a rivalry in which industry appeared to win. The industrial goods were housed in a permanent glass-and-iron Palais de l'Industrie, the art in a temporary building, and only the industrial products could carry prices, with sale booths beside the fair letting visitors buy them. Hornstein draws on the earlier separation of Salon art from industrial exhibitions, on the official report that refused foreign artists' requests to show prices, and on the illustrated newspaper L'Illustration, which feared that art could not compete. Attendance figures, 3.6 million for industry and 900,000 for the fine arts, are read against Salon numbers to show that the art exhibition was in fact a success. The chapter concludes that the fair deepened a perceived schism between art and industry, and that the later move of the Salon into the industrial palace seemed to confirm it.

Paris 1855
3.2Taking the Factory to the FairAllison C. Marshp. 175

Marsh examines the process exhibit, the working factory set up at world's fairs, from the Libbey Glass Company's furnace on the Midway at Chicago in 1893 to the General Motors and Ford assembly lines at Chicago in 1933 and 1934. The argument is that the factory exhibit changed from an educational display into an advertisement: companies used the sight of production to build trust in their brands, and visitors who watched were offered souvenirs and a product to buy. Marsh traces the idea through guidebooks and exhibition manuals, including Lawrence Weaver's 1925 advice to build a miniature factory, and shows that engineers at the 1893 fair were already sceptical that the public understood the technology. The main cases are Libbey's $100,000 exhibit, which turned a profit through souvenirs, the model shoe factory and Singer demonstrations in the Hide and Leather Building, Ford's 1915 Model T line at the Panama-Pacific fair in San Francisco, and the GM and Ford pavilions at Chicago. Marsh concludes that by 1934 factories had given way to entertainment, as corporations sold images rather than processes.

Chicago 1893Chicago 1933San Francisco 1915
3.3Fordism, Corporate Display, and the American Expositions of the 1930sLisa D. Schrenkp. 181

Schrenk examines how American automotive companies changed their displays at world's fairs in the 1930s, when exhibits that taught visitors about production gave way to pavilions built to reinforce brand recognition. Ford and General Motors competed for visitors through increasingly theatrical buildings, often designed by architects such as Albert Kahn and by industrial designers such as Walter Dorwin Teague. The chapter follows the rivalry through the 1933-34 Century of Progress in Chicago, where GM's Chevrolet assembly line and Ford's 1934 rotunda, with its photomurals, dioramas and rotating globes, were the main attractions, and through Ford's pavilions at San Diego in 1935 and Dallas in 1936, which reused Chicago's displays. It then turns to the 1939 New York fair, where GM's Futurama, designed by Norman Bel Geddes, outdid Ford's Cyclorama of Production. The chapter concludes that the factory had become entertainment by the 1930s, and that the rivalry between the two companies carried on at later fairs.

Chicago 1933San Diego 1935Dallas 1936New York 1939
3.4The Past Was No IllusionWalt Bransfordp. 197

Bransford, an architect who pioneered computer-aided design, argues that world's fairs were a kind of crystal ball, and that the technologies and illusions they staged anticipate today's digital entertainment. The essay first appeared in 1997 as the opening chapter of a volume on the future of entertainment technology, and a foreword by Celia Pearce introduces this reprint. Its main case is the World's Columbian Exposition at Chicago in 1893, where electric lighting, long-distance telephone links and the first Ferris Wheel gave visitors immersive experiences of technology and of a newly connected American landscape. Bransford then turns to Paris in 1900, where the Railway Panorama, the Mareorama and the Cineorama Air-Balloon Panorama used moving screens, rolling platforms and film to simulate a train journey, a sea voyage and a balloon flight. He stresses that these attractions were expensive, shared and sponsored by corporations, and he traces the fairs' decline after New Orleans in 1984. The chapter ends by asking whether an interactive successor to the world's fair can be built online, and it concludes that for creative and entrepreneurial people the future is no illusion.

Chicago 1893Paris 1900
3.5Eames at the FairCelia Pearcep. 207

Pearce traces the work of the Charles and Ray Eames office in communicating science, mathematics and computing to general audiences, principally through world's fair exhibitions and films. The chapter argues that the Eameses brought a design-laboratory method of research, prototyping and modelling to exhibition work, and that their long relationship with IBM produced films, multiscreen shows and museum displays. Its cases are the 1958 Brussels fair, where The Information Machine was shown, the 1959 Moscow exchange exhibition with Glimpses of the U.S.A., the 1962 Seattle pavilion with The House of Science, and above all the IBM Pavilion at the 1964-65 New York fair, with its ovoid theatre and the multiscreen Think. Pearce also covers Mathematica and the puppet shows and carnival-style devices of the IBM pavilion. After the fairs the chapter follows projects such as A Computer Perspective and the 1978 laserdisc experiments Art Game and Merlin and the Time Mobile, which were cut short by Charles Eames's death. It closes by suggesting that, given more time, the office might have pioneered interactive multimedia.

Brussels 1958Moscow 1959Seattle 1962New York 1964
4Design & Architecture Pavilionp. 223
4.1Socialism on Display: The Czechoslovak and Yugoslav Pavilions at the 1958 Brussels World’s FairKimberly Elman Zarecor and Vladimir Kulićp. 225

Zarecor and Kulić compare the Czechoslovak and Yugoslav pavilions at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair, EXPO '58, two small socialist states whose pavilions were among the most admired at a fair dominated by the American and Soviet buildings. They argue that the two countries experienced Stalinism differently: Czechoslovakia implemented Stalinist policies and changed slowly after 1956, while Yugoslavia left Cominform in 1948 and moved towards non-alignment. The Czechoslovak pavilion, designed by Cubr, Hrubý and Pokorný, was a populist and immersive display of 'One Day in Czechoslovakia' with the Laterna Magika and Polyekran shows, and it won the Grand Prix. Yugoslavia's pavilion, by Vjenceslav Richter, was an avant-garde, gallery-like building that won a gold medal but drew under ten per cent of the fair's visitors, and a doll exhibition was needed to attract the press. The chapter concludes that both pavilions hybridized American and Soviet models and offered new answers to the dilemmas of modernity, and it traces how each building survived after the fair.

Brussels 1958
4.2The 1925 Paris Exposition des Arts Decoratifs et Industriels Modernes and Le Pavillon de l’Esprit Nouveau: Le Corbusier’s Modernist ManifestoLynn E. Palermop. 241

Palermo examines the 1925 Paris decorative arts exhibition and, in particular, Le Corbusier's Pavillon de l'Esprit Nouveau built within it. The French organizers hoped to reclaim leadership in the decorative arts with a new style, but the exhibition's art deco favored luxury craft and exotic materials for the wealthy, so Le Corbusier's concrete, steel and glass pavilion stood out as a critique. Inside was a full-size housing cell based on his Dom-Ino principle, and on the terrace was the Plan Voisin, a proposal to raze central Paris for towers. Palermo links these to the postwar housing crisis, to Le Corbusier's idea of the 'homme tout nu', the modern everyman, and to his contrast between Louis XIV's objects of distinction and Lenin sitting in a cafe. The chapter concludes that Le Corbusier's claims to universal human needs were themselves idiosyncratic, so that he had a blind spot about his own assumptions.

Paris 1925
4.3Official and Unofficial Spaces of the Budapest Millennial Exhibition, 1896Dorothy Barenscottp. 249

Barenscott examines the 1896 Budapest Millennial Exhibition, which the author deliberately calls an exhibition rather than a world's fair, and asks how visitors perceived it. The official fairgrounds in a city park offered the conventional repertoire of nineteenth-century expositions: monuments to national heroes, a neo-classical Palace of Art and a tidy map of pavilions, which the foreign press praised as meeting Western standards. Barenscott argues that the most vivid experiences lay beyond the grounds: Budapest's new electric underground railway, guidebooks promoting its cafes, cabarets and baths, and a reconstructed Constantinople on an island in the Danube, which offered night-time illusion and a safe encounter with the Ottoman east. The argument is that the city's position between East and West was packaged as exotic, bohemian and profitable, and that commercialized fairs of the 1890s moved spectacle off the fairgrounds. The text breaks off in the middle of this argument, with a comparison to Chicago in 1893 still open, so no conclusion is given.

Budapest 1896
4.4Expo 67, or Megastructure ReduxInderbir Singh Riarp. 255

Riar examines Expo 67 in Montreal and its theme pavilions, which were conceived as megastructures: flexible, cellular frameworks that would house a mass public and embody the optimism of 1960s architecture. The chapter traces the idea to the van Ginkels, Montreal architects and Team 10 members, who wanted the fair organized around a city theme rather than national pavilions, and to Giedion's reading of nineteenth-century exhibition buildings such as the Crystal Palace, the Galerie des Machines and the Eiffel Tower. Riar then follows the collapse of the master plan into five theme pavilions. The central case is Man the Producer, designed by Arcop with the space-frame engineer Jeffrey Lindsay, whose tetrahedral cells owed much to Buckminster Fuller and whose oversized gusset plates were bolted together in 1966. Riar draws on Reyner Banham's 1967 review, which found the tetrahedral pavilion the only place where people were written into the act, and on the critical reception that photographed it as a dematerializing dreamscape. The chapter concludes that the utopian promise of the megastructure lasted only the six months of the fair.

Montreal 1967
4.5The Restoration of the New York Hall of ScienceRaymond M. Pepi, Christopher Gembinski, Laura Buchnerp. 271

This is a conservation report on the exterior restoration of the Great Hall of the New York Hall of Science, designed by Wallace K. Harrison for the 1964-65 New York World's Fair as a permanent museum and one of the few fair buildings to survive. The authors describe the building: a ninety-foot cast-in-place concrete grid filled with some 5,400 dalle-de-verre panels of cobalt-blue glass, which made it the largest installation of its type. They explain why the concrete deteriorated, mainly through carbonation and corrosion of rebar where the cover was too thin, and why earlier patching had failed by 2005. Much of the chapter sets out the testing programme, including laboratory weathering tests, two years of field monitoring with embedded electrodes, mock-ups of repair mortars and comparisons of crack-injection materials. The repairs, which include over 3,000 concrete patches, about 4,000 routed cracks and replacement epoxy panels, are then described. The authors conclude that most of the original glass was kept, so the interior still reads as the luminous hall its architects intended.

New York 1964
5Operations & Urban Planning Pavilionp. 279
5.1Panorama: Robert Moses’ Modern City and the New York World’s FairsMagdalena Sabatp. 281

Sabat examines the Panorama of New York City, a 9,335-square-foot scale model built for the 1964-65 New York World's Fair under Park Commissioner Robert Moses, and the planning ideas it carried. She places the fairs of 1939-40 and 1964-65 in the context of postwar suburbanization, urban decline and Moses's highway programme, arguing that the fairs presented the city's future as already achieved. The model, shown beside the 1931 Castello Model of New Amsterdam, displayed Moses's public works and some projects not yet begun, and was built to serve as a planning tool after the fair. The chapter contrasts it with the 1939 Futurama and Democracity, which imagined decentralized cities, and argues that the 1964 Panorama envisaged a city of networks and arterials. It notes the defeat of the Lower Manhattan Expressway and Moses's declining standing. Sabat concludes, drawing on Jansson and Lagerkvist and on Benjamin, that the Panorama is now a ghostly relic whose meaning lies in showing the incompleteness of planning without people.

New York 1939New York 1964
5.2The Pass of the Chair Maker: Identity and Visibility at the International Exhibition, 1876Kate LaPradp. 289

LaPrad uses a single photograph admission ticket issued to Elder Robert M. Wagan, a Shaker chair maker from Mount Lebanon, New York, to explore how the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition controlled its visitors. The chapter reconstructs the ticket, a lithographed card with an albumen portrait and a daily punched date, and uses it to show how the Department of Admissions under David Yates handled nearly ten million visitors and some 31,000 exhibitors. The system combined a fixed fifty-cent admission, turnstiles whose counters matched coins, and individual passes that identified exhibitors and workers. The punches on Wagan's pass reveal his repeated visits and suggest that associates ran his stall. LaPrad sets this against the Shaker chair trade, which needed visibility and protection from imitation, and against the administrative culture of the Centennial Commission, whose leaders had military and business backgrounds. The chapter concludes that Yates's photographic passes were an early technology of identity and control, and that the few fraud arrests show the system worked.

Philadelphia 1876
5.3Aucune Usine au Monde: Dreaming Work in the Exposition Universelle, Paris 1878Lawrence Birdp. 299

Bird reads the Palais du Champ de Mars at the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1878 through Marx and Freud, asking what dream the building expresses. The chapter first describes the layout: a central street lined with the Rue des Nations and the Pavillon de Paris, with galleries of exhibits grading from delicate luxury goods to heavy industry, and the Galeries des Machines on either flank. It then turns to the outer edge of the site, where eight smokestacks, the forces motrices, powered the machines and sat beside drinking and eating stalls. Bird calls this a displaced centre in Freud's sense, and reads the transmission network of shafts and belts through Marx's account of machinery in Capital, including his image of the 'mechanical monster'. The argument is that the building's façades of world cultures are a fantasy that disguises an industrial nightmare of alienation. The chapter ends by suggesting that the dream of 1878 still resembles our own world.

Paris 1878
5.4Beyond the Event: World’s Fairs and Urban Transformation Since WWIIGaia Caramellino, Alessandro De Magistris, Federico Deambrosisp. 311

Caramellino, De Magistris and Deambrosis argue that world's fairs should be studied not as enclosed spectacles but as urban transformations that continued long after the events closed. They trace a chronology from the late nineteenth-century exhibitions, which were closely tied to the growth of their host cities, to the postwar fairs, in which planning and architecture became central. Their main cases are Brussels 1958, where the fair helped drive the remaking of the city centre, and Turin 1961, whose durable buildings such as Nervi's Palazzo del Lavoro were linked to the urbanisation of a southern periphery. They also consider the New York fair of 1964-65, which the authors treat as a missed opportunity for urban planning, and Montreal 1967, whose infrastructure reshaped Ile Sainte-Hélène. The chapter then moves through Genoa, Seville and Lisbon in the 1990s and Shanghai 2010, where fairs served as triggers for port, waterfront and metropolitan regeneration. The authors end by noting that European fairs since 2000 have shifted toward smaller, more dispersed projects, while Shanghai 2010 carried the older model of large-scale city regeneration.

Brussels 1958Turin 1961New York 1964Montreal 1967Genoa 1992Seville 1992Lisbon 1998Shanghai 2010
5.5Victor Gruen and the World’s Fair that Wasn’tTimothy Mennelp. 323

Mennel describes Victor Gruen's 1959 proposal for a world's fair near Largo, Maryland, outside Washington, which would have been a permanent, fully functioning town rather than a temporary exhibition. Mennel traces Gruen's earlier work, from the Southdale shopping centre to the Fort Worth Plan and the television programme 1976, to show how the fair proposal extended his ideas about cellular urban form. The fair was to have a pedestrian core on two levels, surrounded by parking and 4,500 acres of open land, and to be converted after the fair into a town of 100,000 people. Mennel argues that the plan depended on central control, which had become politically unpopular, and that it prefigured new towns, Columbia in Maryland, and Baltimore's Harborplace. The proposal also lost to the New York team, and Gruen's attempt to bring a 'World of Tomorrow' pavilion to New York failed too. The chapter closes by linking the plan to transit-oriented developments and New Urbanism, and by arguing that such communities assume a narrow set of users, for whom 'better' is narrowly defined.

Largo, Maryland 1964 (proposed)New York 1964
6Arts, Entertainment & Media Pavilionp. 333
6.1The Theatre Culture of United States International Expositions, 1876-1893Robert Davisp. 335

Davis examines how theatre and popular performance shaped the world's fairs held in the United States between 1876 and 1893. It argues against official claims that fairs were purely educational and against histories that treat amusements as a separate zone. Three cases follow. In Philadelphia in 1876, the 'Centennial City' outside the gates is usually described as a cheap sideshow district, but Davis shows that its model oil well was no different in tone from the machinery exhibits inside, where costumed operators ran looms and band saws for crowds. In New Orleans in 1884-85, the Kiralfy brothers' spectacles and Buffalo Bill's Wild West were treated by the local press as part of the exposition. For Chicago in 1893, Davis describes Buffalo Bill's Wild West, now a more polished show, and Kiralfy's America, which put the fair itself on stage, along with the theatrical demonstrations in Machinery Hall. The sources are playbills, newspapers and fairgoers' diaries, used to argue that the fair and the theatre formed one culture of performance. The conclusion widens the point to panoramas and dime museums, which fairgoers visited alongside the exhibits.

Philadelphia 1876New Orleans 1884Chicago 1893
6.2Film, Technology, and Imperialism at the Pan-American Exposition, 1901Brian R. Jacobsonp. 349

Jacobson examines the films Edison's cameramen James White and Edwin Porter made at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo in 1901. The argument is that the films reproduce the fair's logic of transforming nature through technology, and that their margins reveal more than their foreground attractions do. The chapter first traces White's earlier work at the Paris Exposition of 1900, where the rotating tripod head was tested, and then turns to Pan-American Exposition by Night, a panorama that starts in daylight and continues after dark, so day seems to turn into night. Jacobson links this to the Niagara-powered lighting, which made the fair's artificial light depend on the nature it masked. Close readings of Esquimaux Leap-frog and Spanish Dancers show layered planes of foreground spectacle, middle-ground village or tent, and background wires and chimneys, which Jacobson reads as the Exposition's ideology of 'primitive' peoples set against modern technology. The films also leave out Niagara Falls, a conspicuous absence that marks the fair's uneasy relation to nature. The conclusion argues that, read at their margins, the films show the ideals that structured both fairs and early cinema.

Buffalo 1901Paris 1900
6.3Humphrey Jennings and the Festival Audience: Spare Time, Family Portrait, and the Rhetoric of National IdentityKevin M. Flanaganp. 363

Flanagan revisits two films that Humphrey Jennings made for world's fairs and festivals, Spare Time (1939) for the British Pavilion at the New York World's Fair and Family Portrait (1951) for the Festival of Britain. Flanagan argues that Anderson's influential auteurist reading, which prizes the wartime films, overlooks how fair and festival audiences shaped these works. The chapter sets out the audiences the films had to address. Spare Time shows workers in Sheffield, Lancashire and Wales at leisure, with each section built around a local band's performance. Its American references, such as a Western pulp magazine and a basketball game, were pitched at an American audience. Family Portrait, by contrast, speaks to a British public about austerity, presenting the nation as a family whose history of invention, from Drake to radar, supports the present. The film was sent to twenty-three countries as a sanctioned advertisement for the new national self-image. Together the films show cinema serving as national self-presentation at fairs, and Flanagan concludes that Family Portrait argues for compromise as a way of life, preparing for a welfare state.

New York 1939London 1951
6.4Progress is More Than Just a Word: The Workers Film and Photo League at the 1933 Chicago World’s FairCarla Leshnep. 371

Leshne uses the Workers Film and Photo League's response to the 1933 Chicago 'Century of Progress' fair to show how radical groups tried to counter the official picture of ideal American life during the Depression. Leshne works from three surviving artefacts: two films, Conditions in Chicago and Century of Progress, and the pamphlet Chicago on Parade. The chapter first explains the League's history, which was largely erased in the McCarthy period, and Rydell's account of the fair as a defence of corporate capitalism. It then reads the films the League made: Conditions in Chicago sets images of progress against evictions and Hoovervilles, while Century of Progress uses montage and intertitles to mock the fair's sideshows and corporate pavilions and then turns to a cotton strike in California. Leshne also reconstructs the arrests of members and the pamphlet's photographs, which show hunger marches and shanty towns set against the fair's claims. The conclusion is that these materials recover a body of resistance that the fair and later history obscured.

Chicago 1933
6.5Panic at the Pan 1901: Anarchy, Electricity, Early CinemaChris Kamerbeekp. 379

Kamerbeek reads the Edison film Execution of Czolgosz, and the Pan-American films around it, to argue that early cinema and the fair both turned shock into spectacle. The chapter begins with McKinley's assassination in the Temple of Music at Buffalo in September 1901 and the Edison crew who filmed the panic outside. It then sets the Pan in the lineage of the Chicago 1893 fair, with its Midway and White City, and reads the Pan's planning, from its main axis to its 'Rainbow City' colour scheme, as a way of directing the visitor's gaze. Electricity and the Electric Tower are treated as a technological sublime that doubled as a cinematic model, especially in the slow pan of Pan-American Exposition by Night. Kamerbeek also takes up the anarchist 'mob' that Czolgosz was made to stand for, and the staging of the execution at Auburn with the electric chair as a machine under control. The chapter concludes that Edison's films move from anxiety about the crowd to reassurance through order and ritual, and that the execution film serves state power.

Buffalo 1901Chicago 1893
7Amusements & Recreation Pavilionp. 393
7.1How the Theme Park Got Its Power: The World’s Fair as Cultural FormScott A. Lukasp. 395

Lukas compares world's fairs with theme parks, asking how each shaped the experience of the people who visited and worked in them. He opens with a fictional visitor's walk through a themed space, then sets out five points of comparison: architecture and space, cultural display, sociality, material culture and consumption, and rides. On architecture he notes the fair's temporary monuments, such as the Eiffel Tower and the Trylon and Perisphere, and its site plans, which later amusement parks adopted as landmarks and as a means of controlled space. Under cultural display he traces 'place sampling', the re-creation of places such as the Streets of Cairo at the 1893 Chicago fair, as the origin of theming. The sociality and consumption sections draw on Rydell and Kasson for performers and crowd control, and on the brand-saturated Food Zone of the 1939 New York fair. The chapter closes with rides, notably the Ferris wheel and A Trip to the Moon, and concludes that the fair changed culture itself, even as the world expo now converges with theme parks.

Chicago 1893New York 1939New York 1964
7.2Disney and “This World’s Fair Thing”J. P. Telottep. 409

Telotte argues that Disney's work for the 1964-65 New York fair was a creative turn, not merely a business decision to fund Disneyland attractions. He examines four pavilions: the Ford Magic Skyway, with its WEDway Peoplemover ride through dinosaur and cave-man scenes; the Pepsi-UNICEF 'It's a Small World'; the Illinois 'Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln'; and the General Electric 'Carousel of Progress'. Drawing on Virilio and Casetti, he reads these attractions as cinematized experiences that place viewers both inside and detached from the scene, a development from the dioramas and industrial-design exhibits of the 1930s fairs, including New York 1939. He uses cost and reception details, including Robert Moses's support for Lincoln and a critic's dismissal of the figure as technical mania, to show what was at stake. The chapter ends by noting that Disney died in 1966 and that these exhibits later reappeared in the parks, and by treating them as a blueprint for the planned EPCOT.

New York 1964New York 1939
7.3A World of Fun: The New York World’s Fair 1964/1965David Thomasp. 423

Thomas argues that what set the 1964-65 New York World's Fair apart was its fun, which he defines, after Gregory Bateson, as pleasure in an is/is-not frame, where something is presented as what it is not. He grounds the claim in the fair's official Souvenir Book, which he treats as the most concise record of the event. Its section on fun, its full-size replica of Columbus's Santa Maria shown beside an original map, its Disney dinosaur scenes, and its mix of earnest and silly material all frame the serious themes of progress and corporate promotion in play. He quotes Robert Moses's introduction, in which Moses declines to compete with the city's museums, to show the fair's self-consciously unserious stance. The chapter argues that this fun had long-term significance, since its legacy passed to Disney and its permanent fair at Epcot. In conclusion Thomas asks whether fun explains both the fair's dismissal by critics and its enduring place in visitors' memories.

New York 1964
7.4A History of Picnics at World’s FairsVan Troi Tranp. 435

Tran argues that picnics, though a visible presence on fairgrounds, have been largely ignored in histories of world's fairs. Using press reports, official reports, caricatures and advice columns, the chapter reconstructs picnicking at Paris 1889 and 1900, Chicago 1893, New York 1964-65, Montreal 1967 and Shanghai 2010. It reads the picnic in several ways: as a social leveler that inverted class distinctions, with millionaires in the Eiffel Tower and workers on the lawns; as a thrifty alternative to crowded and costly restaurants, which guidebooks promoted; and as a source of sociability and calm amid the sensory strain of the fair. It also traces the market for picnic gear and box lunches. The sharpest episode is Auguste Escoffier's attack on picnicking in Paris, set against French ideas of national cuisine and contrasted with the pastoral, Sunday-school image of the American picnic. The chapter ends with Shanghai 2010, where airport-style checks barred cooked food and take-away meals for fear of food poisoning.

Paris 1889Paris 1900Chicago 1893New York 1964Montreal 1967Shanghai 2010
7.5EPCOT: Disney’s (sort of) World’s FairStacy Warrenp. 447

Warren argues that Epcot, though not a world's fair, works as a permanent one and inherits the fair's preoccupations with technology and empire. The chapter begins with Walt Disney's experience of earlier fairs, especially the 1964 New York fair, where corporate sponsors shaped attractions that Disney then wove into familiar narratives. The main evidence is Epcot's organization into Future World, a set of corporate pavilions such as Spaceship Earth, Universe of Energy and The Living Seas, and World Showcase, a ring of national pavilions. Warren shows how both halves depended on sponsors and governments whose contracts ran out, so that exhibits were abandoned, replaced or rewritten. Communicore, Spaceship Earth after AT&T's exit, and Norway's decaying pavilion, which Disney refused to update, are the main examples. The chapter ends by describing Epcot as a mirror held up to a mirror, a living forum in which messages of technology and empire are absorbed, rewritten or rejected, and asks how such narratives change when they are fixed permanently in the landscape.

New York 1964
8Pavilion of the Futurep. 457
8.1The Cartoons of Tomorrow’s ConveniencesBobby Schweizerp. 459

Schweizer examines three animated shorts of the 1930s that drew on the fair's promise of modern convenience: Disney's Modern Inventions (1937), Fleischer's All's Fair at the Fair (1938), made for a newsreel on the 1939 New York fair, and Warner Bros.' Dog Gone Modern (1939). The argument is that the cartoons respond to the fair's rhetoric of the future in different ways. Modern Inventions and Dog Gone Modern treat automation with suspicion, and the chapter reads their gags, from a robot butler to a bundle-wrapping machine and a dishwasher that drags a dog through the sink, as cautionary and as echoes of Chaplin's Modern Times. All's Fair at the Fair is the exception, a celebration in which the country couple Elmer and Miranda are remade by robotic barbers, beauty treatments and a vending-machine car. The chapter sets this against the Century of Progress fair of 1933 and the home-of-tomorrow tradition. It concludes that the shorts gave audiences a space to explore the pleasures and fears of new technology, which Schweizer relates to Michael O'Pray's idea of animation as a phantasy of control.

New York 1939Chicago 1933
8.2The Japan Pavilion at the 1964/65 New York World’s Fair: A Vision of the Near FutureLori C. Waltersp. 467

Walters examines the promotional materials of the Japan Pavilion at the 1964-65 New York World's Fair, arguing that they signaled an industrial challenge to American manufacturers rather than a cultural exchange. Against the background of the Second World War and the cheap goods Americans associated with Japan, the pavilion's brochures, give-away cards and advertisements stressed industrial rankings, the Shinkansen bullet train and the 1964 Tokyo Olympics. Walters focuses on consumer electronics: Matsushita's cards praising transistor production, the Seiko walking robot Tik-Tok, Sony's portable Videocorder, and Hitachi's 1965 advertisement claiming that Made in Japan means quality. Toray's synthetic fibers, shown in kimonos, and the automobile material, which was modest beside the American pavilions, complete the survey. The chapter also tracks the guidebook advertising, with fourteen Japanese advertisements in 1964 and twelve in 1965, a level matched only by the American hard-liquor industry. It concludes that the pavilion pointed to an industrial future that the fair's American displays had not foreseen.

New York 1964
8.3To Work and Play and Live in the Year 2000: Creating the Future at the 1962 Seattle World’s FairStacy Warrenp. 473

Warren argues that the 1962 Seattle fair, the Century 21 Exposition, was the boldest attempt yet to use a world's fair as a tool of urban redevelopment. Its planners cleared the old Warren neighborhood, demolishing 203 buildings, and designed a compact site of 74 acres as a suburban image of city life, with Disney supplying behind-the-scenes management advice rather than attractions. The chapter moves through the fair's five worlds. The World of Science, centered on Minoru Yamasaki's U.S. Science Exhibit and a film by Charles and Ray Eames, is the most fully described. Warren then sets the pessimistic World of Tomorrow, whose Threshold and Threat presentation mixed visions of Seattle in 2000 with images of atomic war, against the commercial pavilions, the Gayway midway and the adult attractions of Show Street. Attendance of 9.6 million and a small profit serve as the evidence of success. Warren ends by tracing how the site became Seattle Center, with its Fun Forest until 2011, and how a 1980s proposal to use Disney as urban consultants was rejected by residents.

Seattle 1962
8.4A World Fair for the Future: A Study of the Legacy of the Expo ‘98 Urban ModelPatricia Simões Aelbrechtp. 485

Aelbrecht argues that Expo '98 marked a third model for world's fairs, after Paris 1889 and Brussels 1958: the fair as a catalyst of urban renewal, with its site planned from the start as a neighbourhood. The evidence comes from the archives of Parque Expo and of the Bureau International des Expositions, from interviews with the planners, and from a close reading of the plan's four public axes, its mixed-use zoning and its double-function public spaces. Aelbrecht shows how Parque Expo chose Vancouver, Brisbane, Seville and Barcelona as models and what it took from each. The second half turns to reception: a small audited loss, the railway line that cut the new district off from its western neighbours, a largely affluent population, and a model that has spread slowly, with Shanghai 2010 the closest follower. The chapter closes with two lessons for future expos: choose a site inside the city's strategic plan, and plan the post-use from the start.

Lisbon 1998Shanghai 2010
8.5Flying to the World of Tomorrow: The Ascension Theme at the 1939 New York World’s FairAdnan Morshedp. 503

Morshed argues that the ascension theme of flight, wings and aerial viewpoints gave the 1939 New York World's Fair its vision of the 'World of Tomorrow', and that the fair marked the last burst of utopian technological culture before the Second World War. The evidence is visual and material: Binder's winning poster, the official guidebook's aerial drawing, the documentary The City (1939), and the wing sculptures of Foster and Whitney. Morshed also shows how Grover Whalen tied the fair to Howard Hughes's 1938 round-the-world flight. The central cases are General Motors' Futurama, whose conveyor-belt ride simulated a flight over a 1960 America, and the Perisphere's Democracity, where visitors looked down on a planned metropolis from revolving balconies. The Trylon, Perisphere and Helicline are read as the stage for this aerial gaze. Morshed ends by arguing that the aerial view let Depression-era visitors see an uncertain future as attainable, a view the corporate sponsors used to sell consumer utopia.

New York 1939
EpilogueIsaac Asimovp. 517

Asimov, writing in 1964, uses the New York World's Fair of that year as a starting point for guessing what the fair of 2014 will show. He imagines homes with glowing walls and underground houses, automated kitchens, batteries run on radioisotopes, and transport on compressed-air jets, moving pavements and robot-driven cars. He also expects video telephones, laser links to the moon, undersea cities and algae foods. The essay turns grim in its later pages, arguing that population growth will outrun technology, that birth control must be pushed through a worldwide propaganda drive, and that automation will leave people bored. It closes on the thought that, in a society of enforced leisure, work will have become the most glorious word in the vocabulary. The piece is a speculative magazine essay rather than a scholarly chapter, and it cites no sources.

New York 1964
Author Biosp. 525
Hopson, Nathan. “‘A Bad Peace?’: The 1937 Nagoya Pan-Pacific Peace Exhibition.” Journal article.Asia: central5 chapter overviews

Overview

Hopson examines the 1937 Nagoya Pan-Pacific Peace Exhibition, a city-branding event meant to present Nagoya as an industrial and cultural centre. Its ideal of capitalist peace through trade was compromised by the Imperial Japanese Army, which forced in a national defence hall and live-fire displays, and by pressure from Tokyo. Hopson argues that the expo still shows the diversity of Japanese politics before the war with China. After an introduction, the article covers local promotion, accommodation with the army, a comparison with Paris 1937 and a conclusion.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

The article concerns a Japanese exhibition in Nagoya, so Japan is its subject throughout. The chapter 'Local Promotion and Capitalist Peace in the Pacific Age' carries most of this, covering the prefectural, colonial and firm pavilions such as Toyota, Mayor Ōiwa's 'Great Nagoya' campaign and the expo's place in a new Japan-led 'Pacific Age'. 'Accommodation and Survival' treats the Imperial Japanese Army's demands and the recruitment of Prince Higashikuni as chairman, and the introduction places the expo in the diversity of Japanese politics before the war with China.

Beyond Japan, East Asian participation is limited to Japan's colonies and puppet regimes. The pavilions of Manchukuo and the East Hebei regime, and the Taiwanese and Korean pavilions named in the conclusion, are presented as Japanese imperial display, and the East Hebei Hall and Day are read as evidence of Japan's ambitions in China. Southeast Asia is slight: a Dutch Indies exhibit appears among pavilions of other imperial powers, alongside Ceylon, a South Asian case outside the question. Visitors are described as mostly from Japan and its colonial possessions, and no Southeast Asian participation or colonial display of people is discussed.

Contents

Abstractp. 137
Introductionp. 137

Hopson introduces the 1937 Nagoya Pan-Pacific Peace Exhibition as a city-branding event. Although army concessions made it look like a cynical misuse of capitalist peace, Hopson argues that Nagoya's elites still clung to a 1920s vision of peace through trade rather than autarky. Drawing on mega-event theory and regional histories of interwar Japan, the introduction presents the expo as evidence of the diversity of Japanese politics before the war with China.

Nagoya 1937
Local Promotion and Capitalist Peace in the Pacific Agep. 139

Hopson shows how the Nagoya expo, planned in 1934 as a port anniversary and widened into a pan-Pacific peace event, was shaped by compromise between Nagoya's city-branding ambitions, its trade-based prosperity and the need to avoid friction with Tokyo. Its vision was a capitalist peace of free trade in a new 'Pacific Age', yet exhibits of modern science and industry dominated, with the Peace Tower as centrepiece, pavilions from Japan's colonies and puppet regimes, and local firms such as Toyota. Most Western governments stayed away, though business groups from San Francisco, Seattle and Dallas came. The article traces Nagoya's rise from castle town to industrial hub and Mayor Ōiwa's hope of rebranding the city as 'Great Nagoya'. It ends with the planners' anxieties about autarky and the distrust that followed Manchukuo.

Nagoya 1937
Accommodation and Survivalp. 144

Hopson shows how the expo survived pressure from Tokyo and the Imperial Japanese Army. Concern not to rival Tokyo or upstage the 1940 Olympics led the mayor to keep the scale modest and call the event pan-Pacific. The army's demands produced a Hall of National Defense and Aviation, with a panorama of modern warfare and a radio tour in April 1937. The mayor's defence was to recruit Prince Higashikuni as chairman, which shielded the expo from direct military criticism.

Nagoya 1937
Nagoya and Parisp. 147

Hopson compares the Nagoya expo with Paris 1937, arguing that both were spectacles of self-promotion in industry, trade and science, both were integrated into their cities, and both were shaped by rising tensions, the Japanese army in Nagoya and Germany in Paris. Both went through two planning stages and both added peace themes that could not stop the war. Herbert's phrase 'strange marriage of audacity and uncertainty' fits Nagoya as well as Paris.

Nagoya 1937Paris 1937
Conclusionp. 148

Hopson concludes that the expo's idea of peace, though weak, belonged to a serious interwar doctrine of capitalist peace, and that its promoters' bylaws and publicity promised amity and prosperity around the Pacific. In practice, Hopson suggests, visitors remembered the Hall of National Defense, live-fire drills and naval torpedoes more than peace, and the expo, like Japan itself, was massive and diverse.

Nagoya 1937
Referencesp. 149
Hotta-Lister, Ayako. The Japan-British Exhibition of 1910: Gateway to the Island Empire of the East. Richmond: Japan Library, 1999.Asia: central9 chapter overviews

Overview

Hotta-Lister studies the Japan-British Exhibition, held at the White City in London from May to October 1910. Its argument is that the Japanese government treated the exhibition as a national undertaking, meant to correct British views of Japan and to serve political and economic aims. The book covers the background from 1905 to 1910, the preparations in Japan and London, the sponsors' objectives, the opening months, British and Japanese reactions, and the aftermath in trade, loans and diplomacy. Its final chapter judges the exhibition on balance a success and compares it with the 1981-82 Great Japan Exhibition and the 1991 Japan Festival. Appendices list Japan's exhibition participation from 1873 to 1910 and the main exhibits.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the subject of the whole book, so its coverage is central. Japan is sponsor, exhibitor and object of display, and state participation runs through every chapter: the commissioners, the Exhibitors Association, the 1.8 million yen budget, the Palace of the Orient and the Japanese Village. Korea and Manchuria appear mainly as politics: in chapter 1, Background of the Time, on the open door dispute and the annexation of Korea, and in chapter 3, Exhibition Objectives, which sets the Palace of the Orient, with its Korean and Formosan displays, beside the colonial sections of the 1908 Franco-British Exhibition. Chapter 5, Reactions, and chapter 6, Aftermath, treat the Ainu and Formosan displays and the Chinese displays as embarrassments to Japanese residents. China also enters through the Osaka domestic exhibition of 1903 and Chinese student protests against it.

Southeast Asia is slight. Indochina appears as a French possession in a list of annexations cited for Korea (chapter 3) and as a pavilion at the 1908 exhibition (chapter 5). The Philippines are mentioned in the 1905 Taft agreement (chapter 1) and as Filipino natives at St Louis in 1904 (chapter 5). Singapore is one of the new trade posts of 1910 (chapter 1), and chapter 7, Some Concluding Reflections, cites Japanese wartime atrocities in Thailand and Burma. The Dutch East Indies appear only as a participant at Osaka in 1903 (Appendix A). Siam, Malaya and Borneo are not discussed.

Contents

Prefacep. vii
Acknowledgementsp. ix

Hotta-Lister thanks the archives, libraries and individuals who made the study possible. The sources were the British and Japanese Official Reports on the 1910 exhibition, British Foreign Office papers, Japanese diplomatic and political archives, and newspapers in English and Japanese. Thanks also go to people who supplied photographs, information on the 1991 Japan Festival, and advice, above all Professor Nish, who guided the project.

List of Illustrations (Plate Section)p. xi
List of Tablesp. xiii
Abbreviationsp. xv
Introductionp. 1

Hotta-Lister introduces the 1910 exhibition at the White City in London, which ran from May to October and drew over eight million visitors, and places it within the history of nineteenth-century international exhibitions. The study's argument is that the Japanese government saw the event as a national undertaking meant to educate the British public about Japan and to pursue political and economic aims. Quotations from ministers and ambassadors call the two countries 'Island Empires', and the author reads this language as a claim to equal footing. The introduction then surveys the Great Exhibition of 1851, the spread of thematic and imperial displays, and the Franco-British exhibition of 1908 that used the same site. It sets out the book's plan: background on Anglo-Japanese relations, preparations, the opening period, British and Japanese reactions, and the aftermath. It also notes that the book is not a report on the exhibition itself, and that the final chapter compares it with the 1991 Japan Festival.

London 1910London 1851
1Background of the Time (1905-10)p. 9

Hotta-Lister sets out the diplomatic and economic setting for the exhibition in the years 1905 to 1910. Japan had become a great power after the Russo-Japanese War, and its legations in London, Washington and other capitals were upgraded to embassies between 1906 and 1908. The chapter then traces strains in the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, which British newspapers and officials increasingly questioned over Manchuria, the 'open door' pledge and Japanese immigration. It goes on to tariff revision, which Komura pursued against British objections, and to Japan's trade deficit and reliance on foreign loans. Its last sections cover the annexation of Korea in August 1910 and the rivalry between Katsura and Saionji. It also surveys the Japanese and English-language newspapers on which much of the study relies, including The Times, the Japan Weekly Mail and the Chuo Shimbun. The chapter concludes that these pressures explain why the government was so committed to the exhibition.

2Preparationsp. 38

Hotta-Lister shows how deeply the Japanese government committed itself to the London exhibition and how far the two sides differed in approach. The idea came from the entrepreneur Imre Kiralfy, who had staged imperial spectacles and organised the White City site; Komura took it up in Tokyo, while Kato, Mutsu Hirokichi and the commissioners Wada and Beppu handled it in London. The chapter reconstructs the earlier rejections of Kiralfy's plan and the rivalry with possible American and Russian exhibitions. It then covers the 1.8 million yen budget, the exhibitors' association, the selection of 19,943 articles from 1,286 exhibitors, and the gardens, models and entertainers shipped from Japan. British responses were lukewarm: the Board of Trade and Grey gave little official support, while a General Committee under the Duke of Norfolk formed and the Japan Society was given its own space. It ends with the opening on 14 May 1910, two days late after the death of Edward VII.

London 1910Tokyo 1912
3Exhibition Objectivesp. 74

This chapter asks why the Japanese government sponsored the Japan-British Exhibition and what it hoped to gain. Hotta-Lister divide the aims into political and diplomatic, economic and educational groups. The political case is tied to three issues then pending with Britain: revision of Japan's commercial tariffs, renewal of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, and the annexation of Korea, which took place in August 1910 while the Exhibition was open. Working through speeches, newspapers and diplomatic correspondence, the authors argue that Komura and Katsura saw the Exhibition as a platform for Japan's imperial role, and they set the Palace of the Orient, with its Korean and Formosan displays, beside the colonial exhibits of the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908. The economic section covers City loans, exports to Britain and the trade imbalance. The educational section shows Japanese leaders trying to correct British views of Japan as warlike or backward, through the book Japan Today and The Times Japanese Edition. The chapter ends with these publications.

London 1910
4From the Opening Day Until the End of the Exhibitionp. 100

This chapter narrates the Exhibition from its opening on 14 May 1910 to the receipt of the official reports in 1912. Hotta-Lister estimate attendance at over eight million and describe the evening illuminations, fireworks and package tours that drew crowds. Most of the chapter is a dated record of visits and events: Prince Fushimi's attendance at King Edward's funeral, banquets for British and Japanese dignitaries, Japan Day, and visits by Kitchener, Marie Stopes, the Swedish royal couple and the Brazilian president-elect. It also records a private viewing of retrospective Japanese art for about 350 European experts. The authors then trace the afterlife of the exhibits, which were shipped home, given to British and European institutions, or sent to exhibitions in Budapest, Dresden and Turin. Little is argued here; the chapter is a record of ceremony and diplomacy that frames the reactions discussed next.

London 1910
5Reactions to the Exhibitionp. 110

This chapter weighs the reception of the Exhibition in Britain and Japan. Hotta-Lister conclude that it did not change British attitudes toward Japan in diplomacy or trade, though publications about Japan rose sharply in 1910 and 1911. The British press praised the Japanese fine arts, gardens and wooden buildings, including the Chokushimon gate later re-erected at Kew, while some critics judged them by European standards as barbaric or childlike. Japanese opinion was largely hostile. Elite residents in London were embarrassed by the Japanese Village, the Ainu and Formosan displays and the sumo wrestlers, and their complaints reached the Diet, where Kurahara and Nishimura attacked Komura and the promoter Kiralfy. The authors read the colonial displays as part of a common imperial genre. The chapter ends with British manufacturers doubting that exhibitions paid, and with a 1910 proposal for a British-only exhibition in Japan.

London 1910
6Aftermath of the Exhibitionp. 153

Hotta-Lister asks whether the 1910 Japan-British Exhibition in London was, as Japanese opinion held, a failure, and tests its effects in economic, financial, diplomatic and racial terms. On trade, the author sets Japanese and British statistics beside the exhibitors' sales figures to show that Japanese exports to Britain fell overall in 1910 and 1911, while matting, raw silk, shell buttons and toys rose, and treats the Exhibition as one plausible contributor. Loans get the same caution: the government's conversion loans and the municipal and South Manchurian Railway issues were raised largely through the usual banks, so the Exhibition at most reinforced existing confidence. The chapter then follows the tariff dispute, the annexation of Korea in August 1910 and the renewal of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance in July 1911, drawing heavily on British press reactions. Its racial discussion centres on the Official Guide's claims of similarity between Japanese and British people and on Japanese complaints about Chinese and Ainu displays. It concludes that the Exhibition had only a limited effect, though it was not the failure that Japanese critics claimed.

London 1910
7Some Concluding Reflectionsp. 186

Hotta-Lister gives an overall verdict on the 1910 Exhibition, concluding that it was on balance a success rather than the failure of Japanese opinion. The argument rests on the partnership between Imre Kiralfy, the commercial entrepreneur, and the Japanese government under Komura, which the author sees as the seed of later controversy in the Diet. Komura's aims were mainly diplomatic, to ease anti-Japanese feeling and support the Alliance, with trade and loans as secondary goals, and the proposed Grand Japanese Exhibition of 1917 is shown to have been a further reason for the venture. The Japanese negative reviews are traced to Kiralfy's popular attractions and to the elite's embarrassment at Ainu and village displays, which the author compares with exhibitions in the United States. The closing pages set the 1910 event beside the Great Japan Exhibition of 1981/82 and the Japan Festival of 1991 in London, which shared a wish to correct misunderstanding of Japan but differed in scale, funding and educational follow-up. The author concludes that the Exhibition helped turn the Alliance into a link between peoples, though only to a limited extent.
