Hur, Hyungju. “Staging Modern Statehood: World Exhibitions and the Rhetoric of Publishing in Late Qing China, 1851–1910.” Doctoral dissertation.Asia: central8 chapter overviews

Overview

Hur's dissertation examines how the late Qing government tried to present China as a modern state at world exhibitions, and how that effort was undermined by the Imperial Maritime Customs, Japan, and Chinese reformers and revolutionaries. Its argument is that the same official aim was received differently as context changed: the Osaka (1903) and St. Louis (1904) fairs became occasions of national humiliation in the Chinese press, while the Nanyang Industrial Exposition in Nanjing (1910) won brief support once the court promised constitutional reform. The work has an introduction, four chapters running from China's participation before 1903 to the 1910 fair, and a conclusion arguing that the Chinese case does not fit Western theories of exhibitions as hegemonic propaganda or as a stage for the colonized to resist.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the subject of the whole work, which asks how China presented itself at world exhibitions. Japan and Taiwan are active rivals rather than background: the Introduction casts Japan as using the fairs to present itself as Asia’s only modern state, including through its colony Taiwan, and Chapter One compares China with Japan from Philadelphia in 1876 onwards. The densest material is in Chapter Two, “China, the ‘Barbarian’ Guest of Honor at the Osaka Exhibition of 1903”, on the Jinruikan, which planned to display Chinese and other ‘native’ peoples, and on the Taiwan Pavilion; and in Chapter Three, “Recurrence of Trauma at the St. Louis Exposition of 1904”, on a Chinese Village where a bound-foot woman was displayed and on the Japanese section’s wooden map that included Chinese and Korean coasts.

Southeast Asia is marginal. Chapter Four, on the Nanyang Industrial Exposition in Nanjing in 1910, mentions overseas Chinese merchants from Southeast Asia, such as Zhang Zhenxun, and large Japanese visiting groups, and a footnote states that “Nanyang” does not mean Southeast Asia. The Philippine Reservation at St. Louis appears only in a footnote, and Siam, Indochina and the Dutch East Indies are not discussed.

Contents

Abstract

Hur's abstract summarises a dissertation on the Qing government's attempt to stage modern statehood at world exhibitions and how that attempt was undermined. The Imperial Maritime Customs, Japan and Chinese reformers each shaped China's image, and criticism of the Qing grew after Osaka in 1903 and St Louis in 1904. It ends with the Nanyang Industrial Exposition of 1910, which Chinese intellectuals came to support once the government promised constitutional reform.

Osaka 1903St Louis 1904Nanyang 1910
Acknowledgement

Hur's acknowledgement thanks the dissertation committee, with Kai-wing Chow as adviser, and names Ronald Toby, Dan Shao, Teemu Ruskola and Brian Ruppert for their guidance. It names the institutions where the research was carried out and a person who shared photocopies of Meiji papers on the Osaka Exhibition. It closes with family thanks and a dedication to the author's grandmother, so it contains no argument.

Introductionp. 1

Hur opens with the Shanghai World Exposition of 2010, set against Liang Qichao's novel The Future of New China (1902), which imagined a Great Exhibition in Shanghai in 2062. The dissertation's contention is that the late Qing government's aim of showing modern statehood through world exhibitions was repeatedly challenged. Hur identifies three agents: the Imperial Maritime Customs, largely staffed by foreigners, which selected and shipped China's exhibits; Japan, which used the exhibitions to present itself as Asia's only modern state, including through its colony Taiwan; and Chinese reformers and revolutionaries, whose transnational press attacked the Qing government over national humiliation. The four chapters move from the early history of China's participation to the Osaka Exhibition of 1903, the St Louis Exposition of 1904 and the Nanyang Industrial Exposition of 1910. The argument is that the same objective was received differently as the historical context changed, and that the Nanyang exposition marked a brief reconciliation between the government and its critics.

Osaka 1903St Louis 1904Nanyang 1910
OneChina and the World Exhibitions before 1903p. 11

Chapter One traces China's presence at world exhibitions from London in 1851 to the Paris exposition of 1900, and argues that the foreign-staffed Imperial Maritime Customs shaped how China was shown. The Customs took charge of Chinese exhibits from Vienna in 1873, and the foreign commissioners' selections of local curiosities, including bound-feet shoes and opium tools, later became a target for Chinese critics. Early travelogues by Bin Chun, Li Gui, Guo Songtao and Zeng Jize describe Philadelphia in 1876 and Paris in 1878, and reformers such as Zheng Guanying argued from the 1890s that China should hold its own exhibitions. The chapter also compares China with Japan, whose exhibits from Philadelphia onwards outshone China's, including at Chicago in 1893, and it ends with the Qing court's return to Beijing in 1902, when the reformers' hold on the debate began to change.

London 1851Paris 1867Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876Paris 1878Chicago 1893
TwoChina, the “Barbarian” Guest of Honor at the Osaka Exhibition of 1903p. 47

Hur examines the Fifth Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibition, held in Osaka in 1903, which Japan staged as a semi-international show and a rehearsal for a future world exposition. The chapter first shows how the Meiji government courted Chinese officials and gentry with invitations and complimentary tickets, and how Japanese newspapers cast Japan as a model for Chinese reform. Its main case is the Jinruikan, an entertainment building beside a zoo that planned to display 'native' peoples, including Chinese. Hur follows the protests of Chinese students and merchants in Japan, the involvement of the Chinese minister Cai Jun, and the coverage in Chinese newspapers, then turns to the Taiwan Pavilion and a Taiwanese woman mistaken for a Chinese exhibit. The chapter concludes that Zaizhen's imperial commission made Osaka China's first meaningful step into official overseas exhibiting, but that press distrust of the court was already visible in these disputes.

Osaka 1903
ThreeRecurrence of Trauma at the St. Louis Exposition of 1904p. 86

Hur looks at China's official participation in the Louisiana Purchase Exposition at St. Louis in 1904, the first Qing participation in a Western world fair. The chapter argues that Chinese newspapers read the fair through the Jinruikan trauma of Osaka, so that a run of episodes at St. Louis were framed as national shame. It works through four cases: a portrait of the Empress Dowager painted by the American artist Katharine Carl, which Chinese papers denounced as an insult; a tableau of a bound-foot woman and an opium smoker in the Palace of Liberal Arts; a 'Chinese Village' on the Pike where a bound-foot woman was displayed; and the Japanese section, with its wooden map that included parts of China. Hur also weighs the rumors of embezzlement against Huang Kaijia, the vice commissioner who built the Chinese Pavilion, and finds the charge uncorroborated. The chapter concludes that the fair left a lasting image of official incompetence, which later reappeared at the Liege exposition of 1905.

St. Louis 1904
FourThe Nanyang Industrial Exposition of 1910, the Last Show of the Qing Dynastyp. 124

Hur turns to the Nanyang Industrial Exposition, held in Nanjing from June to November 1910, the first national exposition hosted by China and the last of the Qing dynasty. The chapter traces the project to Duanfang, the Manchu governor-general who proposed it in 1908 and modeled its regulations on Japan's domestic exhibitions, and to his successor Zhang Renjun after Duanfang's transfer in 1909. Hur describes the preparations, including a site of about 165 acres, pavilions for twenty-two provinces, foreign samples buildings, and the security measures taken amid fears of unrest in Nanjing. The main argument concerns the Chinese press, which, unlike its coverage of Osaka and St. Louis, was mostly descriptive or positive, a shift Hur ties to the constitutional movement and to newspapers and organizers who backed it. The chapter also covers the large Japanese visiting groups and the overseas Chinese merchants from Southeast Asia. It concludes that the exposition was a momentary display of an integrated, constitutional China that faded with the Xinhai Revolution of 1911.

Nanjing 1910Brussels 1910
Conclusionp. 163

Hur concludes the dissertation by arguing that the Qing government saw world exhibitions as a diplomatic arena in which to present China as a modern state, while Chinese reformers and revolutionaries used the same displays to attack the court. Osaka, St. Louis and Nanjing are recalled as cases in which Chinese exhibits were exaggerated, distorted or ignored by the press. The chapter notes that 'national humiliation' rhetoric, which had targeted foreign powers, was turned inward against the Qing. Hur then argues that the Chinese case does not fit Western theories that treat exhibitions either as hegemonic propaganda or as a stage for the colonized to resist, and calls for audience-oriented approaches. The conclusion ends with comparisons between Chinese and Japanese exhibition traditions, and with a note on the transnational Chinese press and a late Qing public sphere that extended beyond the national boundary.

Osaka 1903St. Louis 1904Nanjing 1910

Kaiser, Wolfram. “The Great Derby Race: Strategies of Cultural Representation at Nineteenth-Century World Exhibitions.” Article.Asia: substantial1 chapter overview

Overview

Kaiser asks how states used nineteenth-century world exhibitions to represent themselves. Governments, he argues, were the most cohesive actors in a contest that was also a global public space, pursuing a favourable image abroad, alliances, and agendas through culture transfer. France, the United States and Japan anchor the argument, with the Paris exhibitions of 1855 to 1900, Philadelphia in 1876 and Chicago in 1893 as the main cases. The article ends by doubting how far states controlled what visitors took away.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is one of the three anchor cases, and Japan is the article's fullest example of a state using exhibitions to present itself abroad. Japanese sections at the 1867 and 1873 exhibitions and later at Philadelphia (1876), Chicago (1893) and Paris (1900) are read as a way of entering the industrialised Atlantic world. Kaiser quotes the Japanese ambassador Gozo Tateno, who called the Chicago section Japan's 'formal introduction to the West', and argues that the display of readiness to adopt Western production and culture was a 'highly effective cultural shield against imperial intrusion', even as Japan itself fought China in 1894 and annexed Taiwan in 1895. The Japanese case is set within Meiji modernisation and is supported by a 1900 interview with Tadamasa Hayashi.

China serves as the contrast. Its first official representation came only in 1904, its earlier unofficial displays, organised by Western businessmen or regional dignitaries, are called weak, and it is described as 'conservative' and unwilling to adopt Western modernity. Southeast Asia does not appear in the text. The native villages of the Paris and St Louis exhibitions are described without naming any region, and the only non-European region named in the examples is British India, in 1851, which is South Asia and is mentioned for its objects alone.

Contents

Part IICULTURE AND THE STATEp. 43
2The Great Derby Race: Strategies of Cultural Representation at Nineteenth-Century World ExhibitionsWolfram Kaiserp. 45

Kaiser asks how states used the nineteenth-century world exhibitions to represent themselves, and argues that governments were the most cohesive actors in a contest that was also a global public space. He identifies three goals: projecting a favourable national image abroad, forming national or ideological alliances, and setting international or domestic agendas through culture transfer. France, the United States and Japan anchor the argument, with the Paris exhibitions of 1855 to 1900, Philadelphia in 1876 and Chicago in 1893 as the main cases. The means included the layout and architecture of the grounds, monuments such as the Statue of Liberty, machinery such as the Corliss engine, colonial villages with people on display, and state visits and boycotts. The republican delegations of 1889 and the monarchies' boycott show how ideology shaped diplomacy. In the last section Kaiser qualifies the argument, noting that women's and workers' groups occupied parts of the space and that visitors often read colonial displays differently from their organisers. States were largely in charge of the exhibitions, but Kaiser doubts how far they controlled what visitors took from them.

Kargon, Robert H., Karen Fiss, Morris Low and Arthur P. Molella. World’s Fairs on the Eve of War: Science, Technology, and Modernity, 1937–1942. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2015.Asia: substantial7 chapter overviews

Overview

Kargon and colleagues examine five international expositions planned in the years before the Second World War: Paris 1937, Düsseldorf 1937 and New York 1939, which were built, and Tokyo 1940 and Rome 1942, which were planned but never opened. The volume argues that these fairs were arenas of ideological struggle in which liberal, communist, fascist and militarist regimes competed to define modernity and to prepare their peoples for war. The introduction sets them against the history of fairs from the Crystal Palace of 1851 and the crises of the 1930s, and each chapter treats one fair through its planning documents and press coverage. The book closes with the first postwar universal exposition, Brussels 1958, which carried the Cold War rivalry into a fair devoted to peaceful atomic energy.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia figure as one case rather than as a theme. Japan is the only Asian nation with a substantial role, and its treatment is concentrated in chapter 5, "Modernity on Display: The 1940 Grand International Exposition of Japan", on the Tokyo and Yokohama exposition cancelled in 1938: the Commemoration Hall competition, the Nippon Kōbō studio, Bruno Taut's writings on Japanese architecture and the 1942 "Overcoming Modernity" symposium. Japan's participation in fairs run by others is briefer: the Paris 1937 pavilion by Sakakura Junzō (chapter 2), the New York 1939 displays (chapters 4 and 5), and the low-profile exhibit at Brussels 1958 (chapter 7). Chapter 3 mentions a visit to Düsseldorf by Prince Chichibu.

Elsewhere Asia is context or comparison. Chapter 5 links the exposition to the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, the Manchukuo express "Asia", Kenzō Tange's 1942 remark that admiring Angkor Wat was "the mark of an amateur", and a Thai proposal for a Japan-Thailand cultural centre in Bangkok. China appears as the war that cancelled the Tokyo fair and, in chapter 1, as the Manchurian crisis of 1931. Apart from Japan, the passages show no East or Southeast Asian nation exhibiting at these fairs and no Asian colonial display. The only exhibition held in Asia is Osaka 1970, mentioned in passing in chapter 7.

Contents

Acknowledgmentsp. vii
1Introduction: World’s Fairs, Modernity, and the Demand for Authenticityp. 1

The introduction sets out a comparative study of five fairs planned in the 1930s, three built (Paris 1937, Düsseldorf 1937 and New York 1939) and two planned but never opened (Tokyo 1940 and Rome 1942). Its argument is that these fairs became arenas of ideological struggle over modernity, as liberal, communist, fascist and militarist regimes competed to define the future. It traces how world's fairs since the Crystal Palace of 1851 taught populations to accept industrial change as progress, and how after the First World War, with the older empires gone, nations sought a unifying authenticity to animate modern technology. It then sketches the international crises of 1931 to 1936, from Manchuria to the Rhineland, which made the fairs' messages more confrontational. The national messages are outlined in turn: imperial Rome, racial unity in Germany, Japan's pan-Asian mastery, and the democratic displays of France and the United States. The introduction ends by describing the fairs as propaganda contests that preceded a war of armies, and by noting that the war of ideas proved significant for its outcome.

Paris 1937Düsseldorf 1937New York 1939Tokyo 1940Rome 1942
2Modernity à la française: The 1937 Paris Expositionp. 7

The chapter examines the 1937 Exposition internationale des arts et techniques dans la vie moderne in Paris and how it defined a French version of modernity. It argues that the fair, planned under the Third Republic, presented France as a third way between subsistence production and American standardised mass production, with human creativity and artisanship at its centre. The evidence comes from the fair's official magazine, the commissioners' reports and a planning history that began in 1928 and was reshaped after the 1934 Stavisky riots. Edmond Labbé and Paul Léon are the main planners, and the chapter works closely through Jean Perrin's Palais de la Découverte, with its Léger mural, and the modernist commissions the Blum government added. It then turns to the foreign pavilions, where the Soviet and German buildings drew the largest crowds and the Italian and Japanese pavilions blended modernism with tradition, while the American building was judged weak. It concludes that France's claim to be a rational middle way between ideologies looks, in retrospect, fragile.

Paris 1937
3Fantasies of Consumption at Schaffendes Volk: National Socialism and the Four-Year Planp. 30

The chapter examines Schaffendes Volk, the 1937 'international' exhibition in Düsseldorf, as a means of steering German consumers towards the goals of the Four-Year Plan. Its argument is that the fair sold consumer pleasure and wartime sacrifice together, promising abundance from synthetics while asking Germans to accept shortages. The author works through the Ehrenhalle's raw-materials displays, the Lebensraum hall with its large relief map, and a model housing estate that was unfinished at the opening. Women are treated as the key audience, addressed through the Women's Bureau and through advertising for synthetic textiles. The Coca-Cola bottling plant and the modernist industrial design on show illustrate how commercial modernism was absorbed into Nazi propaganda. The chapter then sets the fair against the German pavilion in Paris, which it reads as retrograde, and concludes that the regime reconciled private desire with collective duty by making consumption a form of civic mobilisation.

Düsseldorf 1937Paris 1937
4Whose Modernity?: Utopia and Commerce at the 1939 New York World’s Fairp. 57

The chapter examines the 1939 New York World's Fair as the site of a debate over what progress and modernity should mean for the United States during the Depression. It argues that the official theme, Building the World of Tomorrow with the Tools of Today, was contested between New Deal reformers who wanted public education about planned cities and corporate sponsors who wanted to sell products and free enterprise. The author traces the fair's origins in the Fair of the Future committee, which included Lewis Mumford, and the shift towards corporate pavilions after the renewed economic stress of 1937. The main cases are three visions of the American city: Democracity in the Perisphere, General Motors' Futurama, and the film The City, scripted by Mumford. Foreign pavilions, including those of Britain, Japan, Italy and the Soviet Union, are read as propaganda that the approaching war increasingly overshadowed. The chapter concludes that the fair's uneasy mix of public planning and private enterprise was a compromise, and that by the 1964 fair the corporate path to modernity had become dominant.

New York 1939New York 1964
5Modernity on Display: The 1940 Grand International Exposition of Japanp. 83

The chapter examines the planning of the 1940 Grand International Exposition of Japan, which was to be held in Tokyo and Yokohama to mark the 2,600th anniversary of the mythical accession of Emperor Jimmu, and which was suspended in July 1938. Its argument is that the event, never held, shows how Japan combined modernist technology and architecture with an emperor-centred ideology, a pattern the author tests against Jeffrey Herf's concept of reactionary modernism. The case material includes the Commemoration Hall design competition, an administrative building later used for wounded soldiers, the Nippon Kōbō photographic studio, Bruno Taut's writings on Japanese architecture, and the 1942 'Overcoming Modernity' symposium. Japan's displays at the 1939 New York World's Fair are also discussed. The chapter concludes that Japanese modernism was presented as a native, aesthetic alternative to the West, a move that the author links to the Axis powers and to later postmodern architecture.

Tokyo 1940New York 1939
6EUR: Mussolini’s Appian Way to Modernityp. 108

Mussolini's planned Esposizione Universale di Roma, E42, was to open in 1942 to mark twenty years of Fascism, but it never did. This chapter uses its unbuilt plans and the surviving archive as evidence of Fascist culture. Its argument is that E42 fused Roman antiquity with faith in science and technology, a combination it calls the paradoxes of Fascist modernism. The central case is the Arco dell'Impero, a 240-metre triumphal arch by Adalberto Libera and engineers, intended as the fair's emblem and abandoned when technical problems mounted. The chapter then moves through the Marconi obelisk, the Mostra della rivoluzione fascista, the Augustan exhibition that became the Museo della civiltà romana, and the planned Museo delle scienze, whose committees never agreed on the history of science. It ends with the EUR district that was built, read as a monument to totalitarian planning and later as a symbol of postwar alienation in films by Antonioni, Fellini and Pasolini. The fair's future-facing rhetoric, it concludes, rested on a backward-looking myth.

Rome 1942
7Redefining Cultural Conflict: The First Postwar International Expositionp. 138

Brussels 1958 was the first postwar universal exposition, and this chapter argues that it carried the superpower rivalry of the 1930s into a fair officially devoted to cooperation and peaceful atomic energy. The main evidence is the Soviet and American pavilions. The Soviet pavilion, planned from 1956, was reshaped after the Sputniks and displayed industrial goods, space models and national pride. The American pavilion, whose original $15 million budget was cut, offered a soft sell, and its Unfinished Work exhibit, which admitted racial problems and urban blight, was removed after complaints from Southern politicians. The chapter also covers Belgian motives, tied to the new European communities based in Brussels, the Atomium symbol, and the low-profile pavilions of Germany, Italy and Japan. American and European press reactions are compared, with Art Buchwald's jibes about the soft sell quoted. It closes with a White House pamphlet on space, issued as the fair opened, which the chapter says was redeemed at Osaka in 1970 by the Apollo 11 exhibit.

Brussels 1958
