Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991.Asia: substantial24 chapter overviews

Overview

Exhibiting Cultures, edited by Ivan Karp and Steven D. Lavine, grew out of a 1988 Smithsonian conference on the poetics and politics of representation. Its central claim, made in the editors' introduction and repeated across the volume, is that every exhibition embodies the assumptions and authority of its makers, so displays of other cultures are contested. The chapters take up art museums and the Houston Hispanic art show, ethnographic and history museums, Northwest Coast centres in British Columbia, folklife festivals, and world's fairs, with Hinsley on Chicago in 1893 as the main fair case. Most cases are American or European, with Zimbabwe and Indian examples. The book has five parts: culture and representation; art museums, national identity and minority cultures; museum practices; festivals; and other cultures in museum perspective.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia get substantial but uneven attention, and no sustained study of Asian participation in exhibitions. The fullest treatment is Yamaguchi's chapter 4, wholly on Japan, which treats Japanese display forms such as mitate and the tokonoma as an exposition culture set against the Paris Exposition of 1867. Tanen's chapter 19 mentions the Japan Today series and describes a planned 1990-91 Indonesian festival in the United States, the volume's main Southeast Asian case. Elsewhere Asians appear as displayed people rather than organisers: Chinese figures in Nathan Dunn's collection and Balinese performances (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, chapter 20), and the Tonkinese group at Paris 1889 (Hinsley, chapter 18).

Southeast Asia is most fully treated in Boon's chapter 15, which discusses Bali at length as a place shaped by Dutch and British interests and by tourism, and as a 'living museum'; Javanese dancers at the Brighton Aquarium appear in the same chapter. Duncan's chapter 6 reads the Manila museum that Imelda Marcos opened in 1975 as a showpiece of Philippine alignment with the United States. Clifford's chapter 14 mentions China, Japan and Indonesia in the visible storage of the UBC museum. Apart from the Manila museum, no exhibition held in East or Southeast Asia is discussed, and South Asia, chiefly India through the Festival of India, receives far more attention.

Contents

Cover
Title Page
Copyright
Acknowledgements

The acknowledgements explain that the essays grew out of a 1988 Smithsonian conference, The Poetics and Politics of Representation, the first of two meetings on cultural diversity in museums, both funded by the Rockefeller Foundation. They thank the Rockefeller Foundation and Smithsonian staff, the museums that opened their galleries for conference sessions, the scholars who advised the project, and the Smithsonian Institution Press and the American Association of Museums for co-publishing the book. They close with personal thanks.

Introduction: Museums and MulticulturalismSTEVEN D. LAVINE AND IVAN KARP

Lavine and Karp open the volume by arguing that every museum exhibition draws on the cultural assumptions of its makers, which makes exhibitions contested terrain, and that this contest has grown sharper in the United States with multicultural debate. Their main cases are the 1984 Te Maori exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum, where Maori elders consulted over the loan of taonga rejected the catalogue's background, and Hispanic Art in the United States, organized in Houston, which was admired for quality but faulted for presenting Hispanic culture thinly. They then survey minority and Native American museums, such as the Kwagiulth and U'mista centres in British Columbia, and experiments like Essence of Indian Art and Art/artifact. Their argument is that museums need progress in three areas: communities gaining control over their own presentation, established museums developing expertise in non-Western and minority cultures, and exhibitions that show multiple perspectives or admit their own limits. The chapter ends by proposing that museums can help a nation rethink its pluralism, though not settle it.

PART ICulture and Representation
1The Museum as a Way of SeeingSVETLANA ALPERS

Alpers argues that museums work through a 'museum effect', a way of seeing that isolates objects for attentive looking and so turns crabs, Greek statues and African stools into works of art. Her cases are mostly European and American exhibitions. Masters of Seventeenth-Century Dutch Landscape Painting in Boston arranged its pictures by art-historical type and chronology, although the paintings themselves show other concerns; the 1979 Utrecht exhibition on the 1579 Union of Utrecht buried a political declaration beneath documents, maps and prints; and the Musee d'Orsay makes many paintings hard to see through lighting, siting and distracting hardware. She also considers Art/artifact, the Center for African Art's show of Western perceptions of African objects, and the Museum of Modern Art's separate information room. Alpers proposes that installation should encourage seeing more than it explains, and that the museum's way of seeing can be worked with. She concludes that museums turn other peoples' objects into things we look at, but that they also exercise visual attention and let viewers recognise human affinity, as in a Dutch landscape and a carved Baule heddle pulley.

2Exhibiting Intention: Some Preconditions of the Visual Display of Culturally Purposeful ObjectsMICHAEL BAXANDALL

Baxandall proposes that an anthropological exhibition is best understood as a field in which three agents, the maker, the exhibitor and the viewer, play different games, rather than as a static representation of a culture. Its central illustration is a Kota mbulu-ngulu, a brass-sheeted guardian figure from Gabon, placed beside a Fang bieri and a 1907 Picasso; Baxandall follows how a viewer shuttles between the object and the label, seeking causes and then looking again for their traces. He argues that the viewer works mainly with posited intention, that a pointed cultural fact or a foreign concept, such as the Fang notion of bibwe, makes the viewer work, and that exhibitors should enlarge the space between label and object rather than control the viewer's mind. He adds that objects made for visual display are least likely to be misread, and that juxtaposing cultures signals their difference. The chapter concludes that exhibitors cannot represent cultures, and should set up stimulating conditions between their own selection and labels and the maker's object, leaving the rest to the viewer.

3Resonance and WonderSTEPHEN GREENBLATT

Greenblatt contrasts two models of museum display: resonance, the power of an object to evoke the cultural forces that produced it, and wonder, the power to arrest the viewer and hold attention on a unique object. His main example of resonance is the State Jewish Museum in Prague, housed in former synagogues, whose collections the Nazis assembled from confiscated Jewish property in the early 1940s, and which now includes a wall of victims' names and Terezin children's drawings. For wonder he turns to Renaissance cabinets, the Kunstkammer of Rudolf II, and Durer's account of Mexican objects sent to Charles V, in which the artist recognised their beauty and the ingenuity of their makers. He also notes a Coca-Cola stand at Coba that had more resonance for him than the ruins. Greenblatt is sceptical of turning museums into temples of resonance, using the Musee d'Orsay as the leading case, but concludes that most exhibitions combine both models. He proposes that they should begin with wonder and move to resonance, creating strong hybrids.

4The Poetics of Exhibition in Japanese CultureMASAO YAMAGUCHI

Yamaguchi argues that exposition is a basic cultural form, and sets Japanese practices against the Western exposition. He begins with fairground booths, shop windows and the tokonoma alcove, and with mitate, the act of linking an object to a classical reference, which he traces through Sei Shonagon's snow-covered mound, Noh, kabuki costume and the tsukuri arrangement of raw fish shaped as Mount Meru. The chief contrast is with the Paris Exposition of 1867, which Louis Napoleon used to present everyday objects as emblems of his regime and which, Yamaguchi says, raised commodities to the status of art by setting them beside mythic paintings. He then argues that museums turn time into space, that totemism is an imaginary museum, and that classification begins with the noise of unclassifiable things, as in the Renaissance cabinet of curiosities. His conclusion is that all exhibitions are in some sense fake, but that they acquire authenticity when placed in a theatrical context, as Japanese representation has done self-consciously.

Paris 1867
5Another Past, Another Context: Exhibiting Indian Art AbroadB. N. GOSWAMY

Goswamy explains the reasoning behind Rasa: les neuf visages de l'art Indien, the Paris exhibition of 1986 that travelled to San Francisco as Essence of Indian Art. Rather than a chronological survey of Indian art or a selection of masterpieces, Goswamy organised nearly three hundred works around the nine rasas, the aesthetic sentiments of classical Indian theory, such as the erotic, the heroic and the quiescent. Goswamy traces the idea through Bharata Muni's Natyasastra and later rasa theory, arguing that rasa is an experience belonging to the viewer rather than the object, so an exhibition could only point towards it. The chapter then reports the practical choices: sculpture set beside miniature paintings, no chronological frame, minimal dates in the catalogue, polygonal tables for viewing miniature series, and, in San Francisco, galleries painted in the colour assigned to each rasa. Goswamy closes with doubt about how a non-Indian audience understood the show, and with one plan that was never realised: an acoustically dead room for a single viewer before a major sculpture.

Paris 1986San Francisco 1986
PART 2Art Museums, National Identity, and the Status of Minority Cultures: The Case of Hispanic Art in the United States
6Art Museums and the Ritual of CitizenshipCAROL DUNCAN

Duncan argues that public art museums are ceremonial monuments that present the state and its citizens in a flattering light, and that they do so through ritual rather than neutral display. Duncan starts with the Louvre, which the Revolutionary government declared a public museum in 1793, and with the Manila and Tehran museums built to win Western favour. The museum's route, architecture and rationalised installations work like a temple, carrying visitors through a programmed narrative of art history that presents national triumphs as the achievements of individual genius. Princely galleries, Duncan notes, were recast in the nineteenth century as displays of civic virtue, with ceilings that celebrated patrons and Great Artists, and the Louvre's arrangement by national school became the model for museums in the United States. Duncan then reads the Metropolitan and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and finds that the modern wings and the new primitive-art galleries at the Metropolitan undercut the older civic story. Duncan concludes that controlling a museum means controlling how a community represents its identity and who is counted within it.

7The Poetics and Politics of Hispanic Art: A New PerspectiveJANE LIVINGSTON AND JOHN BEARDSLEY

Livingston and Beardsley reflect on the making of Hispanic Art in the United States: Thirty Contemporary Painters and Sculptors, which they organised between 1984 and 1987 for the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, and which then toured American cities. They explain how they found artists through local networks and restricted the show to contemporary painting and sculpture, leaving out murals, posters, photography and video. Their selection pairs very different artists, such as Ibsen Espada and Jesús Bautista Moroles, and they note that images of the Madonna, the outlaw and the mask recur as a shared refrain. Much of the chapter answers critics, chiefly Shifra Goldman, who argued that the term 'Hispanic' and the emphasis on folkloric imagery homogenised the artists, and others who faulted the show for lacking politics. The authors reply that the show was saturated with images of social alienation, that 'Hispanic' was the least incorrect term available, and that the artists' work draws on modernism as much as on folk culture. The chapter concludes that the debate concerns Hispanic art's place in the mainstream, and that its warm popular reception rewarded the risk.

Houston 1987
8Minorities and Fine-Arts Museums in the United StatesPETER C. MARZIO

Marzio, director of the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, answers Livingston and Beardsley from the museum side. Marzio describes the difficulty of finding curators and research for contemporary Hispanic art, the 150,000 visitors and the community outreach that followed, and the decision to show contemporary artists alongside Old Masters. Marzio argues that general art museums and specialised minority museums need each other, and that the real obstacle is the public's lack of exposure more than bigotry.

Houston 1987
9The Chicano Movement/The Movement of Chicano ArtTOMAS YBARRA-FRAUSTO

Ybarra-Frausto traces Chicano art from 1965 to 1990, dividing the history into two phases. The first phase, 1965 to 1975, covers the creation of a movement linked to the farmworkers' cause, the student movement and civil-rights struggles, when artists made posters, murals and newspaper art drawing on vernacular sources such as almanaques, estampas, altares and carteles. Ybarra-Frausto presents rasquachismo as an attitude rather than a style: an underdog sensibility of making do with what is at hand and of favouring bright, elaborate surfaces. The second phase, 1975 to 1990, examines how the movement's aims were absorbed by the mainstream art circuit, which often received Chicano work as colourful and folkloric, and how artists answered with performance, portable murals and a continental view of the Americas. Ybarra-Frausto identifies two competing strategies, a defiant otherness and new links with other Latino groups, and concludes that no single current dominates Chicano art, and that artists' task of recoding themselves and moving beyond dichotomies remains open.

PART 3Museum Practices
10Locating Authenticity: Fragments of a DialogueSPENCER R. CREW AND JAMES E. SIMS

Crew and Sims argue that authenticity in history museums is a matter of authority rather than of the object's factual origin. They open with two cases where the object misleads: a colonial-revival room at the National Museum of American History, left unpainted, and the Mullikin-Spragins house, whose earlier misreading of its construction was kept in place. They then explain why social-history exhibitions struggled, since collections favoured objects of the well-to-do, and set out three options: wait for artefacts, show only what the objects allow, or let historical themes drive the display. They favour idea-driven exhibitions, in which a research database rather than the object supplies authority and generic objects stand for the types used in a setting, such as the northern home room in Field to Factory. The chapter ends by treating the exhibition as an event in which visitors become co-creators of meaning, drawing on Brecht's alienation and Aristotle's Poetics.

Washington Field to Factory
11Noodling Around with Exhibition OpportunitiesELAINE HEUMANN GURIAN

Gurian argues that museum designers impose barriers to learning through unexamined beliefs about visitors, and that the style of an exhibition, rather than its content, decides whether a visitor feels empowered or excluded. Drawing on Bourdieu, Gurian suggests that some producers and traditional visitors share an interest in keeping the museum exclusive, and that the reluctance to use sensory, emotional or playful methods reflects a wish to appear academic. Gurian draws on the hands-on work of Frank Oppenheimer and Michael Spock and on Charles Eames's cluttered displays, which gave visitors room to choose, and on labels that treat the visitor as a partner. Gurian then turns to the novice learner, arguing that exhibitions should define terms, give social context and accommodate varied learning styles, citing Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences. The chapter also covers label copy, identifying the curator and the museum as a social space, and concludes that exhibition teams should state their assumptions about visitors early, since an exhibition is closer to a theatre piece than to any other form.

12Always True to the Object, in Our FashionSUSAN VOGEL

Vogel argues that almost nothing shown in museums was made to be seen there, so every exhibition is a mediation, and that museums should say which parts of a display come from the artist and which from the curator. Drawing on African-art exhibitions Vogel curated, the chapter examines how Western museums recontextualise objects never meant for museum walls. Vogel describes three exhibitions from the Center for African Art: The Art of Collecting African Art, which showed passed-over and forged objects; Perspectives: Angles on African Art, with signed labels from its cocurators; and Art/artifact, which displayed objects in five different styles. Perspectives asked ten cocurators, Africans and Americans, to choose objects and discuss them, and the chapter reports their divide between aesthetic appreciation and cultural understanding, with artists such as Nancy Graves approaching the objects as pure form. Vogel argues that the museum itself teaches political values through its banners, staffing, lighting and labels, and that a museum should admit it is a tightly focused lens rather than a broad frame.

New York 1987New York 1988
13The Poetic Image and Native American ArtPATRICK T. HOULIHAN

Houlihan, a museum director with nineteen years' experience of Native American collections, sets aside the politics of representation to ask what makes an exhibit poetic. Drawing on Gaston Bachelard, he argues that a memorable display should reverberate in the viewer, changing them, rather than merely resonate with familiar categories such as art or subsistence. His main case is the U'mista Cultural Center at Alert Bay, where potlatch masks are arranged on the seating platforms of a big house, so that visitors walk past objects in the places of spectators and object and viewer seem to swap roles. He then offers three examples of material rich in imagery: turquoise in Pueblo and Navajo cosmology, a Navajo string game that teaches star patterns, and an Athabaskan word that Haida and Tlingit speakers use for a spoon, a comb and a branch. His caveats are that an exhibit must show what matters within the culture and that misunderstanding indigenous languages distorts it. He concludes that a few such displays, rather than survey shows repeated in every museum, can carry knowledge from cultures older than industrialization.

14Four Northwest Coast Museums: Travel ReflectionsJAMES CLIFFORD

Clifford, writing as a visitor, compares four Northwest Coast museums in British Columbia: the UBC Museum of Anthropology in Vancouver, the Royal British Columbia Museum in Victoria, and two Kwagiulth tribal centers at Alert Bay and Cape Mudge Village. He sets their aesthetic, historical and tribal approaches against one another, arguing that majority museums claim cosmopolitan patrimony through art and history, while tribal museums assert local kinship, ownership and political opposition. The central case is the potlatch regalia seized by the Canadian government in 1922 and later returned to two museums. At Alert Bay, texts from Indian agents and chiefs surround unlabeled masks in a big house, and Clifford reads the display as storytelling that implicates the viewer. At Cape Mudge, objects are labeled by family owner, and postcards and conversations show how family memory differs from the wider history. He concludes that no museum can fix the meaning of its objects, and that tribal centers are unsettling majority collections.

15Why Museums Make Me SadJAMES A. BOON

Boon argues that museums make him sad because they are built from fragments torn out of their contexts, so every display refers to more museum rather than to a real past. He builds the case through a chain of examples: Robert Burton's quotation-built Anatomy of Melancholy, seventeenth-century curiosity cabinets, P. T. Barnum's American Museum, and the Brighton Aquarium, which gave its tanks over to giants and other human curiosities. The longest case is Henry James's memoir A Small Boy and Others, where a Barnum show and a New York imitation of the Crystal Palace shape his sense of Europe, and his travel writing on Venice, which Boon reads as a city turned into a museum by Ruskin, Proust and tourism. He adds Tahitian feather cloaks kept as relics of contact and Balinese culture shaped by colonial and tourist interests. The chapter then turns on itself, since writing about museums repeats the pillaging it describes, and ends with loose notes on museum-going.

PART 4Festivals
16The Politics of Participation in Folklife FestivalsRICHARD BAUMAN AND PATRICIA SAWIN

Bauman and Sawin study the 1987 Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife from the standpoint of its participants rather than its folklorist organizers. Drawing on an ethnographic study of about twenty Michigan participants, they argue that a folklife festival is a political field where performers, craftspeople and workers must work out what they are doing on the Mall. Their central concept is framing: participants recast their activity as performance, demonstration, instruction, exhibition or work, and demonstration proves the most workable because it allows process without finished products. Cases include a fiddler, Great Lakes fishermen, a polka band, a family string band and a Finnish singing group, whose difficulties arose from thin briefing, cramped stages and clashing staff agendas. The authors also show participants resisting being cast as folk, from an extension agent who disclaimed folklife to a river guide who turned interviews back on presenters. Participants were more positive afterwards and at the smaller East Lansing festival. They conclude that participants are reflexive agents rather than passive display objects, and that a fairer politics of festival representation must take their experience into account.

Washington 1987
17Cultural Conservation through Representation: Festival of India Folklife Exhibitions at the Smithsonian InstitutionRICHARD KURIN

Kurin argues that museum exhibitions can help conserve a culture rather than only record it, and he tests the claim on Aditi and Mela, the two exhibitions the Smithsonian mounted in Washington in 1985 as part of the Festival of India. Aditi was a life-cycle display in the Natural History museum with thousands of objects and forty folk artists, many of them members of a squatters' cooperative from Shadipur in Delhi; Mela was an outdoor composite fair of rituals, crafts, performances and a bazaar on the Mall. Kurin describes the crowds and press, the political gains the artists won back in India, and the ways Indian participants reshaped the displays, from a puja in the museum foyer to a facsimile temple that became a working shrine. He also records the friction with Smithsonian safety rules and business staff over the coconut-leaf roofs and the sales. He concludes that museums can legitimate people and generate the rhetoric and programmes communities need, and that a culture survives only when its bearers can revise it.

Washington 1985
18The World as Marketplace: Commodification of the Exotic at the World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago, 1893CURTIS M. HINSLEY

Hinsley argues that the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893 turned other peoples into commodities, and that its serious anthropology was overwhelmed by the commercial display of exotic people. He sets the work of Frederick Ward Putnam and Franz Boas in the Anthropological Building and the outdoor Kwakiutl village against the Midway Plaisance, where the Street in Cairo, donkey boys, camel procession and Congress of Beauty offered entertainment for a fee. Tracing the history of human display back to Hagenbeck's touring groups and the ethnographic villages of Paris 1889, he shows how photograph albums, captions and a cartoon kept visitors at a safe distance while the Midway taught them that everyone has a price. Putnam's frustrated plans, the strolling vocabulary of the Midway guidebooks and the figure of the flâneur serve as evidence. He concludes that the market turned the exotic into an early form of tourist consumption, and that its 'reasonable others' prefigured later imperial policy.

Chicago 1893Paris 1889
19Festivals and DiplomacyTED M. G. TANEN

Tanen argues that Americans know little about other countries, and that a festival, a concentrated and carefully directed presentation of one country's culture, is a way to change that. Drawing on his Foreign Service work and the 1985-86 Festival of India, he sets out what a festival needs: clear goals, realistic limits on money, and programmes that outlast it. He concludes that a festival should make a broad public aware of another culture and start lasting binational exchange.

United States 1985-86
PART 5Other Cultures in Museum Perspective
20Objects of EthnographyBARBARA KIRSHENBLATT-GIMBLETT

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett argues that ethnographic objects are made by the act of detaching them, so museums, fairs and festivals must then restore context to them. She distinguishes in-situ from in-context display, and shows how Goode's labels and object lessons turned specimens into texts, using Washington Matthews's lecture on Navajo sacred objects as a case. The chapter then turns to human display, from Bullock's Egyptian Hall and Hagenbeck's caravans to Skansen, the Chinese figures of Nathan Dunn and the Midway, where the museum effect made the everyday life of others into spectacle. Later sections compare folk festivals with the Mela at the 1985 Festival of American Folklife and with the Old Ways in the New World programme, showing how the ascetic staging ideals of folklorists sit against tourism and nationalism. She concludes that all interest is vested, so the first task is to examine the conventions by which displays constitute their subjects.

Chicago 1893Washington 1985
21Refocusing or Reorientation? The Exhibit or the Populace: Zimbabwe on the ThresholdDAWSON MUNJERI

Munjeri argues that Zimbabwe's national museums served the white minority under colonial rule and failed the African majority before and after independence. The chapter traces the parastatal from its geological origins, showing how collecting relied on white donors and third parties and how the 1979–81 centralization stripped regional museums of ethnographic material. A 1960 'witchcraft' display and a white settler history exhibition reinforced that exclusion. Munjeri concludes that museums must reconcile their traditional roles with social and cultural issues.

22How Misleading Does an Ethnographical Museum Have to Be?KENNETH HUDSON

Hudson asks how far an ethnographical museum must mislead. The chapter argues that such displays show only the surface of a society, and that objects alone cannot convey smell, climate, poverty or fear. Its evidence is a London exhibition on Canadian Eskimo life, an American museum's odourless New England rooms, and staged 'tribal' dances for visitors. Hudson concludes that museums should organize displays by climate and region, with paid interpreters, and show present struggles of the peoples they portray.

Contributors
Kwon, Hyeokhui. “An Analysis of Korean Intellectual Responses to the Exhibition of Koreans at Japanese Expositions: Nationalism and the Discourse on Northeast Asian Solidarity at the Turn of the Century.” Journal article.Asia: central6 chapter overviews

Overview

Kwon examines Korean intellectual responses to two Japanese exhibitions that displayed Koreans: the Anthropological Pavilion at the Fifth National Industrial Exposition in Osaka in 1903 and the Crystal Pavilion of the Tokyo Industrial Exhibition in 1907. The article argues that the human displays combined social Darwinist classification with commercial entertainment, and that Korean responses, traced in newspapers and magazines of the period, moved from hope in Northeast Asian solidarity under a common race and culture to nationalist resistance once Japan imposed the 1905 Protectorate Treaty. It is organised as an introduction, a section on each exhibition and its Korean reactions, a comparative section on changing perceptions, and a conclusion.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the whole setting, though the article treats only Korea, Japan and China within it. Korea is central: the 1903 Anthropological Pavilion (Osaka) and the 1907 Crystal Pavilion (Tokyo) are read as Japanese displays of Koreans, and chapters 2 to 5 concentrate on the Korean press (Taehan maeil sinbo, T'aegŭk hakpo, Mansebo) and on intellectuals such as Yun Ch'i-ho and Chang Chi-yŏn. Japan is the organiser and the imperial power at issue; the Ainu, Ryukyuans and Taiwanese seiban shown in 1903 appear as its internal and colonial subjects. China appears in chapter 4 through the Chinese display cancelled before opening after protests by students in Japan, which the Korean protests are set beside.

Southeast Asia is marginal. Javanese are named in the 1903 prospectus and in the Chinese protest, where they are called among 'the world's lowliest races', but nothing further is said of them. Manchuria appears only as a site of Japanese overseas research, and the Indians in the 1903 display serve as a South Asian contrast. The article does not discuss exhibitions held elsewhere in Asia or Asian visitors beyond the Korean and Chinese students in Japan.

Contents

ABSTRACTp. 19
Introductionp. 19

Kwon introduces the human displays at Japanese expositions, which combined social Darwinist evolutionary schemes with freak-show entertainment and colonial ideology. Kwon argues that earlier work on the 1903 Anthropological Pavilion in Osaka has focused on the Japanese organisers and overlooked Korean responses, as well as the 1907 Crystal Pavilion in Tokyo. The article traces how Korean intellectuals moved from hope in Northeast Asian solidarity with Japan to nationalist resistance, using newspapers and magazines of the period.

Korean Reactions to the 1903 Display at the Anthropological Pavilionp. 20

Kwon begins with the 1903 Anthropological Pavilion at the Fifth National Industrial Exposition in Osaka, a Japanese version of the Western native-village exhibit that the Tokyo Anthropological Institute helped to organise. The Japanese organisers arranged the peoples on display by a social Darwinist scale of civilisation, and the Korean display differed from the family groups of Ainu and Taiwanese. Kwon argues that the Korean display consisted of two women who were in fact kisaeng entertainers, shown in performance dress and reproduced on souvenir postcards. The exhibit mixed classification with commercial entertainment, and its smaller scale may have reflected Korea's position outside Japan's colonial borders. The section closes by framing the displays as part of a discourse of Northeast Asian unity that Korean responses would later test.

Osaka 1903
The 1907 Crystal Pavilion and Its Representation of Koreansp. 24

Kwon turns to the 1907 Crystal Pavilion at the Tokyo Industrial Exhibition, which Japanese merchants built beside a small Korea hall to draw visitors. It was a fantasy and terror attraction with a dark cave, mirror illusions and a final room where a Korean man and woman sat in traditional dress, and no anthropologists took part. Kwon reconstructs the pair's identities from competing Japanese and Korean newspapers, which disagree over names, origins and whether the woman had come willingly. A table sets out how the display was described, and Korean newspapers likened it to the exhibition of animals. Kwon concludes that the Crystal Pavilion was both educational and commercial, like the 1903 display, and that both were withdrawn after Korean protests stirred ethnic feeling against Japan.

Tokyo 1907
The Anthropological Pavilion and Korean Responsesp. 27

Kwon's longest section follows the protests that brought about the withdrawal of the 1903 Korean display. Japanese officials, worried about relations with Korea and China, ordered the display removed after a protest by three Koreans living in Japan, who appealed to shared race and culture. Kwon notes that these protesters were pro-Japanese bureaucrats, and sets their stance beside the Chinese students' fierce objections to a Chinese display cancelled before it opened. Turning to 1907, Kwon argues that Korean newspapers and the T'aegŭk hakpo responded with far more emotion, condemning the display as racist and as national shame. The Japanese Yomiuri, by contrast, framed the affair as women's liberation and downplayed discrimination. The section ends by linking these reactions to the nationalism of the Patriotic Enlightenment movement after the 1905 Protectorate Treaty.

Osaka 1903Tokyo 1907
The Transformation in Korean People’s Perceptions of the Display of Koreansp. 34

Kwon's penultimate section traces how Korean intellectuals' views of the displays changed between 1903 and 1907. Kwon places both reactions within social Darwinism and the idea of a racial struggle that Japanese politicians such as Itō Hirobumi promoted, and argues that elites at first hoped Japan would lead a yellow-race solidarity against the West. The 1903 protest grew from that hope, Kwon suggests, but the Russo-Japanese War and the 1905 Protectorate Treaty weakened it. Quoting the diaries of Yun Ch'i-ho and the editorials of Chang Chi-yŏn, Kwon shows that the 1907 reaction was angrier and more nationalist as Japan took control of the Korean state. The section notes that the display coincided with the emperor's envoys to The Hague and the later dethronement of the emperor. It concludes that Korean intellectuals turned from solidarity to nationalism.

Osaka 1903Tokyo 1907
Conclusionp. 37

Kwon concludes that the Korean displays combined social Darwinist classification with commercial spectacle, and that Korean responses reveal the shifting politics of Northeast Asia. The Anthropological Pavilion claimed scientific authority, while the Crystal Pavilion was mainly entertainment, yet both drew public curiosity. Korean intellectuals first trusted in common race and culture, Kwon argues, then turned to nationalism as Japan's imperial ambitions became clear. Common race, the chapter concludes, became a rationale for Japanese imperialism.

Osaka 1903Tokyo 1907
GLOSSARYp. 38
REFERENCESp. 38
Lawn, Martin, ed. Modelling the Future: Exhibitions and the Materiality of Education. Oxford: Symposium Books, 2009.Asia: substantial10 chapter overviews

Overview

Edited by Martin Lawn, this volume argues that world's fairs from London in 1851 onward shaped education through their displays of objects, classifications and comparisons between nations, and that the museums they spawned carried these materials into schools. Its 'materiality of education' approach studies objects, captions, displays and technologies, not fairs as temporary spectacle. The chapters, by different authors, cover Britain (London 1851, Wembley 1924, Glasgow 1888-1988), the United States (Chicago 1893 to San Francisco 1915), Germany, Spain, Argentina and Japan, and the introduction ends with a chronology of exhibitions from 1851 to New York 1939.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

Chapter 4, Komatsu on the Educational Museum in Ueno Park, is the only chapter built around East Asia, and it gives Japan's own participation close attention. It covers Japanese government and private exhibitors at Vienna in 1873 and Philadelphia in 1876, the first Domestic Exhibition of 1877, and the Educational Museum, where foreign apparatus was displayed beside Japanese copies made for domestic sale. Komatsu traces the museum's decline after 1885 and the replacement of Pestalozzian teaching by Herbartian method.

Elsewhere the region appears only in passing, and there is no sustained account of Southeast Asia or of Chinese, Korean or Siamese participation. Chapter 5 (Sobe and Rackers) describes a Philippine ethnographic exhibit at St Louis in 1904, where one group judged 'most advanced' took daily lessons, as an instance of 'colonial schooling' shown to spectators. Chapter 6 (Grosvenor, Wembley 1924) lists Malays, Burmans and Hong Kong Chinese among the 'Races in Residence' and Chinese 'Christian natives' in mission bungalows, all within a racial hierarchy of empire, with India and Ceylon discussed far more fully. The introduction's chronology names Hanoi 1902-03 and Nanking 1910 without comment, and Lawn's chapter 1 notes a New South Wales museum's purchase of Chinese 'articles' in 1885. Glasgow's 'Oriental' architecture in chapter 9 is a style, not a reference to Asia.

Contents

IntroductionMartin Lawnp. 7

Lawn introduces the volume by arguing that world exhibitions, from London in 1851 onward, shaped education through their displays of objects, their classifications and their comparisons between nations, and that educational historians have largely ignored them. He describes museums, the exhibitions' offspring, as catalogues of the future that have since lost that outlook and turned towards the past. The introduction proposes a 'materiality of education' approach that studies objects, captions, displays and technologies, rather than treating fairs as temporary spectacles. Its examples include Krumbiegel's imagined education museum and Patrick Geddes's proposed 'Index Museum', which he tied to his summer school at the Paris Expo of 1904. It ends with a chronology of international exhibitions from London 1851 to New York 1939, and with the claim that the future of education was crystallised in the nineteenth-century exhibitions and museums.

London 1851
Sites of the Future: comparing and ordering new educational actualitiesMartin Lawnp. 15

Lawn argues that world exhibitions from London in 1851 onward created the standards and classifications that became 'technologies of rule' in modern education, and that these spread through museums, models and periodicals. His starting point is Michael Sadler's 1902 memorandum urging a government-organised British education exhibit at the St Louis fair of 1904. Most of the chapter examines the 1851 Exhibition's classification scheme, which applied to the British exhibits alone, and the South Kensington museums built from its proceeds and salvaged materials. Lawn then traces colonial museums in New South Wales, which bought classroom models and object-lesson cards in 1885 on the same Empire-wide classification, and the Harvard psychology laboratory exhibit at St Louis. Cassell's illustrated periodicals and the Montessori classroom at the 1915 Panama-Pacific fair show how display became pedagogy. The conclusion holds that education became a field of national competition, and that comparison produced similar teaching materials across many countries.

London 1851St Louis 1904San Francisco 1915
Ethnohistory and Materiality of Education: in the setting of the Universal ExhibitionsAgustin Escolano Benitop. 31

Escolano Benito argues that the Universal Exhibitions of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries built a lasting 'imaginary' of distant peoples and nations, and that school manuals, classroom murals and pedagogical museums passed these images on to generations of pupils. He calls for historians of education to treat school material culture, including manuals, objects and their images, as a source to be read semiotically, in the manner of Ginzburg's evidential paradigm. The evidence is a set of case images and tables: a Spanish arithmetic textbook, a Barcelona publisher's cover showing a European child with children of other races, and Danish and Senegalese classrooms. The central case is Vallin's 1878 statistical map and comparative table of popular instruction in Europe, which ranked nations by schooling and provoked a diplomatic complaint from Spain; the chapter also draws on Carderera's and Perez Galdos's accounts of Spain at the London 1862 and Paris 1867 fairs. It ends by calling for public exhibitions of school heritage, shaped by consensus among practitioners, academics and politicians, as a way of educating citizens about their past.

Paris 1867Paris 1878London 1862
All the World into the School: World's Fairs and the emergence of the school museum in the nineteenth centuryEckhardt Fuchsp. 51

Fuchs traces how school museums emerged in Germany and abroad from the second half of the nineteenth century, arguing that they grew out of temporary education exhibits at world's fairs and were shaped by teachers' bid for professional status. The chapter distinguishes three developments: fair exhibitions converted into permanent museum displays, school museums serving the professional aims of elementary teachers, and a wider school-reform movement around 1900. The evidence is institutional. Fuchs follows the education section of the Paris 1867 fair into the Musee Pedagogique founded in 1879, and the German exhibitions at Chicago 1893 and St Louis 1904, which did not become a national museum. A national-scale German institute followed only after the Brussels fair of 1910, opening as the Central Institute for Education in 1915. Two tables list school museums founded in Germany and abroad, most set up by teachers' associations, and most were small, local and limited to teaching materials. The founding boom faded after 1920, when teacher training improved and schools were better equipped.

Paris 1867Chicago 1893St Louis 1904Brussels 1910
Formation and Transformation of Education in Japan through Exhibitions: focused on the Educational Museum founded in 1877Kayoko Komatsup. 73

Komatsu asks how international and domestic exhibitions helped to modernise education in early Meiji Japan, using the Educational Museum that opened in Ueno Park in 1877 as the main case. Japanese participation in the Vienna (1873) and Philadelphia (1876) fairs and the first Domestic Exhibition supplied the museum with foreign apparatus and books, many bought at fairs and displayed beside Japanese copies made from them. Komatsu uses the museum's guidebook, visitor figures and departmental reports to show how this arrangement pointed Japan towards European materials, and how private makers were encouraged to imitate European physics and chemistry machines for sale to schools. The second half traces the museum's decline after 1885, when it was incorporated into the Tokyo Library and its building passed to the Tokyo Art School, and relates this to the replacement of the Pestalozzian 'Developmental Mode of Teaching' by Herbartian method. The conclusion presents the fairs and the museum as two 'nodes' in a network that carried modern educational materials into Japanese schools.

Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876Paris 1878Tokyo 1877
Fashioning Writing Machines: typewriting and handwriting exhibits at US World's Fairs, 1893-1915Noah W. Sobe & Carrie B. Rackersp. 87

Sobe and Rackers examine handwriting and typewriting exhibits at American world's fairs between 1893 and 1915, arguing that both were displayed as ways of producing a 'writing machine' in which the human body and the mechanism were fused. The handwriting section traces penmanship from Spencer's natural forms to A.N. Palmer's push-pull 'muscular movement' method, which Palmer showed at St Louis in 1904 and in a Palmer Method classroom at San Francisco in 1915, where it won a medal. The typewriting section covers the machines, the Remington and Underwood exhibits, Brown's Business College's working school at St Louis, and the 1915 Standard Commercial School, where forty students were taught shorthand and typing in a glass-walled room watched from a balcony. Drawing on Kittler, the authors conclude that the fairs presented schooling as the means of automating writing and forming subjects who could match the machine, and that handwriting and typewriting were modelled together rather than set against each other.

Chicago 1893St Louis 1904San Francisco 1915
Teaching the Empire: the weekly Bulletin of Empire Study and the British Empire Exhibition, London, 1924Ian Grosvenorp. 107

Grosvenor looks at the Weekly Bulletin of Empire Study, the classroom series issued in 1924 to prepare schoolchildren for the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley, and asks what ideas of empire it carried into schools and how far the Exhibition reflected them. The Bulletin's 24 weekly parts, which circulated at least 125,000 copies a week, began with lessons on imperial history, then turned to individual territories, and carried two recurring themes, 'race character' and a 'hierarchy of Empire'. Grosvenor argues that this racial hierarchy, which called Africans 'child peoples', was matched at Wembley, where people from Nigeria, the Gold Coast and Sierra Leone were shown in reconstructed villages beside the British Government Pavilion, the most imposing building of the Exhibition. The chapter follows the preparation, the school visits and a route through the site, and concludes that Wembley worked as a 'training school' for imperial virtues that were located in 'race', and links the children who visited to the 1951 Festival of Britain and to Enoch Powell's 1968 speech.

London 1924
The Spectacle of Schooling and the Construction of the Nation in Argentina's Participation in World Exhibitions, 1867-1889Inés Dusselp. 129

Dussel examines the Argentine sections on schooling at the Paris exhibitions of 1867 and 1889, treating them as a 'spectacle of schooling' through which the new republic sought investment and migrants. The 1867 consignment, documented in a published report, is presented as a sales catalogue of rural and mining goods, with a few objects from schooling such as Marcos Sastre's desks and benches, fossils and photographs, and it was shaped by a dispute over whether to display 'indigenous' people and gauchos. For 1889 the chapter shows a shift to European iconography, with a palace-style pavilion by the French architect Charles Ballu and photographs of Buenos Aires schools by Samuel Boote, and reads the school section through the report of José Zubiaur, who judged that school books and homework did not satisfy visitors' aesthetic tastes. The final section treats Boote's classroom and school photographs as ambivalent images that show little that is distinctively Argentine, and concludes that they are opaque material that a more critical history could set against claims for a spectacular pedagogy.

Paris 1867Paris 1889
The Bull and the Book: images of Spain and Spanish education in the World Fairs of the nineteenth century, 1851-1900Maria del Mar del Pozo Andrésp. 153

Del Pozo Andrés asks how Spain presented itself through education at the nineteenth-century world fairs, from London in 1851 to Paris in 1900. The argument is that Spanish participation was driven by a wish to restore national pride after imperial decline, and that the fairs staged a contradictory nationalism, boastful about prizes yet anxious about backwardness. The evidence comes from official catalogues, commissioners' reports and the press. Cases include the absence of Spanish teaching materials in London in 1862, the Paris pavilion of 1867 with its stuffed bull, the Philadelphia display of some 715 deluxe books that won ninety-three prizes in 1876, the dispute over an illiteracy chart at Paris in 1878, the pedagogic congress held in Barcelona in 1888 and the Paris pavilion of 1900. The chapter also follows Martin de Martin y Ruiz, a deaf, dumb and blind student shown in Vienna in 1873. It concludes that the fairs supplied new ideas, but that Spanish schools adopted them slowly, and graded schools took hold only after the loss of the colonies in 1898.

London 1862Paris 1867Vienna 1873Philadelphia 1876Paris 1878Barcelona 1888Paris 1900
More of a school than a show? Events in Glasgow, 1888-1988David Limondp. 183

Limond traces how the educational aims of Glasgow's exhibitions changed over a century, using the 1888 International Exhibition, the 1938 Empire Exhibition, the 1951 Exhibition of Industrial Power and the 1988 Garden Festival. The argument is that the nineteenth-century event relied on self-improvement and left visitors to draw their own conclusions, that the 1938 and 1951 events were openly didactic and modernist, and that by 1988 the organisers had abandoned educational purpose, offering school parties a 'day out'. Evidence comes from contemporary press reports, guide-catalogues and an interview with the 1988 principal architect. The 1888 event is read as a response to Glasgow's reputation for poverty and violence, the 1938 event as an imperial showcase whose schoolchildren the city paid to attend, and the 1951 show as a story of uninterrupted technological progress. The chapter ends by arguing that the earlier aspirations were sincere, if paternalistic, and that their loss reflects a wider retreat from exhibitions as teaching.

Glasgow 1888Glasgow 1938Glasgow 1951Glasgow 1988
Notes on Contributorsp. 205
Maloney, Cathy Jean. World’s Fair Gardens: Shaping American Landscapes. Charlottesville: University of Virginia Press, 2012.Asia: substantial11 chapter overviews

Overview

Maloney's World's Fair Gardens (2012) traces the horticulture and landscape design of United States world's fairs from Philadelphia in 1876 to New York in 1939-40, and their lasting effect on public parks and gardens. Its main argument is that the fairs' temporary grounds left durable green spaces, such as Fairmount Park, Jackson Park and Flushing Meadows, and that the pressure to create mature landscapes within months advanced transplanting, irrigation, lighting and cold storage. The book has an introduction, one chapter on each of nine fairs (Philadelphia 1876, New Orleans 1884-85, Chicago 1893, Buffalo 1901, St. Louis 1904, Jamestown 1907, San Francisco 1915, Chicago 1933-34 and New York 1939-40), an epilogue on what the fairs left behind, and back matter with notes, reading list and index.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia, and Japan above all, is a substantial but secondary thread. Japanese gardens and exhibitors recur in six of the nine fair chapters, and the region is never the subject. Its heaviest concentration is in three chapters: Philadelphia 1876 (ch. 2, Centennial Exhibition), where Japan's bazaar, dwelling and garden helped set off a lasting American taste for things Japanesque; Chicago 1893 (ch. 4, World's Columbian Exposition), where the Japanese garden on Wooded Island, laid out by the gardener Izawa, won Olmsted's tacit approval although horticulturists found it inauthentic; and San Francisco 1915 (ch. 8, Panama-Pacific), where a three-acre Japanese garden was shipped in with more than 1,400 trees.

Later chapters continue the pattern. St. Louis 1904 (ch. 6) has a Japanese display of nearly 150,000 square feet beside a Chinese pavilion garden; Chicago 1933 (ch. 9) has an 'Authentic Japanese Garden' tableau and Chinese dioramas; New York 1939 (ch. 10, The World of Tomorrow) has a Japanese pavilion and garden by Tamura and Sakurai that the city kept after the fair. Asian participation comes mostly through exhibits and gardens, not visitors. Southeast Asia is nearly absent: San Francisco's offered Siamese building was declined for lack of funds, and no Indonesian, Philippine or Indochinese display is discussed. The New Orleans chapter (ch. 3) has almost no Asian content.

Contents

Acknowledgmentsp. ix
Introductionp. 1

Maloney introduces the book's subject: the horticulture and landscape design of United States world's fairs between 1850 and 1940, and their lasting influence on public parks and gardens. He argues that the fairs' temporary grounds left durable green spaces, from Jackson Park in Chicago to Flushing Meadows in New York, and that the need to create mature landscapes in a few months drove advances in tree transplantation, irrigation, lighting and cold storage. The chapter traces the spread of the fair from London in 1851 to the United States, where cities with room to grow offered campus-like sites, and notes the designers, nurserymen and horticultural societies who shaped these fairs. It then explains the criteria for choosing the nine featured fairs, from Philadelphia in 1876 to New York in 1939-40, and sets out a table of their sites, attendance and finances. Maloney concludes that understanding the original design intent of these landscapes may help people appreciate and preserve the surviving remnants.

Centennial Exhibition, Philadelphia, 1876: The Debut of American Horticulture on the World Stagep. 13

Maloney describes the horticulture and landscape of the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition, which he presents as the debut of American horticulture on the world stage. He argues that the grounds, laid out by Hermann Schwarzmann, whose background lay in engineering and architecture, were a pragmatic, piecemeal product that put buildings before plantings, yet the horticultural displays had lasting influence on American gardens. The chapter moves through Fairmount Park, the Japanese Bazaar, Horticultural Hall, the sunken carpet-bedding parterre and the rhododendron show by the English nurseryman Anthony Waterer, drawing on reports by Thomas Meehan and George Thurber and on professional disputes between engineers, nurserymen and landscape gardeners. Maloney concludes that the Centennial set a precedent for later fairs, and that its legacies, from Memorial Hall and the Japanese garden to the replacement Horticulture Center, remain in Fairmount Park.

Philadelphia 1876
World's Industrial and Cotton Centennial Exposition, New Orleans, 1884-1885: North Meets South in a Winter Gardenp. 39

Maloney turns to the World's Industrial and Cotton Centennial Exposition in New Orleans, which ran from December 1884 to June 1885 and struggled to present the New South as both industrial and agrarian. He argues that its grounds, laid out within about a year on a former marsh and plantation site, reflected engineering and military expediency, and that railway delays, failed cold storage and summer heat undermined its horticultural displays. The chapter describes the Mississippi Valley Horticultural Society, which ran the horticultural department and renamed itself the American Horticultural Society at the fair, and then the Mexican garden, the live oak avenues, the fruit displays and the cacti. It follows the fair's sale to a company headed by George Pullman and the slow development of Audubon Park, whose plan was commissioned from John Charles Olmsted. Maloney concludes that the fair achieved only some of its goals, though its puttyless glazing, lighting and cactus displays left a legacy for later exhibitions.

New Orleans 1884
World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago, 1893: Landscape Architecture Frames the City Beautifulp. 55

This chapter reconstructs the landscape of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. It begins with the city's rebuilding after the 1871 fire and its horticultural culture, then turns to Frederick Law Olmsted's choice of the swampy Jackson Park site, which he had initially dismissed as unpromising. Maloney's central case is the Wooded Island and the lagoons and Court of Honor that Olmsted designed around it, with naturalistic shorelines planted with native aquatics. The chapter then shows how this vision was compromised. The Horticulture Department, led by John Samuels, filled ten acres of the island with floral displays and a Japanese garden, while the Horticulture Palace housed a controversial floral mound. Maloney draws on Olmsted's letters, Rudolph Ulrich's reports from the site, and reviews by horticulturists such as L. H. Bailey. It ends by assessing the fair's legacy: a permanent Jackson Park, the City Beautiful movement, and the founding of the American Society of Landscape Architects.

Chicago 1893
Pan-American Exposition, Buffalo, 1901: Electric Rainbows of Colorful Flowersp. 83

This chapter examines the landscape of the 1901 Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, which it presents as a deliberate reversal of the subdued naturalism of Chicago in 1893. It first sets out the fair's background, including the Spanish-American War and President McKinley's assassination during the fair, then traces how the Rumsey farm site was chosen and transformed. Rudolph Ulrich, working with the florist William Scott, planted the bright flower beds that earned Buffalo the name 'Rainbow City', while architects including John Carrere and William Bosworth favoured formal French-style parterres, vases and fountains. The evidence comes mainly from the display gardens, such as a tulip display, a rose garden of two thousand hardy roses and the water-lily basins, and from the Horticulture Building, whose underground cold storage Frederic Taylor championed. The chapter ends with the first attempt to light flower beds at night, which it treats as a precedent for later fairs, and with the fair's uncertain legacy: the surviving New York State Building and a debate over keeping the grounds as parkland, which local officials resisted.

Buffalo 1901
Louisiana Purchase Exposition, St. Louis, 1904: A Fair in the Forest Cityp. 99

This chapter examines the landscape of the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition in St. Louis, which it describes as the largest world's fair by acreage and the first US fair required to return its site to a park. It begins with St. Louis's park and horticultural traditions and with the foreign-style gardens then fashionable in America, which the fair reproduced at large scale. The site began as the western half of Forest Park and grew to 1,270 acres, and the chapter explains the fan-shaped plan of the Main Picture, with the Cascades falling to the Grand Basin. Landscape architect George Kessler's work is set against Olmsted's Chicago design, because Agriculture Hill was handed to the horticulture department and planted by exhibiting nurserymen and florists. Evidence comes from the Horticulture Building's fruit storage, the Floral Clock, the Sunken Gardens, the Wildflower Garden and the national gardens, especially Japan's. The chapter ends with the nine-year effort to restore Forest Park and with the fair's legacy in foreign gardens, native plantings and the flower clock.

St. Louis 1904
Jamestown Exposition, Jamestown, 1907: Native Plantings Frame City Planningp. 117

This chapter examines the landscape of the 1907 Jamestown Exposition in Virginia, a fair that never captured the nation's attention and is often treated as a footnote. Its central claim is that Warren Manning's design is a fine example of urban planning, since the fairground was intended to become a residential town after the fair. The chapter sets out the fair's financial problems, its military and maritime emphasis and a budget that kept shrinking. It then shows how Manning drained the swampy site, relied on native plants, had more than three thousand large trees moved and built a living fence of honeysuckle and roses. The evidence includes the street plan and its signature tree species, the Powhatan Oak, Flirtation Walk and the Canoe Trail, and the States Palace, which stood in place of a separate horticulture building. Manning's 1907 essay 'Civic Horticulture and Improvement' supplies the principles that the chapter applies to the plantings. It ends by arguing that the fair's small-town character, its native plantings and its waterfront design shaped later exposition planning.

Jamestown 1907
Panama-Pacific International Exposition, San Francisco, 1915: East Meets West in the Gardenp. 133

This chapter examines the landscape of the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco, which it presents as a fair that joined Eastern and Western garden traditions on land made from the bay. It explains how the Harbor View site was created by dredging, and how Edward Bennett's block plan of courtyards was undermined when he resigned in 1912 after accusing the city's Department of Works of pernicious influence. Most of the chapter concerns John McLaren, the local landscape designer whose plantings are described in detail: the ice plant hedge that imitated an aged wall, the palm and cypress avenues, and the courts that the chapter treats as early small-space gardens. Its other principal cases are the Palace of Fine Arts and its lagoon, the Japanese garden, and the Horticulture Palace, whose exhibits moved from single fruit specimens to commercial processes. The chapter also covers the quarantine inspections that imported plants required. It ends by tracing the fair's legacy through the trees planted in Golden Gate Park and the de Sabla garden at El Cerrito.

San Francisco 1915
Century of Progress Exposition, Chicago, 1933-1934: Modernism Meets the Midwestp. 155

Maloney examines the Century of Progress Exposition of 1933–34 in Chicago as a break from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, arguing that its modernist architecture and lighting produced smaller themed gardens and a move toward corporate display. The chapter follows the planning of the fairground, from the 1928 decision on windowless, terraced buildings to the landfill and tree planting that prepared the site. Its main case is the Horticultural Building, where a dispute between Kate Brewster's committee and commercial florists led to resignations and a restructured program of flower shows and garden tableaux. Maloney also surveys the Victorian, rose and modern gardens, the water gardens, and the state and corporate landscapes, including Sinclair Oil's dinosaur display and the Good Housekeeping garden. The chapter ends by concluding that the fair's copyable backyard gardens and its corporate sponsorship marked the beginning of the end of regionalism in fair gardens.

Chicago 1933Chicago 1893
The World of Tomorrow, New York, 1939-1940: Fair of the Futurep. 173

Maloney turns to the New York World's Fair of 1939–40, held on the Corona ash dump in Flushing Meadows, and argues that its landscapes made corporate identity and modern design the norm for American fair gardens. The chapter explains how Robert Moses and the chief landscape architect Gilmore Clarke reclaimed the site and planted about ten thousand trees. Its central cases are the color-coded exhibit zones, the clipped-hedge designs of Constitution Mall and the Theme Center, and the automobile gardens around the Ford and General Motors buildings. Maloney also examines the corporate gardens of Equitable and AT&T, the Japanese garden by Tamura and Sakurai, and the Gardens on Parade horticultural exhibit, led by Harriet Barnes Pratt. The final sections follow the disposal of the site, in which Moses's plans were slowed by war and the exhibit became the Queens Botanical Gardens. The chapter concludes that the fair introduced the modern garden and the corporate style to the American public, while weakening regional expression.

New York 1939
Epiloguep. 199

Maloney's epilogue asks what the American fairs of 1870 to 1940 left behind. It argues that their legacies lie in urban parks such as Fairmount Park, Jackson Park and Flushing Meadows, in improved methods of shipping perishable produce, in the spread of diverse landscape styles, in hybridization competitions, and in lighting and water effects. Maloney contrasts the 1939–40 fair with the 1854 New York Crystal Palace, where a horticultural exhibit once consisted of dried potatoes. He then turns to the decline of U.S. participation after 1940, which he links to disappointing finances, the rise of radio and film, the shift from professional horticultural societies to garden clubs, and the patenting of new plants. A Century of Progress gladiolus sidebar shows how nursery catalogues carried fair displays into homes. The epilogue ends with the growth of public gardens and the 2020 bid efforts, concluding that the fairs' garden legacies remain present in the country's landscapes.

New York 1939Chicago 1933

Mandell, Richard D. Paris 1900: The Great World’s Fair. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1967.Asia: occasional8 chapter overviews

Overview

Mandell's book is a study of the Paris Exposition of 1900 set against the history of nineteenth-century world's fairs. Its argument is that the fair, planned as a display of French confidence, was shaped by politics: the state controlled it, opponents such as the Nancy editor Goulette campaigned against it, and the Dreyfus Affair was quietly suspended while it ran. The early chapters cover the French industrial exhibitions from 1798, the London exhibition of 1851 and the Paris expositions of 1855 to 1889. The rest follows the planning and opposition, a tour of the grounds, the political background, the verdict on success and the end of the era of great French expositions. The scope is Paris and France, with attention to national pavilions, decorative arts and finance.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia receive occasional attention in this book, which mentions them in some 47 of its 7,866 lines, most of them in Chapter Four, 'At the Fair', where the coverage is substantial. Japan is named most often: its art made a sensation in Paris in 1867 and Vienna in 1873 (Chapter One), its request for more space was repeatedly refused and its delegation found the space insufficient (Chapter Three), and de Vogue judged that Japan surpassed France in taste (Chapter Six). China appears mainly in passing, such as a Chinese boy serving tea at the Asiatic Russia pavilion (Chapter Four).

Chapter Four treats Asia as material on display, organised by others. The colonial section at the Trocadero held the pavilion of Indo-China, which Mandell says was grander than those of several sovereign states, and the Dutch East Indies; the Tour du Monde offered dioramas including Angkor Wat, and Javanese dancers and the Japanese performer Sadda Yakko drew crowds. Korean and Siamese pavilions appear only in plate captions. Siam is among the minor states that declined the invitation (Chapter Two). Southeast Asia beyond Indo-China, Java and Siam is not discussed, and no Asian visitors or observers are described.

Contents

Prefacep. ix

Mandell's preface sets out the purpose of a study of the Paris Exposition of 1900. He describes the crowds, rivalry and medal competitions of nineteenth-century fairs, and argues that historians have neglected world's fairs as sources for political, intellectual and artistic history. The fair is presented as a comprehensive picture of its age, and the book is said to address the Dreyfus Affair, French nationalism and Art Nouveau. The preface ends with notes on terminology and the libraries consulted.

Paris 1900
OneIntroduction: Exhibitions in the Nineteenth Centuryp. 3

Mandell traces exhibitions in the nineteenth century as the background to the Paris Exposition of 1900. He begins with markets and medieval fairs, then with the Paris salons and the first French industrial exhibitions from 1798, which made prizes and medals central and tied displays to state policy under Napoleon and later regimes. The chapter follows the spread of national and international shows: the London Crystal Palace of 1851, with its jury system and surplus, and the French universal expositions of 1855, 1867, 1878 and 1889, each assessed by its organisers, finances and political purpose. Mandell argues that the French state, unlike private organisers elsewhere, controlled these events. The chapter ends with the 1889 triumph and its reputation for French prestige, followed by the political troubles of the next decade.

Paris 1798London 1851Paris 1855Paris 1867Paris 1878Paris 1889
TwoOrigins and Oppositionp. 25

Mandell examines the political opposition to the Exposition of 1900. Beginning with the Republic's 1889 triumph and its later scandals, economic stagnation and demographic anxiety, the chapter shows how French fears of German power produced a race to hold a fair first: a German plan for Berlin prompted the government to announce Paris 1900 in July 1892. It then describes the control of Commissioner General Alfred Picard, the foreign invitations and the American and German demands for space, with Chicago 1893 as a point of comparison. The main argument concerns the opposition of 1895 and 1896, led by the Nancy editor Goulette through the decentralist pamphlet Pas d'Exposition en 1900! and Barres's moral and provincial objections. Mandell concludes that the Chamber and Senate approved the project in 1896 because invitations had already been sent and national honour was engaged.

Paris 1900Chicago 1893Paris 1889
ThreePreparationsp. 52

Mandell describes how the fair was prepared between 1896 and its opening in April 1900. Picard's architectural competition drew 108 accepted projects, but a jury dominated by Ecole des Beaux-Arts graduates gave the first prizes to academic designs, so the architecture turned away from the engineering of 1889. Picard also struggled with the allocation of space among nations, especially the United States, whose share was increased under French government pressure. The chapter then covers construction delays and public mockery: the slow progress of buildings, the controversy over the statue of Paris on the Porte de la Concorde, a plague scare, and an opening date that Picard refused to change. It ends with the official opening on 14 April 1900, with speeches by Loubet and Millerand and a procession over the Pont Alexandre III.

Paris 1900
FourAt the Fairp. 62

Mandell's chapter is a walking tour of the Paris Exposition of 1900, first across its central grounds and then through the arguments about art, architecture and national competition that the fair raised. The tour covers the layout of the site, the commercial amusements, the colonial pavilions, the congresses and the sports competitions, before turning to the decorative arts, where Binet's Porte de la Concorde, the Art Nouveau work shown by Bing, Gallé, Lalique and Guimard, and Saarinen's Finnish pavilion serve as the main cases. The national pavilions on the Quai des Nations, especially those of Russia, Britain, the United States and Germany, are assessed as rivals in a contest between nations. The chapter ends with the festivals, the Banquet des Maires, the fall and recovery of attendance, and the closing night, presenting the fair as a last great display of nineteenth-century confidence that the following years would not share.

Paris 1900
FiveThe Affair and the Fair: Politics and the Expositionp. 89

Mandell argues that the Exposition of 1900 cannot be understood apart from the Dreyfus Affair, which was at its height as the fair was being prepared. The chapter traces how French diplomatic humiliations of the late 1890s, including Fashoda, and the Rennes retrial of September 1899 provoked a wave of foreign boycott threats against the fair, from Chicago and London to Calcutta and Melbourne. It then shows how President Loubet and the Waldeck-Rousseau ministry secured Dreyfus's pardon, and how a campaign of official silence, the truce of the exposition, was pressed on journalists and politicians alike, with Reinach agreeing to keep the peace and Clemenceau refusing. The evidence is mainly from newspapers, parliamentary debates and the published inquiry into appeasement. The chapter ends by suggesting that the fair served as a political tranquilliser, so that the amnesties of 1900 went through quietly and Dreyfus was declared innocent only in 1906.

Paris 1900
SixWas it a Success?p. 104

Mandell takes up the question that observers asked once the fair closed, 'Was it a success?', and answers it on several fronts. The chapter lists the setbacks that dogged the fair, from late building work and faulty machinery to weather, plague scares and diplomatic strain. On finance it sets a deficit of about 42 million francs against the permanent gifts to Paris, which reduce the loss to 7 million francs and, with subsidies counted as receipts, to 2 million, and it records the anger of the concession holders. Attendance of about 50.9 million fell short of the 60 million planned. The core of the chapter is the verdict of critics such as de Vogue, Geddes, Naumann and Henry Adams, who found French power diminished, the displays overwhelming and the nineteenth-century faith in progress spent. It closes with Picard's new classification scheme, which critics found unworkable, and treats the failure of that scheme as a sign of the same loss of confidence.

Paris 1900Paris 1889
Conclusion: The End of an Erap. 118

Mandell's conclusion argues that the Exposition of 1900 closed an era of great French universal expositions, and that the country grew wary of them afterwards. It follows Alfred Picard's later career, the reorganisation of the Comité français des expositions, which gained official recognition in 1901 and came to control French fair policy, and the smaller and less political exhibitions of the twentieth century, from Brussels in 1958 to New York in 1964-65. The chapter then asks whether the fair changed France and answers that the more lasting change lay in France's image of itself, which seemed weaker and more defensive. The final case is the set of European commentators who saw in the fair a failure of nineteenth-century faith in progress and cosmopolitan co-operation, with the Americans, Japanese and Germans named as the winners of a contest in which France was barely a contestant.

Paris 1900
