Mathur, Saloni. India by Design: Colonial History and Cultural Display. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2007.Asia: occasional8 chapter overviews

Overview

Mathur's India by Design (2007) asks how an image of a timeless, craft-based 'traditional India' was made and circulated in Britain from the 1880s. It is organised in three moments: imperial, nationalist and postcolonial. Each chapter takes one site of production: the Liberty department store and its 1885 living village (chapter 1); the living display at the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition, with jail inmates and the petitioner Tulsi Ram (chapter 2); Rudolf Swoboda's portraits for Queen Victoria (chapter 3); colonial postcards (chapter 4); and a dispute over two Buddhist relics at the Victoria and Albert Museum (chapter 5). The argument is that the categories of caste, tradition, village and craftsman still organise how India is staged.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are a slight presence in this book, which is about South Asia. The one substantial regional thread is Burma in chapter 5, 'A Parable of Postcolonial Return'. The V&A's Buddhist displays had rooms on Burma, and in the years before the 1952 reburial the Sanchi relics were shown across Burma from Mandalay to Rangoon, as well as in Calcutta and Nepal. The Burmese government and the Burmese premier, who attended the reburial, shaped that tour. Mathur reads these displays as the new state's use of the relics as national symbols.

Elsewhere the region is passing. A Malay dressmaker is among Swoboda's portraits for the Queen (chapter 3), and Malays are listed among the peoples housed at the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition (chapter 2). Natives from Hong Kong attended the Windsor luncheon (chapter 2), and Tulsi Ram worked in Rangoon before reaching London (chapter 2). Liberty's Paris bazaar of 1889 stocked Chinese lanterns (chapter 1), and the introduction cites the Great Exhibition's China exhibit only as a foil for India's section. Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Siam, Indonesia and Indochina are not discussed.

Contents

List of Figuresp. vii
Acknowledgmentsp. ix

Mathur's acknowledgments trace the book's path from doctoral dissertation to manuscript. She thanks staff at colonial and art collections in India, Britain and the United States, names the funders and fellowships, and credits a 2002-03 London exhibition on Indian portraits for Queen Victoria, whose research became chapter 3. Teachers, colleagues and friends in New York, Los Angeles and Delhi are also thanked, along with her press editor.

Introduction. Colonial Patterns, Indian Stylesp. 1

Mathur opens with the recent boom in contemporary Indian art, Dover's copyright-free Indian design books and the marketing of paisley and pashmina, and argues that these present-day phenomena carry meanings made in the colonial encounter. The book's subject is the image of a timeless, craft-based 'traditional India' that circulated in Britain from the 1880s onwards through exhibitions, department stores, museums, oil painting and picture postcards. Mathur treats the Great Exhibition of 1851 as the first systematic reading of Indian culture through its material goods, and Owen Jones's Grammar of Ornament as its Victorian design legacy. The introduction then sets out the frame: Bennett's 'exhibitionary complex', Said's contrapuntal reading of metropole and colony, and postcolonial work on the Subaltern Studies collective. India in London emerges as an archive that was anxiously constructed, contested by Indian nationalists and internally incoherent. The introduction closes by previewing the five chapters, which move from a department store and a failed village display to painted portraits, postcards and a long dispute over Buddhist relics.

London 1851
1The Indian Village in Victorian Space: The Department Store and the Cult of the Craftsmanp. 27

Mathur's first chapter examines the 'cult of the craftsman', the fascination with the village artisan that first took hold among Europeans in the 1880s and was then taken up by Indian nationalists. Its case study is Liberty's department store on Regent Street, which sold imported Indian goods and English-made imitations, such as the Umritza Cashmere shawl, as authentic products from India. The central episode is Liberty's 'living village' at the Albert Palace in Battersea in 1885, when forty-two villagers were brought from India and then left without food or wages in the cold. Mathur reconstructs the failure from Indian newspapers and legal disputes. The chapter then traces the craftsman through George Birdwood's preservationist writing, R. C. Dutt's economic critique, the swadeshi boycott in Bengal, Coomaraswamy and Havell's art criticism, and Gandhi's adoption of the spinning wheel. Mathur argues that the craftsman symbol was overdetermined by the colonial economy, serving imperial nostalgia and nationalist revival alike. The chapter closes by citing K. G. Subramanyam's critique of colonial stereotypes and pointing ahead to the 1886 exhibition.

London 1885
2"To Visit the Queen": On Display at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886p. 52

Mathur's second chapter reconstructs the living ethnological display of Indian craftsmen at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London in 1886. Most of the men were inmates of the Agra Central Jail, recruited through the prison superintendent Dr John William Tyler, and the chapter shows how the prison-reform training behind their skills was hidden by the image of the timeless village. The focus then falls on Tulsi Ram, a Punjabi peasant who came to London to seek redress for a land dispute, was repeatedly arrested for vagrancy outside Windsor Castle, and was finally placed in the display as a 'sweetmeat maker from Agra'. Using workhouse, police and India Office files and Tulsi Ram's own petitions, Mathur shows how officials mapped London's East End as an imperial other and labelled a 'petitioner class' to be removed. T. N. Mukharji's travelogue supplies the elite Indian viewpoint, including his discomfort at being stared at. The chapter concludes that the men's journeys and petitions were never fully contained by the display.

London 1886
3The Discrepant Portraiture of Empire: Oil Painting in a Global Fieldp. 80

Mathur's third chapter examines the oil portraits of Indian subjects that Rudolf Swoboda painted for Queen Victoria from 1886, now hung at Osborne House and recently shown at the National Gallery. Set against the photographic catalogue The People of India, which presented its subjects as scientific specimens, the paintings are read as decorative 'beautiful things' whose authority was never scientific. The chapter follows Swoboda's commission from the 1886 exhibition through his stay in India, including time with Lockwood Kipling in Lahore, and reads his painting A Peep at the Train as an image of the village set against the railway. The second half turns to the colonial art schools, with their emphasis on copying and their split between crafts and fine arts, which shaped the Indian oil painter. It contrasts Swoboda with Raja Ravi Varma, whose portraits for the Chicago World's Fair were placed in the ethnographic section rather than the fine arts pavilion. Mathur concludes that Swoboda's 'peep' gives a contrapuntal view of the asymmetries that still shape portraiture and the legacy of the craftsman image.

London 1886Chicago 1893
4Collecting Colonial Postcards: Gender and the Visual Archivep. 109

Mathur treats the colonial picture postcard of India as a gendered visual genre long dismissed as low culture. The chapter begins with a postcard album compiled by Josephine Eppes around 1900 and traces the postcard's history from the Austrian postal card of 1869 to the picture card of the 1890s, when mass production, anonymous printers and collecting clubs spread it across Europe and America. Its main evidence is the 'native view' cards of India: caste and occupational types such as the Hindu tailor, the Raphael Tuck oilette series, and the 'Darjeeling: A Dandy' image of a European woman carried by four men. Mathur sorts these into native views, tourist cards and missionary cards to show that Indian and European women are placed in hierarchical relation to each other. The chapter answers Alloula's reading of French cards of Algerian women as a story of visual violation by insisting that European women were also collectors and producers. It concludes that restoring this female consumer history is needed to understand the racism and benevolence the cards stage.

5A Parable of Postcolonial Return: Museums and the Discourse of Restitutionp. 133

Mathur uses a thirty-year custody dispute over two Buddhist relics to examine the restitution of cultural property. The relics, said to be the ashes of the Buddha's disciples Sariputta and Moggallana, were taken from Sanchi in 1851 and ended up in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. The chapter follows the dispute through five scenes, from the Maha Bodhi Society's appeal in 1932 to the relics' reburial at Sanchi in 1952. It shows how the museum, the Buddhist groups and the postcolonial state each invested the relics with different kinds of value, and that this value was produced through exchanges between museum officials and their constituencies rather than inhering in the bones or caskets. The case is set against the 'universal museum' defence and the claims of the new Indian nation. The chapter concludes that the dispute is a parable of postcolonial return, since the home to which objects go back has itself been reshaped by the colonial past.

Epilogue. Historical Afterimagesp. 165

Mathur's epilogue returns the book's three moments, imperial, nationalist and postcolonial, to the present. It starts with the 1980s Festival of India and the 1997 independence anniversary exhibitions in American museums, which it reads as a replay of the state's use of culture. Mathur then turns to the heritage industry, from Dakshin Chitra and Dilli Haat to the Khalsa Heritage Complex at Anandpur Sahib, a museum under construction that borrows from Bilbao and Yad Vashem. Contemporary artists such as Dayanita Singh, Pushpamala N, Shahzia Sikander and Vivan Sundaram are discussed as still troubled by belatedness and by the 'ethnic slot'. The argument is that the categories of caste, tradition, village and craftsman still organise how India is staged, so colonial visual frames have been reworked rather than resolved. The epilogue concludes that 'India' has been repeatedly remade across the three historical phases.

Mitchell, Timothy. “The World as Exhibition.” Comparative Studies in Society and History 31, no. 2 (1989): 217–236.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Mitchell's article argues that nineteenth-century Europe organised the world as an exhibition: a set of models arranged before a viewer so that the real seemed to be on display. He opens with the Egyptian delegation at the 1889 Paris Exposition, whose reconstructed Cairo street disgusted its visitors, and with the same delegation treated as exhibits at the Stockholm Congress of Orientalists. He then turns to Arabic accounts of travel to Europe, to the Egyptian sections of the 1867 and 1889 Paris fairs, and to Flaubert, Lane, Gautier and Nerval in Cairo. His main claim is that the exhibition promises an external reality beyond representation, but that this reality always turns out to be a further representation. The essay has seven sections, the last on the contradiction within Orientalism and its citationary character.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia and Southeast Asia are close to absent. Mitchell's 'Orient' is Egypt, the Arabic-speaking world and the Middle East, and the subject is how nineteenth-century Europeans represented those places. East Asia appears only in passing. In chapter 0, The World as Exhibition, Max Müller at an earlier Berlin Congress 'produced two rival Japanese priests' before an audience, one of several examples of scholars presenting non-Europeans as exhibits. In chapter 1, An Object-World, Sacy's planned Orientalist museum is described as letting a student feel transported into 'a Mongolian tribe or of the Chinese race', the only place where China or Mongolia figures as a subject of study. An Indian pandit at the same Berlin Congress is a South Asian case outside this question.

Southeast Asia does not appear. The article does not treat exhibitions held in Asia, Asian commissioners or pavilions, or Asian merchants and visitors. The non-European participants it discusses are Egyptians and Arab writers, whose delegation, exhibition sections, bazaar and travel accounts carry the argument, and the colonial reading in chapter 3, The Labyrinth Without Exits, is confined to Egypt and the Middle East.

Contents

The World as Exhibitionp. 217

Mitchell opens with the Egyptian delegation to the 1889 Paris Exposition, where a reconstructed Cairo street left the visitors disgusted. The same delegation was then treated as exhibits at the Stockholm Congress of Orientalists. Mitchell takes these episodes to show that nineteenth-century Europeans routinely put the non-European world on display. The essay will examine the exhibition as a mechanism of order and meaning in the modern West.

Paris 1889
An Object-Worldp. 219

Mitchell turns to Arabic writers who visited Europe and found themselves stared at, and argues that this curiosity corresponded to an objectness in European life. Egyptian students in Paris in the 1820s were parodied on the stage as objects of entertainment, and Middle Eastern rulers who attended exhibitions became part of their machinery, as the Khedive did when he stayed in a mock palace. Mitchell then traces how panoramas, dioramas and museums set the world up as a picture to be viewed, citing Sacy's planned Orientalist museum and the 1889 Paris display of human labour, which was to be an object lesson. By the 1890s more than half the Arabic accounts of journeys to Europe described an exhibition or congress, and their authors found the same ordering in streets, gardens, zoos and railways. For these visitors Europe was a place where the world was always a model of something further.

Paris 1889
The Certainty of Representationp. 222

Mitchell argues that exhibitions gave visitors certainty about the world, because each model seemed to match an external reality. The Egyptian section at the 1867 Paris Exhibition, with a pharaonic temple, an Arab palace and a caravanserai side by side, is his main example. The certainty depended on the gap between representation and reality and on an observer standing outside the display. The exhibition's boundaries were hard to draw, since Paris beyond the gates resembled the exhibition.

Paris 1867
The Labyrinth Without Exitsp. 224

Mitchell follows the Egyptian bazaar at the Paris exhibition, where the street felt real because its goods were sold for real money, and argues that exhibitions came to resemble the commercial world of department stores, with merchandise arranged behind glass. He is careful to say that this is not a commodity-fetishism argument, since that critique still relies on a gap between representation and a true reality beneath it. The exhibition instead creates the effect of an external reality against which alienation can be felt. An 1882 Arabic novel, in which two Egyptians lose their way through a Paris warehouse of endless mirrored corridors, serves as the image of this labyrinth. Mitchell identifies three features of the world-as-exhibition: a claim to certainty, a paradox in which the real turns out to be more representation, and a colonial character, since the age of exhibitions was the age of colonial power and global economy. The section ends by turning to the Middle East.

Paris 1889
The East Itselfp. 227

Mitchell asks what Europeans experienced on leaving the exhibition for the 'East itself', beginning with Flaubert's letters from Egypt, where Cairo appeared as a chaos of colour that he could grasp only by turning it into a picture. Travellers responded by drawing and photographing, and the photograph promised a new mechanical certainty of correspondence between image and reality. Edward Lane's ethnography, made with a camera lucida, is presented as the classic example of writing that lets the Orient stand before the reader. The real problem, Mitchell argues, was to create the distance that made the East look like a picture, which meant finding a viewpoint set apart from the scene. The hill outside Cairo used by Lane, the Great Pyramid turned into a viewing platform and the minaret used as a tower for surveying the town show how travellers sought such positions. Bentham's complaint about being mobbed for a peep from a minaret, and the ideal of seeing without being seen, close the section.

Participant Observationp. 231

Mitchell describes the double position of the European traveller, who wanted both to immerse himself in the East and to stand apart from it. Gérard de Nerval, guided by a photographer into the labyrinthine streets of Cairo, and Edward Lane, who hid behind Muslim dress to observe Egyptians unobserved, are the examples. Lane's disguise gave his ethnography its objectivity, and Mitchell argues that modern tourists, Orientalists and anthropologists inherited this way of treating the world as a representation.

The Orient That Escapesp. 233

Mitchell argues that Orientalism was caught in a contradiction. Its writers brought the habits of the exhibition to the Middle East, seeking the real Orient as a picture, yet they arrived already holding pictures they had seen in Paris, so the Orient seemed always something to be rediscovered. Gautier, who went to Cairo after seeing the Egyptian exhibit at a Paris world exhibition, and Gérard de Nerval, who despaired of finding a real Cairo beyond the facades of an exhibition, illustrate the dismay this produced. Nerval spent much of his stay in the libraries of the French Institute, and his book largely repeats Lane's ethnography. Mitchell borrows Said's term 'citationary' for this chain of references, in which the 'East itself' is never a place but a further set of representations. The point, he concludes, is not that the real is never reached, but that the idea of a real beyond representation keeps convincing, which makes Orientalism part of a method of order and truth central to the modern world.

Molella, Arthur P., and Scott Gabriel Knowles, eds. World’s Fairs in the Cold War: Science, Technology, and the Culture of Progress. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2019.Asia: substantial18 chapter overviews

Overview

This edited volume, by Arthur P. Molella and Scott Gabriel Knowles, examines world's fairs as arenas of Cold War rivalry over science, technology and culture. Its sixteen chapters argue that the fairs both reflected and shaped Cold War ideas of progress, the space race, atomic energy, consumer technology, fashion, religion and urban renewal. Its main cases run from Brussels 1958 through New York 1964-1965, Montreal 1967, San Antonio 1968 and Osaka 1970 to Brisbane 1988, and the last chapters look at the fairs after 1989 up to Shanghai 2010. The chapters are grouped in five parts: the opening Brussels and Soviet-American contest, North American fairs, cultural conflict at the fairs, Asia and Australia, and endings and new beginnings. The sources include archives, press, films and visitor surveys.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia and Southeast Asia receive substantial attention, concentrated in two chapters devoted wholly to them. Chapter 3, Morris Low's 'Atoms for Peace in Brussels and Osaka', treats Japan's pavilions at Brussels 1958, where a Hiroshima image confronted visitors, and at Osaka 1970 as ways of selling nuclear power to Japanese audiences. It draws on US Information Service surveys of Japanese opinion and on exit surveys of Japanese visitors to the American and Soviet pavilions. Chapter 13, Ellan F. Spero's 'A Garden City for Progress and Harmony', studies Singapore's Osaka pavilion, its film and stamps, and the government's planning papers, and argues that the pavilion left out colonial rule, the Japanese occupation and the brief union with Malaysia.

Other chapters touch the region more briefly. Chapter 21 by Luca Massidda calls Osaka 1970 the first Asian world exposition and includes it in his table of fairs. Chapter 22 by Scott Gabriel Knowles presents Daejeon 1993 as South Korea's 'new road' of democratic development, with a pavilion for North Korean products, and Shanghai 2010 as a display of urban China with its Chinese visitors. Chapter 14 notes the strong Asian and Pacific representation at Brisbane 1988, and Chapter 16 mentions scrolls sent to women in fourteen Asian and Pacific countries and the queen of Thailand as a member of the Woman's Pavilion. The Philippines, Indonesia, Indochina and Burma do not appear as places of exhibitions in the passages examined, and the volume's centre of gravity remains the United States, Europe and the Soviet Union.

Contents

Acknowledgmentsp. ix

The acknowledgments thank the chapter contributors and the sponsors of two workshops, one at the Smithsonian's Lemelson Center in Washington in 2014 and a second co-sponsored by the University of Milan and timed to coincide with Expo 2015 in Milan. They also name the institutions and individuals who gave research access, translation help, editorial support and anonymous review, and close by looking forward to Dubai 2020.

The World’s Fair in the Era of the Cold War: Science, Technology, and the Culture of ProgressArthur P. Molella and Scott Gabriel Knowlesp. 3

The introduction argues that world's fairs both mirrored and helped shape Cold War culture, and that the fairs of 1958 to 1970 were proxy fronts in the rivalry between the United States and the USSR over science and technology. Molella and Knowles open with Brussels 1958, where replicas of Sputnik drew attention, and with the American responses at Seattle in 1962 and New York in 1964-1965. They then set out the recurring themes of the volume: space and atomic energy, the communications revolution, modern architecture, and the anxieties that technological change produced. The Bureau International des Expositions and the United States' uneasy relationship with it receive attention, from Robert Moses's defiance in 1964 to the 1999 funding restrictions. The chapter ends by sketching the five parts of the book, which move from Brussels to North America, then to Asia and Australia, and finally to the end of the Cold War. For an undergraduate it is a clear map of the volume's scope and its global, interdisciplinary framing.

Brussels 1958Seattle 1962New York 1964
Part ISetting the Stage: The World’s Fair in the Era of the Cold Warp. 9
1Expo ’58: Nucleus for a New EuropeStuart W. Leslie and Joris Mercelisp. 11

Leslie and Mercelis examine Expo '58 in Brussels as a stage for Belgium's ambition to make the city the capital of a united Europe. They describe the Atomium, whose motto was 'Atom = Hope', and show that its nuclear exhibits, like those of the other national pavilions, promoted national programmes over collaboration. The European Coal and Steel Community pavilion is read as a public-relations effort that promoted integration through narratives of progress, while Euratom, which had no pavilion, is treated as the next step. The chapter then turns to urban change: the fair justified new ring roads, parking and office complexes, and it gave Belgian architects commissions that shaped the city. A further section contrasts the American pavilion, with its 'soft pitch', Stone's circular building and the fashion show, with the Soviet pavilion, whose Sputnik models drew the crowds. A brief epilogue moves on to Seattle 1962 and the Space Needle. The authors conclude that Brussels gained the European institutions, but that the fair's promise of supranational unity was only partly realised.

Brussels 1958Seattle 1962
2Soviet-American Rivalry at Expo ’58Anthony Swiftp. 27

Swift compares the Soviet and American pavilions at Expo '58 to show how each superpower sought to win the approval of visitors. He reconstructs Soviet planning from Central Committee resolutions, committee minutes and the views of commissioner Dmitrii Ryzhkov and deputy Iakov Lomko, and shows how Sputnik, launched weeks before the fair opened, moved satellite models to the centre of the Soviet exhibits. The American side is traced through the State Department, the USIA and commissioner Howard Cullman, who used warnings of Soviet victory to win more funding. Swift describes the exhibits in detail: in the Soviet pavilion, heavy machinery, statistics and before-and-after narratives of progress; in the American pavilion, the fashion show, Steinberg's mural, Circarama and the 'Islands of Living'. He then weighs Belgian press reviews and visitor surveys, which generally rated the Soviet exhibits higher, and argues that the Soviets were the more effective propagandists because they showed facts and things. The chapter concludes that the Soviets achieved more with visitors, though most opinions did not change.

Brussels 1958
3Atoms for Peace in Brussels and Osaka: World’s Fairs and the Shaping of Japanese Attitudes to Nuclear PowerMorris Lowp. 46

Low asks how world's fairs helped sell the peaceful atom to Japanese audiences during the Cold War. He begins with the Atoms for Peace campaign and a 1956 US Information Service survey in which many Japanese expected atomic energy to become a curse, and then covers the Japan Pavilion at Brussels 1958, where a Hiroshima image confronted visitors before the exhibits of instruments and crafts. The main case is Expo '70 in Osaka: Low describes Kono's tapestries in the atomic towers, the moon rock, and the Fujipan Robot Pavilion, where Tezuka's Astro Boy helped to counter Japan's 'nuclear allergy'. He also draws on exit surveys of the American and Soviet pavilions, which show Japanese visitors preferring the American display and reading the Soviet one as propaganda. The conclusion is that the fairs helped build a nuclear partnership with the United States, since the Japanese government chose American reactors and most Japanese supported building new plants.

Brussels 1958Osaka 1970
Part IITheater of Conflict: North America and the Cold War Statep. 55
4Bringing the Fair to Town: Harrison “Buzz” Price and International Expositions in the United States after 1945James D. Skeep. 57

Skee follows Harrison 'Buzz' Price, the consultant whose firms Economics Research Associates and Harrison Price Company produced attendance estimates and feasibility studies for several American world's fairs. The chapter begins with Price's background, from wartime bombing surveys to SRI, and with Century 21 in Seattle, where his firm replaced an SRI estimate with a more cautious one based on comparable attractions such as zoos. Skee then turns to HemisFair '68 in San Antonio, where Price's team argued that Mexican American residents had discretionary income to spend, and to the Louisiana World Exposition of 1984, where the projection of 11 million visitors was not met, the city forced the fair into bankruptcy, and 7.3 million attended. Skee argues that Price's quantitative, systems-based methods belonged to a Cold War consensus among American advisers, and that the disclaimers Price adopted after New Orleans turned his forecasts into assumptions rather than promises. The coda ties this to the later spread of data analytics.

Seattle 1962San Antonio 1968New Orleans 1984
5“The Future Isn’t What It Used to Be”: Optimism and Anxiety, 1939 and 1964Robert H. Kargonp. 66

Kargon compares the two New York world's fairs, of 1939-1940 and 1964-1965, through their visions of the future, using General Motors' Futurama as the main case. He argues that the 1939 fair framed the future as rational planning, shaped by Lewis Mumford's call for a 'Fair of the Future' and by Norman Bel Geddes's Futurama, which drew over twenty-seven million visitors and offered an optimistic, collective vision against the Depression and the coming war. In 1964 the future was instead a matter of unfinished technologies for new frontiers such as the moon, Antarctica and the oceans, presented in a corporate and consumerist idiom that critics such as Vincent Scully attacked. Kargon then sets the forecasts beside each other, weighing Robert Millikan's 1939 prediction about coal and oil against Isaac Asimov's 1964 account of the fair of 2014. The conclusion is that both Futuramas are useful indicators of the moments that produced them, since their optimism was shaped by the anxieties of those years.

New York 1939New York 1964
61964 and the State of the CityKatie Uvap. 77

Uva reads the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair as a showcase of midcentury urbanism, the planning ideas of slum clearance, highways and suburbs that New York had pursued since 1939. She sets the Democracity and Futurama of 1939 beside 1964 exhibits such as Moses's Panorama, Disney's rides and the Ford Magical Skyway, and argues that the later fair repeated the earlier vision just as critics were attacking it. Her main evidence is the public contest over the fair: Moses's resignation from the slum-clearance committee, the critiques by Jacobs and Mumford, protests by CORE and tenants in Harlem, and Frank O'Hara's poem on the fair's whitewashing of the city. She notes that the fair projected 70 million visitors but drew 51 million, and that it lost money. The chapter concludes that a shift was under way, one that undermined the utopian authority of the fair's exhibitors and eroded the consensus on which the fair depended.

New York 1939New York 1964
Part IIITheater of Conflict: North America and Cold War Culturep. 85
7Advancing an Optimistic Technological Narrative in an Age of Skepticism: General Electric and Walt Disney’s Progressland at the 1964–1965 New York World’s FairMichelle Demeterp. 87

Demeter examines General Electric's Progressland pavilion at the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair, and above all Disney's 'Carousel of Progress', built with Audio-Animatronic figures. She places the attraction in the Cold War setting of the 1959 Kitchen Debate, arguing that GE's appliances and Disney's domestic vignettes presented technological progress as a source of freedom, time saved and consumer choice. The chapter also covers GE's demonstration of nuclear fusion, which was presented as a safe and peaceful source of energy and was carefully reassured to the public. Demeter describes the carousel's six rotating stages, its robot family, and the way Disney's figures were named and designed to seem friendly rather than threatening, unlike the robots of 1950s science fiction. Her main argument is that the attraction's version of American history is hyperreal and nostalgic, and that its final scene, now dated, has become a retro-future. The conclusion is that GE and Disney used the fair to present American technological superiority as a promise of abundance.

New York 1964
8The Human Spirit in an Age of Machines: The Pietà and the Computer at the 1964–1965 New York World’s FairArthur P. Molellap. 96

Molella uses the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair to revisit Henry Adams's contrast between the dynamo and the Virgin, first set at the Paris Exposition of 1900. The central case is the Vatican Pavilion's Michelangelo Pieta, which was X-rayed and shipped with elaborate precautions, then displayed behind bulletproof Plexiglas and a people-mover, drawing more than 27 million visitors; Molella reads this technical framing as a sign that the sacred had been absorbed into modern technology. He then turns to the IBM Pavilion, with its Eames films and mainframe displays, and to Olivetti's Programma 101, shown at a trade show near the fair and presented as a machine that would free ordinary people from the computer's priesthood. He notes the Cold War subtext of IBM's SAGE work and the rumour that Olivetti was pushed out of computing for political reasons. The conclusion is that Olivetti aimed to show that technology could have a soul, while the fair revealed the unease about machines that Adams had foreseen.

New York 1964
9Cold War Food: Consumption and Technology at the New York World’s Fair, 1964–1965Emanuela Scarpellinip. 109

Scarpellini examines the World of Food Pavilion, planned for the 1964–1965 New York World's Fair but abandoned in 1964 after construction had begun, and two displays intended for it: the RCA-Whirlpool 'Miracle Kitchen' and the 'Supermarket of Tomorrow'. Drawing on archival records and press material, the chapter traces the pavilion's design, cost and construction. Its argument is that both displays marked a shift in the Cold War story of technology, from producers to consumers, and that they addressed women directly as buyers and as users of new machines. The kitchen is set against precedents such as the 1956 Frigidaire 'Kitchen of Tomorrow' and the 1959 Moscow kitchen of the Kitchen Debate, and the supermarket's menu, product-information and checkout systems are described in detail. The chapter ends by noting that the pavilion mixed futuristic displays with traditional foods, so that it bridged past and future in the name of progress.

New York 1964–1965
10Billy Graham: The Fifth Dimension at the 1964−1965 New York World’s FairMary Ann Bordenp. 118

Borden examines the Billy Graham Pavilion, a separate evangelical building at the 1964–1965 New York World's Fair that the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association secured in 1962 after declining space in the Protestant Center. The argument is that the pavilion and its film, Man in the 5th Dimension, turned the fair's theme of 'Peace through Understanding' towards religious conversion, in response to Cold War anxieties and a rise in church attendance after Kennedy's assassination. The chapter works through the negotiations with the fair commission, the octagonal design by Edward Durell Stone, the globe of jewelled cities that recorded Graham's crusades, and the film itself, with its multilingual soundtracks and its counselling of visitors. Success is measured in attendance of over five million, some 590,000 public decisions for Christ in 1964, and the film's later rental to churches. Borden also considers the few critics, including a Methodist writer who found the film phoney. The chapter ends by presenting the pavilion as a 'fifth dimension' experience for millions, and as the only one of the four religious pavilions not backed by a single church to break even.

New York 1964–1965
11“Massy and Classy”: Dressing American Women at Expo ’67Daniela Sheininp. 128

Sheinin examines the US Pavilion at Expo '67 in Montreal, where women guides wore uniforms designed by the fashion designer Bill Blass. The argument is that the United States Information Agency, under its design chief Jack Masey, used fashion rather than technology or commerce to claim American leadership, and that the fashion industry presented American ready-to-wear clothing as a Cold War asset. The chapter draws on the pavilion's planning, the newsletters of the Fashion Group International, and fashion and news magazines, and sets the pavilion against the French Pavilion and the Soviet Pavilion's fashion shows. Sheinin traces how the 'Sputnik style' rhetoric of the 1950s, with its moon-themed cosmetics and talk of fabric laboratories, framed American clothing as modern and scientific, and how DuPont and Burlington Industries backed the pavilion and its uniforms. The later sections follow Blass's rise as a designer celebrity, which the chapter presents as the start of a fashion economy in which the designer's name mattered as much as the fabric. The chapter ends by describing Expo '67 as a turning point in the marketing of American women's fashion.

Montreal 1967
12“The Changing Role of Women in a Changing World”: Universal Womanhood at HemisFair ’68Abigail M. Markwynp. 137

Markwyn examines the Woman's Pavilion at HemisFair '68 in San Antonio, a building that local club women initiated, funded through subscriptions and designed around the theme 'The Changing Role of Women in a Changing World'. The argument is that the pavilion belonged to a regional, midcentury women's organising that predates the second wave of feminism, and that it promoted a hemispheric 'universal womanhood' while leaving race, colonialism and gender inequality largely unaddressed. The chapter follows the project from its origins in 1966, through fundraising and charter membership, to the narratives that shaped its exhibits. It weighs the architecture, the displays and a fashion film, which reinforced gender stereotypes, against the fair's displacement of 1,600 residents and its treatment of Black and Mexican American communities. Markwyn compares the pavilion with the 1893 Chicago Woman's Building and with the Texas debate over the Equal Rights Amendment. The chapter ends by treating the pavilion as a grassroots step towards the feminism of the 1970s, still bounded by Cold War internationalism and settler colonialism.

San Antonio 1968
Part IVTheater of Conflict: Asia and Australiap. 159
13A Garden City for Progress and Harmony: Singapore at the Osaka 1970 ExpoEllan F. Sperop. 161

Spero examines Singapore's pavilion at Expo '70 in Osaka, a tropical garden with a film and a series of postage stamps, shown by a country that had been independent for only five years. The argument is that the pavilion presented Singapore as a multicultural, non-aligned and prosperous state, and that this was a deliberate choice which played down colonial rule, the Japanese occupation and the brief union with Malaysia. The chapter draws on the planning papers of the Ministry of Culture and the Tourist Promotion Board, the Shell-produced film Singapore Island City, and the stamps' design history. It recounts the government's initial reluctance to take part, the Japanese invitation, and the tourism and political aims considered for the pavilion. Spero describes the aviary, aquarium and two stand-alone huts, the film's origin myth and its treatment of trade, housing and diversity, and the four stamp designs. The chapter ends by suggesting that the garden is best understood through what it hides, the labour and planning behind its apparent naturalness.

Osaka 1970
14Cultural Diplomacy Down Under: US Sports Diplomacy at Brisbane’s Expo ’88Martin J. Manningp. 172

Manning examines the US Pavilion at Expo '88 in Brisbane, whose theme was 'Sport and Its Science', and argues that it was a piece of sports diplomacy at the close of the Cold War. The chapter places Brisbane within the sequence of American participation in world's fairs run by the United States Information Agency, from Brussels in 1958, and within the longer American effort, dating from the 1952 Olympics, to win the sporting rivalry with the USSR. It draws on USIA and Expo materials, including the pavilion's press kit, and describes the collateral programme of sports-science seminars, a drugs conference, and the outdoor Sports Court where teams performed. Manning also details the exhibits, from baseball and basketball relics to the radar 'Match the Athletes' display. The chapter ends by judging Brisbane a success, with 18.5 million visitors and a Soviet pavilion reduced in profile, and as the last fair run by the USIA, after which Congress ended government funding for US participation.

Brisbane 1988
Part VEndings and New Beginningsp. 181
15The Cold War, a Cool Medium, and the Postmodern Death of World ExposLuca Massiddap. 183

Massidda asks why world expositions disappeared after Osaka 1970, with no BIE-recognised universal exposition until Seville in 1992. The argument is that the expo's cultural form was structurally incompatible with late capitalism, the crisis of the city and the dominance of television, which made the Olympics a more effective 'media event'. The chapter has two parts. The first examines Brussels 1958, Montreal 1967 and Osaka 1970 at their peak, with attendances of 41 to 64 million, Cold War superpower pavilions, and new technology such as the Bell Pavilion's 360-degree screen. The second, covering 1970 to 1992, draws on McLuhan and Meyrowitz to argue that television dissolved the physical public space on which expos depended, and it presents a table of smaller specialised fairs in the period. Massidda concludes that the digital and networked media of the 1990s returned the city to the centre of the social system and gave the expo a new opportunity, as Seville showed.

Brussels 1958Montreal 1967Osaka 1970
16Does the World’s Fair Still Matter? Discovering New Worlds after 1989Scott Gabriel Knowlesp. 194

Knowles asks whether the world's fair still matters after 1989, and examines the fairs planned during or after the Cold War, from Plovdiv in 1991 to Shanghai in 2010. The argument is that these fairs were shaped by the political changes of their moment and in turn helped to shape them, as host cities used them for urban renewal, national self-presentation and reform. The chapter moves fair by fair. Plovdiv's young-inventors expositions of 1985 and 1991 are read as a shift from Cold War showcase to a sign of Bulgarian transition, and Seville 1992, Lisbon 1998 and Hannover 2000 as bids for European integration, reunification and a sustainable image. Daejeon 1993 is presented as South Korea's 'new road' of democratic development, and Shanghai 2010 as a display of urban China. Knowles relies on press reports, Bureau of International Expositions assessments and the fairs' own films, and records the American difficulties at Seville and Hannover. The chapter ends by pointing to Dubai 2020 and a possible American return, presenting the fairs as theatres for national visions.

Park, Young-Sin. “Making ‘Modern’ Korean Subjects: The Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition of 1915.” Journal article.Asia: central5 chapter overviews

Overview

Park's article examines the Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition held in Seoul from September to October 1915, five years after Japan's annexation of Korea. Park argues against reading the event mainly as colonial propaganda and treats it as a cultural machinery that addressed Korean visitors as modern subjects, drawing on Foucault's panopticon and apparatus. It traces how the exposition idea entered Korea from the 1880s, analyses the Western-style pavilions and the 'old' palace space at Kyŏngbok Palace, and examines visitors' responses to discipline, spectacle and commodities. A brief conclusion places the exhibition at the start of colonial exposition culture in Korea.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the whole subject, since the exhibition took place in Korea under Japanese rule, and Korea is discussed in every chapter. The attention is central, concentrated in the chapters on the introduction of the exposition idea and on 'Modern Korea', with the visitor chapter on Koreans' experience. Japan is the second presence: as colonial government it designed the Western-style pavilions in the palace grounds on the model of the Tokyo Taisho Exhibition of 1914, and it sold Japanese goods through merchants such as Mitsukoshi. China appears only as the former power over Korea, whose troops suppressed the 1884 coup.

Korean participation abroad is traced in the introduction: the Chicago exposition of 1893 and the Paris exposition of 1900, where Korea showed itself as an independent empire but was read as a 'Hermit Kingdom', and the Kyŏngsŏng Exposition of 1907. Koreans are otherwise the audience: over a million visitors came in 1915, and folk arts and customs were shown in the 'old' palace space to set off Japanese progress. Chinese visitors and exhibitors do not appear in the text as read. Southeast Asia is absent: none of its countries, colonies or peoples is named.

Contents

Introductionp. 1

Park's introduction presents the 1915 Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition in Seoul as a spectacle that addressed Korean visitors as modern subjects. It argues against the literature that reads the event mainly as colonial propaganda, and treats it as a cultural machine that disciplined and seduced visitors, drawing on Foucault's panopticon and apparatus. The introduction then sets out the article's plan: how the exposition idea reached Korea, how the exhibition represented 'modern Korea', and how visitors experienced it.

Seoul 1915
The Introduction of an International Exposition into Korea as a Symbol of Modernityp. 3

Park traces how the idea of the international exposition, pangnamhoe, entered Korean public life between the 1880s and the early 1900s. The main evidence is the Pobingsa mission to the United States in 1883, Pak Chŏng-yang's report on the Tokyo national exhibition of 1881, Yu Kil-chun's book Sŏyu kyŏnmun of 1895, and newspaper articles of 1884 and 1900. Park argues that Korean understanding came mainly through Japan but also through direct contact with the West. Expositions became a symbol of civilisation, self-strengthening and national prosperity. Korea's participation at Chicago in 1893 and Paris in 1900, the Japanese-Korean Merchandise Exposition at Pusan in 1906 and the Kyŏngsŏng Exposition of 1907 are presented as steps towards the kongjinhoe, or industrial exhibition, that prepared the 1915 event. The chapter ends by reading these early exhibitions as expressions both of Korean reform and of Japanese justification for annexation.

Tokyo 1881Chicago 1893Paris 1900Pusan 1906Seoul 1907
Representations of “Modern Korea” in the 1915 Exhibitionp. 7

Park examines the architecture, layout and display of the 1915 exhibition as a way of representing 'modern Korea'. The chapter draws on the official report, the exhibition guide and visitor routes printed in Maeil shinbo and Keijō nippō, and on posters, photographs and postcards. It shows that the organisers built Western-style pavilions on the east of the Kyŏngbok Palace site, destroying a large part of its structures, and kept older palace halls on the west as small exhibition rooms. Visitors followed a numbered route from the 'modern' pavilions to the 'premodern' or 'old' space. Displays of penal and hygiene systems, provincial development and products were arranged to show Korean backwardness against Japanese progress. Park situates the architecture in the Tokyo Taisho exhibition of 1914 and in Renaissance and Secession styles, and concludes that the buildings served the colonial claim to have made a 'new modern' Korea.

Seoul 1915Tokyo 1914
Experiencing Modernity and “New Modern Subjects”p. 15

Park turns from the organisers to the visitors, asking how ordinary Koreans experienced and responded to the exhibition. The main sources are the Maeil shinbo's reports, the American missionaries Edwin Wade Koons and William Arthur Noble, and a survey of visitors' favourite sites. Park argues that the exhibition aimed to produce disciplined, 'civilised' viewers through rules on dress, behaviour, toilets and sanitary inspection, but that many visitors were drawn instead to electric illumination, rides, the entertainment area and shopping. Souvenirs and the Mitsukoshi kimono shop show the exhibition as a 'universe of commodities'. Reformist commentators such as Chang Chi-yŏn and Yun Pong-kyun welcomed it as a means of industrial growth and self-strengthening. The chapter concludes that the Korean subject shaped by the exhibition was divided between the disciplined citizen, the consumer and the colonised subject.

Seoul 1915
Conclusionp. 21

The brief conclusion treats 1915 as the start of colonial exposition culture in Korea, with some thirty large and small expositions held between 1915 and 1940. Park argues that the exhibition was a cultural machinery producing a conflicted Korean subject, shaped by seduction and spectacle, education and discipline, and coercive colonial control. It ends by linking this to a Korean nationalism understood as an ambivalent response to uneven development.

Seoul 1915
Reference Listp. 22
Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020.Asia: central11 chapter overviews

Overview

Peterson's book examines how independent Asian states sought to control their own representation at Western world's fairs between 1915 and 2015. Its case studies are San Francisco 1915, New York 1939-40, Brisbane 1988, New York 1964-65 and Milan 2015, each centred on the pavilions or concessions of Japan, China, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia or South Korea. The introduction argues that Japan, and to a lesser extent Thailand, were arguably the only Asian nations that consistently presented themselves, and proposes a move from a colonial order of display to a performative order of live encounters, drawing on Mitchell and Greenhalgh. Each case is a chapter, organised by fair, using archival and ethnographic methods. The conclusion argues that state-directed national representation has declined as the form became costly for host cities, and that Asia has become the leading host of expositions.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East and Southeast Asia are the whole subject of this work, and their coverage is central. Japan is the main case in chapters 2 and 4 (the government site, 'Japan Beautiful' concession and fine arts galleries at San Francisco 1915; the pavilion and Takarazuka Revue at New York 1939-40). China fills chapter 3 (the official site and the Chinese Village at San Francisco 1915, with Chinatown's role) and chapter 5 (Expo '88 in Brisbane). The Philippines (chapter 6) and Indonesia (chapter 7) are studied through their New York 1964-65 pavilions, South Korea (chapter 8) and Thailand (chapter 9) through Milan 2015, and chapter 10 treats the Chinese Milan pavilion and Asia's rise as host.

Most of the participation is by states, commissioners and merchants: the Japanese Commission, the Chinese commissioners Chen Qi and T.C. Chu, and the Six Companies running the Joy Zone village. Displays organised by others are also discussed. Chapter 2 notes that a Formosa tea house names a Japanese colony and reads Japan's Red Cross display as propaganda, and chapter 4 describes New York critics who wanted Japan as cherry blossoms and willowy maidens. Asian women are mainly performers and press subjects, notably in chapters 6 and 7. Asian visitors feature only as crowds at the Chinese Village groundbreaking. Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Burma and the Malay states are not discussed in the chapter overviews.

Contents

List of Figuresp. 8
Acknowledgementsp. 11

The acknowledgements trace Peterson's interest in fairs to childhood visits to the 1964-65 New York World's Fair, and link the book to the COVID-19 pandemic and the Anthropocene. Peterson thanks family, Georgetown teachers, a former colleague, Maryrose Casey, and archivists in New York, Queensland and San Francisco who gave access to the materials. Funding came from Flinders University, and a 2018 visiting fellowship at the International Institute for Asian Studies in Leiden is also acknowledged.

Note on Works Citedp. 13
Note on Asian Namesp. 14
1Introductionp. 15

Peterson introduces a study of how independent Asian nations sought to control their own representation at Western world's fairs between 1915 and 2015. Peterson argues that Japan, and to a lesser extent Thailand, were arguably the only Asian nations that consistently presented themselves at these fairs rather than being presented by Western powers, and that the story of Asian agency begins in San Francisco in 1915. Drawing on Timothy Mitchell and Greenhalgh, Peterson proposes a move from an exhibitionary order of colonial display to a performative order of live encounters within pavilions. Three modes of performance are distinguished: cultural shows, guides who perform national identity, and the metrics of neoliberal productivity. The case studies cover San Francisco 1915, New York 1939-40, Brisbane 1988, New York 1964-65 and Milan 2015, and the introduction explains the archival and ethnographic methods and their limits. It concludes that state-directed self-representation at expositions has declined as the form became costly for host cities.

San Francisco 1915New York 1939Brisbane 1988New York 1964Milan 2015
2The Master of the Formp. 39

Peterson argues that by 1915 Japan had become the master of the international exhibition format, and that its self-representation at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco was built on staged encounters rather than on objects alone. He starts with diplomacy: the 1912 groundbreaking, the gold 'Loving Cup' and the public performances of Japanese and American officials that presented the two countries as peaceful partners on the Pacific. The first and longest case is the Japanese government site, with its temple-like pavilion and garden, where Peterson reads photographs of kimono-clad women as evidence of how fairgoers performed an emotional attachment to the place. He then turns to the commercial 'Japan Beautiful' concession in the Joy Zone, with its miniature Asakusa-style village, geisha and Mount Fuji tea house, then to the trade halls selling ceramics, lacquer and silk, and to the fine arts galleries, where San Francisco critics praised traditional work and dismissed Western-style painting. The chapter ends by arguing that Japan knew what America wanted to see, a pre-modern and refined nation, and supplied it.

San Francisco 1915
3The New China and Chinese-Americannessp. 79

Peterson argues that the new Republic of China, emerging from the Qing dynasty, used the San Francisco fair to present itself as both an heir to ancient civilisation and a modern nation, while San Francisco's Chinese community performed family values and assimilation. The official site, a walled garden around a hall modelled on a Forbidden City palace, held carved furniture and porcelain, while trade goods and a set of pagoda models made by orphaned boys presented China as ancient and handcrafted. Peterson's main concern, though, is the Chinese Village in the Joy Zone, where the community's groundbreaking had projected family respectability and an 'Underground Chinatown' exhibit of opium and gambling mannequins, shut in March 1915 after protests in the Chinese-language press, threatened to undo that work. He also covers a 1914 row over the clothes of Chinese craftsmen building the government site and the 1939 New York fair, where a Chinese village failed to raise funds. The chapter concludes that Chinese-American identity was forged in San Francisco's and New York's Chinatowns, which competed with anything the fairgrounds could show.

San Francisco 1915Saint Louis 1904New York 1939
4Performing Japan in the ‘World of Tomorrow’p. 113

Peterson argues that Japan's pavilion at the 1939-1940 New York World's Fair staged a gendered performance of diplomacy and femininity for American audiences, at a time when Japan was moving towards war. The pavilion, reputedly modelled on the Ise-Jingū Shrine and designed by Nippon Kōbō, combined halls and a garden in which kimono-clad women reeled silk, served tea and arranged flowers, and the press releases pitched these scenes to newspapers' women's pages. Peterson then turns to the 1939 and 1940 Japan Day ceremonies, where diplomats recited a love-fest narrative of friendship and Perry's opening of Japan, even as relations soured. The Takarazuka Revue, which played the fairgrounds in May 1939 with a gender-bending, modern show, was dismissed by New York critics who wanted a Japan of cherry blossoms and willowy maidens. The chapter concludes that Americans wanted Japan to stay a fixed image of tradition, and that Japan's own staging helped keep that image in place until Pearl Harbor.

New York 1939
5From ‘Panda Diplomacy’ to Acrobat Diplomacyp. 139

Peterson examines how the People's Republic of China presented itself at Expo '88 in Brisbane, a privately financed 'specialized exposition' open from April to October 1988. Its argument is that, a year before Tiananmen, China drew on three cultural assets, pandas, terracotta warriors and acrobats, to win goodwill in Australia, a country that had recognised the PRC in 1972 and was uneasy about Japanese investment. The main evidence is the China pavilion: its Chinese gate, its 360-degree film 'A Glimpse of China', its gift shop and family restaurant, and above all the resident artisans whose live work in embroidery, cork and ivory carving is read through press reviews, fair guides and private scrapbooks held in Queensland archives. Much of the chapter then follows the three acrobatic troupes that performed in the open-air Piazza across the fair's run, placing them within Australia's own circus tradition. It closes with a national tour of Wu Zuguang's Beijing Opera The Three Beatings of Tao San Chun, sponsored by Australia's foreign affairs department, which Peterson reads as a sign of hope before the Tiananmen Square massacre of June 1989.

Brisbane 1988
6Fashion, Dance, and Representing the Filipinap. 167

Peterson looks at the Philippine pavilion at the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair, a non-official fair built to make a profit, and asks how fashion and dance presented the newly independent nation to Americans. The argument is that the pavilion staged a modern, cosmopolitan Philippines, but that its women, who were central to that image, were framed by a press that fixed on Asian women's appearance. The evidence runs roughly in order: the 1963 groundbreaking, where Governor Poletti's remarks and the reception photographs of Filipiniana dress are examined; the President's daughter Gloria Macapagal, who represented her father during Philippines Week in June 1964; the pavilion's open, farmer's-hat-shaped roof; and its 'Hospitality Corps' of guides, whom press releases described as drawn from the nation's best families. The chapter then reconstructs Philippines Week, with the Bayanihan dance company at Lincoln Center, the Karilagan designers' fashion shows and a Manhattan motorcade. It ends by using the Filipino word grabe, or 'too-muchness', to describe the pavilion's excess, and its porousness as a metaphor for a nation that looked outward.

New York 1964-1965
7Performing Modernity under Sukarno’s ‘Roving Eye’p. 195

Peterson examines Indonesia's pavilion at the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair and argues that President Sukarno's personal control shaped both its content and the way the American press received its women. The chapter first sets out Sukarno's career and the cultural policy of the Indonesian state, which since the 1950s had treated regional dance as the basis of national identity. It then turns to the pavilion, a modernist building with Balinese touches, whose theatre restaurant staged four shows a day, and to press coverage such as Newsday's 'Girl Watching at the Fair' and the Sunday News's praise of Sukarno's own painting. Peterson reads the dances, including the Perang Kembang battle between Arjun and Buta Cakil and the choreographed Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, as works that mixed regional traditions with modern dance training. The chapter follows the pavilion's decline through the Malaysian dispute, Sukarno's halting of plans in March 1965 and the events of 1 October 1965, and ends by noting that the image of exotic Bali and Java outlived both the pavilion and the violence.

New York 1964-1965
8Maximizing Affect, Minimizing Impact with Hansikp. 227

Peterson examines South Korea's pavilion at the 2015 Milan Expo, whose theme was 'Feeding the Planet'. Korea presented hansik, its vegetable-heavy fermented cuisine, as a solution to hunger and obesity, and Peterson, who visited the pavilion repeatedly, describes its sequence of art-installation-like galleries in detail: a gallery of obese figures linked to food, a video hologram of a starving child, a multimedia 'Symphony of Food', a sensor-driven virtual cooking table, and a fermentation gallery of 365 projected clay pots set to Arirang. He argues that these spaces generated strong visual and aural affect but never engaged taste or smell, and that treating hansik as a science experiment clashed with the place-based, social food culture of Italy. Peterson supports the point with contrasts to the Argentine pavilion next door and to Korea Week performances in Milan, and by noting that Korean restaurants were scarce in the city. The chapter concludes that the pavilion succeeded in its ambition to feed the planet but failed to win converts to hansik.

Milan 2015
9Hard and Soft Power in the Thai Pavilionp. 255

Peterson's chapter examines the Thai pavilion at the 2015 Milan Expo, which opened while King Bhumibol was gravely ill and Thailand was ruled by a military junta. Peterson argues that the pavilion, presenting Thailand as the 'Golden Land' and 'Kitchen to the World', was overwhelmed by these domestic anxieties. He walks the reader through three spaces: a 360-degree film of abundant land and sea, a room of projected images of corporate food production and packaged brands, and a closing film that presents the King as the 'Farmer King' and 'Royal Rainmaker'. A gift shop stocked with frozen meals beside a wall of microwaves forms the commercial end point of the route. Drawing on Nye, Jackson's 'regime of images' and Göhler's distinction between power to and power over, Peterson contends that the pavilion addressed Italian visitors as children being instructed by an authority, blunting both its message and its aim of selling Thai processed food. The chapter concludes that the pavilion performed compliance before an absent Thai audience.

Milan 2015
10Conclusionp. 279

Peterson's conclusion looks beyond Milan to the future of national representation at world's fairs. He argues that the 2015 Milan Expo, with its cost overruns, unfinished pavilions and protests, suggests that the grand European exposition is unlikely to be revived. Asia has taken the lead as host, and Peterson weighs Shanghai 2010, with its 73 million visitors and forced displacement of residents, against Dubai 2020, whose site relied on migrant labor. The Chinese pavilion at Milan, with its animated family film and live Hani dancers, is read as a more effective affective encounter than the Korean and Thai pavilions. Drawing on Volcic and Andrejvic, Peterson proposes that states now 'nationalize the sell', so that future expositions are more likely to exploit national identity than to say anything meaningful about it. He ends by arguing that the analytical frameworks for studying these displays must change, though they will remain performative, visual and increasingly virtual.

Milan 2015Shanghai 2010Dubai 2020

Qureshi, Sadiah. Peoples on Parade: Exhibitions, Empire, and Anthropology in Nineteenth-Century Britain. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2011.Asia: occasional10 chapter overviews

Overview

Qureshi's book studies the display of living foreign peoples in nineteenth-century London, from the San exhibition at Exeter Hall in 1847 to Savage South Africa at Earl's Court in 1899. Its argument is that these shows were a large commercial entertainment, shaped by London's streets, printed promotion, managers and performers who consented on their own terms, and that they fed into ethnology and the scientific study of race rather than being only racist spectacle. Part One covers the streets, Part Two the promotion, the managers and the recruitment of performers, and Part Three the audiences' interpretations, the natural history court at the Crystal Palace and the learned societies, ending with the shift toward entertainment and imperial spectacle. The scope is London, with comparisons to Paris in 1889, Chicago in 1893 and the Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are present in this book as one group among many displayed peoples and as a frequent comparison, but not as a central subject. The text names them in about 74 of its 17,790 lines, mostly in Chapters Six and Seven and the notes. Chinese people appear in Chapter One as physiognomic types in Eliza Lynn's 'Passing Faces' and as settlers stranded in the London docks, and Japanese and Chinese shows are named in the introduction. Chapter Six gives the most sustained attention: Latham's natural history court at the Crystal Palace displayed Chinese, Tibetans, Malaysians and Javanese, and the guidebook's classification of the Chinese as the most civilized of the Mongolians is discussed.

Chapter Seven adds Asian displays at other fairs, used as comparisons with London: the 1886 Colonial and Indian Exhibition's 'Malay' and Straits Settlements performers and Chinese junks from Hong Kong, the Cochin-China settlement and Kampong-Javanese camp of Paris 1889, and the Chicago 1893 Midway with its Chinese and Javanese villages and Japanese bazaar. The book says little about the Asian performers themselves or their experiences in London, and South Asia, through the Empire of India exhibition of 1895, receives more attention as a contrast.

Contents

Introduction: Ladies and Gentlemen, I Bring You . . .p. 1

Qureshi opens with the San exhibition that the anatomist Robert Knox staged at Exeter Hall, London, in 1847, where a lecture on the group's natural history gave way to performance and members of the audience engaged with the performers. The introduction uses this case to argue that displays of living foreign peoples were a large commercial entertainment in nineteenth-century Britain, and that their links to racism and empire must be shown historically rather than assumed. It places the shows against the making of the professional scientist, the contested status of ethnology and anthropology, and the politics of slavery and missionary philanthropy. Qureshi also explains the thin source base, since showmen and performers left few records, and the book's choices about historical terms and images. It closes with a plan in three parts: London's streets, the showmen and performers, and the learned societies and international fairs.

London 1847
Part OneStreet Spectaclesp. 13
1Glimpsing Urban Savagesp. 15

Qureshi argues that the market for displayed peoples was prepared on London's streets, which writers presented as a spectacle for visual inspection. The chapter opens with Punch's 1849 print of Regent Street and reads Eliza Lynn's essay 'Passing Faces' and Henry Mayhew's London Labour and the London Poor. It shows how Mayhew classed the urban poor as wandering nomads, aligning costers and street patterers with foreign peoples through the ethnology of Smith and Prichard and through physiognomic and cranial ideas. Qureshi then surveys the literature of street life from Lamb and Mudie to tourists such as Simond and Pückler-Muskau, and the etiquette of detached looking. Typological images by Haydon, Beard and Woolnoth supplied the visual codes by which spectators read faces and trades. The chapter ends by arguing that London's Jewish, Asian and black residents made the city an intercultural contact zone, so that shows of foreign peoples did not rely on colour alone to appear alien.

2Artful Promotionp. 47

Qureshi argues that the printed promotional material of London's human displays, including posters, playbills, handbills, newspaper advertisements and pamphlets, shaped how audiences were invited to understand the shows, and that historians have wrongly treated it as evidence of audience reception. After opening with a Punch piece on billposting, the chapter traces how showmen used typefaces, woodcuts and, later, images to stress ethnic origin and venue. Its main cases are the Sámi at the Egyptian Hall in 1822, Caldecott's Zulus in 1853, the Aztec children Maximo and Bartola, and Farini's Zulus in 1879. Qureshi shows that pamphlets borrowed long passages from travel writers such as Isaacs and Lichtenstein, and that reviews and handbills recycled one another's wording. The chapter concludes that promotion supplied the frameworks through which patrons made sense of what they saw, so it reveals how showmen framed the shows rather than how paying visitors actually responded.

London 1822London 1847London 1853London 1879
Part TwoMetropolitan Encountersp. 99
3Managing Performancep. 101

Qureshi argues that exhibition managers were not simply profiteers but active shapers of how foreign peoples were received, and that historians have overemphasised P. T. Barnum while neglecting the managers. The chapter profiles several: Catlin, who toured Native American delegations while publicising their plight; Bullock, the Liverpool Museum and Egyptian Hall proprietor; Knox, the anatomist who lectured on the San; Maungwudaus (George Henry), an Anishinabe who managed his own troupe; and Farini and Imre Kiralfy, later professional showmen. Qureshi then examines the techniques managers used to frame performances: lectures, costumes, painted and panoramic scenery, imported artefacts, and staged rites such as Zulu marriages and Bakhoje dances, all chosen to meet audience expectations. The lectures of Knox and Tyler on the San, which drew on travel literature to explain the group's mental and moral traits, show how talks tied performers to racial classification and political debate. The chapter concludes that managers mediated the knowledge audiences formed and also recruited the performers themselves, a point taken up in the next chapter.

London 1822London 1840London 1847London 1853London 1885
4Recruiting Entertainersp. 126

Qureshi asks how foreign peoples were recruited into the shows and how far they consented, arguing that neither victimhood nor simple agency captures their situation. The chapter covers the San children Flora and Martinus, taken in Africa by a merchant and later raised by a Croydon family, and the Aztec children Maximo and Bartola, who were probably sold by a trader. It then turns to Sara Baartman, who chose to sail to London, the Bakhoje and Anishinabe groups recruited through missionaries, the Zulus gathered by A. T. Caldecott in 1853, and prisoners drawn from Indian and Cape jails. Wild West and 1899 Savage South Africa performers appear under contracts that became standardised. Qureshi tests these arrangements against Herzog and Gerber's consent criteria and finds them largely unmet, but court cases involving the Zulu chiefs Manyos and Larcher show performers pressing their own demands. The chapter concludes that performers resisted, formed relationships and kept some dignity, while the consent obtained mainly served managers and officials.

London 1810London 1844London 1853London 1886London 1899
5Interpreting Exhibitionsp. 155

Qureshi asks how audiences made sense of the London shows of displayed peoples, a question the chapter admits is hard to answer because most spectators left no records. Drawing on press reviews, satirical periodicals, images and travel literature, it maps a range of responses to performers including San, Zulu, Bakhoje and Anishinabe groups. Its main cases are the San children at the Egyptian Hall in 1845, the Zulu shows of 1853 and 1879, and Savage South Africa at Earl's Court in 1899, where a press campaign over women touching performers led the organisers to exclude women from the kraal. Patrons shook hands, gave gifts and questioned performers, while critics disputed whether they were authentic, and reviewers read the displays through travel accounts such as Lichtenstein's on the San and Isaacs's on the Zulus. Satirical papers turned the shows against fashionable society and humanitarian campaigners. The chapter concludes that spectators were critical interpreters rather than passive viewers, and that the shows' receptions were too varied to reduce to a single racist gaze.

London 1899London 1879London 1853London 1845
Part ThreeThe Natural History of Racep. 183
6Transforming “Unfruitful Wonder”p. 185

Qureshi challenges John Conolly's 1855 address, which called displayed peoples 'unfruitful wonder', and argues that London's shows were in fact used by ethnologists as material for research. The chapter shows how press reviews of the San exhibition of 1847 and other shows cast performers as scientific specimens, and how Conolly himself observed groups of San, Anishinabe and Zulu people across the 1840s and 1850s. Its central case is Maximo and Bartola, the children exhibited as Aztecs in 1853, whom Richard Owen, Robert Knox and a phrenologist assessed in conflicting ways, a dispute the chapter reads as a contest over the nature of human variety. It then turns to Robert Gordon Latham's natural history court at the Crystal Palace in Sydenham, where casts of performers were displayed in tableaux and his guidebook stressed human unity. The chapter ends by tracing the split between the Ethnological and Anthropological Societies in 1863, and concludes that displayed peoples helped shape ethnological method, making their bodies valuable to research even after death.

London 1854London 1853
7The End of an Affairp. 222

Qureshi uses Frank Fillis's Savage South Africa, staged at Earl's Court in 1899, to show how African and Afrikaner performers were displayed in late Victorian London. The argument rests on the show's mock kraal, its reenactments of the Ndebele wars and the press coverage that framed them. Qureshi sets these against earlier British fairs, above all the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886, where performers worked as attendants and craftsmen inside the main displays rather than in segregated villages. Paris in 1889 and Chicago in 1893 supply the contrasting model of the native village and the Midway. The chapter then turns to anthropologists such as Galton and Rivers, who used performers and collections at the 1886 exhibition, and argues that British researchers exploited displayed peoples less systematically than their German counterparts. It ends by suggesting that by 1900 the shows had become detached from anthropology and tied to entertainment and imperial spectacle.

London 1899London 1886London 1851Paris 1889Chicago 1893
Conclusion: Afterlivesp. 271

Qureshi's conclusion argues that displayed peoples were more varied, and more central to knowledge production, than the common picture of racist spectacle allows. It opens with a 2002 Zulu show at Cambridge's Corn Exchange and traces the century's changes: from small private ventures to fairs with state, corporate and public funding, and from simple stages to immersive, purpose-built villages. Qureshi argues that colour-based definitions of race are too narrow for the period, that performers and patrons built relationships ranging from day trips to marriage, and that anthropologists used the shows for measurement and training. The discussion then moves to modern cases, including the Augsburg Zoo village, a mock Afghan village in Norfolk and the 1992 'Two Undiscovered Amerindians' installation, to show how easily audiences slip into the same voyeurism. It closes with Sara Baartman and Tambo, whose repatriations are politically charged, and warns against reducing the performers to icons of oppression.

London 1851London 1886
Acknowledgmentsp. 285

Qureshi thanks colleagues and institutions in the Department of History and Philosophy of Science at Cambridge, names Jim Secord as a principal mentor, and lists the readers who commented on drafts and on earlier work about Sara Baartman. Funding came from the Arts and Humanities Research Board, a Leverhulme fellowship and the Getty Foundation, and archivists and the University of Chicago Press are also thanked. The section ends with thanks to family.
