Raizman, David, and Ethan Robey, eds. Expanding Nationalisms at World’s Fairs: Identity, Diversity, and Exchange, 1851–1915. London: Routledge, 2018.Asia: substantial11 chapter overviews

Overview

The volume, edited by David Raizman and Ethan Robey, collects eleven essays on how nations used the world's fairs between 1851 and 1915 to present national identity through manufactured goods and architecture. The editors' introduction, drawing on Benedict Anderson's 'imagined communities', argues that earlier design history treated the fairs as a foil to modernism, and that they were networks of exchange rather than single unified displays. Each chapter is a case study of one national display: Tunisia, Denmark's Nordic Exhibition, Italy at Antwerp, Japan's Hôôden at Chicago, the Musée Centennal in Paris, Finland, Hungary, China's expositions and the American touring art show in South America. The cases run from London and Paris to Chicago, Copenhagen, St. Louis, Nanjing, San Francisco and Buenos Aires.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is substantial but confined to two chapters. Chapter 5, by Hannah Sigur, examines the Hôôden, Japan's pavilion at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, treated as a state project: the commissioners Kuki Ryûichi, Okakura Kakuzô and Yamataka Nobutsura, the architect Kuru Masamichi, and the nihonga paintings of the Tokyo Academy of Art, which presented Japanese art as ancient and authentic. Chapter 9, by Susan Fernsebner, is about China's own participation at St. Louis (1904), Nanjing (1910) and San Francisco (1915): officials and merchants such as Chen Qi, the Six Companies, the protest against the China Pavilion's teahouse and the closure of the 'Underground Chinatown' concession. The introduction names both chapters, and Sigur also covers the 1867 and 1889 Paris fairs, where the French imposed fanciful 'Japanese' facades on Japan's display.

Southeast Asia is nearly absent. Fernsebner notes that overseas Chinese at Nanjing used Southeast Asian native goods to show a hierarchy of civilisation, and that 'Nanyang' in the exposition's name refers to Southeast Asia, but no Southeast Asian territory or people is the subject of any essay. Elsewhere East Asia appears in passing: Hanson's chapter 1 uses 'the East' to mean North Africa, the Middle East, Turkey, India and Persia, with China and Japan excluded; Houze notes Japanese exhibits along the Esplanade in Paris in 1900; Guldberg notes Japanese-inspired ceramics and Bing's Japanese prints in Copenhagen.

Contents

List of illustrationsp. vii
List of contributorsp. xi
Introduction: communities real and imagined: world’s fairs and political meaningsDavid Raizman and Ethan Robeyp. 1

Raizman and Robey introduce the volume by asking how the world's fairs of 1851 to 1915 used manufactured goods to express national identity. They argue that earlier design history treated fairs as a foil to modernism, and that the fairs were networks of exchange rather than single, unified displays. Pevsner's dismissal of the Crystal Palace is challenged by later critics, from Banham and Sparke to Greenhalgh, Bennett and Mitchell, the last three reading the fairs as imperial spectacle. The editors use Anderson's 'imagined communities' to tie national identity to material culture. Their evidence is the Albert Memorial, Owen Jones's interior and Grammar of Ornament, and the contributors' cases: the 1888 Copenhagen Nordic Exhibition, the Nanjing and South American centenaries of 1910, Italy at Brussels and Antwerp, and the Finnish pavilion at Paris in 1900. They end with the outbreak of World War I, when the ideal of 'peaceful competition' broke down.

London 1851Brussels 1880Antwerp 1885Copenhagen 1888Paris 1900Nanjing 1910
1East meets West: re-presenting the Arab-Islamic world at the nineteenth-century world’s fairsDebra Hansonp. 15

Hanson asks how the Arab-Islamic world was represented at nineteenth-century world's fairs, arguing that the fairs turned 'the East' into an exotic, consumable product that served Western nationalism and imperial power. It starts at the 1851 Crystal Palace, where Owen Jones's interior drew on the Alhambra and The Arabian Nights, and where the floor plan set India and other 'Oriental' nations apart from Britain's half. Her main case is Tunisia. Its display, under Ahmed Bey's supervision, included a Bedouin tent and a bazaar staffed by attendants, and Hanson shows how design reformers praised the same goods that a humorous view-book mocked. She then follows Tunisian displays to the 1867 Paris Bardo pavilion and to the Cairo Street and Tunisian village at Chicago in 1893, where live performance replaces object display. Hanson concludes that Tunisia used the fairs for its own self-presentation, but within frameworks set by the host, and that these displays fixed Orientalist stereotypes.

London 1851Paris 1867Chicago 1893
2From London to Paris (via Cairo): the world expositions and the making of a modern architect, 1862–1867Christian A. Hedrickp. 33

Hedrick follows the Prussian architect Carl von Diebitsch from the London exhibition of 1862 to his Cairo practice and the 1867 Paris Exposition Universelle. He argues that Diebitsch's prize-winning zinc vase, with its arabesques and German portrait frieze, was an early attempt to cast Islamic ornament in modern metal, and that a commission from the banker Henry Oppenheim, whom he met at the fair in the Viceroy Sa'id Pasha's party, took him to Egypt. In Cairo he built the cast-iron and zinc mausoleum of Sulayman Pasha and other prefabricated projects. For Paris he designed a portable 'Moorish Kiosk' but exhibited it in the Prussian section, not the Egyptian one the Khedive wanted, a choice Hedrick links to his decline. Set against Chapon's Bardo pavilion, the kiosk shows that Diebitsch's Islamic style was modern rather than Orientalist, and Hedrick concludes that his work belongs in the history of modern architecture.

London 1862Paris 1867
3The Belgian reception of Italy at the 1885 Antwerp World Exhibition: converging artistic, economic, and political strategies on displayDaniela N. Prinap. 50

Prina examines how Italy and Belgium, two young nation-states, each tried to link art, industry and education, and how the Italian government used foreign models to reform its own system. The starting point is a mission of 1880 by Baldassarre Odescalchi and Raffaele Erculei, who inspected the Brussels Jubilee Exhibition and the art-industry institutions of Belgium. The chapter then follows Italy's display at the Turin exhibition of 1884, notably the Borgo Medievale that Alfredo d'Andrade built as a recreation of medieval Piedmont, and its large showing at the Antwerp world's fair of 1885, where 570 of the 665 Italian exhibitors received awards. A Belgian architect, Théophile Fumière, wrote a book on the Italian section that praised Italian ceramics and the regional school system as a model for Belgian design reform. Prina ends with the Brussels decorative arts school and museum of the 1880s and with Italian interest in Belgian religious art and Art Nouveau, leading towards the Turin decorative arts exhibition of 1902.

Antwerp 1885Turin 1884Brussels 1880
4A Danish spectacle: balancing national interests at the 1888 Nordic Exhibition of Industry, Agriculture, and Art in CopenhagenJørn Guldbergp. 71

Guldberg reads the Nordic Exhibition of Industry, Agriculture and Art, held in Copenhagen in 1888, as part of the Copenhagen Industrial Association's campaign for applied art. The exhibition drew about 1.5 million visitors and some 6,000 exhibitors, mostly Scandinavian, and it celebrated three anniversaries. The chapter describes Martin Nyrop's wooden buildings in a national-romantic style, the largely historicist foreign sections, and the ceramics of the Royal Porcelain Factory, where Arnold Krog's naturalistic decoration stood out against the eclectic work of Ipsen's factory. It then sets against this the vernacular ceramics of the Association of Decorators, which critics dismissed as one-off art objects rather than prototypes. The most distinctive part is the analysis of display: packaged goods and sanitary fittings were shown as pagodas and mosques built of bottles and cans, while machines were run for effect with no link to what they made. The conclusion places the exhibition within the rise of Danish cooperatives and the undemocratic rule of the 1880s, and reads the working dairy as a sign of industrial things to come.

Copenhagen 1888
5A neoclassical translation: the Hôôden at the 1893 World’s Columbian ExpositionHannah L. Sigurp. 92

Sigur examines the Hôôden, the Japanese pavilion at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, a wooden building modelled on the Byōdō-in Phoenix Hall at Uji. The argument is that the pavilion translated Japanese identity into the neoclassical language that Western fairs treated as the mark of civilization. The chapter traces how the Japanese commissioners struggled with the fairs' art categories, and how the architect Kuru Masamichi, trained in Beaux-Arts theory, merged three period interiors into one symmetrical building on the Wooded Island. It then turns to the interiors, where nihonga paintings by Tokyo Academy of Art faculty, devised by Okakura Kakuzō and Ernest Fenollosa, were meant to present Japanese art as ancient and authentic. Sigur shows that this stress on authenticity concealed invented pedigrees, including Itô Chûta's Greek reading of Hôryûji. The conclusion is that the exterior, not the paintings, carried the pavilion's message, and that its success set the pattern for architects designing Japan's national pavilions at later fairs.

Chicago 1893
6Paris, 1900: the Musée Centennal du Mobilier et de la Décoration and the formulation of a nineteenth-century national design identityAnca I. Lascp. 109

Lasc examines the Musée Centennal du Mobilier et de la Décoration, a display of furniture and decorative arts on the Esplanade des Invalides at the 1900 Exposition Universelle in Paris. The argument is that the museum used a sequence of eight period rooms, each tied to a political era from Louis XVI to Napoléon III, to present French decorative arts as a continuous national tradition. Lasc places these rooms among other immersive attractions of the fair, such as the Paris en 1400 reconstruction, the Palais du Costume with its mannequins, and the Village Suisse, a copy of Alpine scenery built with real Swiss inhabitants. Lasc ties the museum to the anxieties of the period, after defeat in 1870 and the Panama, Boulanger and Dreyfus affairs, which made French critics wary of foreign modern design including Siegfried Bing's Art Nouveau. The Musée Centennal, Lasc concludes, recast the fairs' historicism as nationalist confidence, so that the Third Republic's modern makers, Gallé, Majorelle and Chéret, appeared as the culmination of the historical sequence.

Paris 1900
7“Our country has never been as popular as it is now!”: Finland at the 1900 Exposition UniverselleBart Pushawp. 130

Pushaw asks how Finland, then a Grand Duchy under Russian rule, won its own pavilion at the 1900 Exposition Universelle, and what the pavilion's appearance of national unity concealed. The chapter reconstructs the campaign of Leo Mechelin, Albert Edelfelt and Robert Runeberg, which secured a site on condition that the building be labelled a Russian section, and the choice of a stone church design by Gesellius, Lindgren and Saarinen. Its central case is Beda Stjernschantz's painting The Glassblowers, which Pushaw reads against her letters and Russian-language pamphlets about the factory it shows. The workers there were Russian-speaking and Orthodox, so a seemingly Finnish image of industry was in fact Russian. Gallen-Kallela's Kalevala frescoes and Emil Halonen's relief of a Sámi reindeer herder receive shorter treatment, as examples of how Finnish identity was defined against Russian and Indigenous others. The pavilion's cohesion, Pushaw argues, was a constructed spectacle of national solidarity. The chapter ends by noting its influence on Estonian and Latvian artists, who faced similar multiethnic conditions.

Paris 1900
8“A revelation of grace and pride”: cultural memory and international aspiration in early twentieth-century Hungarian designRebecca Houzep. 147

Houze follows Hungarian decorative art through four international exhibitions, Paris 1900, Turin 1902, St. Louis 1904 and Milan 1906, asking how these displays built a national identity that moved between folk and cosmopolitan models. Her starting point is Hungary's position within Austria-Hungary, which pushed designers to find forms distinct from Austrian ones, drawing on folk motifs and a supposed Eastern origin of the Magyars. In Paris a historicist national pavilion stood beside Bálint and Jámbor's ornate installation, and critics divided over its folk emphasis. Pál Horti's Turin entrance, with stylised Art Nouveau arabesques, won praise from an Austrian reviewer. His St. Louis display of wooden towers and a Székely gate turned the village into a market stall and led to commissions from American furniture makers. Géza Maróti's Milan rooms, admired by Alfredo Melani, burned in August 1906 and were rebuilt in less grand form. Houze concludes that the fairs made Hungarian identity an elusive, fashionable and commercial construct.

Paris 1900Turin 1902St. Louis 1904Milan 1906
9When the local is the global: case studies in early twentieth-century Chinese exposition projectsSusan R. Fernsebnerp. 173

Fernsebner follows Chinese exposition managers, mostly state officials and commercial elites, through three fairs: St. Louis in 1904, China's first national exposition at Nanjing in 1910, and the Panama-Pacific fair in San Francisco in 1915. Her argument is that these elites sought control over how China was represented. At St. Louis they protested against displays arranged by the Western-staffed Qing Customs Service, including bound-foot shoes and opium pipes. At Nanjing they used the fair to promote economic nationalism and to train a 'new people', drawing on provincial displays of soap, furniture and textiles and on a hall for overseas Chinese. The San Francisco section centres on a complaint about the China Pavilion's teahouse and on 'Underground Chinatown', an attraction that the Six Companies and commissioner-general Chen Qi protested and that closed in March 1915. The chapter concludes that these disputes joined local, transnational and global concerns, and that the same dynamics recur in China's later hosting of Expo 2010.

St. Louis 1904Nanjing 1910San Francisco 1915
10The 1910 Centenary Exhibition in Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay: manufacturing fine art and cultural diplomacy in South AmericaM. Elizabeth Boonep. 195

Boone examines the touring exhibition of 120 paintings and 41 sculptures that the United States sent to the centenary celebrations of Argentina and Chile in 1910, and then to Uruguay in 1911. She treats it as an early case of cultural diplomacy under the Taft administration's Dollar Diplomacy. Her main evidence is a set of political cartoons from Caras y Caretas, Zig-Zag and Sucesos, which mock the American paintings and their viewers, from an Argentine mayor who discusses paintings in the terms of horse breeding to a Chilean landowner who mistakes a painting for livestock. Boone also weighs the Philadelphia jury's conservative choices, which favoured landscapes and academic nudes from the Northeast and Midwest, and the reviews by Pedro Lira and others that praised American painting as a rival to Europe. She argues that the stress on similarity avoided disputes such as the Alsop Claim and the Panama Canal. The chapter closes with works still held in Uruguayan state buildings, still performing diplomacy.

Buenos Aires 1910Santiago 1910Montevideo 1911

Roche, Maurice. Mega-Events and Modernity: Olympics and Expos in the Growth of Global Culture. London: Routledge, 2000.Asia: substantial10 chapter overviews

Overview

Mega-Events and Modernity (2000) is Roche's sociological study of the modern world's mega-events, chiefly international expos and the Olympic Games. It argues that these events shaped public culture, cultural citizenship and the inclusion or exclusion of populations from the mid-nineteenth century onwards, and it proposes a multi-perspectival method combining a dramaturgical view of the event, a political-sociological account of its production and a long-run view of modernity. Part 1 (chapters 2-4) covers expos as instruments of national and imperial cultural policy, their mass audiences and racial and gender exclusion, and the inter-war Olympics. Part 2 (chapters 5-7) covers expos and Olympics in host cities and tourism, the media and television, and global citizenship in the Olympic movement. Chapter 8 is theoretical.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia receives substantial but uneven attention, centred on Korea. The Seoul Olympics of 1988 are the main case: chapter 6 (Mega-events and media culture) gives them the longest treatment, testing Katz and Dayan's media-event theory against Larson and Park's account of the Games as political communication by a military government. Chapter 5 (Mega-events, cities and tourist culture) presents Seoul as a 'media city', and chapter 7 (Mega-events and global citizenship) cites Seoul among repressive host states. Japan appears in chapter 4 (The Olympics, internationalism and supernationalism), where the IOC's handling of the 1940 Games is narrated, and in chapter 3 (Mega-events and cultural citizenship), where Japanese and Chinese national pavilions are said to project a positive national identity. China figures in chapter 5 through the Beijing 2000 bid and in chapter 7 through human rights and doping.

Southeast Asia appears only in colonial and imperial displays. The Philippines are present in chapter 2 (Expos and cultural power), where a 47-acre Philippines site at St Louis 1904 is noted as a sign of American control, and in chapter 3 among the peoples shown in 'native village' displays. Malaya, Burma and Hong Kong appear only in the list of colonies at Wembley 1924/5. The Dutch East Indies, Indochina, Siam and Singapore are not discussed. Expos held in Asia, such as Osaka 1970 and Taejon 1993, appear only in passing.

Contents

Tables and illustrations
Preface

Roche explains that the project grew out of Sheffield's bid for the 1991 World Student Games, and that sociology colleagues found mega-events trivial. Roche argues that mega-events are real problems of the modern world, and notes that the book appeared in 2000, a year of Millennium and Expo events. The preface links the Millennium Dome to the 1951 Festival of Britain and sets Britain's and South Africa's bids beside the nation-building aims of their governments.

Acknowledgements

Roche thanks colleagues at Sheffield and elsewhere who discussed events, tourism and citizenship, and names doctoral students and conference hosts. The list of archives consulted includes the Bureau of International Expositions in Paris, the International Olympic Committee, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the National Fair Archive in Sheffield. Thanks also go to the Routledge editors and to family, and the publishers note the permissions granted for the images reproduced in the book.

1Mega-events and modernity: perspectives and themesp. 1

Roche's introduction defines mega-events and explains how the book will study them. These are large cultural, commercial and sporting occasions with mass appeal and international reach, and the book concentrates on world fairs (expos) and the Olympic Games. Roche argues that they have shaped public culture, cultural citizenship and inclusion or exclusion in modern societies. Roche proposes a multi-perspectival method that combines a dramatological view of the event, a contextual political sociology of its production and a long-run account of modernity. The chapter weighs this against rival approaches, from ethnography and textualism to economic and critical functionalism. It then previews the later chapters, and it closes by arguing that mega-events matter both for personal identity and for social structure in global society.

Paris 1900
Part 1Mega-events and the growth of international culturep. 31
2Expos and cultural power: capitalism, nationalism and imperialismp. 30

Roche reviews the international and imperial expos held between 1851 and 1939 and argues that they were major instruments of national cultural policy, through which elites expressed and reinforced capitalism, nationalism and imperialism. The chapter first tests Hobsbawm's 'invented traditions' and Bennett's 'exhibitionary complex' against the expos, and proposes a 'performance complex' in which mass participation mattered as much as display. It then traces the genre's French origins and its development in Paris, London, Philadelphia, Chicago and St Louis, drawing on attendance and profit figures. The 1851 Crystal Palace exhibition is the main international case, including its building and the 'Albertopolis' complex of museums and colleges later developed on the profits. Wembley 1924/5 is the imperial case, examined through its origins, its Pageant of Empire and its trade and emigration aims. Roche concludes that expos were recurrent forms of elite cultural policy, and leads on to the question of how mass publics consumed them.

London 1851Wembley 1924/5Paris 1889Chicago 1893
3Mega-events and cultural citizenship: consumerism, inclusion/exclusion and internationalismp. 65

Roche examines how expos reached mass publics and how far they included or excluded them, arguing that expos anticipated the touristic consumerism and urban cosmopolitanism of later popular culture. Thomas Cook's excursions to the 1851 London exhibition and the commodity displays at expos are offered as evidence. The chapter then tests inclusion against class, gender and race. It finds that expos offered conditional citizenship to the white working class, confined women largely to domestic roles, and displayed non-white peoples in 'native village' and imperial shows, most notoriously the Dahomeyan village at Chicago 1893. Philadelphia 1876, Chicago 1893 and St Louis 1904 provide much of the evidence for this. The last section moves to internationalism, tracing how expos shaped the early Olympic Games at Paris 1900, St Louis 1904 and London 1908, and how the BIE and FIFA later set up international regulation for expos and football. Roche ends by stating that the next chapter will treat the inter-war Olympics and supernationalism.

London 1851Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893Paris 1900St Louis 1904
4The Olympics, internationalism and supernationalism: international sports events and movements in the inter-war periodp. 99

Roche's chapter traces how international sport developed between the wars and how supernationalist, socialist and feminist movements shaped the Olympic movement. It starts with imperial British sport and the Empire Games, first held in Hamilton in 1930, and with Soviet mass events such as the Pre-Olympiad of 1920 and the 1928 Spartakiad, which were set against the 'bourgeois' Olympics. It then examines the socialist Workers' Olympics in Frankfurt (1925) and Vienna (1931) and the women's World Games from 1922, both presented as alternatives later absorbed into mainstream sport. The main case study is Berlin 1936: Nazi racism in German sport, the propaganda role given to Goebbels and Speer, the torch relay, and the IOC's refusal to act against boycott calls. Roche argues that the IOC's collaboration with fascism was a serious failure of its ideals, and the chapter ends by linking these inter-war rituals to the later Olympics, which Part 2 takes up.

Part 2Mega-events and the growth of global culturep. 123
5Mega-events, cities and tourist culture: Olympics and exposp. 125

Roche's chapter examines expos and Olympic Games as urban events, asking what they do to host cities' tourism, image, infrastructure and politics. It begins with the link between expos and theme parks: Disneyland and its successors are treated as permanent expos, and Zukin's comparison of Disney World with the 1939 New York fair supports the point. It then turns to post-war expos, mainly Vancouver 1986 and Seville 1992, weighing visitor figures, deficits and permanent heritage against uneven economic results. The Olympic half centres on Barcelona 1992, with figures on public investment, the Olympic village and the Montjuic stadium, and on the telecommunications build-outs that made Seoul and Barcelona 'media cities'. The final section examines bidding, tracing corruption through the 1990s bids for Sydney 2000 and Salt Lake City 2002. It closes by arguing that the urban leaderships pursuing these projects weakened local democratic accountability.

Vancouver 1986Seville 1992New York 1939
6Mega-events and media culture: sport and the Olympicsp. 159

Roche examines how television and the media shape mega-events, taking sport and the Olympics as the main case. The first section reviews three American dramatological approaches: Katz and Dayan on media events, MacAloon on the Games as a mix of festival, ritual, spectacle and game, and Real on Olympic TV as ritual and myth. The second section turns to political economy, tracing Murdoch's use of sport to build television markets in the USA, Britain and Europe, the blocked BSkyB bid for Manchester United, and the revised British list of events that must stay free to air. The chapter then studies two Games as media events. Larson and Park present Seoul 1988 as a political stage for South Korean democratisation, while the Spa team study of the Barcelona 1992 opening ceremony in twenty-four national broadcasts shows how each broadcaster reshaped the spectacle for its own audience. Roche concludes that Olympic television mixes commercial and Olympic messages in ways the IOC cannot control, and that the regulation of media sport is a contest over cultural citizenship.

Seoul 1988Barcelona 1992
7Mega-events and global citizenship: Olympic problems and responsesp. 194

Roche asks whether the Olympic movement lives up to ideals of global citizenship, and sets out four dimensions to test it: universal citizenship based on human rights, mediatised citizenship of audiences, movement citizenship of inclusion and democracy within sport, and corporate citizenship in global governance. The chapter first describes the movement's universalist ideology, the self-recruiting IOC and its growing ties with the UN, UNESCO, the ILO and the WHO. Against this it sets a record of host states with repressive governments, from Mexico 1968 to Seoul 1988, and the IOC's failure to take a firm line on China's bid. It then examines media problems, including the commercialisation of Olympic TV, the drift of rights to pay television, and the limits of internet access. Drug abuse, from East German state doping to Ben Johnson and the 1998 cases, is treated as a failure of IOC testing. The bidding corruption crisis, the Pound Inquiry and the 1999 reforms are followed by the Olympic Truce agreed with the UN. Roche concludes that the IOC's credibility remains doubtful until its reforms are rigorously enforced.

8Mega-events, identity and global society: theoretical reflectionsp. 217

Roche's concluding chapter steps back from the case studies to ask what mega-events mean for individuals and for global society. Its first half argues that expos and sport mega-events help people in late modernity resist threats to identity, using the concepts of time-structure, lived space and agency. Staging an event gives a bounded, deadline-driven project and a sense of temporal distance and place that everyday life, shaped by flows and media, tends to erode. The second half turns to meso-social processes. Drawing on Castells's network vocabulary, Roche describes mega-events as hubs and switches that link elites with mass publics and generations, and as temporary bridges between the space of flows and the space of places. Houlihan's work on sport and international politics supports a pluralist reading of sport's role in global governance. Roche concludes that mega-events matter for understanding agency, structure and continuity in modernity, and presents the chapter as a preliminary research agenda.

Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.Asia: substantial11 chapter overviews

Overview

Rydell's study examines the American world's fairs held between 1876 and 1916, from Philadelphia's Centennial to the San Francisco and San Diego expositions of 1915, and argues that they gave visitors a ritual confirmation of progress that legitimised white supremacy and the authority of corporate, political and scientific leaders. Each chapter takes one exposition or a group of them: Philadelphia, Chicago 1893, the southern fairs, Omaha, Buffalo, Saint Louis, Portland and Seattle, and San Francisco and San Diego. Midway villages, anthropology displays and federal exhibits are read as lessons in racial hierarchy and imperial expansion. The introduction sets out the argument, and the conclusion presents the fairs as tools by which the United States began to manage the world from its own imperial perspective.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a substantial strand of the book, not its centre; African Americans, Native Americans and Mexicans receive as much attention. The Philippines is the most concentrated theme: it is the central case of chapter 6, 'The Coronation of Civilization' (Saint Louis, 1904), where Igorot and Negrito villages on the Philippine Reservation are set against Scouts and Constabulary. Chapter 5 (Buffalo) and chapter 7 (Portland and Seattle) also follow Filipino villages. China and Japan recur in chapters 1, 2 and 8, most fully in chapter 2 (Chicago 1893) and chapter 8 (San Francisco and San Diego).

Asia appears as participant, as the subject of displays organised by others, and as visitors whose treatment was contested. Japan built its Ho-o-den at Chicago with Japanese workers, a Japanese delegation toured Seattle in 1909, and China's official Forbidden City was reassembled at San Francisco. Chinese villages were staged at Chicago, Omaha and New Orleans, Japanese and Chinese villages at San Francisco, and the Mysterious Asia bazaars at Saint Louis included streets in Rangoon. Chinese protests closed one concession at San Francisco, and Dosch reported that Asian exhibitors were discouraged from Portland by their treatment at Saint Louis. Rydell reads these displays as lessons in racial hierarchy rather than as Asian agency.

Contents

Acknowledgments

Rydell's acknowledgments thank the teachers and mentors who shaped the interest in American culture and fairs, from undergraduate study at Berkeley to the UCLA seminar led by Saxton, and the colleagues who read drafts. Debts are recorded to the staff of more than two dozen archives and libraries, especially the Smithsonian and the Fresno exposition collection, and to the grants and journals that supported the work. The section ends with thanks to family and a spouse.

Introduction

Rydell's introduction sets out the argument that America's world's fairs between 1876 and 1916 were 'symbolic universes' that legitimised white supremacy and the authority of corporate, political and scientific leaders. Drawing on Berger and Luckmann, and on the idea of hegemony, Rydell argues that fairs gave visitors a ritual confirmation of progress, which the planners equated with economic growth and racial hierarchy. Chicago's 1893 Columbian Exposition recurs as evidence: Henry Adams's religious reading of its dynamos, the Smithsonian's struggles to supply exhibits, and the living ethnological 'villages' that Rydell describes as honky-tonk concessions beside the amusements. The Smithsonian and anthropologists are introduced as the scientific authority that lent the fairs credibility. Rydell notes that the book concentrates on American fairs, which were part of a worldwide movement tied to imperial expansion. The introduction ends by framing the expositions as tools by which the United States began to manage the world from its own imperial perspective.

Chicago 1893
1The Centennial Exhibition, Philadelphia, 1876: The Exposition as a “Moral Influence”

This chapter examines the Centennial Exhibition held in Philadelphia in 1876 as a lesson in national values. Rydell argues that its organisers, drawn from a small circle of wealthy investors, officials and scientists, used the fair to answer the doubts left by Reconstruction and the 1873 depression, presenting America as a nation of progress and unity. Its evidence comes mainly from the planning and display: William P. Blake's classification system, which moved from raw materials to the higher achievements of intellect, and the Main Building, where exhibits were arranged by race. The Smithsonian's Indian display, assembled under Baird, Mason and Rau, presents Native Americans as a vanishing people, while black Americans are almost absent except as entertainers. The chapter also looks at the workers and miners brought in by employers, and at the Centennial City shantytown on Elm Street, which was demolished because it offered a rival to the fair's values. Rydell concludes that Welsh and the directors claimed a 'moral influence' for the exhibition, a claim that gave them grounds to speak with authority in the decades after.

Philadelphia 1876
2The Chicago World’s Columbian Exposition of 1893: “And Was Jerusalem Builded Here?”

This chapter treats the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893 as the fair in which a utopian vision of American progress was made fully explicit. Rydell argues that the neoclassical White City was matched by the Midway Plaisance, where non-white peoples were displayed as evidence of an evolutionary hierarchy, so that the two halves of the fair supported one another. Its evidence comes from the financing of the fair by Chicago businessmen, G. Brown Goode's classification of exhibits as an 'illustrated encyclopedia of civilization', the Midway villages, including the Dahomeyan and Chinese displays, and Frederic Putnam's anthropology department. The chapter also shows how black Americans were excluded or mocked, through the rejection of separate exhibits, Jubilee Day and Harper's cartoons, and how Frederick Douglass protested from the Haitian Building. It closes by tracing the fair's legacy in the Field Museum, the City Beautiful movement and later fairs, which Rydell presents as attempts to hasten the realisation of the same utopia.

Chicago 1893
3The New Orleans, Atlanta, and Nashville Expositions: New Markets, “New Negroes,” and a New South

This chapter examines the southern expositions at New Orleans (1885), Atlanta (1895) and Nashville (1897) as a regional version of the fair's ideology of progress, one that tied the New South's recovery to new markets in Latin America and Asia and to the subordination of black Americans. Rydell argues that these fairs were not simple imitations of Philadelphia and Chicago, since their directors addressed the 'Negro question' through separate Negro departments. The evidence includes Booker T. Washington's Atlanta address, the Negro buildings and the responses of black leaders, who both accepted and resisted the terms, and the Old Plantation and Midway villages that displayed Mexicans, Chinese and Native Americans. The chapter also covers Isaac Avery's campaign to win Latin American exhibitors, the railroads' and northern investors' stake in the fairs, and the Smithsonian's evolutionary displays. It concludes that the southern fairs joined race and progress in a New South ideology that prepared the way for Plessy v. Ferguson and immigration restriction, and that the Parthenon at Nashville became its lasting monument.

New Orleans 1885Atlanta 1895Nashville 1897
4The Trans-Mississippi and International Exposition, Omaha, 1898: “Concomitant to Empire”

Rydell reads the Trans-Mississippi and International Exposition of 1898 as an ideological event staged as the Spanish-American War began. He traces how Omaha's businessmen and the Knights of Ak-Sar-Ben backed the fair, and how Edward Rosewater and the Bureau of American Ethnology's James Mooney shaped its Indian Congress, a display first imagined as a vast encampment of all tribes. The main evidence is the Congress itself: its staged sham battle, the parade before President McKinley, and Mooney's complaints that the show had become a Wild West show. Midway villages of African Americans, Chinese, and Filipinos, and the Buffalo Bill day, are read as lessons in racial hierarchy and empire. The chapter closes with the fair's record attendance and the Greater America Exposition that followed the next year, which turned the exposition movement toward the colonies.

Omaha 1898
5The Pan-American Exposition, Buffalo: “Pax 1901”

Rydell argues that the Pan-American Exposition at Buffalo in 1901 presented American progress as an evolutionary story, with a color scheme and sculpture that moved from the strongest colors near the entrances to refined ivory and gold at the Electric Tower. The chapter explains how the directors, led by John Milburn and William Buchanan, reused experienced exposition makers, and how the architect John Carrère, the sculptor Karl Bitter and the painter Charles Turner gave the fair its design. Its central cases are the Ethnology Building, where artifacts were arranged in racial order, and the midway villages of Africans, African Americans, Filipinos and Mexicans. The government's Philippine collection, gathered by Frank Hilder, shows how colonial acquisitions were presented as lessons in tutelage. The chapter ends with McKinley's assassination in the Temple of Music, which Rydell reads as a test of the fair's promise of shared faith in progress.

Buffalo 1901
6The Louisiana Purchase Exposition, Saint Louis, 1904: “The Coronation of Civilization”

Rydell argues that the Louisiana Purchase Exposition of 1904 made anthropology the scientific core of a fair devoted to racial and material progress, and turned the Philippines into its central lesson. The chapter follows W J McGee, head of the Anthropology Department, from his theory of racial grades to the living ethnological exhibits, the anthropometric laboratories and the Anthropology Day contests. Its main case is the Philippine Reservation, planned by William Powell Wilson and Gustavo Niederlein with federal backing, where Igorot and Negrito villages were set against Scouts and Constabulary. When press ridicule led the government to plan clothing for the villagers, Frederick Starr argued that dress would ruin the exhibit, the Board of Lady Managers concurred, and the plan was dropped. Rydell also reads the Pike, the Japanese exhibits and the American Federation of Labor's display as lessons in comparative progress. The chapter closes by tracing how the fair's memory lingered in Missouri and how its imperial vision passed to the Pacific Northwest.

Saint Louis 1904
7The Expositions in Portland and Seattle: “To Celebrate the Past and to Exploit the Future”

Rydell argues that the Lewis and Clark Centennial in Portland (1905) and the Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition in Seattle (1909) were built to link the Pacific Northwest to Asian markets and an American commercial empire, and that organized labor contested both. The chapter traces the closed-shop dispute, the referendum drive and the open-shop hiring that led to the Labor Day protest at Woodland Park. Its evidence is the exhibits and villages: the Igorot village on Portland's Trail and Seattle's Pay Streak, the Smithsonian and War Department displays of the Pacific possessions, the Oriental Exhibits Building, and the Japanese delegation's visit to Seattle under the slogan hands across the sea. Rydell also follows the concessionaires Felder and Schneidewind and their Igorot troupe through amusement parks, where a complaint that the performers wanted to go home was answered with higher wages. The chapter ends with the fairs' legacies in Portland's Guild Lake industrial district and the University of Washington campus.

Portland 1905Seattle 1909
8The Expositions in San Francisco and San Diego: Toward the World of Tomorrow

Rydell examines the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco and the Panama-California Exposition in San Diego, both of 1915, which celebrated the opening of the Panama Canal. Rydell argues that the two fairs staged a racial history of the American West in which white conquest appeared as natural progress, and that their wealthy promoters used this message to present an orderly, racially ranked future. The chapter reconstructs the rivalry between the two cities and the federal politics that gave San Diego only a narrower recognition. Its central evidence is San Diego's physical anthropology display, assembled with Smithsonian anthropologists, whose busts and skulls ranked peoples within an evolutionary and eugenic framework. Rydell then turns to San Francisco's Race Betterment congress and to the Joy Zone and Isthmus concessions, where Mexican, Samoan, African, Chinese, Japanese and Native American villages were staged as entertainment. The chapter closes with the fairs' legacy in Balboa Park and Forest Lawn cemetery, where the vision outlived the exhibitions.

San Francisco 1915San Diego 1915
Conclusion

Rydell concludes that the expositions of 1876 to 1916 were upper-class creations, sustained by federal funds and Smithsonian expertise. Midway shows, once shunned, were brought into the main grounds by 1904, and they both entertained and legitimised an imperialist world view. Nationalism and racism, Rydell argues, blurred class divisions among whites after the railroad strikes of 1877. The fairs shaped American culture, the chapter ends, and left an enduring vision of empire.

Overview

Rydell's book examines the American world's fairs of the 1920s and 1930s, the century-of-progress expositions, and argues that they were theatres of power offering abundance and consumption within a racially exclusive social hierarchy during the Depression. He places them in continuity with the Victorian fairs, tracing ethnological villages, eugenics displays, colonial exhibitions in Europe, scientists' exhibits and African American protests from Philadelphia in 1926 through Chicago, New York, Dallas and San Francisco to Brussels in 1958. The first part, An Exhibitionary Culture, covers forerunners and eugenics exhibitions; the second, The Century-of-Progress Expositions, moves through colonial modernism, science, future-oriented displays and racial politics. A closing chapter argues that the fairs helped shore up faith in government and the economic order.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a substantial strand of the book, though the centre of gravity is the American fairs themselves. The material is concentrated in Chapter One, 'Forerunners of the Century-of-Progress Expositions', and Chapter Three, 'Coloniale Moderne'. The Philippines is the main Southeast Asian case: the 1904 St Louis Philippines Reservation is read as a display of Filipinos as commodities of American empire, Igorot and Filipino villages at Seattle and Buffalo are ethnological displays organised by others, and the American annex at the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition is set against the Filipino and Puerto Rican protests that the official display erased. French Indochina recurs through the Angkor Wat replica at Paris in 1931 and the Indochina pavilion at San Francisco in 1939, where the Dutch East Indies and Johore also had pavilions in the Pacific Basin. Living displays of Malays, Burmans and Hong Kong Chinese at Wembley in 1924, and Chinese from a village concession used to promote the Nashville fair in 1897, show Asians as displayed peoples.

Asian participation as exhibitors is marginal. Japan appears among the foreign pavilions at the 1926 Philadelphia Sesquicentennial and Japanese restaurants on the San Francisco Gayway are passing mentions. Asian visitors and Asian-held exhibitions are not discussed. The Brussels chapter and the science and African American chapters say nothing about the region. The Indian Village at Chicago in 1933 falls outside the question.

Acknowledgmentsp. ix

Rydell thanks the institutions that supported the research, among them the National Museum of American History, Montana State University and the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study, and the scholars who criticised the manuscript. He also acknowledges librarians and archivists who handled unprocessed world's fair materials, along with students and the publisher's staff. The book is dedicated to his wife, Kiki Leigh Rydell, to his daughters, and to Alex and Trudy Saxton.

Introductionp. 1

Rydell opens with the depression-era world's fairs, which drew nearly one hundred million Americans to Chicago, San Diego, Dallas, Cleveland, San Francisco and New York, and asks why people paid to visit something so ephemeral while unemployment and political instability were so severe. Expositions, he argues, had long deflected criticism of the social order, and the interwar fairs, in modernistic dress, were built to restore faith in government, business, science and intellectual leaders. Their promise was of abundance and consumption within a racially exclusive social hierarchy, which he presents as continuous with the Victorian fairs rather than a break from them. The chapters take up colonial modernism, eugenics, the scientists' campaign to popularise science, a consumption-oriented welfare state, African American resistance and the American pavilion at Brussels in 1958. Rydell concludes that the century-of-progress expositions were theatres of power that gave a depression a sense of meaning.

Part OneAn Exhibitionary Culturep. 12
OneForerunners of the Century-of-Progress Expositionsp. 15

Rydell traces the roots of the interwar fairs to the Victorian expositions from London in 1851 to San Francisco in 1915, arguing that these fairs fused a culture of abundance with a vision of empire. Exposition authorities organised themselves like corporations, ran publicity departments and turned to trained scientists to classify exhibits, and at nearly every American fair after 1893 ethnological villages placed people along a scale from savagery to civilisation. The 1904 St Louis fair, with its Philippines Reservation, is the central case, where Filipinos were displayed as commodities of the American empire. Rydell then follows the publicity machinery at Chicago in 1893 and St Louis, and the Montana state board, whose silver statue of Justice drew the state into the fair's imperial vision before the silver was melted down. The Philadelphia Commercial Museum, founded from Chicago's exhibits to promote foreign trade, is presented as a permanent fair. The last pages cover postwar plans for fairs in Philadelphia and Chicago, and the 1920s 'fitter family' displays that carried eugenics into the New York fair.

Chicago 1893St Louis 1904Philadelphia 1899
Two“Fitter Families for Future Firesides”: Eugenics Exhibitions between the Warsp. 38

Rydell shows how American eugenicists used exhibitions between the wars to turn race betterment into a popular cause. The chapter begins with the Race Betterment Foundation's booth and pageant at the 1915 San Francisco fair, then moves to the Second International Congress of Eugenics, held at the American Museum of Natural History in New York in 1921. Henry Laughlin's congress exhibits, including racial casts, pedigree charts and anthropometric instruments, went after the congress to a House committee on immigration, which Rydell treats as a direct route from display to policy. The central case is the 'Fitter Families' contest that Mary Watts and Florence Brown Sherbon began at the 1920 Kansas Free Fair, where families were examined and scored and the scorecards went to Charles Davenport. The contest spread to state and county fairs, and a mobile tent exhibit carried it further. The chapter closes with the 1932 Third Congress, the four small eugenics panels at Chicago in 1933, and the 'Typical American Families' display at the 1940 New York fair. Rydell concludes that eugenics was a subterranean strand of the exhibition culture rather than a fringe doctrine.

Part TwoThe Century-of-Progress Expositionsp. 59
ThreeColoniale Modernep. 61

Rydell argues that colonial expositions between the wars made empire look like part of modernity, a fusion he calls coloniale moderne, and that American fairs adopted it. He begins with the Marseilles colonial fair of 1922 and the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley in 1924-25, where living colonial subjects and a pageant of empire were shown, and then the 1925 Paris decorative arts fair, where French colonial pavilions were given modernistic designs. The central case is the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition, with its Angkor Wat replica and the U.S. government's prefabricated Mount Vernon, stocked with artifacts from the overseas territories. Rydell shows how protests in Puerto Rico and the Philippines were erased from the American display. The chapter then turns to Chicago's 1933 fair, which borrowed the colonial villages idea, and to San Francisco's 1939 Golden Gate exposition, where Pacific Basin pavilions and a Latin American court presented the West as a market for American goods. Rydell concludes that these fairs tied American expansion to the imperial policies of European powers.

Marseilles 1922London 1924Paris 1925Paris 1931Chicago 1933San Francisco 1939
FourThe Empire of Sciencep. 92

Rydell argues that American scientists used the Chicago 1933-34 and New York 1939-40 fairs to present scientific progress as the work of corporations, a creed the organizers called scientific idealism. The chapter begins with the link between Chicago's organizers and the National Research Council, whose Science Advisory Committee, led by Frank Jewett, shaped the fair's philosophy. It then looks at the Hall of Science, where a periodic table, an oil refinery and the Transparent Man presented science as a modern faith, and at social-science exhibits such as an Indian Village beside a replica Mayan temple. For New York, Rydell shows how industrial exhibitors took over science displays from academic scientists, how Gerald Wendt's advisory committee won a converted building for science, and how Wendt's book Science for the World of Tomorrow called for a Henry Ford for the American home. The chapter concludes that these scientists gave the corporation-run state intellectual support into the postwar period, and left Americans poorly prepared for the nuclear age.

Chicago 1933New York 1939
FiveFuture Perfectp. 115

Rydell argues that the century-of-progress fairs were ideological constructs, funded by corporate capital, that presented corporate power and rational planning as the route out of the Depression. The chapter begins with the financing of the 1933-34 Chicago fair by the Dawes brothers and their guarantors, and with the modernistic architecture and corporate pavilions, such as General Foods and Bell Telephone, that told visitors to modernize. It then moves to San Francisco's Pacific Basin pavilions and Vacationland exhibits, which sold the American West as a leisure economy. The main case is New York's 1939-40 fair, with Democracity and Norman Bel Geddes's General Motors Futurama, which Rydell reads as advertising for publicly financed superhighways. Striptease shows such as the Crystal Lassies are linked to the same visions of the future. The chapter closes with Roosevelt's endorsement of the fairs and with African American challenges to their racial order.

Chicago 1933San Francisco 1939New York 1939
SixAfrican Americans in the World of Tomorrowp. 157

Rydell examines how African Americans tried to turn the white supremacist world's fairs of the 1920s and 1930s into arenas for social change. He argues that each struggle over representation reflected shifting class and political alignments within the African-American community, as older Republican elites gave way to labour organisers and radical intellectuals. The chapter moves through five fairs: Philadelphia's 1926 Sesquicentennial, where A. Philip Randolph gave an opening-day address amid protests over a planned Ku Klux Klan presence; Chicago's 1933-34 Century of Progress, where the NAACP and a state anti-discrimination law confronted concessionaires; Dallas's 1936 Texas Centennial, where a federally funded Hall of Negro Life embodied an accommodationist compromise and was later demolished; New York's 1939-40 World's Fair, where picket lines met official denials of discrimination; and the 1940 Chicago American Negro Exposition, which federal agencies helped stage. Evidence comes from newspapers, official correspondence and interviews. Rydell concludes that the fairs were battlegrounds rather than mere showcases, though sponsors repeatedly steered reform towards accommodation.

Philadelphia 1926Chicago 1933Dallas 1936New York 1939Chicago 1940
SevenThe New Day Dawns: The American Pavilion at the 1958 Brussels World’s Fairp. 193

Rydell traces how the American Pavilion at the 1958 Brussels world's fair was planned as a cold war statement. He argues that government planners, drawing on business leaders, media executives, labour leaders and an MIT symposium, presented America as a 'society in ferment' while masking a preoccupation with national security. The chapter follows the pavilion's design by Edward Stone, the congressional fight over funding after Sputnik, and the exhibits themselves: the Face of America display, voting machines turned into cultural vending machines, the Circarama film, and the Unfinished Work exhibit on social problems, which was altered after objections from the US Information Agency. It also examines intelligence gathering at the site and the security vetting of performers. Rydell concludes that by fusing consumerism with science and leisure, the pavilion carried the mass-consumption vision of the century-of-progress fairs into postwar Europe and America.

Brussels 1958
Conclusionp. 213

Rydell's conclusion argues that the century-of-progress expositions of the 1930s were calculated responses to the Depression, the Bolshevik Revolution and industrial strikes, and that their blueprints for modernisation were tied to corporate, government and scientific authority. He contrasts them with the Victorian fairs, noting that entertainment became central to the modernising strategies of promoters, so that the Midway had triumphed over the White City by 1958. Although African-American and other dissenting voices were real, Rydell argues that those who controlled the expositions held the power to define social reality. Scientists, now mostly tied to corporate laboratories, lent legitimacy to the claim that business and government could plan the nation's future. The fairs thus helped shore up faith in government and the economic order. The closing paragraph notes that white supremacy, women's subordinate roles and American imperial ambitions survived in the Brussels pavilion, even though the modernising scaffolding of the 1930s had been taken down.

Rydell, Robert W., John E. Findling and Kimberly D. Pelle. Fair America: World’s Fairs in the United States. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 2000.Asia: substantial7 chapter overviews

Overview

Rydell, Findling and Pelle write the history of world's fairs held in the United States, from the Crystal Palace in London in 1851 and Philadelphia in 1876 to the New York and San Francisco fairs of 1939-40, the postwar fairs and a closing look at Seville in 1992 and Hannover in 2000. Their argument is that American fairs carried the political reconstruction of the nation after the Civil War into culture, and that business elites used them to promote overseas expansion and racial hierarchy as remedies for class conflict. The book runs in six chapters, from industrial fairs of 1876-97 and imperial fairs of 1898-1915 through interwar and atomic-age fairs to a conclusion on whether fairs can help the species survive.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

Asia is a substantial but uneven theme, concentrated in Chapter 2, 'Fairs of the Imperial Era', where the Philippines is the central case. A Philippine Reservation at Buffalo in 1901, with Negrito and Igorot villages and Philippine Scouts, presented the islands as stages of American uplift. The federally backed Filipino village at St. Louis in 1904, the Igorot village at Portland in 1905 and the Filipino building at Seattle in 1909 followed. These were displays of Filipinos organised by American officials, promoters and anthropologists, not Filipino participation. China appears in a Chinese Village at Omaha in 1898, which the authors call little more than a souvenir shop, and in the Chinese village at San Francisco in 1915, which framed China as ripe for American investment. Japan appears through the Fair Japan concession at St. Louis, with its Ainu display, and through Japanese exhibits sent to Portland, which were hampered by reported discrimination against Asians at St. Louis.

Elsewhere coverage is slight. The interwar chapter notes the Asian ornamental elements and Pacific Basin focus of San Francisco's 1939-40 fair, with elephant towers modelled on Cambodia's Angkor Wat. The atomic-age chapter mentions exhibits from newly independent Asian nations at New York in 1964-65, China's relics at Knoxville in 1982 and Korea at Taejon in 1993. The introduction and conclusion name Osaka 1970 and Aichi 2005 as later Japanese fairs. No passage mentions Thailand, Indochina or the Dutch East Indies.

Acknowledgmentsp. ix

The acknowledgments thank the collectors, documentary makers and librarians whose work made the book possible, singling out the interlibrary loan staff at Montana State and Indiana University Southeast, the Smithsonian Institution Libraries, and the Henry Madden Library at California State University, Fresno. They also thank Mark Hirsch of the Smithsonian Institution Press, Ruth Thomson for shaping the prose into a single voice, and three reviewers, Thomas J. Schlereth, Eric J. Sandeen and Keith Walden.

Introduction

The introduction presents world's fairs as a formative part of modern life, drawing around 100 million visitors to American fairs between 1876 and the First World War and shaping amusement parks, technologies and city design. It then sorts the scholarship on fairs into six schools, from producer-centred readings of cultural hegemony and audience-centred accounts of how visitors made their own meanings, to counter-hegemonic studies of the people displayed, Benedict's potlatch model with Susman's liminality, documentary histories of technology, and the collectors' tradition. Rydell, Findling and Pelle argue that American fairs carried the political reconstruction of the nation after the Civil War into culture, moving from the Crystal Palace model through Philadelphia in 1876 to Chicago in 1893 and Atlanta in 1895, and promoting overseas expansion and racial hierarchy as remedies for class conflict. The authors close by asking whether fairs, now tied to transnational corporations, will address the nuclear and ecological crises of the present or leave us whistling in the dark.

London 1851Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893Atlanta 1895
1Fairs in the Age of Industrialism’s Advance

Rydell, Findling and Pelle trace the world's fair from London's Crystal Palace of 1851, which drew over six million visitors and set the model for later fairs, to the American fairs of the industrial era. Their main cases are the failed New York Crystal Palace of 1853, the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial, where foreign exhibits were arranged by race and Smithsonian displays cast Native Americans as savage counterparts to civilised whites, and a run of southern fairs in Atlanta, New Orleans and Nashville that sought industrial and export markets. Chicago's 1893 Columbian Exposition receives the fullest treatment: its planning and White City design, the Midway's commercial exoticism, the anthropology displays of Putnam and Boas, and the Colored People's Day that Douglass and Ida B. Wells contested. The authors argue that fairs from 1876 to 1897 were run by business elites to persuade middle-class visitors of Anglo-Saxon superiority. The chapter ends with the turn after 1898, when the acquisition of an overseas empire gave fairs a new imperial purpose.

London 1851New York 1853Philadelphia 1876Atlanta 1881New Orleans 1885Chicago 1893Atlanta 1895Nashville 1897San Francisco 1894
2Fairs of the Imperial Erap. 45

Rydell, Findling and Pelle examine how American fairs from 1898 to 1915 presented the new overseas empire as natural and the racial hierarchy that justified it. They begin with the Trans-Mississippi Exposition in Omaha, where an Indian Congress, staged battles and an Old Plantation Village taught visitors about conquest and slavery, and move to Buffalo in 1901, where a color scheme ranked races from dark to light and a Filipino village cast American rule as uplift. St. Louis in 1904 receives the most space, for its anthropology displays and the Olympic events held alongside the fair. The authors then cover the Portland and Seattle fairs, which relied on Igorot and Eskimo villages, and the 1915 fairs in San Francisco, with its eugenics congresses, and San Diego, which reinvented the city's Spanish past and displayed human evolution. The evidence comes from fair records, newspapers and visitors' recollections. The chapter argues that these fairs were designed to show the desirability of colonialism and to justify racial hierarchy, and it closes by noting that the war which followed would reshape the next generation of fairs.

Omaha 1898Buffalo 1901St. Louis 1904Portland 1905Seattle 1909San Francisco 1915San Diego 1915
3Fairs between the World Warsp. 72

Rydell, Findling and Pelle argue that fairs between the world wars turned to science, corporate pavilions and the Depression economy, and that they kept African Americans at the margins. The chapter opens with the 1920s boom and Philadelphia's Sesqui-Centennial of 1926, a historical fair that opened unfinished in the rain, and with Long Beach's 1928 fair, built around a North African theme. Its central case is Chicago's Century of Progress of 1933-34, where modernist buildings, Sally Rand's fan dance and a Hall of Science drew crowds, while demeaning attractions and a poorly attended Negro Day marked its treatment of black visitors. The authors then cover San Diego in 1935-36, the regional fairs in Dallas and Cleveland in 1936, where the Dallas Hall of Negro Life was hidden behind shrubbery, and the New York and Golden Gate fairs of 1939-40, with General Motors' Futurama and the Trylon and Perisphere. The evidence comes from fair publicity, press reports and official histories. The chapter concludes that these fairs offered hope in hard times, and suggests that they may help explain why the United States avoided political revolution in the 1930s.

Philadelphia 1926Long Beach 1928Chicago 1933-34San Diego 1935-36Dallas 1936Cleveland 1936-37New York 1939-40San Francisco 1939-40
4Fairs in the Atomic Agep. 100

Rydell, Findling and Pelle follow fairs from the Cold War decades onward, when the medium shifted toward corporate sponsorship, civil rights protest and smaller host cities. The chapter begins with Brussels in 1958, where the Soviet and American pavilions staged a Cold War contest, and then treats Seattle's Century 21 of 1962, a science fair partly prompted by Sputnik, with its Space Needle and competing religious and science pavilions. Its central case is the New York World's Fair of 1964-65, whose poor attendance, finances and civil rights protests explain its failure. Shorter sections cover Alaska '67, HemisFair in San Antonio in 1968, Expo '74 in Spokane, Knoxville's energy fair of 1982 and the New Orleans fair of 1984, which the authors call a disaster from start to finish. The chapter also traces the planned Chicago fair of 1992, which collapsed after public opposition and the withdrawal of state funding. The evidence comes mainly from press coverage and critics. The chapter argues that corporations and smaller cities increasingly carried fairs, and it ends by noting that after New Orleans few American cities pursued a world's fair.

Seattle 1962New York 1964-65San Antonio 1968Spokane 1974Knoxville 1982New Orleans 1984Chicago 1992
Cultural Dinosaurs? World’s Fairs and the Survival of the Speciesp. 131

Rydell, Findling and Pelle use this conclusion to ask whether the cultural armor that world's fairs have built will help the human species survive, when fairs themselves may look like cultural dinosaurs. They argue that since 1851 fairs have manufactured consent for national and imperial policy, from Colt's revolver at London's Crystal Palace, which carried an allegory of imperial conquest, to the cold war and the neoimperialism of the 1920s and 1930s. The authors trace a faith in technology as the path to utopia through Chicago in 1893 and 1933-34, the New York fair of 1939-40 and its Futurama exhibit, and the nuclear-age fairs of the 1950s and 1960s. They note the growing power of corporations at Seville in 1992 and then turn to Hannover's Expo 2000, whose sustainability theme they doubt can escape the ideology of earlier fairs. They conclude that the armor fairs have built may give a false sense of security.

Samuel, Lawrence R. The End of the Innocence: The 1964–1965 New York World’s Fair. Syracuse: Syracuse University Press, 2007.Asia: substantial8 chapter overviews

Overview

Samuel's book is a history of the 1964–65 New York World's Fair, from Robert Kopple's 1958 proposal through the planning under Robert Moses, the two seasons of 1964 and 1965, and the sale of the pavilions afterwards. Its argument is that the Fair's theme of 'peace through understanding' was contradicted by its practice: commercial sponsors shaped nearly every pavilion, civil rights and Vietnam protests intruded on the grounds, and the corporation's finances collapsed. The book has two parts, 'Peace Through Understanding' (chapters 1 to 3, the planning and the two seasons) and 'Tomorrow Begins Today' (chapters 4 to 6, corporate exhibits, the International Area and science), then a conclusion on the Fair's popular memory.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia receive substantial attention, mostly as exhibitors and sights at the Fair. The densest treatment is Chapter 5, Global Holiday, on the foreign pavilions: Japan's Toyota and Datsun cars and Sony electronics, the Shikoku artisans who built a Japanese castle and clashed with American union rules, the hostesses at the Japanese, Korean and Indonesian restaurants (Sukarno chose the Indonesian staff), the Indonesian pavilion's withdrawal for 1965 over Malaysia, Nationalist China's 370 products, and the exclusion of Communist China. Elsewhere the region appears in chapters on the Fair's operations and afterlife: Chapter 2 on the Chun King Chinese Inn and on pilferage from the Hong Kong and Japanese pavilions, Chapter 3 on the auction of Philippine wood panels and the removal of Japan's stone wall and Thailand's shrine, Chapter 4 on Thai and Philippine goods and Japanese hostesses, and Chapter 6 on the Japanese pavilion's Fujitsu computer.

The region is treated from outside and mostly as commerce and display, not through the politics of Asian participation. Vietnam and Southeast Asia appear in the introduction only as the war behind the Fair's politics. South Korean workers who stayed past their visas get a short case in Chapter 5, and Asian Americans in Flushing are noted at the end of Chapter 6. India gets comparable space through its essay contest, a contrast here.

Illustrations
Acknowledgments
Introduction

Samuel argues that the 1964-65 New York World's Fair, dismissed as a failure, is better remembered for its optimism. The introduction sets the fair against the civil rights struggle, the Vietnam War and the 1965 counterculture, arguing that its conservatism was a key to its appeal. It then outlines the book's chronological and thematic parts and its period sources and Cotter's photographs. It ends with the hope that the book will preserve the fair's memory.

New York 1964Brussels 1958Seattle 1962
PART ONEPeace Through Understanding
1The Greatest Event in History

Samuel traces how the 1964–65 New York World's Fair was conceived and built, from Robert Kopple's 1958 proposal that a fair could teach children about other nations to the opening day in April 1964. The chapter centres on Robert Moses, installed as the corporation's president in 1960, and on the decisions that shaped the event: its finances and forecast attendance, the choice to let exhibitors design their own pavilions on the 1939 grid, the Unisphere, the highway and transit programme, and the ban on a midway. Samuel shows how the entertainment and religious pavilions were policed for taste, and how hiring disputes, school ticket prices and planned civil rights protests exposed the gap between the Fair's theme of 'peace through understanding' and its practice. The chapter closes on the opening-day parade and speeches, as the Fair opened amid political conflict and high expectations.

New York 1964New York 1939Seattle 1962
2Heigh Ho, Ho Hum

Samuel follows the Fair's first season, from its opening day on 22 April 1964 to its closing in October. The chapter's main case is opening day, when civil rights protesters drowned out President Johnson's speech and CORE's planned stall-in on the highways fizzled, and it follows the legal fights over picketing that came after. The rest of the season is treated as a sequence of problems: architecture that critics called 'Motleyland, USA', unionised maintenance costs, theft and mishaps, the failing Lake Amusement Area, the closure of weaker state pavilions and restaurants, and the religious pavilions and the Jordanian mural dispute. Attendance is set against Moses's forecasts and his attacks on the press. Samuel ends with the closing day and the first season's deficit, and with a student essay contest that offers a more hopeful reading of the Fair's purpose.

New York 1964
3Second Time Around

Samuel covers the Fair's second and final season, from the winter of 1964–65 to its closing in October 1965, when the corporation's finances were exposed as insolvent. The chapter argues that the WFC tried to revive attendance with a new film, a $2.50 adult price, reworked exhibits and discotheques in the pavilions, while cutting staff. Its main evidence is the audit fight between Moses, Beame, the bankers and Mayor Wagner, the unpaid $24 million owed to the city, and the rejected night-time fare. Samuel then turns to the sale and demolition of the pavilions, the survival of the Unisphere and the Spanish Pavilion, and Moses's plan to use Triborough funds for a Queens park. It ends with the final attendance of 51.6 million and the New York Times's view that the Fair's memories would outlast its recriminations.

New York 1964
PART TWOTomorrow Begins Today
4The House of Good Taste

Samuel argues that the 1964–65 New York World's Fair was, above all, a trade show in which corporate sponsors shaped nearly every part of the grounds. The chapter draws mainly on contemporary press criticism, from the Nation, Time and the New York Times, to show how commerce set the tone of the Pool of Industry, the executive lounges and the corporate pavilions. It then works through General Motors' Futurama, Ford's Magic Skyway, Disney's animatronics and the Better Living Center, with its Clairol, Simmons and Borden exhibits, before turning to the model homes of the House of Good Taste and the Underground World Home. Its conclusion is that exhibitors spent far more than they had budgeted, and that many decided fairs were no longer worth the investment, though the brand loyalties they built lasted for decades.

New York 1964New York 1939
5Global Holiday

Samuel examines the International Area and the Federal and State Area of the 1964–65 New York World's Fair and asks how far they delivered the Fair's promise of peace through understanding. The chapter begins with the American pavilions, including the Federal Pavilion's Hall of Presidents, the state pavilions and New York's own pavilions, before turning to the foreign ones. Its central story is the diplomatic campaign to recruit nations, which it follows through the disputes over Soviet, Italian and French participation and the Vatican's loan of Michelangelo's Pietà. Evidence comes from the pavilions' food, dance and hosting, the Japanese exhibits, the Burundian and South African dancers, and the Indian essay contest. Samuel concludes that the International Area mixed real cultural exchange with commercial promotion, and that the Fair's lasting legacy lay in what visitors came to think about the world.

New York 1964
6Sermons from Science

Samuel examines how science and technology were put on display at the 1964–65 New York World's Fair, where exhibitors offered what one called 'sermons of science' to millions of visitors. The chapter moves through the fair's exhibits by sector. It starts with the Hall of Science, whose future as a permanent museum was disputed, and its Atomic Energy Commission display 'Atomsville, USA' for children. It then covers chemical and plastics firms, notably Du Pont's musical revue Wonderful World of Chemistry, energy and communications exhibits such as General Electric's Progressland with its 'Fusion on Earth' show and Bell's Picturephone, transport and space displays from Greyhound and Sinclair to NASA's U.S. Space Park, IBM's computer pavilion, and General Motors' Futurama. Samuel's main point is that corporations used these exhibits to promote a better future, often ignoring its costs. The chapter ends with the Hall of Science's later history, a museum far smaller than its planners wanted, and the park that replaced the fairground.

New York 1964-65
Conclusion

Samuel's conclusion weighs the 1964–65 New York World's Fair's poor reputation against its popular success. It argues that Robert Moses, whose career was already damaged, achieved much of his original vision by turning the Flushing Meadows valley of ashes into a large public park. Samuel contrasts the fair's official memory, a business and political failure, with its popular memory: fifty-two million visitors who found it enjoyable and, for many children and teenagers, formative. He presents it as the most attended American world's fair, and as a celebration of what Henry Luce had called 'the American century'. The main criticism is that the fair excluded popular music, youth culture and African American expression, so it missed a chance to educate visitors about the wider world. The chapter ends by describing the fair as the end of postwar innocence, with a different chapter in American history to follow.
