Shepherdson-Scott, Kari. “Conflicting Politics and Contesting Borders: Exhibiting (Japanese) Manchuria at the Chicago World’s Fair, 1933–34.” Journal article.Asia: central5 chapter overviews

Overview

Shepherdson-Scott examines the Manchuria pavilion that the South Manchuria Railway Company and the Manchukuo government sponsored at Chicago's A Century of Progress fair in 1933 and 1934, months after Manchukuo was founded and Japan left the League of Nations. The argument is that this small building, which drew about two percent of fairgoers, was a diplomatic instrument aimed at American opinion, and that Mantetsu let the exhibit present Manchuria as an economic project rather than a political one. The paper also treats the American-sponsored Golden Temple of Jehol, whose site and authenticity contested the pavilion's maps, which placed the recently occupied province of Jehol inside Manchukuo. It concludes that the fair never sold a single idea of Manchuria.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

Manchuria is the subject of the whole article, so East Asia is central, but the coverage is confined to a few states. Japan is the organiser: the government, the Kwantung Army, Mantetsu and the exhibition committees shape the pavilion, which chapter 2 reads against Japan's own Kyoto Manchuria pavilion of 1915 and the Qing-inspired architecture it dropped. Manchukuo is treated as a new state whose sovereignty the exhibit had to perform. China enters as the party whose planned display prompted Japan to participate, and chapter 3 is concentrated on the Golden Temple of Jehol, a replica built in Beijing by Chinese craftsmen and sited beside the China and Japan exhibits. Mongolia appears through Jehol and the Sino-Mongolian culture Bendix claimed to conserve. Korea appears only as a Japanese colony shown on Mantetsu's map, its border with Manchukuo blurred.

Southeast Asia is absent. None of its countries, colonies or peoples is named in the text, and it discusses no exhibition held in Southeast Asia. Its Asian comparisons are confined to Japan, China, Korea and Manchuria, and the wider 'Asia' language is used for the Japanese imperial project in Northeast Asia.

Contents

Introductionp. 539

Shepherdson-Scott introduces a small Manchuria pavilion at Chicago's 1933-34 fair, A Century of Progress, built on the Japanese exhibition grounds months after the Kwantung Army had created Manchukuo and Japan had left the League of Nations. The argument is that this modest building, which drew only about two percent of fairgoers, carried great diplomatic weight in a bid to sway American opinion. The paper traces how the Japanese government and army, the Manchukuo government and the South Manchuria Railway Company (Mantetsu) shaped the pavilion's sponsorship and name, and how Mantetsu's role let the exhibit present Manchuria as an economic project rather than a political one. The introduction then previews the paper's three parts: the building and its displays, the Japanese bargaining over how Manchuria should appear, and the American-sponsored Golden Temple of Jehol, which contested Manchukuo's borders.

Chicago 1933
MANCHUKUO: CHILD OF CONFLICTp. 542

Shepherdson-Scott sets the Manchuria pavilion against the diplomatic crisis of 1931 to 1933. The chapter reviews the Mukden Incident, the founding of Manchukuo in February 1932, the Stimson Doctrine, the Lytton Commission's report and Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations, and shows that few powers had recognized the new state by the time the fair opened in May 1933. It then turns to the decisions behind the exhibit. Japan had first declined to exhibit, changed course when China planned a display, and saw a film on Manchukuo rejected for American screening. Mantetsu and the Manchukuo government funded the pavilion, which was named the South Manchuria Railway Building and attached to the Japan pavilion. Shepherdson-Scott describes Mantetsu's role as a masterstroke: as the company that dominated the region, it let the exhibit promote development and Open Door trade without foregrounding the new state's sovereignty.

Chicago 1933
SELLING JAPANESE MANCHURIAp. 546

Shepherdson-Scott examines how the pavilion's architecture and displays presented a Japanese-led Manchuria to American visitors. The building shared the wood cladding and green tile roof of the Japan pavilion but dropped its karahafu gables and continental motifs, distancing Manchuria from China in a way that contrasts with the Qing-inspired Manchuria pavilion shown at Kyoto in 1915. Inside, a life-size diorama of a Manchu family, with Chinese calligraphy on the wall, casts Japan as the paternal guide, since few Americans could read the inscription. Paintings of Mukden and Dalian 'before and after' and a large relief map of Manchuria with Jehol inside its borders show development as already completed under Japanese control. Shepherdson-Scott argues that the displays presented Japan as the determined facilitator of Manchurian modernization and claimed Jehol for Manchukuo, leaving little room for American fantasies of development. Mantetsu pamphlets and Kawakami's Open Door arguments back this reading.

Chicago 1933
CONTESTED BOUNDARIES: THE GOLDEN TEMPLE OF JEHOLp. 557

Shepherdson-Scott turns to the Golden Temple of Jehol, a replica of the Potala of Jehol sponsored by the Chicago industrialist Vincent Bendix and placed where the roads to the Japan and Chinese exhibits met. Built in Beijing by Chinese craftsmen, with plans prepared by the architect W. H. Liang on the advice of the explorer Sven Hedin, the temple took on an aura of authenticity that the fair exploited. Its gilded interior made it one of the premier attractions, and the official guidebook gave it far more pages than the Manchuria pavilion. Shepherdson-Scott argues that Bendix cast himself as a conservator of Sino-Mongolian culture, challenging Japan's claim to be the patriarchal guide of East Asia. The temple's location and its politics, sharpened by the Kwantung Army's occupation of Jehol in May 1933, contested the borders that the Manchuria displays had drawn. The section ends by noting that the official View Book of the fair removed the Manchuria exhibit altogether.

Chicago 1933
CONCLUSIONp. 561

Shepherdson-Scott concludes that the Manchuria exhibits could not sell a single, settled idea of Manchuria at Chicago in 1933. The official literature never used the name Manchukuo, and the Japanese displays were undermined by the American-sponsored Golden Temple of Jehol and by the fair's own catalogues. The geopolitical idea of Manchuria was therefore fluid, held between multiple perspectives and interests in Chicago and beyond.

Chicago 1933
List of Referencesp. 562
Thomas, Nicholas. Entangled Objects: Exchange, Material Culture, and Colonialism in the Pacific. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1991.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Thomas's Entangled Objects argues against Marcel Mauss's theory of the gift and against the opposition between gifts and commodities, which it says should be detached from the split between European and indigenous societies. Its claim is that objects are what exchange and colonial contact have made them, not what their makers intended. The scope is the Pacific, above all Fiji, with the Marquesas, Niue, the western Solomons and Massim exchange, and the period from Cook's voyages to the contemporary Fijian village. After an introduction, five chapters cover anthropological exchange theory, Pacific exchange systems, indigenous appropriation of European goods, European collecting of Pacific objects, and gift exchange in present-day Fiji. The fairs at Sydney in 1879 and Melbourne in 1880 are treated briefly within the collecting chapter.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are slight in this work and appear almost only in passing. The Introduction quotes a missionary's remark that Indians, like the Chinese, prized their own goods over European ones, and Thomas answers it through Forster. Chapter 3 names Canton and Manila as the markets for beche-de-mer and tortoiseshell that ships carried through Fiji, which is trade, not display. In Chapter 4 the catalogue of the Missionary Museum lists idols from China and India among other objects, and a Fijian curiosity list includes a 'Malay war mask and creese'. Javanese objects appear in Chapter 4 as an example of how things change meaning, and Geertz's Balinese negara is discussed in Chapter 1 as an ethnographic case. Indonesia and India appear in the Introduction as places that anthropology has treated as authentic and stable, and Chapter 5 cites East Asian manufacturing against the view that Asian consumer goods show the appeal of Western ones. The book discusses no Asian pavilion, no colonial display of Asian people, no Asian visitor and no exhibition held in Asia. Indian caste and cowrie money appear only as contrast.

Contents

Maps
Illustrations
Acknowledgmentsp. xi

Thomas thanks the people, institutions and readers who helped with the book. The acknowledgments state its aim: to take apart Marcel Mauss's theory of the gift and to study exchange through colonial histories and the cultural constitution of objects. They credit fieldwork in Fiji in 1988, the funders who supported it, and the critics who shaped the argument. The final thanks go to the Suguvanua family of Korolevu, Navosa, who adopted the author.

Introductionp. 1

Thomas opens with a missionary's 1800 remark that Indians ignored European furniture and utensils, and with Forster's reply that poverty, hostility and climate explained this, not custom. The book extends Forster's critique to anthropology's 'discourse of alterity' and its denial of colonial history. It argues that the gift and commodity opposition should be detached from the split between European and indigenous societies, and that objects are what they have become rather than what they were made to be.

1Objects, Exchange, Anthropologyp. 7

Thomas reviews how exchange theory has treated gifts and commodities, beginning with Frazer's questionnaire and its silent-film image of barter, then Malinowski's kula, which Thomas argues was presented as purely ceremonial and cut off from barter. The main argument engages Mauss and the work built on him: Gregory's contrast between gifts that create indebtedness between people and commodities that create equivalence between strangers, Weiner's inalienable wealth, Appadurai's social lives of things, and Miller's objectification. Thomas keeps the gift and commodity distinction at an abstract level but insists it must be tied to particular economies. The evidence is a wedding ring passed from mother to daughter, a Tubetube kitomwa, and the sentimental and historical associations that can override systemic value. The chapter ends by calling the gift a foil for differences rather than an ideal type.

2The Permutations of Debt: Exchange Systems in the Pacificp. 35

Thomas argues that Pacific exchange regimes differed in how they converted things, persons and debts, and that these differences shaped the conditions for colonial encounters. The cases are Fiji, the early Marquesas, the New Georgia system of the western Solomons and Massim exchange. In Fiji, solevu presentations of valuables create and discharge debts of relatedness, and services become debts repaid in other forms. In the Marquesas, feasting is a competitive matching of food with food. The myth of Tabua, who obtains a wife with whale teeth, is read as showing that tabua were meant to be alienated and carry no histories. Thomas also argues against Strathern's claim that Melanesian work cannot be alienated and against the Maussian model of the gift. The chapter closes by stressing that these systems had their own histories, including Tongan contact in Fiji, and that the past remains partly unknowable.

3The Indigenous Appropriation of European Thingsp. 83

Thomas argues against the story, told in Western liberal writing and in some indigenous histories, that European goods drew Pacific peoples into dependence through barter. He treats objects as culturally mutable: an axe or a musket gained its value from local practice and from ideas about the foreign visitors who brought it. Three cases carry the argument. On Niue, islanders traded weapons for knives and fishhooks while keeping women out of exchange and resisting prolonged contact. In the Marquesas, pigs were too valuable to sell until David Porter's intervention in 1813 made guns the prized trade item and tied local prestige to his alliance. In Fiji, whale teeth moved through chiefly ceremony and marriage politics, and trade adjusted existing polities rather than overturning them. The chapter concludes that precolonial systems shaped how later colonial histories unfolded, and that foreign goods never simply carried their makers' meanings.

4The European Appropriation of Indigenous Thingsp. 125

Thomas turns from indigenous appropriation to European collecting, from Cook's voyages to the early twentieth century. Sailors and naturalists bought curiosities, and observers called objects curious without judging them, a vagueness Thomas links to the absence of any developed anthropological language of material culture. Later collectors gave objects narrative weight: Keate's Pelew bowl stood for a king's generosity, missionaries displayed burned idols as proof of conversion, and settlers in Fiji treated clubs and cannibal forks as evidence of murder. Anatole Von Hugel's systematic collecting and Governor Gordon's display of clubs and bowls at Government House in Levuka ordered Fijian culture into a totality for the colonial state. Fijian exhibits at Sydney 1879 and Melbourne 1880 showed craft with few weapons. The chapter ends with Frank Hurley's Papuan collecting, which it reads as a denial of the people who made the objects, and concludes that both sides reworked the meanings of things.

Sydney 1879Melbourne 1880
5The Discovery of the Gift: Exchange and Identity in the Contemporary Pacificp. 185

Thomas examines gift exchange and objects in colonial and postcolonial Oceania, centring on rural Fiji. Its main case is the solevu and marriage presentations of Fijian villages, where mats, drums of kerosene, cattle and whale teeth (tabua) are given in quantities that men describe as the price of the bride, while women explain the same exchanges through the sacredness of women. Thomas argues that these forms are not timeless but have been reshaped by colonial trade, wage labour and cash cropping, so that Fijians now set a way of the land against a way of money and present custom as a moral alternative to commerce. Comparative material comes from Kahn's account of Wamira taro exchange and Linnekin's work on Hawaii. The closing Discoveries section draws these strands together: gift and commodity cannot be fitted into one model, and the colonial encounter made Pacific cultures explicit in oppositional ways. It ends by describing people and objects as entangled in unstable outcomes that run beyond what either side expects.

Notesp. 211
Indexp. 257
Weimann, Jeanne Madeline. The Fair Women: The Story of the Woman’s Building, World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893. Chicago: Academy Chicago, 1981.Asia: occasional24 chapter overviews

Overview

Weimann's study recounts the Woman's Building at the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 in Chicago, and the Board of Lady Managers that ran it under Bertha Palmer. Its argument is that the building was a real achievement for women but a constrained one: Congress created the Board with almost no defined duties, it depended on male commissioners and the Fair's architects, and it was split between clubwomen, suffragists and class and sectional loyalties. The book moves in rough chronological order, from the Philadelphia Centennial of 1876 and Chicago's bid for the Fair, through the Board's quarrels, its building, art, library, congresses and exhibits, to the aftermath of 1893 and later women's buildings up to Chicago in 1933. Its scope is American women's organised work at one fair, with the wider world entering through foreign commissions and exhibits.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia enter the book mainly as part of the Board's foreign work, and the coverage is occasional and scattered. It is concentrated in Chapter VII, 'Circling the Globe', and Chapter XI, 'Women in the White City'. In Chapter VII, Japan's women's committee is described as formed under the Empress, who paid for it, while China's participation fails: Palmer's hope for a semi-official Chinese women's committee, with Lord Li's wife in charge, comes to nothing, and only a few embroideries and weavings arrive without a representative. Chapter XI describes the Japanese exhibit, funded by the Empress and run by Princess Yasu Mori, with rooms furnished by forty-four women artisans, a Japanese Parlor filled by the commissioner, and the Siamese pavilion, a reproduction of a Buddhist temple with heirlooms of the Queen of Siam. Ceylon appears alongside as a contrast.

Elsewhere Asia is passing material: Siamese cradles in the Children's Building nursery (Chapter XIII), Japanese and Chinese embroidery praised by the Committee on Awards (Chapter XV), the Japanese book Nippon Fajin and Japan's statistics in the library (Chapter XIV), the Siamese queen's album and the Siamese commissioner's wife (Chapter XXI), and a Japanese temperance bell (Chapter XIX). Missionary societies in the Organizations room are said to uplift the Chinese and Japanese, which the book does not examine. Asian women are almost never voices in the book, and colonial display of Southeast Asia does not feature.

Contents

Author's Acknowledgementsp. vi
IntroductionAnita Millerp. vii

Miller introduces Weimann's book on the Woman's Building at the 1893 Chicago fair. She contrasts the White City's architecture, which Adams and Mumford disparaged, with the building's craftswomen and philanthropy. She asks what the building achieved, finds little effect on the vote but some gains in education, and says the book aims to recreate it.

Chicago 1893
Preludep. 1

Weimann opens with the Philadelphia Centennial of 1876, where the Woman's Pavilion was planned, funded and managed by women after the Centennial Board had initially left them out. Elizabeth Gillespie's committee raised more than $90,000, then was told at the last minute that there was no space in the Main Building, and the pavilion went up as a separate wooden hall. The chapter describes its exhibits, including the New Century newspaper, the butter sculpture of Iolanthe, and the Declaration of Rights for Women that Susan Anthony read on Independence Square on July 4 after the Centennial Committee refused it a place in the programme. Weimann then turns to Chicago, where wealthy women of the new elite began demanding a place in the 1893 fair, and concludes that the Philadelphia experience shaped those demands.

Philadelphia 1876
IQueen of the Westp. 7

Weimann describes Chicago from the 1850s to the 1889 fair as a city whose wealth and social life were shaped by men such as Potter Palmer and the families around him. The chapter follows the Palmers' marriage in 1870, the loss of the Palmer House and the Honore fortunes in the 1871 fire, and the rebuilding that followed. It then turns to women's public work: the Fortnightly and the Chicago Woman's Club, led by Ellen Henrotin and Bertha Palmer, which pressed for reforms in asylums, prisons and police stations, and Jane Addams's Hull House among the immigrants of the west side. Haymarket, labour unrest and the Woman's Temple show the city's tensions. Weimann concludes that by 1889 Chicago was ready to assert its place as a centre of industry and intellect.

IIGovernment Discovers Chicagop. 21

Weimann traces how Chicago won the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition from New York, St Louis and Washington between 1889 and 1890. Newspapers on each side traded insults, Chicago's business elite set up the Corporation and its fund-raising committees, and the House vote of February 24, 1890 followed the city's support across the Midwest, the West and the South. Women's contributions form a second thread: the Women's Auxiliary and Myra Bradwell recalled the Sanitary Fair of 1863, which women had run in Chicago, and both the Auxiliary and the Isabella Association sought control over women's representation. The chapter ends with the Fair Bill signed on April 25, 1890, and concludes that Chicago profited from its rivals' failures as well as from its own organisation.

Chicago 1893Chicago 1863
IIIGovernment Discovers Womenp. 35

Weimann examines the Springer amendment of 1890, which created the Board of Lady Managers with almost no defined duties, and the disputes over who should control it. The chapter sets out the Corporation's officers and the National Commission's appointments, including the nine Chicago delegates. It contrasts the Auxiliary, which wanted a women's industries pavilion and stressed philanthropy, with the Isabella Association, which argued for equal rights and a statue of Queen Isabella. Frances Willard's and other women's comments on the Board's title are quoted, and the author weighs suffragist claims to have created the Board against the political motives of Representative Springer. The chapter concludes that the Board's first divisions reflected a split within the women's movement between general reform and women's own equal rights.

Chicago 1893
IVThe Chivalric Chimerap. 43

Weimann follows the Board of Lady Managers from its first meeting in Chicago in November 1890 to its struggle over a separate building. Bertha Palmer is elected president by roll call, Phoebe Couzins is elected secretary after a contested ballot, and the Board's plan for a Woman's Building draws criticism in the Chicago press, which calls the Board a 'chivalric chimera'. The main evidence is the correspondence between the Board, the Directory and the Isabella Association, which asked for space for a bronze statue of Queen Isabella by Harriet Hosmer and for a club pavilion. The Directory refused on the grounds that it had a rule against club buildings, and Palmer kept the Isabellas off the grounds. Mary Newbury Adams's history of the Board was revised at Palmer's direction, and Adams later had her name removed. The chapter concludes with Palmer's victory over the Isabellas and the statue's later journey to San Francisco.

Chicago 1893
VPhoebe Couzinsp. 73

Weimann tells the story of Phoebe Couzins, the lawyer and suffragist elected Secretary of the Board of Lady Managers for the Chicago fair of 1893, and of her removal from office in April 1891. The chapter follows the quarrel from late 1890, when a bylaw on the Executive Committee was found altered in pencil, through the intervention of the Board of Reference and Control, to the resolutions that gave Bertha Palmer, the Board's president, command of its committees and correspondence. Its evidence is the Board's minutes, the letters among the Lady Managers, newspaper reports and Couzins's own testimony to a House committee in 1892. Weimann shows how the dispute split the Board along lines of class, politics and sectional loyalty, with the suffragist 'Isabella' faction, led by Isabella Beecher Hooker, opposing Palmer's clubwomen. The chapter ends with Couzins's suit, which failed in the courts, and with her later bitterness, which Weimann presents as the cost of a fight that nearly destroyed the Board.

Chicago 1893
VIParian and Ebonyp. 103

Weimann's chapter examines how African American women sought a place for black exhibits at the Chicago fair, and how the Board of Lady Managers responded. It opens with a November 1890 resolution from Chicago's 'colored women', referred by the Board to the Commission, and follows the rival black organisations of 1891, among them Lettie Trent's group and the Women's Columbian Auxiliary Association. Drawing on Board correspondence, circulars and pledges, Weimann shows how Bertha Palmer, who disliked being 'supplemented', chose Mary Cantrill to represent black interests, and how equal treatment without a separate exhibit left the groups out. A parallel section covers Palmer's European trip of 1891 and the few black appointments that followed, among them Hallie Brown and Fannie Barrier Williams. It closes with the White City's few black staff, the embarrassed 'Colored People's Day' of August 1893, and Mrs A.J. Cooper's claim at the Congress of Representative Women that woman's cause could not be won while any group was left out.

Chicago 1893
VIICircling the Globep. 125

Weimann follows the Board of Lady Managers' effort between 1891 and 1893 to build networks of state and foreign committees for the Chicago fair. The first half concerns the state boards, which Palmer reported at the second full Board meeting as covering thirty-seven states and territories; it shows women in New York, Connecticut, Iowa and Colorado recruiting members, raising money and forming county associations, often against unwilling legislatures. The second half turns abroad, to Palmer's European journey of 1892, her letter to Queen Victoria, the exchange with Carmen de Diaz in Mexico and the obstacles in China, Japan, Tunis and Syria. These are set against the slow work of the State Department and Thomas Cridler, whom Palmer pressed to act faster. Evidence comes from the Board's circulars and reports, the Lady Managers' letters and the Woman's Journal. The chapter closes with Palmer's count of forty-one responding countries, which Palmer attributed to a 'freemasonry' among women, and with the view that women had to work for women where governments would not.

Chicago 1893
VIIIThe Ladies Lovely Childp. 141

Weimann follows the making of the Woman's Building at the World's Columbian Exposition, from the Board of Lady Managers' first resolution of 1890 to the building's opening in 1893. The Board wanted its architect chosen by a competition open only to women, but the design had to fit the schedule and budget of Daniel Burnham's Department of Construction. Weimann works through the thirteen entries, the prize-winning design by Sophia Hayden, and the changes made by Burnham's office and by Charles Atwood, the consulting architect, including a third storey and a roof garden. Board members then pressed donated carved panels, columns and tiles on the building, which Hayden found could do little good. A second competition, for the figures on the exterior, won by Alice Rideout, and the Board's handling of Enid Yandell, who modelled the caryatids, show how the Ladies' patronage worked in practice. The chapter ends with Hayden's breakdown in the summer of 1892 and her absence from the Fair, which Weimann reads as the cost of a building that others had to finish.

Chicago 1893
IXThe Decoratorsp. 181

Weimann describes how the two large murals in the main gallery of the Woman's Building were commissioned and painted. Bertha Palmer's search for muralists was guided by Sara Hallowell, the Chicago art adviser whose bid to become Director of Fine Arts had failed, and Weimann traces the loan collection Hallowell assembled for the Fine Arts Palace, drawing on the Impressionist paintings she had shown in Chicago in 1890. The chapter follows the letters among Palmer, Hallowell and the painters: Elizabeth Gardner declined, and Mary MacMonnies and Mary Cassatt accepted. Their contracts put the cost of the work on the artists and set an October deadline they found too close, and the terms were disputed with Frank Millet until the date moved to February 1893. Weimann then covers Palmer's objections to the nudity in MacMonnies's design, her telegram about the scale of the borders, and the artists' replies, which show their frustration. The chapter ends with the murals hung high in the Hall of Honor, and Weimann argues that Cassatt's fears about their height had been well founded.

Chicago 1893Chicago 1890
XProdigies of Preparationp. 215

Weimann covers the months before the Fair opened, when the Board of Lady Managers fought for a place in the Dedication Ceremonies of October 1892 and in the wider programme. The contest centred on Amy Beach's Jubilate, which the Music Bureau dropped, on Harriet Monroe's Columbian Ode, which the Committee on Ceremonies tried to hand to the Board, and on James Ellsworth, who opposed the Ladies at each stage. Weimann follows these disputes through Amey Starkweather's letters, the eight minutes allotted to the Board, Palmer's reluctant speech, and Monroe's unsuccessful attempts to sell the printed Ode. The chapter then turns to the interior of the building, where Candace Wheeler's ivory and gold scheme and the gifts from the states had to be fitted into space already squeezed by the Fair's shortage. Weimann closes with the fight over women jurors, which Springer pressed in Congress and John Thatcher tried to reduce, and with the April 1893 reception at which the gifts were acknowledged, after which Wheeler, who never received a contract, was paid by cheque.

Chicago 1893
XIWomen in the White Cityp. 241

Weimann begins with the opening of the Columbian Exposition on 1 May 1893, reconstructed from the Fair's official History and press reports, then walks through the Court of Honor and into the Woman's Building run by the Board of Lady Managers under Bertha Palmer. The chapter argues that the building was a necessity rather than an afterthought, because women's work done alongside men was otherwise credited to men, though critics called it a white elephant. Its evidence is concrete: the opening luncheon and ceremony, Palmer's speech on women's wage labour and the 'sphere' of home, critics' gendered readings of the building's architecture, the crowded rooms and rooftop restaurant, and the state, foreign and royal exhibits. It ends by setting the building's popularity with visitors against the Board's struggle to justify it, and by quoting the Fair's own verdict that such a gathering of women's work could not be repeated.

Chicago 1893
XIIA Glorious Wealth of Mediocrityp. 279

Weimann follows the Board of Lady Managers' attempt to build a 'Gallery of Honor' of women's fine art in the Woman's Building, meant to rival the Fine Arts Palace. The chapter argues that the gallery fell short because few women artists were thought to merit a separate show, and because Bertha Palmer's efforts to borrow major works, including Rosa Bonheur's The Horse Fair, were refused. Its evidence comes from correspondence between Palmer, Sara Hallowell, Candace Wheeler and Mary Logan, and from the sculptors Harriet Hosmer, Anne Whitney, Vinnie Ream Hoxie and Adelaide Johnson, whose busts of Susan B. Anthony and other suffragists became a dispute over display. Weimann also works through the Keppel print collection, which the chapter treats as the strongest display, and through the murals by Mary Cassatt and Mary MacMonnies, whose press reception is quoted at length. It closes by judging Palmer to have done her best, and by setting the gallery's mediocrity against the general weakness of American art of the period.

Chicago 1893
XIIICots and Cribsp. 325

Weimann turns to the two philanthropic projects of the Chicago women at the Fair: the Woman's Dormitory, a low-cost lodging house for visitors, and the Children's Building. The chapter argues that both depended on unpaid female labour and fund-raising rather than Fair money. For the Dormitory it follows the sale of stock, the Hyde Park site, the crowded summer of 1893 when twelve hundred women sought beds in a building meant for one thousand, and the final accounts. For the Children's Building it traces the state quotas, the kindergarten and kitchen-garden exhibits, the Garrett sisters' deaf-education display, the library, and the day nursery, which the press mocked as a 'baby farm'. It closes with Julia Shattuck's remark that the women, without an appropriation, did what their hands found to do.

Chicago 1893
XIVMob of Scribbling Womenp. 353

Weimann describes the library that the Board of Lady Managers set up in the Woman's Building as a showcase of women's writing. The chapter concentrates on the New York contribution of some 2,400 volumes, club records and periodical folios, which the New York women insisted should stay together as a state exhibit against the national plan to shelve books by subject. Connecticut's exhibit, built around Harriet Beecher Stowe's works and a marble bust, and the smaller collections from New Jersey and Massachusetts are set beside it, while Candace Wheeler and Dora Wheeler Keith's blue-green decoration and painted ceiling give the room its look. The later sections turn to Edith Clarke's cataloguing, where married and pen names and foreign naming habits made each entry a problem, and the work ran over budget until the Board halted it in September 1893. Weimann ends with visitors' astonishment at how many books women had written, and with the remaining books passing to the Chicago Public Library.

Chicago 1893
XVWomen in Savageryp. 393

Weimann traces the Board's attempt to prove that women invented the primitive industries, a theme that the Smithsonian's loan of ethnographic material was meant to carry. The chapter follows the quarrels between Bertha Palmer, Mary Lockwood and Smithsonian staff over cases and placement, and the eighty cases of 'Woman's Work in Savagery' that reached the building only in June, after a Congressional resolution authorised the loan. It then shows the theme breaking apart: the Italian laces and the Burano lace revival, Lady Aberdeen's Irish Home Industries, the Turkish Compassionate Fund's embroidery and its failed sales, and Mexican and Royal School of Art Needlework work all crowd beside it. Pottery and woodcarving bring in the dispute between Mary Louise McLaughlin and Maria Longworth Nichols Storer over the underglaze process, and the Sales Room, which took $42,882 mostly from cheap souvenirs. Weimann closes with cottage workers who could not compete with machine production and with a nostalgic remark from the wife of Governor Harrison that handmade work could never come again.

Chicago 1893
XVIRare and Interesting Lines of Workp. 427

Weimann uses the Board's call for 'rare and interesting lines of work' to examine exhibits that moved beyond domestic crafts into inventions, science and exploration. The Inventions Room, built from the patents that Mary Lockwood collected, was crowded with kitchen gadgets, and only Martha Costen's night signals, which the Navy had tested, are singled out as important. The science display, thin because few women scientists could be found, is set around a tribute to Maria Mitchell, Harriet Strong's pampas-grass storage dams and Anna Comstock's engravings. The second half follows May French Sheldon's East African caravan and Kate Marsden's Siberian leper mission, along with the Royal Geographical Society's refusal to admit women as ordinary Fellows. Weimann ends with Marsden's exhibit and the rumours of fraud that Bertha Palmer repeated in 1894, then Marsden's own 1921 defence, leaving the impression that women's unusual work was accepted only on fragile terms.

Chicago 1893
XVIIRefined Avenues of Effortp. 449

Weimann moves from the Woman's Building's nursing and domestic displays to the case that nursing and housekeeping could be recast as professions. The chapter starts with the Illinois women's hospital pavilion, which the Board first refused and later allowed to be built on the Fairgrounds, and traces nurse training from Nightingale's Scutari and the American Civil War to the schools at Bellevue and the Woman's Medical College of Philadelphia. The central case is Ethel Bedford-Fenwick's campaign for a register of nurses, shown in a room under a Nightingale portrait and opposed by Nightingale and others. Weimann then looks at the Columbian Association of Housekeepers and the Model Kitchen, where Sarah Tyson Rorer ran corn cookery demonstrations for 225,000 visitors, and at Ellen Richards's rival Rumford Kitchen. The chapter closes with Fernald's complaint that domestic science was underrepresented and Alice Freeman Palmer's view that housekeeping could become a learned profession.

Chicago 1893
XVIIIMementoes of an Emancipated Erap. 465

This chapter follows how the Board of Lady Managers turned the Woman's Building at the 1893 Chicago fair into a commercial enterprise, selling souvenirs to raise money for a memorial fund. Weimann covers the silk bookmarks woven with Bertha Palmer's likeness, the postcards, the souvenir spoons made by a Chicago wholesale jeweller, and a Columbian cookbook that Carrie Shuman proposed and Rand McNally published. The argument is that Palmer's control over these ventures was constant and often heavy-handed, and that it produced quarrels with manufacturers, sellers and the women whose support the Board needed. The longest case is the Isabella quarter, a commemorative coin whose design was fought over between the Board, the sculptor Caroline Peddle and the Mint. It ended as a crownless Isabella on one side and a kneeling woman with a distaff on the other, a design the Ladies themselves disliked. The chapter closes with the coins' poor sales, the remelting of part of the stock, and the unaccounted-for remainder, and with a numismatist's praise for the coin's lack of mottoes.

Chicago 1893
XIXOrganizationsp. 487

Organizations follows the Board of Lady Managers' attempt to present the women's associations of 1893 in one Organizations Room in the Woman's Building, which Rebecca Felton was asked to run. Weimann traces how floor space was allotted among groups including the YWCA, the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, the suffragists, the Federation of Women's Clubs, the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Association of Collegiate Alumnae, and how the Board's inquiries into working women's organizations went nowhere. Its cases include the YWCA's withdrawal and return of space, Charlotte Smith's public clash with the cosmetics promoter Madame Yale, and Grace Dodge's refusal to complete the Board's questionnaire on working women. The argument is that the Board's aim of showing women united was repeatedly undermined by rivalry, politics and class difference among the organizations. The chapter ends with Helen Barker's Encyclopedia of Organizations, which was completed but never published, and Felton's later complaint about it.

Chicago 1893
XXNot Things but Women: The Congressesp. 523

Not Things but Women covers the women's congresses held in Chicago in 1893, concentrating on the Congress of Representative Women, which May Wright Sewall organized under the International Council of Women and which Bertha Palmer and Ellen Henrotin tried to bring under the Board's control. Weimann recounts the dispute over stationery, committee secretaries and rival networks of suffragists, clubwomen and conservatives, then the congress's crowded May sessions in the Art Palace. Much of the evidence comes from the dress reform debates, where Rachel Foster Avery and Annie Jenness Miller spoke in unconventional costume, and from talks on domestic service by Jane Addams, on Polish women by Helena Modjeska, and on race by Fannie Coppin. The argument is that the congresses gave a wide range of women a public platform while leaving unresolved the tensions between feminist, professional and conservative positions. The chapter notes Lucy Stone's death in October 1893 and ends with her last speech, on the legal disabilities of married women, which she presents as recent reform.

Chicago 1893
XXIThe Summer Sessions: Not Enough of the Duchessp. 551

Weimann follows the Board of Lady Managers through its 1893 summer sessions at the Chicago World's Fair, when quarrels over ceremonies, jurors and social favour became a public scandal. The chapter opens with Katharine Minor's proposal to rotate the Committee on Ceremonies, Mary Logan's objections, and the exclusion of many Ladies from the opening-day events. It then moves to Bertha Palmer's entertaining, the protests of the Couzins faction, and the Infanta Eulalia's late and sulky appearance at Palmer's reception. Letters, newspaper reports and the journal of the alternate Sallie Cotten show how the wrangling looked from inside the Board. The later sections concern the juror appointments and the feud between Ida Ball and Virginia Meredith, which ended with Ball's removal from the Committee on Awards. The Treasury Secretary halted the session on 12 August after thirty-six days. The chapter closes with the quieter October meetings, which Weimann describes as an ending conducted with some dignity.

Chicago 1893
XXIIAfter the Fair is Overp. 579

Weimann follows the Board of Lady Managers after the Chicago fair closed in 1893. The chapter covers the final session, the packing of some eighty thousand exhibits, and the Board's plan for a permanent Woman's Memorial Building, with Sophia Hayden's designs, Potter Palmer's $200,000 pledge and Juana Neal's insurance scheme, which Bertha Palmer abandoned in 1894. It records the disappearance of the Cassatt and MacMonnies murals and other goods from a Chicago warehouse, and the later demolition of the White City. Palmer's career after the fair, including her Paris commission in 1900 and the Legion of Honor, is set beside the work of Ellen Henrotin and other women. A survey of later women's buildings, from Atlanta and Omaha to St Louis, San Francisco and Chicago in 1933, shows how the model faded. Weimann ends by setting the predictions of Kate Field and Alice Freeman Palmer, that women's boards would soon be unnecessary, against what followed, and closes with Bertha Palmer's farewell to the Lady Managers.

Çelik, Zeynep. Displaying the Orient: Architecture of Islam at Nineteenth-Century World’s Fairs. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Çelik examines how Islamic architecture was built, displayed and read at nineteenth-century world's fairs, centred on the Paris expositions of 1867, 1878, 1889 and 1900, Vienna in 1873 and Chicago in 1893. His argument is that the fairs claimed scientific accuracy while indulging fantasy, so that the Islamic quarters and national pavilions show both how Europeans constructed the Orient and how Ottoman and Egyptian rulers sought a modern cultural identity. The chapters move from the visitors and displayed peoples, to the street-level quarters, to the national pavilions of the Ottoman Empire, Egypt, Iran, Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria, to the Ottoman and Egyptian exposition experience, and then to the influence of pavilion design on neo-Islamic building in Istanbul, Cairo and the West.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive slight attention, and the mentions are passing. In chapter 2 (Islamic Quarters) the account of Garnier's History of Habitation at the Paris 1889 exposition quotes a classification that places Chinese and Japanese dwellings among "contemporary versions of primitive civilizations", a display organised by a French architect for European visitors, and Drevet's 1878 Paris facades for the Siamese and Annamese pavilions are said to need a symbolic architecture alongside the Muslim nations. In chapter 3 (National Pavilions) Drevet's 1878 foreign section again includes Siam and Annam, and Çelik notes that Luxembourg, Greece, China, Japan and Russia also commissioned French architects, but no Chinese or Japanese building is described.

Javanese figures in a parade description quoted in chapter 1, and a Javanese village appears in a Midway description at Chicago in 1893 in chapter 2. Asian participation, state commissioners, merchants and Asian visitors are not discussed at all, and the Introduction sets aside colonial discourse about occupied territories, so Indochina and the Dutch East Indies get no treatment as such.

Contents

List of Illustrationsp. viii
Acknowledgmentsp. xiv
Introductionp. 1–2

Celik introduces a study of how Islamic architecture was displayed at nineteenth-century world's fairs, focusing on the Paris expositions of 1867, 1878, 1889 and 1900, Vienna in 1873 and the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. He argues that the fairs claimed scientific accuracy while indulging fantasy, and that their Islamic pavilions show both how Europeans constructed the Orient and how Muslim states tried to define a modern cultural identity. Celik gives three reasons for choosing Islam: it stood as Europe's binary opposite, it raises a debate about modernity that is still live, and non-Western perspectives reveal a more complex nineteenth-century world. He surveys the political history of the Ottoman Empire, Egypt, Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco and Iran to show how colonial control varied, and sketches the thought of Ibrahim Sinasi, al-Tahtawi and Khayr al-Din, who saw European progress as compatible with Islam. The chapter ends by previewing the book's chapters on site plans, pavilion styles, Ottoman and Egyptian displays and Western architects' use of Islamic styles.

Paris 1867Paris 1878Paris 1889Paris 1900Vienna 1873Chicago 1893
1Muslim Visitors to World's Fairsp. 17

Celik examines the Muslim visitors and displayed peoples at the fairs, both official sovereigns and commissioners and the performers and craftsmen shown as anthropological types. The chapter first looks at indigenous displays, which organisers arranged in racial hierarchies, citing the Tunisian craft section of 1900 and the Cairo Street at Chicago in 1893. It then turns to the theatre and belly dancing that drew crowds to Paris in 1889 and to Chicago, and to the visits of Isma'il Pasha and Abdulaziz to the 1867 exhibition, which Celik reads as attempts to display modernisation and to win European lenders. Celik shows how the scientific language of racial types and the harem caricature reinforced one another. Egyptian writers, including Muhammad Sharif Salim, Ahmad Zaki and Muhammad al-Muwaylihi, objected to the dancers and cafe stereotypes as a distortion of their country's image. The chapter ends by noting that such self-images were rarely corrective, and that European stereotypes of the East remained dominant.

Paris 1867Paris 1889Paris 1900Chicago 1893
2Islamic Quarters in Western Citiesp. 51

Celik's fourth chapter examines the Islamic quarters built as street-level spectacle in Western cities, from the Ottoman and Egyptian sections at Paris in 1867 to the Cairo Street and Ottoman village at Chicago in 1893. Celik argues that the designers pursued authenticity through collected fragments and irregular plans, yet their settings were ahistorical, collapsing periods and regions into single structures that made Islamic cultures appear incapable of change. The chapter follows how the layouts moved from the picturesque, as in the 1867 Egyptian and Tunisian pavilions and Vienna in 1873, to the regularised and axial Tunisian village of 1900. Its key case is the Rue du Caire that Delort de Gleon built in 1889 from recycled Cairo fragments, which Celik reads as a blend of archaeological claim and commerce, and whose mosque was used as a coffeehouse according to one Egyptian visitor. The chapter concludes that after four decades the Islamic world no longer seemed exotic, and that with colonial expansion the exotic increasingly belonged to the Western powers.

Paris 1867Vienna 1873Paris 1878Paris 1889Chicago 1893Paris 1900
3Search for Identity: Architecture of National Pavilionsp. 95

Çelik asks how the national pavilions of Islamic states and colonies at nineteenth-century world's fairs were designed, and what image of Islamic architecture they gave Western visitors. The chapter moves roughly chronologically through the Ottoman Empire, Egypt, Iran, Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria, beginning with the Ottoman buildings in Paris in 1867, where Leon Parvillee used measured drawings of Bursa to argue that Ottoman architecture followed geometric rules. It then follows replicas of Istanbul monuments, such as the Sultan Ahmed Fountain at Vienna in 1873, the Egyptian temple modelled on Philae, and the Persian and Tunisian palaces, to the colonial palaces of Algeria and Tunisia at Paris in 1878, 1889 and 1900. Çelik shows that most of the architects were French and academically trained, and that they drew on publications more than firsthand knowledge. The conclusion is that regional differences at the fairs were stylistic rather than a matter of building type, and that in the colonies France used Islamic forms to display its own power.

Paris 1867Vienna 1873Paris 1878Paris 1889Paris 1900Chicago 1893
4Exposition Fever Carried Eastp. 139

Çelik traces how exposition fever reached the Ottoman Empire and Egypt, where governments used fairs to show they belonged to modern civilisation. The Ottoman General Exposition of 1863 filled a large hall on the Istanbul Hippodrome, designed by Bourgeois and Parvillee in a 'new manner' that mixed Islamic and European details. The planned 1894 Istanbul Agricultural and Industrial Exposition, designed by Raimondo D'Aronco, was never built after an earthquake, and only its drawings and model survive in part. In Egypt, the opening of the Suez Canal at Ismailiyya in 1869 was staged with tents, temporary pavilions and a palace for the khedive, and the guest lists and press accounts show how the ceremony presented a spectacle of local peoples. The chapter ends with the Cairo press predicting that the city would become the 'Paris of the Orient' after the festivities.

Istanbul 1863Istanbul 1894Ismailiyya 1869
5The Impactp. 153

Çelik argues that world's fairs affected architecture far beyond the fairgrounds, because Western architects learned Islamic forms from the pavilions and Ottoman architects reconsidered their own traditions in the same exhibitions. The chapter starts with drawing: Western plan, section and elevation conventions, as used by Parvillee, became the norm in Ottoman publications such as Usul-u mimari-i Osmani (1873). It then turns to neo-Islamic buildings in Istanbul designed mostly by European architects, from the gate of the Ministry of Defense to the Public Debt Administration Building by Antoine Vallaury, and to neo-Arabic architecture in Cairo. The central section examines Western case studies: Owen Jones's interior for the Crystal Palace in 1851, Frank Furness's Brazilian pavilion at Philadelphia in 1876, the Trocadero Palace in Paris in 1878, Adler and Sullivan's Transportation Building in Chicago in 1893, and Eugène Henard's Palace of Electricity in Paris in 1900. The conclusion is that the pavilions were forerunners of neo-Islamic styles in the Ottoman Empire and Egypt, while in the colonies the ruling power appropriated Islamic architecture for its own repertoire.

London 1851Philadelphia 1876Paris 1878Chicago 1893Paris 1900
Epiloguep. 181

Çelik examines what happened to the representational habits of the nineteenth-century fairs in the twentieth century, arguing that the non-Western quarters persisted even as fairs became more specialised. The chapter describes the colonial exhibitions in France, notably the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition, whose Tunisian quarter reconstructed a souk peopled by Tunisian craftsmen, and the Museum of the Colonies, which mixed Greco-Latin architecture with colonial motifs. It then shows how the Turkish pavilion at New York in 1939 and the Moroccan pavilion at Montreal in 1967 reused familiar North African imagery, and how the Musée de l'Homme of 1938 presented other cultures while leaving the modern West unexhibited. The second half compares Albert Laprade's new madina at Casablanca and Hassan Fathy's village of New Gourna with the paternalism of colonial planners. Çelik ends with the restored Soğukçeşme Street in Istanbul and the immigrant quarters of European cities, arguing that staged authenticity and power relations still shape how Islam is represented.
